lessons.briefing:
# 00 — Hello, Dojo (Node.js)

Welcome to the Node track. This course teaches you the Node.js *runtime* — not
JavaScript the language, which you are assumed to know, but the thing that
runs it on a server: one thread, one event loop, an I/O layer built out of
callbacks and streams, and an HTTP server you will write from scratch before
you are allowed near a framework.

Node's whole design follows from one decision. A web server spends almost all
of its life waiting — for a disk, a database, another service — and a thread
that waits is a thread doing nothing while holding a stack, a scheduler slot
and a few hundred kilobytes of memory. Node refuses to wait. It hands the I/O
to the operating system, returns to the loop, and picks your callback back up
when the answer arrives. That is why a single Node process can hold tens of
thousands of open connections, and also why one accidental `while` loop over a
large array freezes every single one of them. Everything you find delightful
about Node and everything you find infuriating about it comes out of that
same trade.

You learn it here the way you learn anything: by writing code that a gate
grades. You edit one file, run one command, and a test tells you whether you
were right — and when you were not, it prints the evidence and names the
section you should reread.

## The loop

Every lesson is a directory under `tracks/node/lessons/`. Inside:

- `README.md` — this file. Read it top to bottom before you write anything.
- `reading.md` — the theory. Read it *after* you attempt the exercises.
- `ex1/`, `ex2/`, … — one directory per exercise. You edit `exN/solution.ts`
  and nothing else.
- `gate.test.ts` — the gate. It imports your file, calls your function and
  asserts on what comes back. It is quoted verbatim at the bottom of this
  README, and always will be: you are never graded by a program you have not
  been shown.

The commands you will live in:

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo        # grade the whole lesson
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex2    # grade just one exercise
uv run dojo hint node 00_hello_dojo ex2    # stuck? reveal the next tier
uv run dojo read node 00_hello_dojo ex2    # the theory behind it
uv run dojo status node                    # the progress dashboard
uv run dojo next node                      # what should I do now?
```

The files are TypeScript, because that is what you will be handed on any Node
codebase written after about 2020, but this is not the TypeScript track: every
signature you need is already written for you. If you want the type system
itself, that course is next door (`uv run dojo status typescript`).

Before you write a single line, run the gate and watch it fail:

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo
```

Three red tests, each one an `Error: exN: ... is not implemented yet`. That is
the correct state of a fresh checkout. Reading a failure you *expected* is the
cheapest way to learn to read the ones you do not.

## Concept — the process is an object you can ask questions

Node hands every program a global called `process`: the running program's view
of itself. It is not a library you import, it is just there.

```ts
process.version;    // "v22.16.0"  - the Node build running this code
process.platform;   // "win32" | "darwin" | "linux" | ...
process.pid;        // 24680       - the OS process id
process.argv;       // ["C:\\Program Files\\nodejs\\node.exe", "C:\\app\\sum.js", "3", "4"]
process.env.PATH;   // strings from the environment, or undefined
```

`process.argv` is the one with a trap in it. It is not "the arguments the user
typed" — it is the *whole* command line as the OS delivered it, so index 0 is
the Node executable, index 1 is the script being run, and the user's arguments
start at index 2. Every CLI you will ever write starts with a `.slice(2)`, and
every CLI written by someone who forgot starts by trying to parse
`C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe` as a number.

The second thing to have in your hands from minute one is the shape of async
code. A function marked `async` always returns a promise, whatever you write
inside it:

```ts
async function loadCount(): Promise<number> {
  return 7;                  // the caller gets Promise<number>, not 7
}
```

`await` unwraps a promise, and — this is the part people forget — if the
promise rejects, `await` *throws* at that line. So the two error worlds are
one world: a rejection inside an async function behaves exactly like an
exception, and an exception inside an async function comes back to the caller
as a rejection.

```ts
async function total(): Promise<number> {
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([loadCount(), loadCount()]);
  return a + b;
}
```

`Promise.all` takes an array of promises and gives you one promise of an array
of results, in the order you passed them in — *not* the order they finished.
If any of them rejects, the promise it returned rejects with that same error,
immediately. Lesson 03 takes this apart properly; today you just need to be
able to use it.

## Exercise 1 — read the runtime you are standing in

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `describeRuntime()` so it returns a single
line describing the running process:

- on this machine, `"Node.js v22.16.0 on win32"`
- on a colleague's laptop, `"Node.js v20.11.1 on darwin"`

Same shape, different values — which is the point. The values must be read
from `process` at call time, not typed in as a literal, because the gate
builds the string it expects the same way and compares character for
character. Mind the `v`: `process.version` already has one.

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the two arguments you did not pass

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `sumOfArgs(argv)`, which takes an array
shaped like `process.argv` and returns the sum of the *user's* arguments:

- `sumOfArgs(["/usr/bin/node", "/app/sum.js", "3", "4"])` → `7`
- `sumOfArgs(["/usr/bin/node", "/app/sum.js"])` → `0`
- `sumOfArgs(["node", "sum.js", "10", "-4", "0.5"])` → `6.5`

Two things decide whether this is right, and they fail differently. Drop the
first two entries, or you will be summing file paths. Convert each remaining
entry from a string to a number, or `"10" + "-4"` gives you the string
`"10-4"` and the gate shows you a diff that looks like nonsense until you
notice the quotes.

Take the array as given — do not mutate it. The caller usually owns
`process.argv` itself.

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — your first async function

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `totalOf(promises)`, which takes an array of
promises of numbers and resolves to their sum:

- `totalOf([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)])` resolves to `3`
- `totalOf([])` resolves to `0`
- if any input promise rejects, `totalOf` rejects **with that same error**

That last line is the actual exercise. The natural first attempt is a loop
that `await`s each promise in turn, and it produces the right answers — but
read the second half of the Concept section again and ask what a rejected
input does to the loop, and what a `try`/`catch` you add to "make it safe"
would do to the error the caller needs to see.

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex3
```

# Reading - node/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. Read it **after** you attempt a problem, whether the gate went
green or red. Failing first and reading second is not a consolation prize; it
is the version of studying that sticks.

## Notes

**What Node actually is.** Node.js is V8 (Chrome's JavaScript engine) bolted
to libuv (a cross-platform asynchronous I/O library) with a standard library
in between. V8 runs your JavaScript on exactly one thread. libuv owns a small
pool of background threads and, more importantly, the operating system's
readiness notification machinery — `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS, IOCP
on Windows. When you ask Node to read a file, your one thread does not sit in
a `read()` syscall waiting for the disk; it hands the request to libuv and
goes back to the event loop, and libuv arranges for your callback to be
queued when the bytes are ready. Everything else in this track is a
consequence of that sentence.

**One thread means one thing at a time.** There is no preemption in your
JavaScript. A function you call runs to completion before any callback,
promise or timer gets a turn — the loop cannot interrupt you, it can only
wait for you to return. That is a gift, because you never need a mutex around
your own data structures, and it is a loaded gun, because a `JSON.parse` of a
90 MB payload or a triple-nested loop over a million rows blocks *every*
connected client for as long as it runs. "Node is fast" is really "Node is
fast at waiting"; it is no faster than anything else at computing, and it has
fewer places to hide when you make it compute.

**Why the runtime is worth a whole course.** JavaScript the language is
mostly portable — a `map` is a `map` in a browser and on a server. The
runtime is not. Browsers have no filesystem, no processes, no `Buffer`, no
streams-with-backpressure, no ports to bind. Node has all of those and no DOM.
Nearly every interview question that separates "writes JavaScript" from
"builds services" lives in this gap: the event loop, streams, error handling
in a process that must not die, module resolution, and what to do about CPU
work. That is exactly the ground lessons 01–11 cover, and the interview part
at the end (`i1`, `i2`, `i3`) is built out of the same material in the shape
an interviewer will hand it to you.

**On TypeScript in this track.** The files are `.ts` and vitest compiles them
for you; nothing here is type-checked as part of grading, and no exercise asks
you to invent a type. Treat the annotations as documentation of what goes in
and what comes out. If a signature is unfamiliar (`Promise<number>[]` in ex3,
say), read it right to left: an array of promises, each resolving to a number.

## ex1 — the process is an object

`process` is a global in the literal sense — it is not imported, it is
installed on `globalThis` before your first line runs — and it is your
program's window onto everything outside its own code: the argument vector,
the environment, the working directory, the streams `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`,
the exit code, and the signals the OS is sending you. Later in this course you
will use `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)` to shut an HTTP server down gracefully,
and `process.exitCode` to fail a script honestly.

The exercise made you read two values rather than hard-code them, which is a
smaller lesson than it looks. `process.platform` in particular is a value
people love to guess: it is `"win32"` on 64-bit Windows (a historical wart,
not a bug), `"darwin"` on macOS, and `"linux"` on Linux. If you ever branch on
it, branch on the value, not on a prettified version of it — and prefer not to
branch at all, which is what `node:path` exists for and what lesson 05 is
about.

The classic interview follow-up here is "how do you know which Node version a
production box is running, and why do you care?" The answer worth having is
that `process.version` tells you at run time, `engines` in `package.json`
declares what you require, and you care because the platform's async features
arrived in specific versions — `fetch` in 18, stable `node:test` in 20, and so
on — and because the LTS line is the only one getting security fixes.

## ex2 — argv, and the two entries nobody asks for

`process.argv` is an array of strings assembled by the runtime: element 0 is
the path to the Node executable, element 1 is the absolute path of the script
that was run, and everything after that is what the user typed. It is not
parsed, not unquoted beyond what the shell already did, and not converted:
`node sum.js 3 4` gives you the *strings* `"3"` and `"4"`.

Both halves of that fact caused the two failure modes the gate probes for.
Forgetting the `.slice(2)` sums the executable path as `NaN` and the whole
answer collapses to `NaN` — a value that is famously not equal to itself,
which is why the gate's diff shows `NaN` against a number instead of the
"nearly right" answer beginners expect. Forgetting the conversion gives you
string concatenation, because `+` is overloaded and JavaScript resolves the
ambiguity in favour of strings the moment either operand is one.

Two footnotes worth carrying. `Number("")` is `0`, not `NaN`, so an empty
argument quietly counts as zero — real CLIs validate rather than trust.
And in production you will use a parser (`node:util`'s `parseArgs`, or a
library) rather than indexing by hand, but every one of them is a `.slice(2)`
underneath.

## ex3 — async is the normal case

An `async` function returns a promise. Not "returns a value wrapped in a
promise if you use await" — always, unconditionally, even if the body is
`return 7`. That is the single most useful sentence about async/await, because
it explains the mistakes that follow from not believing it: calling an async
function without awaiting it gives you a promise object, and `if (promise)` is
always true; returning a promise from an async function does not double-wrap
it, because promises flatten; and a `throw` inside an async function does not
throw at the call site, it produces a rejected promise, which is why a
`try`/`catch` *around a non-awaited call* catches nothing.

The exercise's real content was error propagation. `Promise.all` rejects as
soon as any input rejects — it does not wait for the rest, and it does not
tell you which ones succeeded. That is usually what you want ("if any of these
three services is down, this request has failed"), and when it is not, the
combinator you want is `Promise.allSettled`, which waits for everything and
hands you an array of `{status, value}` / `{status, reason}` records. Lesson
03 makes you use both, along with `race` and `any`, and makes the difference
between them a thing you can say out loud in an interview.

The subtle trap in this exercise is the loop people write instead:

```ts
let total = 0;
for (const p of promises) total += await p;   // sequential, and it works here
```

With promises that are already created, this gives the right answer, because
the work started before you looped. With *functions* that start work when
called — which is what you will actually have in real code — the same shape is
the classic performance bug: three requests that could have taken 100 ms
together take 300 ms one after another. Keep the shape in mind; lesson 03
turns it into an exercise with a stopwatch on it.

## Further reading

- [Introduction to Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/introduction-to-nodejs) — the official orientation, including the V8/libuv split. Fifteen minutes.
- [`process` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html) — the whole surface: `argv`, `env`, `platform`, signals, exit codes. Skim it once now so you know what is in there.
- [MDN: `async function`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function) — the language half of ex3, with the "always returns a promise" rule stated plainly.
- [MDN: `Promise.all()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) — including the fail-fast rejection semantics the gate checks.
- [Vitest: `expect`](https://vitest.dev/api/expect) — the assertion API every gate in this track is written in, including the message argument you keep reading.

```ts
import { describe, expect, test } from "vitest";

import { describeRuntime } from "./ex1/solution";
import { sumOfArgs } from "./ex2/solution";
import { totalOf } from "./ex3/solution";

describe("00_hello_dojo", () => {
  test("ex1 - describeRuntime() reads the process it is running in", () => {
    expect(
      describeRuntime(),
      "the string must be built from process.version and process.platform at " +
        "run time, in the exact shape given in README ex1",
    ).toBe(`Node.js ${process.version} on ${process.platform}`);
    expect(
      describeRuntime().startsWith("Node.js v"),
      "process.version already begins with a v - do not add a second one, and " +
        "do not strip the one that is there",
    ).toBe(true);
  });

  test("ex2 - sumOfArgs() skips the two entries Node puts in front", () => {
    expect(
      sumOfArgs(["/usr/bin/node", "/app/sum.js", "3", "4"]),

        "after those two are user arguments (reread README ex2)",
    ).toBe(7);
    expect(
      sumOfArgs(["/usr/bin/node", "/app/sum.js"]),
      "no user arguments means an empty sum, which is 0 - not NaN and not undefined",
    ).toBe(0);
    expect(
      sumOfArgs(["node", "sum.js", "10", "-4", "0.5"]),
      "argv entries are always strings: Number(\"0.5\") is 0.5, but \"10\" + \"-4\" " +
        "is string concatenation, so convert before you add",
    ).toBe(6.5);
  });

    await expect(
      totalOf([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)]),
      "totalOf() must resolve to the sum of the resolved values, not to an " +
        "array and not to a promise of a promise",
    ).resolves.toBe(3);
    await expect(
      totalOf([]),
      "the sum of nothing is 0 - an empty input is a case, not an accident",
    ).resolves.toBe(0);
    // The gate keeps its own handler on this one so that an unfinished stub
    // cannot turn it into an unhandled rejection and crash the whole run.
    const failing = Promise.reject(new Error("boom"));
    failing.catch(() => {});
    await expect(
      totalOf([Promise.resolve(1), failing, Promise.resolve(3)]),
      "one rejected input must reject the whole thing with that same error - " +
        "do not swallow it and do not replace it with an error of your own",
    ).rejects.toThrow("boom");
  });
});
```

- **ex1** calls your function and compares it against a string the gate builds
  from the same two `process` properties, so a hard-coded version number
  passes on your machine today and fails on any other machine, forever. The
  second check catches the most common typo, a doubled `v`.
- **ex2** calls `sumOfArgs` three times: a normal case, an empty case, and one
  with a decimal and a negative so that an integer-only or string-flavoured
  addition shows up as a wrong number rather than a near miss.
- **ex3** checks the resolved value twice and then checks that a rejection
  travels *through* your function unchanged. `rejects.toThrow("boom")` means:
  the promise you returned must reject, and the error it rejects with must
  carry that message.

line vitest prints when the assertion fails, and in this course it always
names the mistake rather than restating the assertion. Read it before you read
the diff.

The habit this lesson builds is *predicting the failure*. You ran the gate
before writing anything, so you know what red looks like; from here on, every

languages, reading a file is a function call that returns a value, and doing
it asynchronously is an advanced topic. In Node it is the reverse: the async
form is the normal form, the synchronous form exists mainly for start-up
scripts, and a library that only offers you the synchronous version is a
library that can stall your entire server. You spent ex3 writing three lines
of that world. The next eleven lessons are about what happens underneath it.

Next: **01_modules**, where you find out why `require` and `import` are two
different systems, and why that is still, in 2026, a thing you have to know.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **00 — Hello, Dojo (Node.js)**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |

# Reading - node/00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole course.
This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the problems you
just solved. Read it **after** you attempt a problem, whether the gate went
green or red. Failing first and reading second is not a consolation prize; it
is the version of studying that sticks.

## Notes

**What Node actually is.** Node.js is V8 (Chrome's JavaScript engine) bolted
to libuv (a cross-platform asynchronous I/O library) with a standard library
in between. V8 runs your JavaScript on exactly one thread. libuv owns a small
pool of background threads and, more importantly, the operating system's
readiness notification machinery — `epoll` on Linux, `kqueue` on macOS, IOCP
on Windows. When you ask Node to read a file, your one thread does not sit in
a `read()` syscall waiting for the disk; it hands the request to libuv and
goes back to the event loop, and libuv arranges for your callback to be
queued when the bytes are ready. Everything else in this track is a
consequence of that sentence.

**One thread means one thing at a time.** There is no preemption in your
JavaScript. A function you call runs to completion before any callback,
promise or timer gets a turn — the loop cannot interrupt you, it can only
wait for you to return. That is a gift, because you never need a mutex around
your own data structures, and it is a loaded gun, because a `JSON.parse` of a
90 MB payload or a triple-nested loop over a million rows blocks *every*
connected client for as long as it runs. "Node is fast" is really "Node is
fast at waiting"; it is no faster than anything else at computing, and it has
fewer places to hide when you make it compute.

**Why the runtime is worth a whole course.** JavaScript the language is
mostly portable — a `map` is a `map` in a browser and on a server. The
runtime is not. Browsers have no filesystem, no processes, no `Buffer`, no
streams-with-backpressure, no ports to bind. Node has all of those and no DOM.
Nearly every interview question that separates "writes JavaScript" from
"builds services" lives in this gap: the event loop, streams, error handling
in a process that must not die, module resolution, and what to do about CPU
work. That is exactly the ground lessons 01–11 cover, and the interview part
at the end (`i1`, `i2`, `i3`) is built out of the same material in the shape
an interviewer will hand it to you.

**On TypeScript in this track.** The files are `.ts` and vitest compiles them
for you; nothing here is type-checked as part of grading, and no exercise asks
you to invent a type. Treat the annotations as documentation of what goes in
and what comes out. If a signature is unfamiliar (`Promise<number>[]` in ex3,
say), read it right to left: an array of promises, each resolving to a number.

## ex1 — the process is an object

`process` is a global in the literal sense — it is not imported, it is
installed on `globalThis` before your first line runs — and it is your
program's window onto everything outside its own code: the argument vector,
the environment, the working directory, the streams `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`,
the exit code, and the signals the OS is sending you. Later in this course you
will use `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)` to shut an HTTP server down gracefully,
and `process.exitCode` to fail a script honestly.

The exercise made you read two values rather than hard-code them, which is a
smaller lesson than it looks. `process.platform` in particular is a value
people love to guess: it is `"win32"` on 64-bit Windows (a historical wart,
not a bug), `"darwin"` on macOS, and `"linux"` on Linux. If you ever branch on
it, branch on the value, not on a prettified version of it — and prefer not to
branch at all, which is what `node:path` exists for and what lesson 05 is
about.

The classic interview follow-up here is "how do you know which Node version a
production box is running, and why do you care?" The answer worth having is
that `process.version` tells you at run time, `engines` in `package.json`
declares what you require, and you care because the platform's async features
arrived in specific versions — `fetch` in 18, stable `node:test` in 20, and so
on — and because the LTS line is the only one getting security fixes.

## ex2 — argv, and the two entries nobody asks for

`process.argv` is an array of strings assembled by the runtime: element 0 is
the path to the Node executable, element 1 is the absolute path of the script
that was run, and everything after that is what the user typed. It is not
parsed, not unquoted beyond what the shell already did, and not converted:
`node sum.js 3 4` gives you the *strings* `"3"` and `"4"`.

Both halves of that fact caused the two failure modes the gate probes for.
Forgetting the `.slice(2)` sums the executable path as `NaN` and the whole
answer collapses to `NaN` — a value that is famously not equal to itself,
which is why the gate's diff shows `NaN` against a number instead of the
"nearly right" answer beginners expect. Forgetting the conversion gives you
string concatenation, because `+` is overloaded and JavaScript resolves the
ambiguity in favour of strings the moment either operand is one.

Two footnotes worth carrying. `Number("")` is `0`, not `NaN`, so an empty
argument quietly counts as zero — real CLIs validate rather than trust.
And in production you will use a parser (`node:util`'s `parseArgs`, or a
library) rather than indexing by hand, but every one of them is a `.slice(2)`
underneath.

## ex3 — async is the normal case

An `async` function returns a promise. Not "returns a value wrapped in a
promise if you use await" — always, unconditionally, even if the body is
`return 7`. That is the single most useful sentence about async/await, because
it explains the mistakes that follow from not believing it: calling an async
function without awaiting it gives you a promise object, and `if (promise)` is
always true; returning a promise from an async function does not double-wrap
it, because promises flatten; and a `throw` inside an async function does not
throw at the call site, it produces a rejected promise, which is why a
`try`/`catch` *around a non-awaited call* catches nothing.

The exercise's real content was error propagation. `Promise.all` rejects as
soon as any input rejects — it does not wait for the rest, and it does not
tell you which ones succeeded. That is usually what you want ("if any of these
three services is down, this request has failed"), and when it is not, the
combinator you want is `Promise.allSettled`, which waits for everything and
hands you an array of `{status, value}` / `{status, reason}` records. Lesson
03 makes you use both, along with `race` and `any`, and makes the difference
between them a thing you can say out loud in an interview.

The subtle trap in this exercise is the loop people write instead:

```ts
let total = 0;
for (const p of promises) total += await p;   // sequential, and it works here
```

With promises that are already created, this gives the right answer, because
the work started before you looped. With *functions* that start work when
called — which is what you will actually have in real code — the same shape is
the classic performance bug: three requests that could have taken 100 ms
together take 300 ms one after another. Keep the shape in mind; lesson 03
turns it into an exercise with a stopwatch on it.

## Further reading

- [Introduction to Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/introduction-to-nodejs) — the official orientation, including the V8/libuv split. Fifteen minutes.
- [`process` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html) — the whole surface: `argv`, `env`, `platform`, signals, exit codes. Skim it once now so you know what is in there.
- [MDN: `async function`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function) — the language half of ex3, with the "always returns a promise" rule stated plainly.
- [MDN: `Promise.all()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) — including the fail-fast rejection semantics the gate checks.
- [Vitest: `expect`](https://vitest.dev/api/expect) — the assertion API every gate in this track is written in, including the message argument you keep reading.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — read the runtime you are standing in

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `describeRuntime()` so it returns a single
line describing the running process:

- on this machine, `"Node.js v22.16.0 on win32"`
- on a colleague's laptop, `"Node.js v20.11.1 on darwin"`

Same shape, different values — which is the point. The values must be read
from `process` at call time, not typed in as a literal, because the gate
builds the string it expects the same way and compares character for
character. Mind the `v`: `process.version` already has one.

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

single `return`.

The shape is:

```ts
return `Node.js ${/* which property? */} on ${/* which property? */}`;
```

Two decisions left: which property goes in each slot, and whether you need to
touch either value on the way through. If your string comes out with `vv` at
the front, you added something that was already there.

## Exercise 3 — your first async function

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `totalOf(promises)`, which takes an array of
promises of numbers and resolves to their sum:

- `totalOf([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve(2)])` resolves to `3`
- `totalOf([])` resolves to `0`
- if any input promise rejects, `totalOf` rejects **with that same error**

That last line is the actual exercise. The natural first attempt is a loop
that `await`s each promise in turn, and it produces the right answers — but
read the second half of the Concept section again and ask what a rejected
input does to the loop, and what a `try`/`catch` you add to "make it safe"
would do to the error the caller needs to see.

```
uv run dojo test node 00_hello_dojo ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are handed an array of promises, not an array of numbers. Adding promises
together gives you `"[object Promise][object Promise]"`, which is exactly the
kind of failure the gate is looking for.

So the job splits in two: turn the array of promises into an array of numbers,
then add the numbers up — and you already wrote the adding-up half in ex2.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all(promises)` returns a single promise that resolves to an array of
the resolved values, in input order. `await` it inside your `async` function
and you are back in familiar territory.

The rejection case needs no code at all: `Promise.all` rejects with the first
rejection it sees, and an `await` on a rejected promise throws inside your
function, which turns into a rejection of the promise your function returns.
Do not wrap it in `try`/`catch` — the gate wants that error to escape.

## Hint 3

The shape is two statements:

```ts
const values = await /* what combinator? */;
return values.reduce(/* the same reducer idea as ex2 */);
```

The decision left to you is the reducer and its initial value. Check the empty
array case: `Promise.all([])` resolves immediately to `[]`, so the answer
comes entirely from where your sum starts.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You are handed an array of promises, not an array of numbers. Adding promises
together gives you `"[object Promise][object Promise]"`, which is exactly the
kind of failure the gate is looking for.

So the job splits in two: turn the array of promises into an array of numbers,
then add the numbers up — and you already wrote the adding-up half in ex2.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all(promises)` returns a single promise that resolves to an array of
the resolved values, in input order. `await` it inside your `async` function
and you are back in familiar territory.

The rejection case needs no code at all: `Promise.all` rejects with the first
rejection it sees, and an `await` on a rejected promise throws inside your
function, which turns into a rejection of the promise your function returns.
Do not wrap it in `try`/`catch` — the gate wants that error to escape.

## Hint 3

The shape is two statements:

```ts
const values = await /* what combinator? */;
return values.reduce(/* the same reducer idea as ex2 */);
```

The decision left to you is the reducer and its initial value. Check the empty
array case: `Promise.all([])` resolves immediately to `[]`, so the answer
comes entirely from where your sum starts.

lessons.briefing:
# 01 — Modules: two systems, one runtime

Node shipped in 2009 with a module system it invented, because JavaScript did
not have one: `require()`, `module.exports`, and a resolution algorithm that
walks up the directory tree looking for `node_modules`. That system is
CommonJS, and for a decade it *was* server-side JavaScript. Then the language
itself grew modules — `import`/`export`, standardised in ES2015, designed
around static analysis and asynchronous loading — and Node had to support
both, in the same process, forever.

That is why this is lesson 01 and not an appendix. Every real Node codebase
you touch sits somewhere on the migration: an ESM application depending on a
CommonJS library, a CommonJS test runner loading an ESM helper, a package
publishing both from one `package.json`. When something goes wrong the error
messages are unusually bad — `require is not defined`,
`Cannot use import statement outside a module`,
`[ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]` — and they are only decodable if you know which system was
trying to load what.

The two systems differ in ways that matter more than syntax. CommonJS loads
*synchronously*: `require()` reads the file, runs it and hands you the value
right there, which is why you can `require` inside an `if`. ESM loads in two
phases: the runtime parses every module first, links the import graph, and
only then evaluates anything — which is why an ESM import has to sit at the
top level with a literal specifier, and why `import()` (the function form)
exists for the cases where you genuinely need to decide at run time. CommonJS
gives you `__dirname` and `__filename` for free; ESM gives you `import.meta`,
and you build the rest from it. And exactly one thing is the same in both:
**a module is evaluated once per process and cached**, which turns every
module into a singleton whether you meant it to be one or not.

## Concept — what each system hands you

This track runs as ESM. Files end in `.ts`, are treated as modules, and the
following is what you have:

```ts
import path from "node:path";                 // static: hoisted, resolved before anything runs
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";  // named import
export const NAME = "01_modules";             // a named export
export default function main() {}             // the default export

import.meta.url;      // "file:///C:/Users/Owner/Desktop/buildsql/tracks/node/lessons/01_modules/gate.test.ts"
```

`import.meta.url` is the ESM replacement for `__filename`, and note that it is
a **URL string**, not a path. On Windows the difference is not cosmetic:
`file:///C:/app/my%20dir/index.js` has a leading slash before the drive letter
and a `%20` where the space is. Converting it by hand — `.replace("file://", "")`
— produces a path that looks right in a demo and fails on the first user whose
name has a space in it. `node:url` exports `fileURLToPath` for this, and its
inverse `pathToFileURL`, and between them they are the only correct answer.

For CommonJS, the shape is:

```js
const path = require("node:path");            // synchronous, returns the exports object
module.exports = { RATES, priceWithTax };     // one object is "the exports"
exports.helper = () => {};                    // sugar for module.exports.helper
__dirname;                                    // the directory, already a path
```

From ESM you can `import` a CommonJS module and Node will give you its
`module.exports` as the **default** export. Named imports from CommonJS work
only when Node's static scan can spot the assignments, which it usually can
and sometimes cannot — a genuinely annoying failure mode. The escape hatch,
and the tool this lesson makes you use, is:

```ts
import { createRequire } from "node:module";

const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
const legacy = require("./some-legacy-thing.cjs");   // the real CommonJS require
```

`createRequire` builds a `require` function anchored at a URL you give it, so
relative specifiers resolve the way they would from that file. It is the
supported bridge, not a hack, and it is how you read a JSON file, load a
native addon, or call a package that never made the jump.

The last piece is the module cache. Both systems keep one:

```ts
// counter.ts
let n = 0;
export const bump = () => ++n;

// a.ts:  import { bump } from "./counter";   bump();  // 1
// b.ts:  import { bump } from "./counter";   bump();  // 2  <- same module, same n
```

The module body ran once. Every importer got a reference to the *same*
evaluated module, so `n` is shared process-wide. This is how a database pool
or a config object ends up a singleton without anybody writing a singleton
pattern — and it is also why a module with side effects in its body is a
liability, because you cannot control when, or how often, they happen.

## Exercise 1 — where am I?

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `moduleDirname(metaUrl)`, which takes an
`import.meta.url` string and returns the absolute path of the directory that
contains that module:

- `moduleDirname("file:///C:/app/my%20dir/index.js")` → `C:\app\my dir` on Windows
- the same call on Linux → `/C:/app/my dir` (URLs do not know about drive letters)

You do not need to handle the platform difference yourself — one standard
library function does it — but you do need to pick the right one. The gate
checks the path you return actually exists on disk, and separately feeds you a
URL with an encoded space in it.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — call the old code

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Next to it sits `legacy-pricing.cjs`, a CommonJS
module written years ago that you are not allowed to modify. It exports:

```js
module.exports = { RATES, priceWithTax };
// RATES        = { us: 0.07, de: 0.19, jp: 0.1 }
// priceWithTax = (cents, region) => cents rounded up by that region's rate
```

Implement two functions on top of it:

- `checkout(cents, region)` returns the taxed price by **calling** the legacy
  function — `checkout(1000, "us")` → `1070`, `checkout(2500, "de")` → `2975`.
- `regions()` returns the region codes from `RATES`, sorted:
  `["de", "jp", "us"]`.

Reimplementing the arithmetic instead of calling across the boundary defeats
the exercise, and the gate cannot tell — but you can, and the next legacy
module you meet will have three hundred lines of rules in it rather than one.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one module, one instance

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement an id issuer:

- `nextId()` returns `"job-1"`, then `"job-2"`, then `"job-3"`, …
- `idsIssued()` returns how many ids have been issued so far.

The gate imports your module twice, under two different local names, and
expects the second import to continue the first one's numbering. Nothing in
your code makes that happen; the runtime makes it happen. Your job is to put
the state where the runtime can share it.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — load it when you need it

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Two formatter modules live in `ex4/formatters/`, each
default-exporting a function that turns rows into a string. Implement:

```ts
loadFormatter(kind: "json" | "csv"): Promise<Formatter>
```

It must resolve to the module's default export, and it must throw for an
unknown kind with a message containing `unknown formatter: <kind>`.

The catch, and the reason this exercise exists: **a formatter module must not
be evaluated until it is asked for**. Each of those modules registers itself
in a shared registry when its body runs, and the gate checks the registry is
empty before your function is first called, then that it contains exactly the
formatters you loaded, in order. A pair of static imports at the top of your
file fails on the very first assertion.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex4
```

## Challenge — write the cache yourself

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createModuleCache(load)`, a
memoising loader with the semantics Node's own module cache has:

```ts
const cache = createModuleCache(async (key) => expensiveLoad(key));
cache.get("alpha");   // calls the loader
cache.get("alpha");   // does not
cache.size();         // how many keys are cached
```

Three rules, and the third is the interesting one:

1. Two `get`s for the same key that overlap *in time* must result in exactly
   one call to `load` — the second caller waits on the first caller's work.
2. Once a key has loaded, the loader is never called for it again.
3. If a load **rejects**, the key must not be cached: the next `get` tries
   again. Both callers of a failed load still see the rejection.

Rule 3 mirrors real `require` semantics — a module that throws while being
evaluated is removed from the cache, so the next `require` re-runs it — and it
is the rule people forget, which is how a single blip during start-up becomes
a permanently broken cache entry that only a restart fixes.

Honest difficulty note: rules 1 and 2 are five lines. Rule 3 is where you have
to think about *which* promise you are holding and *what* `.catch()` returns.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules challenge
```

## Review

`review1/solution.ts` comes back on the spaced-review schedule once the core
exercises are green; it is the same idea as ex3 in a different shape. Implement
`firstTimeSeeing(token)`, which returns `true` the first time it sees a given
string and `false` every time after, and `seenCount()`, which reports how many
*distinct* tokens the module has seen.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/01_modules

Modules are the part of Node that people learn by accident, from error
messages, over years. Reading the model once — deliberately — is much cheaper.

## Notes

**Two loaders, one process.** CommonJS resolves and evaluates in a single
synchronous pass: `require("./x")` finds the file, wraps its source in a
function `(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) => {...}`, runs
it, and returns `module.exports`. That wrapper is why `__dirname` exists and
why the top level of a CommonJS file is not really the top level. ESM works in
three phases instead — construction (find and parse every module reachable
from the entry, building a graph), instantiation (link the imports and exports
so each binding points at the right slot), evaluation (run the bodies, deepest
first). Static analysis of the graph before any code runs is exactly what
makes tree-shaking and top-level `await` possible, and exactly what makes
`import x from someVariable` impossible.

**Live bindings, not copies.** An ESM named import is a *view* of the
exporting module's variable, so if the exporter reassigns it, the importer
sees the new value. A CommonJS `require` gives you the value of
`module.exports` at the moment you asked; if the exporter later reassigns
`module.exports`, you keep the old object. The difference shows up in circular
imports: ESM can survive a cycle where CommonJS hands you a half-built
`exports` object. Do not build architectures on either behaviour — but do
recognise the symptom, because "the value was there a second ago" is what a
cycle looks like from inside.

**Resolution, briefly.** For a bare specifier (`"express"`), Node walks up
from the importing file through every `node_modules` directory until it finds
a match, then consults that package's `package.json` — `exports` first
(which can map, and can *block*, subpaths), then `main`, then index files.
For a relative specifier, ESM requires the extension (`./util.js`, not
`./util`), because guessing extensions requires filesystem probing that the
spec deliberately excludes. In this course a bundler-style resolver is
configured for you, which is why the gates import `./ex1/solution` with no
suffix; plain Node would want the extension.

**`.mjs`, `.cjs`, and `"type"`.** A `.mjs` file is always ESM and a `.cjs`
file is always CommonJS, whatever anything says. A plain `.js` file is ESM if
the nearest `package.json` says `"type": "module"` and CommonJS otherwise —
which is why adding one line to a `package.json` can break a whole directory
of files, and why library authors reach for the explicit extensions.

**Everything is cached.** CommonJS keeps `require.cache`, keyed by resolved
absolute filename; ESM keeps an internal module registry keyed by resolved
URL. Either way the body runs once. You can delete a `require.cache` entry to
force a re-evaluation (test frameworks used to do this constantly); there is
no supported way to do it in ESM, which is why vitest gives each *test file*
its own module registry rather than trying to unload modules. That isolation
is also why the ex3 counter starts at 1 every time you run the gate, no
matter how many times you have run it before.

## ex1 — a URL is not a path

The exercise looks like string manipulation and is really about a category
error. `import.meta.url` is a URL: a percent-encoded, forward-slashed,
scheme-prefixed identifier that is legal to hand to `fetch` and illegal to
hand to `fs.readFile`. A filesystem path is platform-specific bytes with a
separator that is `\` on Windows. `fileURLToPath` is the only correct bridge,
and `pathToFileURL` is the way back.

The three checks in the gate correspond to the three ways the string-surgery
version fails. Slicing off `"file://"` leaves `/C:/app/...` on Windows, which
is not absolute in the way Windows means it. Forgetting to decode leaves
`%20` where a space belongs, so the path does not exist. And taking the wrong
level of the path — `basename` instead of `dirname` — gives you a plausible
string that points at nothing.

The interview version of this question is "how do you get `__dirname` in
ESM?", and the answer worth memorising is one line:

```ts
const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
```

The classic follow-up is "and why did they not just keep `__dirname`?" —
because ESM modules are specified in terms of URLs, and a module might not
have come from a filesystem at all. Recent Node versions do add
`import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` as conveniences, which is
worth mentioning as the modern shortcut; know the `fileURLToPath` form anyway,
because it is what every codebase written before that shortcut uses.

## ex2 — the bridge to CommonJS

`createRequire(url)` builds a real CommonJS `require` whose resolution base is
the URL you pass. That is the whole trick, and the reason the argument is
usually `import.meta.url`: you want relative specifiers to mean "relative to
this file". Pass something else and `./legacy-pricing.cjs` resolves somewhere
else — which is occasionally what you want, and usually a bug.

Three things `createRequire` is genuinely used for in production. Loading a
CommonJS-only dependency whose named exports Node cannot statically detect.
Reading a JSON file synchronously at start-up (`require("./config.json")`)
without waiting for import attributes to be everywhere. And getting a
package's own `package.json` — `require("some-pkg/package.json")` — which
several tools do to read a version number.

The performance footnote people ask about: doing the `require` once at module
scope, as the reference does, is not about the file read. It is about not
paying for the cache lookup and the resolution on every call, and about
failing loudly at import time rather than deep inside a request handler if the
module is missing. Start-up is the right place for start-up failures.

## ex3 — the accidental singleton

Every module is a singleton. That sentence explains a surprising amount of
real-world Node behaviour: why a `pool` exported from `db.ts` is shared by
every route file; why a module-level `let currentUser` is a security incident
waiting to happen in a server that handles more than one request; why two
copies of the same library at different versions in `node_modules` produce
"instanceof returns false for a thing that obviously is one".

The gate demonstrates it with two imports of one module, but the more useful
mental model is: the registry is keyed by *resolved URL*, so two specifiers
that resolve to the same file share state, and two that do not — a symlinked
copy, a differently-cased path on a case-insensitive filesystem, the same
package installed twice — do not.

Where this bites in interviews: "how would you implement a singleton in
Node?" The strong answer is that you rarely need a pattern for it, because
module semantics already give you one; you export the instance (or a factory
memoised at module scope) and the cache does the rest. The follow-up is "and
what is the risk?", and the answer is testability — module-level state
persists between tests in the same file, so anything stateful needs a reset
hook or per-test isolation, which is exactly why vitest isolates by file.

## ex4 — importing on purpose

`import()` — the function, not the statement — returns a promise for the
module namespace. It is the escape hatch from the static graph, and it exists
for three real reasons: loading something only under a condition (a plugin, a
platform-specific implementation), deferring an expensive module until it is
needed (start-up time), and loading a module whose specifier is only known at
run time.

The registry trick the gate uses is worth stealing. Side effects in a module
body are normally invisible — you cannot easily prove *when* a module was
evaluated — and the way to make it visible is to have the module record its
own evaluation. This is also how "why is my start-up 900 ms" investigations
go: instrument module bodies, discover that importing a CLI framework at the
top of a lambda handler costs 300 ms whether or not the CLI is used.

The most common mistake, and the one worth carrying into a code review: the
namespace object is not the default export. `const mod = await import("./x")`
then `mod.default` for a default-exported function, `mod.thing` for a named
one. People destructure `const { default: format } = await import(...)`, which
is the same thing with better ergonomics.

## challenge — cache the promise, not the value

This is a small exercise with a big idea in it: **in an async world, the unit
of caching is the promise**. Caching resolved values leaves a window — from
the first call until the first resolution — during which a second caller sees
an empty cache and starts a duplicate load. Under concurrency that window is
where your thundering herd lives: fifty requests arrive, the cache is cold,
fifty database queries go out for the same row. Storing the in-flight promise
closes the window because the promise exists immediately.

Rule 3 is the counterweight. If failures are cached, one transient error is
permanent until restart. Node's own `require` gets this right: a module that
throws during evaluation is deleted from the cache, so the next `require`
re-evaluates it — and if you have ever seen a module "work on the second try",
that is why. The implementation detail that catches people is that
`pending.catch(fn)` returns a *new* promise; the caller must still receive the
original, or the rejection is swallowed and the caller sees `undefined`. The
guard `if (entries.get(key) === pending)` matters for the same reason a
compare-and-swap does: by the time your handler runs, someone may already have
stored a newer attempt.

## review1 — the same rule, a different question

`firstTimeSeeing` is deduplication, which is the shape module state most often
takes in production: a `Set` of processed message ids so a retried webhook is
not applied twice, a `Map` of rate-limit counters, a memo of expensive lookups.
Writing it again from scratch is the point — the review ladder exists because
you remember what you re-derive, not what you recognise.

Two footnotes. A `Set` is the right structure because membership on an array
is a linear scan and gets slow exactly when the set gets big. And a
process-lifetime `Set` grows forever, which is fine for a test and a slow
memory leak in a server: real deduplication caches have a bound (an LRU) or a
TTL, and "how would you keep this from growing without limit?" is the natural
follow-up question in an interview.

## Further reading

# Reading - node/01_modules

Modules are the part of Node that people learn by accident, from error
messages, over years. Reading the model once — deliberately — is much cheaper.

## Notes

**Two loaders, one process.** CommonJS resolves and evaluates in a single
synchronous pass: `require("./x")` finds the file, wraps its source in a
function `(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) => {...}`, runs
it, and returns `module.exports`. That wrapper is why `__dirname` exists and
why the top level of a CommonJS file is not really the top level. ESM works in
three phases instead — construction (find and parse every module reachable
from the entry, building a graph), instantiation (link the imports and exports
so each binding points at the right slot), evaluation (run the bodies, deepest
first). Static analysis of the graph before any code runs is exactly what
makes tree-shaking and top-level `await` possible, and exactly what makes
`import x from someVariable` impossible.

**Live bindings, not copies.** An ESM named import is a *view* of the
exporting module's variable, so if the exporter reassigns it, the importer
sees the new value. A CommonJS `require` gives you the value of
`module.exports` at the moment you asked; if the exporter later reassigns
`module.exports`, you keep the old object. The difference shows up in circular
imports: ESM can survive a cycle where CommonJS hands you a half-built
`exports` object. Do not build architectures on either behaviour — but do
recognise the symptom, because "the value was there a second ago" is what a
cycle looks like from inside.

**Resolution, briefly.** For a bare specifier (`"express"`), Node walks up
from the importing file through every `node_modules` directory until it finds
a match, then consults that package's `package.json` — `exports` first
(which can map, and can *block*, subpaths), then `main`, then index files.
For a relative specifier, ESM requires the extension (`./util.js`, not
`./util`), because guessing extensions requires filesystem probing that the
spec deliberately excludes. In this course a bundler-style resolver is
configured for you, which is why the gates import `./ex1/solution` with no
suffix; plain Node would want the extension.

**`.mjs`, `.cjs`, and `"type"`.** A `.mjs` file is always ESM and a `.cjs`
file is always CommonJS, whatever anything says. A plain `.js` file is ESM if
the nearest `package.json` says `"type": "module"` and CommonJS otherwise —
which is why adding one line to a `package.json` can break a whole directory
of files, and why library authors reach for the explicit extensions.

**Everything is cached.** CommonJS keeps `require.cache`, keyed by resolved
absolute filename; ESM keeps an internal module registry keyed by resolved
URL. Either way the body runs once. You can delete a `require.cache` entry to
force a re-evaluation (test frameworks used to do this constantly); there is
no supported way to do it in ESM, which is why vitest gives each *test file*
its own module registry rather than trying to unload modules. That isolation
is also why the ex3 counter starts at 1 every time you run the gate, no
matter how many times you have run it before.

## ex1 — a URL is not a path

The exercise looks like string manipulation and is really about a category
error. `import.meta.url` is a URL: a percent-encoded, forward-slashed,
scheme-prefixed identifier that is legal to hand to `fetch` and illegal to
hand to `fs.readFile`. A filesystem path is platform-specific bytes with a
separator that is `\` on Windows. `fileURLToPath` is the only correct bridge,
and `pathToFileURL` is the way back.

The three checks in the gate correspond to the three ways the string-surgery
version fails. Slicing off `"file://"` leaves `/C:/app/...` on Windows, which
is not absolute in the way Windows means it. Forgetting to decode leaves
`%20` where a space belongs, so the path does not exist. And taking the wrong
level of the path — `basename` instead of `dirname` — gives you a plausible
string that points at nothing.

The interview version of this question is "how do you get `__dirname` in
ESM?", and the answer worth memorising is one line:

```ts
const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
```

The classic follow-up is "and why did they not just keep `__dirname`?" —
because ESM modules are specified in terms of URLs, and a module might not
have come from a filesystem at all. Recent Node versions do add
`import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` as conveniences, which is
worth mentioning as the modern shortcut; know the `fileURLToPath` form anyway,
because it is what every codebase written before that shortcut uses.

## ex2 — the bridge to CommonJS

`createRequire(url)` builds a real CommonJS `require` whose resolution base is
the URL you pass. That is the whole trick, and the reason the argument is
usually `import.meta.url`: you want relative specifiers to mean "relative to
this file". Pass something else and `./legacy-pricing.cjs` resolves somewhere
else — which is occasionally what you want, and usually a bug.

Three things `createRequire` is genuinely used for in production. Loading a
CommonJS-only dependency whose named exports Node cannot statically detect.
Reading a JSON file synchronously at start-up (`require("./config.json")`)
without waiting for import attributes to be everywhere. And getting a
package's own `package.json` — `require("some-pkg/package.json")` — which
several tools do to read a version number.

The performance footnote people ask about: doing the `require` once at module
scope, as the reference does, is not about the file read. It is about not
paying for the cache lookup and the resolution on every call, and about
failing loudly at import time rather than deep inside a request handler if the
module is missing. Start-up is the right place for start-up failures.

## ex3 — the accidental singleton

Every module is a singleton. That sentence explains a surprising amount of
real-world Node behaviour: why a `pool` exported from `db.ts` is shared by
every route file; why a module-level `let currentUser` is a security incident
waiting to happen in a server that handles more than one request; why two
copies of the same library at different versions in `node_modules` produce
"instanceof returns false for a thing that obviously is one".

The gate demonstrates it with two imports of one module, but the more useful
mental model is: the registry is keyed by *resolved URL*, so two specifiers
that resolve to the same file share state, and two that do not — a symlinked
copy, a differently-cased path on a case-insensitive filesystem, the same
package installed twice — do not.

Where this bites in interviews: "how would you implement a singleton in
Node?" The strong answer is that you rarely need a pattern for it, because
module semantics already give you one; you export the instance (or a factory
memoised at module scope) and the cache does the rest. The follow-up is "and
what is the risk?", and the answer is testability — module-level state
persists between tests in the same file, so anything stateful needs a reset
hook or per-test isolation, which is exactly why vitest isolates by file.

## ex4 — importing on purpose

`import()` — the function, not the statement — returns a promise for the
module namespace. It is the escape hatch from the static graph, and it exists
for three real reasons: loading something only under a condition (a plugin, a
platform-specific implementation), deferring an expensive module until it is
needed (start-up time), and loading a module whose specifier is only known at
run time.

The registry trick the gate uses is worth stealing. Side effects in a module
body are normally invisible — you cannot easily prove *when* a module was
evaluated — and the way to make it visible is to have the module record its
own evaluation. This is also how "why is my start-up 900 ms" investigations
go: instrument module bodies, discover that importing a CLI framework at the
top of a lambda handler costs 300 ms whether or not the CLI is used.

The most common mistake, and the one worth carrying into a code review: the
namespace object is not the default export. `const mod = await import("./x")`
then `mod.default` for a default-exported function, `mod.thing` for a named
one. People destructure `const { default: format } = await import(...)`, which
is the same thing with better ergonomics.

## challenge — cache the promise, not the value

This is a small exercise with a big idea in it: **in an async world, the unit
of caching is the promise**. Caching resolved values leaves a window — from
the first call until the first resolution — during which a second caller sees
an empty cache and starts a duplicate load. Under concurrency that window is
where your thundering herd lives: fifty requests arrive, the cache is cold,
fifty database queries go out for the same row. Storing the in-flight promise
closes the window because the promise exists immediately.

Rule 3 is the counterweight. If failures are cached, one transient error is
permanent until restart. Node's own `require` gets this right: a module that
throws during evaluation is deleted from the cache, so the next `require`
re-evaluates it — and if you have ever seen a module "work on the second try",
that is why. The implementation detail that catches people is that
`pending.catch(fn)` returns a *new* promise; the caller must still receive the
original, or the rejection is swallowed and the caller sees `undefined`. The
guard `if (entries.get(key) === pending)` matters for the same reason a
compare-and-swap does: by the time your handler runs, someone may already have
stored a newer attempt.

## review1 — the same rule, a different question

`firstTimeSeeing` is deduplication, which is the shape module state most often
takes in production: a `Set` of processed message ids so a retried webhook is
not applied twice, a `Map` of rate-limit counters, a memo of expensive lookups.
Writing it again from scratch is the point — the review ladder exists because
you remember what you re-derive, not what you recognise.

Two footnotes. A `Set` is the right structure because membership on an array
is a linear scan and gets slow exactly when the set gets big. And a
process-lifetime `Set` grows forever, which is fine for a test and a slow
memory leak in a server: real deduplication caches have a bound (an LRU) or a
TTL, and "how would you keep this from growing without limit?" is the natural
follow-up question in an interview.

## Further reading

- [Modules: Packages](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html) — the official rules for `"type"`, `exports`, dual packages and interop. Dense, and the source of truth.
- [Modules: ECMAScript modules](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html) — `import.meta`, resolution, and the CommonJS interop section you will come back to.
- [`module.createRequire()`](https://nodejs.org/api/module.html#modulecreaterequirefilename) — the bridge from ex2, in the API docs.
- [MDN: `import()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/import) — dynamic import, including what the namespace object contains.
- [MDN: `Set`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set) — for review1, and for every deduplication you write from here on.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — write the cache yourself

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createModuleCache(load)`, a
memoising loader with the semantics Node's own module cache has:

```ts
const cache = createModuleCache(async (key) => expensiveLoad(key));
cache.get("alpha");   // calls the loader
cache.get("alpha");   // does not
cache.size();         // how many keys are cached
```

Three rules, and the third is the interesting one:

1. Two `get`s for the same key that overlap *in time* must result in exactly
   one call to `load` — the second caller waits on the first caller's work.
2. Once a key has loaded, the loader is never called for it again.
3. If a load **rejects**, the key must not be cached: the next `get` tries
   again. Both callers of a failed load still see the rejection.

Rule 3 mirrors real `require` semantics — a module that throws while being
evaluated is removed from the cache, so the next `require` re-runs it — and it
is the rule people forget, which is how a single blip during start-up becomes
a permanently broken cache entry that only a restart fixes.

Honest difficulty note: rules 1 and 2 are five lines. Rule 3 is where you have
to think about *which* promise you are holding and *what* `.catch()` returns.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three requirements, and they pull against each other:

1. two overlapping `get`s for one key call the loader once,
2. a key that has finished loading never calls the loader again,
3. a key whose load *failed* is forgotten, so the next `get` retries.

Requirement 1 decides your data structure. If you cache the resolved value you
have nothing to hand the second caller while the first load is still in
flight, so cache something that exists earlier than the value does.

## Hint 2

Cache the promise, not the value. A `Map<string, Promise<T>>` satisfies (1)
and (2) at once: `get` looks the key up, returns the stored promise if there
is one, and otherwise calls `load(key)`, stores the promise it got back and
returns it. Promises are freely shareable - awaiting one twice is fine, and
every awaiter of a settled promise gets the same result.

Requirement 3 needs a second step: attach a rejection handler to the promise
you stored that removes the entry from the map. Do that *without* changing
what `get` hands back - the caller still has to see the rejection.

## Hint 3

The skeleton:

```ts
const entries = new Map<string, Promise<T>>();

get(key) {
  const cached = entries.get(key);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;

  const pending = load(key);
  entries.set(key, pending);
  pending.catch(() => { /* remove the entry - but which one? */ });
```

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three requirements, and they pull against each other:

1. two overlapping `get`s for one key call the loader once,
2. a key that has finished loading never calls the loader again,
3. a key whose load *failed* is forgotten, so the next `get` retries.

Requirement 1 decides your data structure. If you cache the resolved value you
have nothing to hand the second caller while the first load is still in
flight, so cache something that exists earlier than the value does.

## Hint 2

Cache the promise, not the value. A `Map<string, Promise<T>>` satisfies (1)
and (2) at once: `get` looks the key up, returns the stored promise if there
is one, and otherwise calls `load(key)`, stores the promise it got back and
returns it. Promises are freely shareable - awaiting one twice is fine, and
every awaiter of a settled promise gets the same result.

Requirement 3 needs a second step: attach a rejection handler to the promise
you stored that removes the entry from the map. Do that *without* changing
what `get` hands back - the caller still has to see the rejection.

## Hint 3

The skeleton:

```ts
const entries = new Map<string, Promise<T>>();

get(key) {
  const cached = entries.get(key);
  if (cached !== undefined) return cached;

  const pending = load(key);
  entries.set(key, pending);
  pending.catch(() => { /* remove the entry - but which one? */ });
  return pending;
}
```

Two decisions left. Inside the `catch`, delete only if the stored promise is
still *this* one (a retry may already have replaced it) - compare before you
delete. And note that `pending.catch(...)` returns a *new* promise: if you
return that instead of `pending`, you have just swallowed the error you were
told to propagate.

## Exercise 1 — where am I?

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `moduleDirname(metaUrl)`, which takes an
`import.meta.url` string and returns the absolute path of the directory that
contains that module:

- `moduleDirname("file:///C:/app/my%20dir/index.js")` → `C:\app\my dir` on Windows
- the same call on Linux → `/C:/app/my dir` (URLs do not know about drive letters)

You do not need to handle the platform difference yourself — one standard
library function does it — but you do need to pick the right one. The gate
checks the path you return actually exists on disk, and separately feeds you a
URL with an encoded space in it.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are given a URL and asked for a path. Those are two notations for the same
location, and the difference is not cosmetic: a URL percent-encodes characters
that are perfectly legal in paths (a space becomes `%20`), and on Windows it
grows a leading slash in front of the drive letter (`file:///C:/app`).

So the first question is: which module in the standard library converts
between the two? The answer is not `node:path`.

## Hint 2

`node:url` exports `fileURLToPath`, the inverse of `pathToFileURL`. It handles
the percent-decoding and the Windows drive-letter rule for you, and it throws
if you hand it something that is not a `file:` URL.

That gets you the path of the *file*. The gate asks for the directory that
contains it, which is a one-call job for `node:path`.

## Hint 3

Two calls, composed:

```ts
import path from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

export function moduleDirname(metaUrl: string): string {
  return path./* which function? */(fileURLToPath(metaUrl));
}
```

The decision left to you is which `node:path` function drops the last segment:
`basename` gives you the last segment, `extname` gives you the suffix, and the
one you want is the third of that family. If you are tempted to write
`metaUrl.replace("file://", "")` instead, run it against the `my dojo` case in
the gate and watch what happens to the space.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You are given a URL and asked for a path. Those are two notations for the same
location, and the difference is not cosmetic: a URL percent-encodes characters
that are perfectly legal in paths (a space becomes `%20`), and on Windows it
grows a leading slash in front of the drive letter (`file:///C:/app`).

So the first question is: which module in the standard library converts
between the two? The answer is not `node:path`.

## Hint 2

`node:url` exports `fileURLToPath`, the inverse of `pathToFileURL`. It handles
the percent-decoding and the Windows drive-letter rule for you, and it throws
if you hand it something that is not a `file:` URL.

That gets you the path of the *file*. The gate asks for the directory that
contains it, which is a one-call job for `node:path`.

## Hint 3

Two calls, composed:

```ts
import path from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

export function moduleDirname(metaUrl: string): string {
  return path./* which function? */(fileURLToPath(metaUrl));
}
```

The decision left to you is which `node:path` function drops the last segment:
`basename` gives you the last segment, `extname` gives you the suffix, and the
one you want is the third of that family. If you are tempted to write
`metaUrl.replace("file://", "")` instead, run it against the `my dojo` case in
the gate and watch what happens to the space.

## Exercise 2 — call the old code

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Next to it sits `legacy-pricing.cjs`, a CommonJS
module written years ago that you are not allowed to modify. It exports:

```js
module.exports = { RATES, priceWithTax };
// RATES        = { us: 0.07, de: 0.19, jp: 0.1 }
// priceWithTax = (cents, region) => cents rounded up by that region's rate
```

Implement two functions on top of it:

- `checkout(cents, region)` returns the taxed price by **calling** the legacy
  function — `checkout(1000, "us")` → `1070`, `checkout(2500, "de")` → `2975`.
- `regions()` returns the region codes from `RATES`, sorted:
  `["de", "jp", "us"]`.

Reimplementing the arithmetic instead of calling across the boundary defeats
the exercise, and the gate cannot tell — but you can, and the next legacy
module you meet will have three hundred lines of rules in it rather than one.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex2
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both functions have to agree about a number and neither of them is given it,
so the number has to live somewhere they can both reach: outside the
functions, at the top level of the module.

The reason that works - the reason the gate can import your module twice and
still see one counter - is the thing this exercise is really teaching. Reread
the "a module is evaluated once" part of the README before you write anything.

## Hint 2

Declare the state with `let` at module scope, above both functions. `nextId`
moves it on by one and returns the string built from the new value;
`idsIssued` just reports it.

Watch the off-by-one: the first id is `job-1`, not `job-0`. Increment before
you build the string, or start the counter at 1 and increment after - pick one
and be consistent.

## Hint 3

The shape:

```ts
let issued = /* what starting value? */;

export function nextId(): string {
  /* move the counter, then return a template literal */
}
```

Do not export `issued` itself and do not wrap it in an object you export -
exported bindings are live views of the module variable, and handing the
counter out is how someone else ends up resetting it. The decision left to you
is where the increment goes relative to the `return`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both functions have to agree about a number and neither of them is given it,
so the number has to live somewhere they can both reach: outside the
functions, at the top level of the module.

The reason that works - the reason the gate can import your module twice and
still see one counter - is the thing this exercise is really teaching. Reread
the "a module is evaluated once" part of the README before you write anything.

## Hint 2

Declare the state with `let` at module scope, above both functions. `nextId`
moves it on by one and returns the string built from the new value;
`idsIssued` just reports it.

Watch the off-by-one: the first id is `job-1`, not `job-0`. Increment before
you build the string, or start the counter at 1 and increment after - pick one
and be consistent.

## Hint 3

The shape:

```ts
let issued = /* what starting value? */;

export function nextId(): string {
  /* move the counter, then return a template literal */
}
```

Do not export `issued` itself and do not wrap it in an object you export -
exported bindings are live views of the module variable, and handing the
counter out is how someone else ends up resetting it. The decision left to you
is where the increment goes relative to the `return`.

## Exercise 4 — load it when you need it

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Two formatter modules live in `ex4/formatters/`, each
default-exporting a function that turns rows into a string. Implement:

```ts
loadFormatter(kind: "json" | "csv"): Promise<Formatter>
```

It must resolve to the module's default export, and it must throw for an
unknown kind with a message containing `unknown formatter: <kind>`.

The catch, and the reason this exercise exists: **a formatter module must not
be evaluated until it is asked for**. Each of those modules registers itself
in a shared registry when its body runs, and the gate checks the registry is
empty before your function is first called, then that it contains exactly the
formatters you loaded, in order. A pair of static imports at the top of your
file fails on the very first assertion.

```
uv run dojo test node 01_modules ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The first assertion in the gate runs before your function is ever called and
checks that *neither* formatter module has been evaluated. That single check
rules out the obvious solution: two `import` statements at the top of your
file would evaluate both modules the moment the gate imports yours.

What you need is the form of import that happens when control reaches it,
returns a promise, and is allowed to sit inside an `if` or a `switch`.

## Hint 2

`await import("./formatters/csv")` gives you the module namespace object - the
same thing `import * as csv from ...` would bind. The function you want to
return is its `default` property, because those modules use `export default`.

Branch on `kind` with a `switch` or an `if`, one `await import` per branch.
Write the specifiers as literal strings: a bundler can only prepare what it
can see, and `import(someVariable)` is the version that bites you later.

For an unknown kind, throw an `Error` whose message contains
`unknown formatter: ` followed by the kind you were given.

## Hint 3

The shape:

```ts
switch (kind) {
  case "csv": {
    const module = await import(/* the literal specifier */);
    return module./* which property? */;
  }
  // ... the json case ...
  default:
    throw new Error(`unknown formatter: ${kind}`);
}
```

Two decisions left: which property of the namespace object carries a default
export, and whether to keep the `default` branch at all. TypeScript says it is
unreachable, which is exactly why the gate calls it through a
`@ts-expect-error` - types are erased before your code runs, and the string
that arrives at run time is whatever the caller had.
