lessons.briefing:
# 04 — Events, and what to do when things break

Node has two ways to say "something happened later". You have spent a lesson
on the first one: a promise, which settles exactly once, with a value or an
error. The second is the `EventEmitter`, which says "something happened"
however many times it likes, to however many listeners are interested, and
never settles at all. HTTP servers, sockets, streams, processes, file watchers
— every long-lived thing in Node is an emitter, so this is not an optional
corner of the platform.

The two models are not competitors; they answer different questions. *Did the
database call succeed?* is a promise: one question, one answer. *What is
arriving on this socket?* is an emitter: an open-ended stream of occurrences,
where "done" is itself just another event. Most real code needs to bridge
them, which is exercise 4.

The other half of this lesson is errors, because in Node the two subjects are
the same subject. A rejected promise nobody handles will, since Node 15,
terminate your process. An `"error"` event nobody listens for **throws** — it
is the one event name with special behaviour, and an unhandled one takes the
process down too. And the decision of whether taking the process down is
*correct* turns out to be one of the sharpest lines in server engineering: the
difference between an operational error and a programmer error.

## Concept — emitters, and the error taxonomy

An emitter is a registry of callbacks keyed by name:

```ts
import { EventEmitter } from "node:events";

const jobs = new EventEmitter();

jobs.on("added", (job, size) => console.log(`${job} queued, ${size} waiting`));
jobs.once("ready", () => console.log("this fires at most once"));

jobs.emit("added", "resize-image", 1);   // calls every "added" listener, now
```

Four facts about `emit` that decide most of the behaviour you will meet:

1. **It is synchronous.** `emit` calls the listeners in registration order and
   returns when the last one has returned. There is no queue and no `await`.
   That is why a slow listener slows down the emitter, and why a listener that
   throws propagates out of the `emit` call.
2. **Order is registration order**, always, and there is no priority system.
3. **`emit` returns a boolean** — `true` if there was at least one listener.
   That is how you can tell an event nobody heard.
4. **Listeners are not removed for you**, except by `once`. An emitter that
   lives for the process lifetime with listeners added per request is a memory
   leak, and Node warns you about it at eleven listeners for one event
   (`MaxListenersExceededWarning`) precisely because that number usually means
   a bug rather than a design.

Then the special case:

```ts
const socket = new EventEmitter();
socket.emit("error", new Error("connection reset"));   // THROWS. No listener.
```

`"error"` is the one name `EventEmitter` treats specially: emitting it with no
listener registered throws the error rather than dropping it. This is
deliberate — a silently ignored error is worse than a crash — and it is why
every stream, socket and server you use needs an error listener.

### Operational vs programmer errors

The distinction comes from Joyent's old Node error-handling guide and it has
outlived nearly everything else from that era:

- An **operational error** is a correct program meeting a wrong world: bad
  user input, a 500 from an upstream service, a connection reset, a missing
  file, a full disk. Your code did nothing wrong. These are *expected*, they
  belong in your control flow, and you handle them — retry, return a 400, log
  and continue.
- A **programmer error** is a bug: reading a property of `undefined`, calling
  a function that does not exist, passing the wrong type. Nothing sensible can
  be done at run time, because the process is now in a state its author never
  intended. The honest response is to crash, let a supervisor restart you, and
  fix the bug.

The reason this matters more in Node than in some other runtimes is that one
process serves many concurrent requests. A `try`/`catch` that swallows a
programmer error keeps a process alive with corrupted state, and it will keep
serving the other nine hundred requests with it.

### Errors are objects you get to design

`throw new Error("bad email")` gives the caller a string to regex. A custom
class gives them something to branch on:

```ts
class NotFoundError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly id: string) {
    super(`no such order: ${id}`);
    this.name = "NotFoundError";      // without this, logs say "Error"
  }
}
```

`instanceof NotFoundError` in a `catch`, `error.id` for the details,
`error.name` in the log. And since ES2022 there is a standard way to keep the
error underneath:

```ts
throw new Error("loading the user profile failed", { cause: originalError });
```

Everything — `console.log`, vitest, most loggers — knows how to print a
`cause` chain, which is why this beats inventing `error.inner`.

## Exercise 1 — an emitter of your own

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `JobQueue`, a class that extends
`EventEmitter`:

- `add(job)` records the job, emits `"added"` with **two** arguments — the
  job and the queue's new size — and returns the new size.
- `flush()` emits `"drained"` with **one** argument, the array of jobs, then
  empties the queue and returns that array. Flushing an empty queue still
  emits, with an empty array.
- `size()` returns how many jobs are waiting.

The gate checks that the listener has already run by the time `add` returns
(emit is synchronous), that a `once` listener fires only once, and that
listeners are called in registration order.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the callback convention, from the other side

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `parseConfig(text, callback)`:

- if `text` is not valid JSON, call back with an `Error` whose `code` is
  `"EPARSE"`;
- if it parses but has no numeric `port`, call back with an `Error` whose
  `code` is `"EMISSING"` and whose message mentions `port`;
- otherwise, call back with `(null, config)`.

And one rule that is not about the error at all: **the callback must never be
called synchronously.** Defer it — `process.nextTick` or `queueMicrotask` —
so that `parseConfig` always returns before the callback runs.

That rule has a name (Isaac Schlueter's "don't release Zalgo") and a real
reason. An API that calls back synchronously *sometimes* — say, when the input
is invalid — runs your callback before the caller has finished setting up,
which produces bugs that appear only on the error path and only under some
inputs. Pick one behaviour and always do it; asynchronous is the one that is
always safe.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — an error class, and a judgement call

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Two things.

First, `ValidationError`, which extends `Error` and carries:
`name` of `"ValidationError"`, the `message` it was constructed with, the
`field` that failed, `status` of `400`, and `isOperational` of `true`.

Second, `classifyError(error)`, returning `"operational"` or `"programmer"`,
by this rule:

1. anything that is not an `Error` instance → `"programmer"` (someone threw a
   string, which is a bug on its own);
2. an error with `isOperational === true` → `"operational"`;
3. everything else → `"programmer"`.

Rule 3 is the interesting one, and it is a deliberate design choice: errors
are guilty until proven innocent. An unrecognised failure gets treated as a
bug, because assuming a mystery is harmless is how a corrupted process stays
up. Real systems mark their operational errors on purpose — which is exactly
what `isOperational` is doing on your `ValidationError`.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — one promise from many events

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `collectUntilEnd(source)`, which watches an
emitter and returns a promise that:

- resolves with an array of every `"data"` payload, in order, when `"end"`
  fires;
- rejects with the error if `"error"` fires first;
- **and removes every listener it added, on both paths.**

The gate checks the listener counts after the promise settles, because that is
the bug this exercise exists to prevent. Attaching listeners to a long-lived
emitter and never removing them is *the* Node memory leak: the emitter holds
your closure, your closure holds the array, the array holds the payloads, and
nothing is ever collected.

One thing to know before you start: `off` (and its older alias
`removeListener`) removes a listener **by identity**. Passing a fresh arrow
function with the same body removes nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex4
```

## Challenge — write EventEmitter yourself

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createEmitter()` returning an object
with `on`, `once`, `off` and `emit`, obeying four rules:

1. listeners run in registration order, synchronously;
2. `emit` returns `true` if at least one listener ran, `false` otherwise;
3. `off` removes exactly the listener it is given — including a listener
   registered with `once`, which is not the function you actually stored;
4. a listener that removes itself (or any other listener) *during* dispatch
   must not disturb the dispatch in progress.

Rule 4 is the one that separates a working implementation from a nearly
working one, and it is why the real `EventEmitter` copies its listener array
before walking it. Rule 3 is the other trap: `once` has to wrap the caller's
function, so `off` needs a way back from the original to the wrapper.

Honest difficulty note: `on`/`emit`/`off` is fifteen minutes. `once` plus
rule 4 is another twenty, and this exact question ("implement EventEmitter")
is a standard mid-level interview task.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors challenge
```

## Review

`review1/solution.ts` comes back on the spaced-review schedule. Implement:

- `wrapError(error, context)` → a new `Error` whose message is
  `` `${context}: ${error.message}` `` and whose `cause` is the original error;
- `rootCause(error)` → walk the `cause` chain and return the error at the
  bottom of it. An error with no cause is its own root cause.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/04_events_errors

Emitters are the oldest abstraction in Node and still the one everything is
built on. Error handling is the topic that separates a service that survives
a bad night from one that does not.

## Notes

**The observer pattern, with one name.** `EventEmitter` is a `Map` from event
name to an array of functions, plus `emit`, and knowing that it is that small
demystifies it. It has no queue, no scheduling, no priorities and no
back-pressure: `emit` calls the listeners and returns. Everything that feels
magical about streams and servers is built on this plus a state machine.

**Synchronous dispatch has consequences.** Because `emit` runs listeners
immediately, a listener that throws propagates out of the `emit` call — into
whatever code was emitting, which is often deep inside Node itself. Because it
is synchronous, a slow listener delays the emitter and everything behind it.
And because it is synchronous, adding a listener *after* the event was emitted
means you missed it forever: there is no replay. That last one bites people
who register a listener in a promise continuation and wonder why nothing
fires.

**`"error"` is special, and only `"error"`.** `emit("error", err)` with no
listener throws the error. Every other event name with no listener is a no-op.
This is why `stream.on("error", ...)` is not optional, why `pipeline()` (next
lesson) is better than `.pipe()` — it wires the error handling for you — and
why a well-behaved emitter documents whether it can emit `"error"` at all.

**Unhandled rejections kill the process, since Node 15.** The default for
`--unhandled-rejections` is `throw`, which raises an uncaught exception if
nothing handles a rejected promise. This was controversial and is right: a
rejection nobody looked at is an error nobody looked at. You can register
`process.on("unhandledRejection", handler)` to log before exiting, but you
should still exit — the state that produced it is unknown.

**`uncaughtException` is not a recovery mechanism.** The handler exists so you
can log, flush metrics, and stop accepting new connections before exiting.
Continuing after one means running a process whose invariants have been
violated by definition. The production pattern is: log, close the server, give
in-flight requests a couple of seconds, `process.exit(1)`, and let systemd,
Kubernetes or PM2 start a fresh one.

**Graceful shutdown belongs in the same mental compartment.** `SIGTERM` is
what an orchestrator sends before it kills you; the polite response is to stop
listening, finish in-flight work, close the pool, and exit. In code that is
`process.on("SIGTERM", () => server.close(...))`, and it is a routine
interview question because a service that drops requests on every deploy is a
service nobody trusts.

## ex1 — an emitter of your own

Subclassing `EventEmitter` is the standard way to expose "things happened" on
your own objects, and the exercise's shape — a method that mutates state and
then announces it — is the shape you will write dozens of times.

Two design notes hide in it. First, `emit` after the state change, never
before: listeners run synchronously and will read the state you just mutated,
so emitting first shows them the old world. Second, `flush` hands out its
internal array and immediately replaces it. Handing out a live reference to
internal state is a bug you only notice later, when a caller mutates it and
the queue mutates with it — the same reasoning behind returning copies from
getters in every language.

The interview version is "when would you use an EventEmitter instead of a
promise, or a callback?" The answer: when the number of occurrences is not one
— zero, many, or unknown — and when multiple independent parts of the program
want to know. And the follow-up worth pre-empting: emitters make control flow
hard to follow, so prefer a promise when the answer really is "one result".

## ex2 — the convention, and Zalgo

Error-first callbacks are a convention, not a type, so the compiler cannot
help you keep them. Three rules make a callback API well behaved: call the
callback exactly once, pass an `Error` (never a string) as the first argument
on failure, and always call it asynchronously.

The third one has a name — "don't release Zalgo", from an essay by Isaac
Schlueter — and the reason is the interesting part. Consider an API that
validates its input synchronously and calls back with an error, but does I/O
and calls back asynchronously on success. Now the caller's code after the call
sometimes runs before the callback and sometimes after. Any state they set up
on the line below is present in one case and missing in the other, so the bug
appears only on the error path, only for some inputs, and never in the tests.
Deferring unconditionally — `process.nextTick(() => cb(err))` — removes the
whole category.

Codes rather than messages is the other durable lesson. Node's own errors do

Writing `EventEmitter` is a favourite interview task because it is small

# Reading - node/04_events_errors

Emitters are the oldest abstraction in Node and still the one everything is
built on. Error handling is the topic that separates a service that survives
a bad night from one that does not.

## Notes

**The observer pattern, with one name.** `EventEmitter` is a `Map` from event
name to an array of functions, plus `emit`, and knowing that it is that small
demystifies it. It has no queue, no scheduling, no priorities and no
back-pressure: `emit` calls the listeners and returns. Everything that feels
magical about streams and servers is built on this plus a state machine.

**Synchronous dispatch has consequences.** Because `emit` runs listeners
immediately, a listener that throws propagates out of the `emit` call — into
whatever code was emitting, which is often deep inside Node itself. Because it
is synchronous, a slow listener delays the emitter and everything behind it.
And because it is synchronous, adding a listener *after* the event was emitted
means you missed it forever: there is no replay. That last one bites people
who register a listener in a promise continuation and wonder why nothing
fires.

**`"error"` is special, and only `"error"`.** `emit("error", err)` with no
listener throws the error. Every other event name with no listener is a no-op.
This is why `stream.on("error", ...)` is not optional, why `pipeline()` (next
lesson) is better than `.pipe()` — it wires the error handling for you — and
why a well-behaved emitter documents whether it can emit `"error"` at all.

**Unhandled rejections kill the process, since Node 15.** The default for
`--unhandled-rejections` is `throw`, which raises an uncaught exception if
nothing handles a rejected promise. This was controversial and is right: a
rejection nobody looked at is an error nobody looked at. You can register
`process.on("unhandledRejection", handler)` to log before exiting, but you
should still exit — the state that produced it is unknown.

**`uncaughtException` is not a recovery mechanism.** The handler exists so you
can log, flush metrics, and stop accepting new connections before exiting.

violated by definition. The production pattern is: log, close the server, give
in-flight requests a couple of seconds, `process.exit(1)`, and let systemd,
Kubernetes or PM2 start a fresh one.

**Graceful shutdown belongs in the same mental compartment.** `SIGTERM` is
what an orchestrator sends before it kills you; the polite response is to stop

before: listeners run synchronously and will read the state you just mutated,
so emitting first shows them the old world. Second, `flush` hands out its
internal array and immediately replaces it. Handing out a live reference to
internal state is a bug you only notice later, when a caller mutates it and
the queue mutates with it — the same reasoning behind returning copies from
getters in every language.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — write EventEmitter yourself

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createEmitter()` returning an object
with `on`, `once`, `off` and `emit`, obeying four rules:

1. listeners run in registration order, synchronously;
2. `emit` returns `true` if at least one listener ran, `false` otherwise;
3. `off` removes exactly the listener it is given — including a listener
   registered with `once`, which is not the function you actually stored;
4. a listener that removes itself (or any other listener) *during* dispatch
   must not disturb the dispatch in progress.

Rule 4 is the one that separates a working implementation from a nearly
working one, and it is why the real `EventEmitter` copies its listener array
before walking it. Rule 3 is the other trap: `once` has to wrap the caller's
function, so `off` needs a way back from the original to the wrapper.

Honest difficulty note: `on`/`emit`/`off` is fifteen minutes. `once` plus
rule 4 is another twenty, and this exact question ("implement EventEmitter")
is a standard mid-level interview task.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The data structure is a `Map<string, Listener[]>`: event name to the listeners
registered for it, in registration order. `on` appends, `off` removes by
identity, `emit` walks the array.

Write those three first and get the ordering and the `false`-when-empty rule
passing. Then come back for `once`, which is where the design decisions are.

## Hint 2

Two rules are easy to get subtly wrong.

**`emit` must iterate over a copy.** A listener is allowed to call `off` (or
`on`) while it runs, and if you are walking the live array, removing the
current element shifts everything down and the next listener gets skipped.
`for (const listener of [...existing])` costs nothing and fixes it.

**`once` needs a wrapper**, because the thing that has to be removed is not
the listener the caller gave you - it is your wrapper. So `off(event,
originalListener)` has to be able to find the wrapper. A second map from
original to wrapper is the simplest way.

## Hint 3

The shape of `once`:

```ts
once(event, listener) {
  const wrapper: Listener = (...args) => {
    /* remove the wrapper FIRST, then call the listener */
  };
  wrappers.set(listener, wrapper);
  emitter.on(event, wrapper);
}
```

Two decisions left. The order inside the wrapper matters: if the listener
throws, having already removed it means it still only ran once. And in `off`,
you have to look for the wrapper *before* falling back to the listener itself
(`wrappers.get(listener) ?? listener`), or `off` will silently do nothing for
every `once` listener - the bug that turns a one-shot handler into a permanent
one.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — an emitter of your own

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `JobQueue`, a class that extends
`EventEmitter`:

- `add(job)` records the job, emits `"added"` with **two** arguments — the
  job and the queue's new size — and returns the new size.
- `flush()` emits `"drained"` with **one** argument, the array of jobs, then
  empties the queue and returns that array. Flushing an empty queue still
  emits, with an empty array.
- `size()` returns how many jobs are waiting.

The gate checks that the listener has already run by the time `add` returns
(emit is synchronous), that a `once` listener fires only once, and that
listeners are called in registration order.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three methods and one piece of state: the array of jobs. Put the array on the
instance (a field, or a `#private` field if you like the privacy) and the
methods almost write themselves.

The part that is new is `this.emit(name, ...args)`, which you inherit from
`EventEmitter`. It calls every listener registered for that name, right now,
in order, with the arguments you pass - and then returns.

## Hint 2

`add` does three things in this order: record the job, announce it, return the
new size. The announcement carries two arguments, the job and the size the
queue has *after* the addition, so emit after you push.

`flush` has a subtlety: you have to hand out the jobs and empty the queue, and
if you empty it by mutating the same array (`this.jobs.length = 0`) the caller
is holding an array you just emptied. Take a reference to the old array and
give the instance a fresh one instead.

## Hint 3

```ts
add(job: string): number {
  this.#jobs.push(job);
  this.emit("added", /* what two arguments? */);
  return this.#jobs.length;
}

flush(): string[] {
  const jobs = this.#jobs;
  this.#jobs = [];
  this.emit(/* which event, with what payload? */);
  return jobs;
}
```

Two decisions left: the exact payloads. Reread the gate's assertions for the
shapes - one event carries two separate arguments, the other carries a single
array - and remember that flushing an empty queue must still emit.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the callback convention, from the other side

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `parseConfig(text, callback)`:

- if `text` is not valid JSON, call back with an `Error` whose `code` is
  `"EPARSE"`;
- if it parses but has no numeric `port`, call back with an `Error` whose
  `code` is `"EMISSING"` and whose message mentions `port`;
- otherwise, call back with `(null, config)`.

And one rule that is not about the error at all: **the callback must never be
called synchronously.** Defer it — `process.nextTick` or `queueMicrotask` —
so that `parseConfig` always returns before the callback runs.

That rule has a name (Isaac Schlueter's "don't release Zalgo") and a real
reason. An API that calls back synchronously *sometimes* — say, when the input
is invalid — runs your callback before the caller has finished setting up,
which produces bugs that appear only on the error path and only under some
inputs. Pick one behaviour and always do it; asynchronous is the one that is
always safe.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three outcomes, one callback, and a rule about *when*.

The outcomes: the text is not JSON at all; the text is JSON but has no numeric
`port`; the text is a usable config. The first two call the callback with an
error and nothing else, the third calls it with `null` and the config.

The rule about when: your callback must not run before `parseConfig` has
returned. The gate checks this by looking at the call log immediately after
calling you.

## Hint 2

`JSON.parse` throws on bad input, so it needs a `try`/`catch` - but the
`catch` must not rethrow. Turn the caught error into your own error and hand
it to the callback. That is the whole point of the convention: the caller has
no `try` around you, because you are asynchronous.

To tag an error with a code, either assign the property
(`Object.assign(new Error(msg), { code: "EPARSE" })`) or set it after
construction. Callers branch on `error.code`, never on message text, because
message text changes and codes do not.

To defer, wrap the whole body in `process.nextTick(() => { ... })` or
`queueMicrotask(...)`.

## Hint 3

The skeleton:

```ts
process.nextTick(() => {
  let parsed: unknown;
  try {
    parsed = JSON.parse(text);
  } catch (error) {
    callback(/* an Error tagged EPARSE */);
    return;                       // <- do not fall through
  }

  const config = parsed as Config;
  if (/* is there a numeric port? */) {
    callback(/* an Error tagged EMISSING, naming the field */);
    return;
  }
  callback(null, config);
});
```

Two decisions left: the port check (`typeof x === "number"` is stricter than
truthiness, and a port of 0 is a real value), and making sure exactly one
callback call happens on every path. Those `return`s after each callback are
the entire reason error-first code is full of them.

## Exercise 3 — an error class, and a judgement call

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Two things.

First, `ValidationError`, which extends `Error` and carries:
`name` of `"ValidationError"`, the `message` it was constructed with, the
`field` that failed, `status` of `400`, and `isOperational` of `true`.

Second, `classifyError(error)`, returning `"operational"` or `"programmer"`,
by this rule:

1. anything that is not an `Error` instance → `"programmer"` (someone threw a
   string, which is a bug on its own);
2. an error with `isOperational === true` → `"operational"`;
3. everything else → `"programmer"`.

Rule 3 is the interesting one, and it is a deliberate design choice: errors
are guilty until proven innocent. An unrecognised failure gets treated as a
bug, because assuming a mystery is harmless is how a corrupted process stays
up. Real systems mark their operational errors on purpose — which is exactly
what `isOperational` is doing on your `ValidationError`.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex3
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — one promise from many events

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `collectUntilEnd(source)`, which watches an
emitter and returns a promise that:

- resolves with an array of every `"data"` payload, in order, when `"end"`
  fires;
- rejects with the error if `"error"` fires first;
- **and removes every listener it added, on both paths.**

The gate checks the listener counts after the promise settles, because that is
the bug this exercise exists to prevent. Attaching listeners to a long-lived
emitter and never removing them is *the* Node memory leak: the emitter holds
your closure, your closure holds the array, the array holds the payloads, and
nothing is ever collected.

One thing to know before you start: `off` (and its older alias
`removeListener`) removes a listener **by identity**. Passing a fresh arrow
function with the same body removes nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test node 04_events_errors ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are bridging two worlds: an emitter that pushes events at you, and a
promise that settles once. The `Promise` constructor is the bridge, because it
hands you `resolve` and `reject` to call from inside your listeners.

Three listeners: one that collects, one that finishes, one that fails. And a
fourth thing that is not a listener - the cleanup that removes all three.

## Hint 2

Name your listeners rather than passing inline arrows, because `off` needs the
*same function reference* you passed to `on`. This is the number one reason
"I removed the listener and it still fires" happens:

```ts
source.on("data", (item) => items.push(item));
source.off("data", (item) => items.push(item));   // a different function!
```

Write a `cleanup()` that calls `off` for all three, and call it from both the
end path and the error path before you settle.

## Hint 3

The skeleton:

```ts
return new Promise<T[]>((resolve, reject) => {
  const items: T[] = [];

  const onData = (item: T): void => { items.push(item); };
  const onEnd = (): void => { cleanup(); resolve(items); };
  const onError = (error: Error): void => { cleanup(); /* ? */ };
  const cleanup = (): void => { /* three off() calls */ };

  source.on("data", onData);
  source.once("end", onEnd);
  source.once("error", onError);
});
```

Two decisions left: what `onError` does with the error, and whether `once` or
`on` is right for each of the three. (`once` already removes its own listener
after firing, which makes `cleanup` partly redundant - and still worth writing,
because the *other* two listeners are the ones that leak.)

lessons.briefing:
# 05 — Files and paths

This is the lesson where Node stops being a language runtime and starts being
an operating-system client. Everything you write from here — reading config,
serving static files, processing uploads, writing logs — goes through two
modules: `node:fs`, which does the I/O, and `node:path`, which does the
arithmetic on the strings that name the files.

Two things make this harder than it looks. The first is that a path is not
really a string: it has a separator that differs between platforms, an
extension whose definition has an edge case, and a normalisation step that
turns `a/b/../c` into `a/c`. Code that treats paths as strings works
perfectly on the machine it was written on. Your Windows box and a Linux
container disagree about `\` versus `/`, and the resulting bug is always
discovered in production.

The second is that the filesystem is a shared, hostile, stateful thing. The
file might not exist. It might exist and be a directory. It might disappear
between your check and your read. Someone else might be writing it right now.
The `fs` API's job is to hand you those failures precisely — through
`error.code` — and yours is to decide, per code, which are expected and which
are not. That is the operational/programmer distinction from lesson 04, now
with real error codes attached.

## Concept — `node:path` first, `node:fs/promises` second

`node:path` is pure string arithmetic; it never touches the disk, so nothing
in it can fail because a file is missing:

```ts
import path from "node:path";

path.join("data", "reports", "q1.json");   // "data\reports\q1.json" on Windows
path.resolve("data", "q1.json");           // absolute, based on process.cwd()
path.dirname("/srv/app/index.js");         // "/srv/app"
path.basename("/srv/app/index.js");        // "index.js"
path.basename("/srv/app/index.js", ".js"); // "index"
path.extname("archive.tar.gz");            // ".gz"  <- the LAST dot onwards
path.parse("/srv/app/index.js");
// { root: "/", dir: "/srv/app", base: "index.js", name: "index", ext: ".js" }
path.relative("/srv/app", "/srv/app/logs/today.log");  // "logs/today.log"
path.sep;                                  // "\" on Windows, "/" elsewhere
```

`join` versus `resolve` is the distinction to keep: `join` glues segments
together and normalises; `resolve` builds an *absolute* path, walking right to
left until it has one, so `path.resolve("/a", "/b")` is `/b`. Use `join` for
"a file inside this directory" and `resolve` for "make this absolute".

Then the filesystem, in its promise flavour:

```ts
import { readFile, writeFile, mkdir, readdir, rm, stat } from "node:fs/promises";

const text = await readFile(file, "utf8");        // without "utf8": a Buffer
await writeFile(file, text, "utf8");              // truncates and replaces
await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });            // no error if it exists
const entries = await readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true });  // Dirent objects
```

`node:fs` has three APIs for everything: callbacks (`fs.readFile`), promises
(`fs/promises`), and synchronous (`fs.readFileSync`). Use the promise one.
The sync one blocks the entire event loop for the duration of the disk I/O,
which is acceptable exactly once — at start-up, before you accept traffic —
and a self-inflicted outage anywhere else.

And the failures, which arrive as an `Error` with a `code`:

| code | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ENOENT` | no such file or directory |
| `EACCES` / `EPERM` | you are not allowed |
| `EEXIST` | it is already there |
| `EISDIR` / `ENOTDIR` | you asked for the wrong kind of thing |
| `EMFILE` | too many open file descriptors |

messages are prose and they change.

## Exercise 1 — path arithmetic

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Three small functions, no disk access at all:

- `reportPath(root, slug, file)` joins the three segments into one path, using
  the platform separator and collapsing a doubled separator if `root` already
  ends with one.
- `splitName(file)` returns `{ name, ext }` for a filename:
  `"report.2026.json"` → `{ name: "report.2026", ext: ".json" }`,
  `"LICENSE"` → `{ name: "LICENSE", ext: "" }`.

  `parent`: `true` for a file in a subdirectory, `false` for anything reached
  by going up, and `false` when the two are the same path.

answer resolves both paths first and asks which direction the journey goes.


- `writeJson(file, data)` — writes `data` as JSON, **creating any missing
  parent directories**, indented with two spaces, ending with a newline.
- `readJson(file)` — reads it back and parses it.

```

```

slashes**, sorted.

```
a.json
notes.txt
nested/b.json
nested/deep/c.json
nested/deep/skip.md

```

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `readJsonOr(file, fallback)`:

```
uv run dojo test node 05_fs_path ex4
```

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `buildIndex(dir)`:

1. find every `.json` file under `dir` (skipping `index.json` itself);
2. read and parse each one, taking `{ id, title }` from it;
3. sort the entries by `id`;

5. return the array.

`cause`. Nothing partial gets written.

this course are deliberately isolated so that one broken file cannot fail two
gates.

things you have just written is exactly the point. The two places people lose
time are forgetting to skip `index.json` (so the second run indexes its own
output) and reporting the error without the filename.

```
uv run dojo test node 05_fs_path challenge
```

## Review

`review1/solution.ts` comes back on the spaced-review schedule. Implement
`ensureUniqueName(dir, name)`: return `name` if nothing in `dir` is called
that, otherwise `name-1`, `name-2`, … until you find a free one — with the
suffix **before** the extension (`report-1.json`, never `report.json-1`), and
working for files with no extension at all.

```

```

# Reading - node/05_fs_path

The filesystem is where a Node program meets the operating system, and where
"it works on my machine" is born.

## Notes

**Three APIs, one filesystem.** `node:fs` exposes callbacks
(`fs.readFile(path, cb)`), promises (`fs/promises`), and synchronous
(`fs.readFileSync`). They do the same work through the same libuv machinery;
what differs is who waits. The promise API is the default for new code. The
sync API is legitimate in exactly two places: a CLI that has nothing else to
do, and a server's start-up path before it accepts connections. Anywhere else
it blocks the event loop for the whole duration of a disk operation — which on
a cold cache or a network filesystem can be tens of milliseconds, during which
your server answers nobody.

**libuv uses a thread pool for file I/O.** Sockets get real asynchronous
notification from the OS (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), but file operations do not have
a portable async interface, so libuv runs them on a pool of four threads by
default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`). This is why a burst of file reads can queue
behind each other while HTTP requests keep flowing, and why the answer to
"should I raise the thread pool size?" is "measure first". `crypto.pbkdf2`,
`zlib` and DNS lookups share that pool, which is a genuinely surprising
interaction and a good interview aside.

**Paths are not strings, and `..` is the enemy.** Path traversal — a
user-supplied name containing `../` that escapes the directory you meant —
remains one of the most commonly exploited web vulnerabilities. The defence is
always the same shape: resolve the candidate to an absolute path, then prove
it is inside the base directory before touching it. Never compare with
`startsWith` on the raw strings (`/uploads-secret` starts with `/uploads`),
and remember that on Windows a path can also escape by changing drive.

**Encoding matters more than it looks.** `readFile(file)` without an encoding
returns a `Buffer`; with `"utf8"` it returns a string, decoded. That decode is
not free and it is not always safe: a multi-byte character split across two
reads decodes to a replacement character, which is why streaming text needs
`StringDecoder` (next lesson). For binary — images, archives, hashes — stay in
`Buffer` and never let a string near it.

**Atomic-ish writes.** `writeFile` truncates the target and then writes; a
crash halfway leaves a truncated file. The standard trick is to write to a
temp file in the same directory and `rename` it over the target, because
`rename` within a filesystem is atomic. Worth knowing when a config file
matters, and a good answer to "how would you make sure a reader never sees a
half-written file?".

**Watch out for `existsSync` before an operation.** The classic
`if (existsSync(f)) readFileSync(f)` is a TOCTOU race: the file can vanish
between the two calls. The correct pattern is to attempt the operation and
handle `ENOENT`, which is exactly what ex4 makes you write.

## ex1 — the six functions worth memorising

`join`, `resolve`, `dirname`, `basename`, `extname`, `parse`, `relative`. That
is most of `node:path`, and knowing them cold removes the temptation to do
string surgery.

Two subtleties in this exercise. `extname` takes the **last** dot onwards, so
`archive.tar.gz` has extension `.gz` and `.gitignore` — a dotfile — has
extension `""` with a name of `.gitignore`, which surprises people. And
`path.relative` answers a question people do not realise they are asking: it
returns the route from A to B, so a route that never goes up means B is
underneath A. That is a much better containment test than any string
comparison, and it handles normalisation (`a/b/../b/c`) for free.

The path-traversal check is worth remembering as a snippet, because you will
need it whenever a filename comes from outside:

```ts
const target = path.resolve(baseDir, userSuppliedName);
const relative = path.relative(baseDir, target);
if (relative.startsWith("..") || path.isAbsolute(relative)) throw new ForbiddenError();
```

The follow-up an interviewer asks: "and what about symlinks?" A symlink inside
the base can point outside it, and the resolution above will not notice.
`fs.realpath` resolves links; whether you need it depends on whether the
directory is user-writable.

## ex2 — the round trip, and the two-space indent

The interesting part is `mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })`, which is both "make
the whole chain of directories" and "do not complain if it is already there".
Before it existed, every codebase had a `mkdirp` dependency and a subtly wrong
`existsSync` check; it is one of the clearest examples of the standard library
absorbing a lesson from the ecosystem.

The formatting details are not fussiness. Two-space indentation means a config
file produces a readable diff when someone changes one field, rather than one
enormous line. The trailing newline means `cat` does not leave your prompt
mid-line, `git` does not report "\ No newline at end of file" forever, and
line-oriented tools count the last line. Both are conventions, both are free,
and both are noticed when missing.

The type-level footnote: `readJson<T>` returns `Promise<T>` while `JSON.parse`
returns `any`. That cast is a promise you are making without evidence. It is
acceptable in a course exercise and it is how a surprising amount of
production code reads external data — until the day the shape changes. The
grown-up answer is a runtime schema check, which is what zod does in lesson
10, and the reason people describe it as "the type you can actually trust".

## ex3 — recursion, and the separator question

`readdir` with `withFileTypes: true` is the efficient shape: one syscall gives
you names *and* types, where the alternative is a `stat` per entry. (Node also
offers `readdir(dir, { recursive: true })` now, which does the walk for you —
write it by hand once, then use the built-in.)

The separator normalisation is a real convention, not a test artefact.
Anything that leaves your process — a JSON manifest, a URL, a log line, a
cache key — is better off with forward slashes, because that string may be
read on a different platform than the one that wrote it. Anything that goes
back into `fs` should be reassembled with `path.join`. Normalise at the
boundary, keep the inside consistent.

Two production notes. Directory trees can be deep, and a recursive walk uses
the JavaScript stack — for pathological trees an explicit stack or queue is
safer. And walking a big tree with `await` per entry is slow; a real
implementation batches with a concurrency limit, which is exactly
`mapWithLimit` from lesson 03 doing its second job.

## ex4 — the narrow try block

This exercise is a single design rule dressed as a function: **catch only the
failure you understand, around only the operation that can produce it**.

The wide version — one `try` around read-and-parse with `return fallback` —
merges "the file is absent" with "the file is corrupt", and the second one
matters. A settings file that fails to parse means something wrote garbage
into it: a crash mid-write, a disk error, a bad migration. Silently replacing
it with defaults destroys the evidence and the user's data in the same move.

`NodeJS.ErrnoException` is the type Node ships for these errors:
`{ code?, errno?, syscall?, path? }` on top of `Error`. The `path` property is
particularly useful in logs, because it tells you *which* file was missing
without you having to interpolate it yourself.

The interview version of this is "how do you check whether a file exists?" The
strong answer: you usually should not — you attempt the operation and handle
`ENOENT`, because any check is stale by the time you act on it. If you truly
need a check (a validation step in a CLI, say), `fs.access` is the honest one
and `existsSync` is fine at start-up.

## challenge — the pipeline shape

Read everything, transform in memory, write once. That ordering is worth
naming because the alternative — write as you go — is what produces half-built
artefacts when input 400 is broken. For a directory of blog posts it is a
nuisance; for a deployment manifest it is an outage.

Skipping `index.json` is the small lesson with the big name: your output lives
in your input's directory, so the operation is not idempotent unless you
exclude it. Build tools hit this constantly, which is why they insist on a
separate output directory.

The error-with-filename requirement is about the 3am experience. "Unexpected
token } in JSON at position 42" tells you nothing when there are nine hundred
files. `posts/nested/bad.json is not valid JSON` plus a `cause` carrying the
original parse error tells you where to look and what the parser thought.
Adding context on the way up the stack, without discarding the original, is
exactly what lesson 04's `cause` chain was for.

## review1 — collisions, and a race you cannot win

Uniquifying a filename is the everyday version of "do not destroy data you
were not asked to destroy". Every browser download folder implements it;
`report(1).pdf` is the same algorithm with different punctuation.

The `path.parse` step is what makes it correct rather than nearly correct:
inserting the suffix before the extension keeps the file openable by whatever
was going to open it. Splitting on the last dot by hand gets `LICENSE` wrong
and `archive.tar.gz` debatable.

And then the honest caveat: the whole approach is a time-of-check to
time-of-use race. Between reading the directory and writing the file, another
process can take the name you chose. In a single-process CLI nobody cares; in
a service handling concurrent uploads it is a real bug, and the fix is to let
the filesystem arbitrate — open with the `"wx"` flag, which fails with
`EEXIST` if the file exists, and retry. Knowing that the naive version has a
name and a fix is the point; you will meet TOCTOU again in every system that
has both a check and an action.

## Further reading

- [`node:path`](https://nodejs.org/api/path.html) — the whole module; short enough to read once, end to end.
- [`node:fs` — Promises API](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#promises-api) — `readFile`, `writeFile`, `mkdir`, `readdir`, `open` and the flags table.
- [Node.js file system errors](https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html#common-system-errors) — the `code` values, which is the vocabulary ex4 is written in.
- [Working with folders in Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/manipulating-files/working-with-folders-in-nodejs) — the official tour of directory operations.
- [MDN: `JSON.stringify()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify) — the replacer and space arguments used in ex2.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a small pipeline

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `buildIndex(dir)`:

1. find every `.json` file under `dir` (skipping `index.json` itself);
2. read and parse each one, taking `{ id, title }` from it;
3. sort the entries by `id`;
4. write them to `<dir>/index.json` in the same format as `writeJson`;
5. return the array.

If any file fails to parse, reject — and the error message must contain the
**relative path of the offending file**, with the original error kept as
`cause`. Nothing partial gets written.

Copy your ex3 walker into this file rather than importing it; exercises in
this course are deliberately isolated so that one broken file cannot fail two
gates.

Honest difficulty note: nothing here is individually hard, and assembling four
things you have just written is exactly the point. The two places people lose
time are forgetting to skip `index.json` (so the second run indexes its own
output) and reporting the error without the filename.

```
uv run dojo test node 05_fs_path challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex2, ex3 and ex4 in a trench coat: walk the tree, read and parse each
file, write one summary out. Copy your ex3 walker into this file - the
exercises are deliberately isolated, so importing from a sibling exercise is
not the idea.

Do the whole read pass before you write anything. A pipeline that writes as it
goes leaves a half-built index behind when file 400 turns out to be corrupt.

## Hint 2

Three details the gate is specific about.

**Skip `index.json` itself.** You are writing it into the same directory you
are reading, so the second run would index its own output.

**Sort by `id`,** not by filename: the fixture is deliberately arranged so
those two orders differ.

**Name the file in the error.** Wrap the parse in a `try`/`catch` and throw a
new error whose message contains the relative path - and pass the original as
`{ cause: error }`, which is exactly what you built in lesson 04.

## Hint 3

The skeleton:

```ts
for (const relative of await jsonFiles(dir)) {
  if (relative === "index.json") continue;
  const text = await readFile(path.join(dir, ...relative.split("/")), "utf8");
  try {
    /* parse and push { id, title } */
  } catch (error) {
    throw new Error(`${relative} is not valid JSON`, { cause: error });
  }
}
```

Two decisions left: how you turn a forward-slash relative path back into a
real path for reading (`relative.split("/")` spread into `path.join` is one
way, and it is the reason the walker normalised the separators in the first
place), and the comparator for the sort. `localeCompare` reads better than
`a < b ? -1 : 1` and behaves for non-ASCII ids.

```ts
for (const relative of await jsonFiles(dir)) {
```

## Exercise 1 — path arithmetic

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Three small functions, no disk access at all:

- `reportPath(root, slug, file)` joins the three segments into one path, using
  the platform separator and collapsing a doubled separator if `root` already
  ends with one.
- `splitName(file)` returns `{ name, ext }` for a filename:
  `"report.2026.json"` → `{ name: "report.2026", ext: ".json" }`,
  `"LICENSE"` → `{ name: "LICENSE", ext: "" }`.
- `isInside(parent, child)` returns whether `child` is strictly below
  `parent`: `true` for a file in a subdirectory, `false` for anything reached
  by going up, and `false` when the two are the same path.

`isInside` is not a toy. It is the check that stops
`GET /files/../../etc/passwd` from serving your password file, and "the
attacker sent `..` in a filename" is one of the oldest live vulnerabilities on
the web. The naive version — does the string start with the base directory? —
passes `/uploads-secret` when the base is `/uploads`, which is why the right
answer resolves both paths first and asks which direction the journey goes.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Import from `node:fs/promises`, not `node:fs`. The callback API and the
promise API live in different modules, and mixing them up is the most common
"why is this undefined" in a first fs program.

`writeJson` has three jobs in order: make sure the directory exists, turn the
data into text, write the text. `readJson` has two: read the text, turn it
back into data.

## Hint 2

`mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` creates every missing level and does *not*
fail if the directory is already there - which is why it replaced the
`if (!existsSync) mkdir` dance you may have seen. The directory you need is
`path.dirname(file)`.

`JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)` is the readable form: `null` for the replacer,
`2` for the indent. It does not add a trailing newline, so you add one.

`readFile(file, "utf8")` gives you a string; without the encoding argument it
gives you a `Buffer`, which `JSON.parse` will coerce - but be explicit.

## Hint 3

```ts
export async function writeJson(file: string, data: unknown): Promise<void> {
  await mkdir(/* which directory? */, { recursive: true });
  await writeFile(file, `${JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}\n`, "utf8");
}
```

The decisions left to you: which directory to create, and what `readJson`
does about types. It is declared `Promise<T>` but `JSON.parse` returns `any` -
the cast is you promising the compiler something you have not checked. That is
honest here and a real risk in production, where the answer is a schema
validator (zod, in lesson 10) rather than a cast.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Import from `node:fs/promises`, not `node:fs`. The callback API and the
promise API live in different modules, and mixing them up is the most common
"why is this undefined" in a first fs program.

`writeJson` has three jobs in order: make sure the directory exists, turn the
data into text, write the text. `readJson` has two: read the text, turn it
back into data.

## Hint 2

`mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` creates every missing level and does *not*
fail if the directory is already there - which is why it replaced the
`if (!existsSync) mkdir` dance you may have seen. The directory you need is
`path.dirname(file)`.

`JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)` is the readable form: `null` for the replacer,
`2` for the indent. It does not add a trailing newline, so you add one.

`readFile(file, "utf8")` gives you a string; without the encoding argument it
gives you a `Buffer`, which `JSON.parse` will coerce - but be explicit.

## Hint 3

```ts
export async function writeJson(file: string, data: unknown): Promise<void> {
  await mkdir(/* which directory? */, { recursive: true });
  await writeFile(file, `${JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)}\n`, "utf8");
}
```

The decisions left to you: which directory to create, and what `readJson`
does about types. It is declared `Promise<T>` but `JSON.parse` returns `any` -
the cast is you promising the compiler something you have not checked. That is
honest here and a real risk in production, where the answer is a schema
validator (zod, in lesson 10) rather than a cast.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — walk the tree

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `listJsonFiles(dir)`: every `.json` file at
any depth below `dir`, as paths **relative to `dir`**, with **forward
slashes**, sorted.

Given this tree:

```
a.json
notes.txt
nested/b.json
nested/deep/c.json
nested/deep/skip.md
```

…the answer is `["a.json", "nested/b.json", "nested/deep/c.json"]`.

Two portability details are deliberate. Relative paths keep the output stable
no matter where the temp directory is; forward slashes keep it stable no
matter which platform you are on. Normalising to POSIX separators at the edge
of your program — and joining with `path.join` again on the way back in — is a
common and sane convention, and it is exactly what the challenge does with the
result.

```
uv run dojo test node 05_fs_path ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A recursive walk with an accumulator. The inner function takes the directory
it is currently looking at; the outer function owns the results array and the
root that every result is relative to.

`readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` is the call you want: it gives you
`Dirent` objects with `name`, `isDirectory()` and `isFile()`, so you do not
have to `stat` every entry separately.

## Hint 2

For each entry, build the full path with `path.join(current, entry.name)` and
then branch: recurse into directories, and for files check the extension with
`path.extname`.

The result has to be relative to the directory you were *originally* given -
not the one you are currently reading - which is why the root has to be
captured by the outer function and passed to `path.relative`.

Then the portability step: `path.relative` returns backslashes on Windows and
the gate expects forward slashes. `.split(path.sep).join("/")` converts one to
the other and does nothing on Linux.

## Hint 3

```ts
const found: string[] = [];

const walk = async (current: string): Promise<void> => {
  const entries = await readdir(current, { withFileTypes: true });
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const full = path.join(current, entry.name);
    if (entry.isDirectory()) await walk(full);
    else if (/* is it .json? */) found.push(/* relative, forward slashes */);
  }
};

await walk(dir);
return /* ? */;
```

Two decisions left: the extension test, and the fact that the gate wants the
list sorted - `readdir` order is filesystem order, which is alphabetical on
some systems and not on others, so sort it yourself rather than hoping.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two parts, and you have written both before in this lesson.

Finding out what is already in the directory: one `readdir` call gives you the
names. Putting them in a `Set` makes "is this taken?" a single fast check, and
you only need to read the directory once.

Taking a name apart so the counter lands in the right place: `path.parse`,
same as ex1. `report.json` has to become `report-1.json`, so the suffix goes
between the stem and the extension.

## Hint 2

The loop is "try 1, try 2, try 3 until one is free". A `for` loop with no end
condition and a `return` inside it is the honest shape here - the exit is
finding a free name, not exhausting a range.

Watch the no-extension case: `path.parse("LICENSE")` gives
`{ name: "LICENSE", ext: "" }`, so the template
`` `${stem}-${suffix}${ext}` `` produces `LICENSE-1` with no trailing dot. If
you build the name by string surgery around the last dot instead, that case is
where it breaks.

## Hint 3

```ts
const taken = new Set(await readdir(dir));
if (!taken.has(name)) return name;

const { name: stem, ext } = path.parse(name);
for (let suffix = 1; ; suffix += 1) {
  const candidate = /* build it */;
  if (!taken.has(candidate)) return candidate;
}
```

The decision left to you is the candidate template. One honest caveat worth
knowing: between your `readdir` and whoever actually writes the file, another
process could take the name - a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. The real
fix is to open the file with the exclusive flag (`fs.open(file, "wx")`) and
retry on `EEXIST`, and knowing that this class of bug has a name is most of
the value of the exercise.

## Hint 1

Two parts, and you have written both before in this lesson.

Finding out what is already in the directory: one `readdir` call gives you the
names. Putting them in a `Set` makes "is this taken?" a single fast check, and
you only need to read the directory once.

Taking a name apart so the counter lands in the right place: `path.parse`,
same as ex1. `report.json` has to become `report-1.json`, so the suffix goes
between the stem and the extension.

## Hint 2

The loop is "try 1, try 2, try 3 until one is free". A `for` loop with no end
condition and a `return` inside it is the honest shape here - the exit is
finding a free name, not exhausting a range.

Watch the no-extension case: `path.parse("LICENSE")` gives
`{ name: "LICENSE", ext: "" }`, so the template
`` `${stem}-${suffix}${ext}` `` produces `LICENSE-1` with no trailing dot. If
you build the name by string surgery around the last dot instead, that case is
where it breaks.

## Hint 3

```ts
const taken = new Set(await readdir(dir));
if (!taken.has(name)) return name;

const { name: stem, ext } = path.parse(name);
for (let suffix = 1; ; suffix += 1) {
  const candidate = /* build it */;
  if (!taken.has(candidate)) return candidate;
}
```

The decision left to you is the candidate template. One honest caveat worth
knowing: between your `readdir` and whoever actually writes the file, another
process could take the name - a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. The real
fix is to open the file with the exclusive flag (`fs.open(file, "wx")`) and
retry on `EEXIST`, and knowing that this class of bug has a name is most of
the value of the exercise.

lessons.briefing:
# 06 — Buffers and streams

Up to now every value you have handled fitted in memory and arrived all at
once. That is a comfortable assumption and it is wrong for most of what
servers actually do. A 4 GB video upload does not fit in memory. A log file
being tailed has no end. A response to a client is not a string you produce
and then hand over; it is bytes you write, at whatever rate the network will
take them.

Node's answer is two abstractions that predate almost everything else in the
platform. A **Buffer** is a fixed-length chunk of raw bytes outside the
JavaScript heap — the thing you get when you read from a socket or a file
without asking for a decoded string. A **stream** is a sequence of those
chunks over time, with a protocol for pushing back when the consumer cannot
keep up.

That last part — backpressure — is the reason streams exist rather than just
"read it all, then process it". Without it, a fast source and a slow sink mean
an ever-growing buffer in the middle, and the only thing that stops it growing
is the process dying. With it, the fast source is told to wait. Every
`.pipe()` you have ever written implements this for you; this lesson makes you
write it by hand once so you know what it is doing.

## Concept — bytes first, then chunks over time

A `Buffer` is a `Uint8Array` with extra methods, and the important thing about
it is what it is *not*: a string.

```ts
const buf = Buffer.from("café", "utf8");
buf.length;                     // 5   <- BYTES, not characters
"café".length;                  // 4   <- characters (UTF-16 code units)
Buffer.byteLength("café");      // 5   <- ask this before you allocate

Buffer.alloc(4);                // 4 zeroed bytes
buf.readUInt16BE(0);            // read a 16-bit big-endian number
buf.subarray(1, 3);             // a VIEW of the same memory, not a copy
Buffer.concat([a, b]);          // a new Buffer holding both
buf.toString("utf8");           // decode - the last step, not the first
buf.toString("hex");            // "636166c3a9"
buf.toString("base64");         // "Y2Fmw6k="
```

Two facts to file away. `Buffer.alloc(n)` zeroes the memory;
`Buffer.allocUnsafe(n)` does not, which is faster and hands you whatever was
in that memory before — a genuine information-disclosure bug if you forget to
overwrite all of it. And `subarray` shares memory with the original, so
writing through the view changes the source; `Buffer.from(view)` copies.

A **stream** is an `EventEmitter` with a state machine. There are four kinds:

| kind | direction | example |
|---|---|---|
| `Readable` | source | `fs.createReadStream`, an HTTP request on the server |
| `Writable` | sink | `fs.createWriteStream`, an HTTP response |
| `Duplex` | both, independently | a TCP socket |
| `Transform` | a Duplex where output derives from input | gzip, a parser (lesson 07) |

Consuming a readable stream, in the modern style:

```ts
for await (const chunk of readable) {
  // chunk is a Buffer, unless the stream is in object mode
}
```

Producing one, with the constructor:

```ts
const source = new Readable({
  read() {
    this.push("some data");   // hand a chunk to the consumer
    this.push(null);          // ...and that was the last one
  },
});
```

Consuming into a sink, and the protocol that matters:

```ts
const ok = writable.write(chunk);   // false = the buffer is over its limit
if (!ok) await once(writable, "drain");   // wait for the sink to catch up
```

`write()` never refuses a chunk — it always accepts it and buffers it. The
boolean is *advice*, and ignoring it is the difference between a program with
bounded memory and one that queues an entire file in RAM. The threshold it
compares against is `highWaterMark`, 64 KB by default for byte streams.

One more thing, because it is the trap the exercises are built around:
**never decode a chunk on its own.** UTF-8 is variable-length, a chunk
boundary can fall in the middle of a character, and decoding each half
produces two replacement characters and permanent corruption. Collect
`Buffer`s, concatenate, decode once — or use `StringDecoder`, which holds
partial characters back until the rest arrives.

## Exercise 1 — read and write a binary frame

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. A "frame" in this lesson is:

```
byte 0     version (uint8)
bytes 1-2  payload length in BYTES (uint16, big-endian)
bytes 3+   the payload, UTF-8
```

Implement `encodeFrame({ version, payload })` → `Buffer`, and
`decodeFrame(buffer)` → `{ version, payload }`.

The gate encodes `"café"`, which is four characters and five bytes — if your
length field says 4, you have measured the wrong thing. It also appends junk
after a valid frame and expects `decodeFrame` to ignore it: a parser trusts
its header, not the end of the buffer it happens to be holding.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — collect a stream without corrupting it

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `collect(readable)`, resolving to a single
`Buffer` holding everything the stream produced.

The gate feeds you `"café"` split so that the two bytes of `é` land in
different chunks. Decode-then-join fails; join-then-decode passes. An empty
stream must give you an empty `Buffer`.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — build a source

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createCounter(limit)`, returning a
`Readable` that emits `"1"`, `"2"`, … up to `limit` and then ends.
`createCounter(0)` emits nothing and still ends.

Two things to get right: `this.push(value)` inside `read()` delivers a chunk,
and `this.push(null)` is the only way to say "there are no more". A stream
that never pushes `null` is a `for await` that never returns — if the gate
hangs for five seconds and then fails, that is what happened.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — build a sink

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `createCollector()`, returning
`{ writable, text() }` where `writable` is a `Writable` that keeps every chunk
written to it, and `text()` decodes all of them as UTF-8.

The rule that catches everyone once: your `write(chunk, encoding, callback)`
implementation **must call `callback()`**. That is how a writable stream says
"send me the next one". Forget it and the pipeline stalls after exactly one
chunk, with no error and no clue.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex4
```

## Challenge — backpressure, by hand

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `writeAll(writable, chunks)`: write
every chunk in order, and whenever `write()` returns `false`, wait for the
stream's `"drain"` event before continuing. Do not call `end()` — the caller
owns the stream.

The gate builds a deliberately slow sink with a 16-byte `highWaterMark` and
records how much data was sitting in its buffer at the worst moment. Write
without checking and that number is ten times the limit; write properly and it
stays at the limit. That number is memory — in a real upload it is the
difference between a constant 64 KB and the whole file.

Honest difficulty note: the code is six lines. Understanding *why* it is six
lines and what each one prevents takes longer, and it is the point.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams challenge
```

## Review

`review1/solution.ts` comes back on the spaced-review schedule. Implement
`readFrames(buffer)`: the same frame format as ex1, but the buffer holds
several frames end to end. Return them all, in order. An empty buffer gives an
empty array, and a frame with an empty payload is still a frame.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams review1
```

# Reading - node/06_buffers_streams

Buffers are Node's answer to "JavaScript has no bytes". Streams are its answer
to "the data is bigger than your memory, and it arrives over time".

## Notes

**Why `Buffer` exists.** When Node was written, JavaScript had no typed
arrays, and a string was the only container for data — which is useless for
binary, because a string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units and any byte
sequence you round-trip through one comes back changed. `Buffer` was invented
to be a byte array, and when `Uint8Array` arrived in ES6 `Buffer` was
re-based on it. Today `Buffer extends Uint8Array`, so anything that accepts a
typed array accepts a Buffer; the extra methods are the read/write helpers
(`readUInt16BE`, `writeInt32LE`, …), the encodings (`toString("hex")`), and
`Buffer.concat`.

**Bytes versus characters, one more time.** `"café".length === 4` counts
UTF-16 code units; `Buffer.byteLength("café") === 5` counts UTF-8 bytes. For
anything with a length prefix, a size limit, or a byte offset, the second
number is the one that matters. This is also why a "1 MB request body limit"
enforced on `text.length` is not a 1 MB limit at all — an attacker sends
multi-byte characters and gets three times the budget.

**`allocUnsafe` is not a micro-optimisation to sprinkle around.**
`Buffer.alloc(n)` zero-fills; `allocUnsafe(n)` hands you recycled memory from
an internal pool. It is measurably faster and it has leaked private data in
real CVEs when the code that used it did not overwrite every byte. Use
`alloc`, and reach for `allocUnsafe` only when you are about to fill the whole
thing immediately.

**Streams are a state machine with an event API.** A `Readable` is in flowing
or paused mode; `.pipe()`, `for await` and a `"data"` listener each put it in
flowing mode, and mixing two of those mechanisms on one stream is how chunks
get lost. Pick one consumption style per stream. `for await` is the one to
default to: it handles pause/resume, propagates errors as rejections, and
destroys the stream if you `break`.

**Backpressure is the whole design.** Every writable keeps an internal buffer
and a `highWaterMark` (64 KB for byte streams, 16 *objects* in object mode).
`write()` returns `false` once the buffer is over that mark; `"drain"` fires
when it has emptied. `.pipe()` and `pipeline()` implement this loop for you.
Doing it by hand is only necessary when you are the one generating chunks — a
loop over database rows, say — and that is exactly when people forget, which
is why "the export job used 8 GB" is such a common incident.

**Object mode.** A stream with `objectMode: true` carries arbitrary
JavaScript values instead of bytes, and its `highWaterMark` counts items, not
bytes. This is what makes streams usable as a data pipeline (rows, parsed
records, log entries) rather than only as a byte pipe — you will use it
throughout lesson 07.

**Web streams exist too.** Node supports `ReadableStream`/`WritableStream`
from the WHATWG spec (the ones `fetch` uses), and `Readable.fromWeb` /
`Readable.toWeb` convert between the two worlds. Node streams remain the
native currency of `fs`, `http` and `zlib`; know that the other family exists
and that they are convertible.

## ex1 — a header is a contract about bytes

Binary framing is how nearly every wire protocol works — HTTP/2, WebSocket,
Postgres, Redis — and they all share this shape: a fixed-size header that
tells you how much variable-size body follows. Writing the encoder and decoder
by hand once makes every protocol document readable afterwards.

Big-endian is called network byte order because that is what the internet
standardised on; `readUInt16BE`/`writeUInt16BE` are the ones you will use for
anything on a wire, and the `LE` variants for file formats that came from x86
(and for anything where a spec says so). Getting it backwards is a classic
bug: 5 written little-endian and read big-endian is 1280, and your parser will
try to read 1280 bytes of payload that are not there.

The "trailing junk" assertion is not a trick. A TCP socket gives you whatever
has arrived — half a frame, one frame, three frames and a bit — so a parser
that assumes "the buffer is exactly one message" works in tests and fails on
the network. The correct shape is exactly what review1 makes you write: a
cursor, a header read, a length-bounded slice, repeat. And in production you
also need the other half, which is buffering the *incomplete* tail until more
bytes arrive.

## ex2 — the split-character bug

This is the single most common streaming bug in Node, and it is invisible
until your input contains a non-ASCII character in an unlucky position. The
chunk boundary is decided by the kernel, the network MTU and the filesystem —
not by your data — so this failure is inherently intermittent, which is the
worst kind.

Two correct answers. Collect Buffers and `Buffer.concat` before decoding —
right when you need the whole thing anyway (a JSON body, a small file). Or use
`node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder`, which keeps incomplete multi-byte
sequences in an internal buffer and emits them once the continuation bytes
arrive — right when you want to process text as it streams. Lesson 07's line
splitter is where the second one earns its keep.

A production note on `collect`: it is exactly what a body parser does, and it
is also exactly how you accidentally hold an unbounded amount of data in
memory. Every real implementation adds a limit — count the bytes as you go and
reject with a 413 past the threshold — which is the shape you will build for
real in lesson 08.

## ex3 — being a source

Implementing `_read` teaches the contract from the other side: the stream
machinery calls it when the consumer wants data, you `push` chunks, and
`push(null)` ends it. The return value of `push` matters in bigger sources —
`false` means "the read buffer is full, stop pushing until `_read` is called
again" — which is the reading half of backpressure.

Two things worth knowing beyond the exercise. `Readable.from(iterable)` builds
a stream out of any iterable or async generator, and for most real cases it is
the better tool: an async generator is far easier to read than a `_read` state
machine, and it gets backpressure right by construction because the generator
is only pulled when the consumer wants more. And `stream.Readable` is an
`EventEmitter`, so a source that fails should `destroy(error)` rather than
throw — that emits `"error"` on the stream, which is where consumers are
listening.

## ex4 — being a sink

The `callback` in `_write` is the entire flow-control protocol, and forgetting
it produces the most confusing failure in the streams API: everything works
for exactly one chunk and then stops, silently, forever. No error, no
timeout — the stream is simply waiting for you.

Calling it with an error (`callback(err)`) is how a sink reports failure; the
stream emits `"error"` and, if you used `pipeline`, the whole chain is torn
down. There is also `_final(callback)` for flush-on-end work (close a file
handle, write a footer) and `_destroy` for cleanup — worth knowing they exist
when you write a sink that owns a resource.

`text()` being a function rather than a property is a small design lesson:
snapshot accessors that are evaluated eagerly are wrong for anything that
accumulates. The same reasoning applies to `res.locals`, to metrics counters,
and to any getter over mutable state.

## challenge — the loop `.pipe()` writes for you

The six lines you wrote are the core of `.pipe()`. Writing them explains three
things that otherwise look arbitrary.

Why `.pipe()` is better than a `"data"` listener that writes: the listener
version ignores the return value of `write`, so a slow sink buffers without
limit. Why `pipeline()` is better than `.pipe()`: `.pipe()` does *not*
propagate errors or destroy the other streams when one fails, leaving leaked
file handles and sockets — `pipeline()` cleans up, and lesson 07 makes you use
it. And why `highWaterMark` is tunable: it is the memory-versus-syscalls
trade-off, so a stream of tiny chunks over a fast link wants a bigger mark and
a memory-constrained process wants a smaller one.

The interview question this maps to is "what is backpressure and how does Node
implement it?" A strong answer names the boolean, the `"drain"` event, the
`highWaterMark`, and the observation that `pipe`/`pipeline` implement the loop
so most code never sees it — plus the case where you *do*: when you are
generating the chunks yourself.

## review1 — the parser loop, again

Reading several frames from one buffer is the shape of every length-prefixed
protocol parser, and the reason to write it twice is that the cursor
arithmetic is where the bugs live. Naming `start = offset + 3` instead of
scattering `offset + 3` through the slice call is the small discipline that
makes it right the first time.

The empty-payload case is deliberate. A frame with a zero-length body is
legitimate — a heartbeat, an acknowledgement, an end-of-stream marker — and a
loop that stops when the length is zero silently drops it. Interviewers who
ask you to write a parser tend to feed it exactly that.

The next question, which the exercise does not ask but the network will: what
do you do when the buffer ends *mid-frame*? A real parser keeps the leftover
bytes and prepends them to the next chunk, which is why a stream parser is
usually a `Transform` with an internal buffer — precisely the structure of the
line splitter in lesson 07.

## Further reading

- [`Buffer` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html) — the whole surface, including the alloc/allocUnsafe discussion and every encoding.
- [Stream — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html) — long, and the sections on implementing `_read`/`_write` are the ones to read now.
- [Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the official essay behind the challenge exercise.
- [`string_decoder`](https://nodejs.org/api/string_decoder.html) — the correct way to decode text as it streams, and the other answer to ex2.
- [MDN: `Uint8Array`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Uint8Array) — what a Buffer actually is underneath.
