(`readUInt16BE`, `writeInt32LE`, …), the encodings (`toString("hex")`), and
`Buffer.concat`.

**Bytes versus characters, one more time.** `"café".length === 4` counts
UTF-16 code units; `Buffer.byteLength("café") === 5` counts UTF-8 bytes. For
anything with a length prefix, a size limit, or a byte offset, the second
number is the one that matters. This is also why a "1 MB request body limit"
enforced on `text.length` is not a 1 MB limit at all — an attacker sends
multi-byte characters and gets three times the budget.

**`allocUnsafe` is not a micro-optimisation to sprinkle around.**
`Buffer.alloc(n)` zero-fills; `allocUnsafe(n)` hands you recycled memory from
an internal pool. It is measurably faster and it has leaked private data in
real CVEs when the code that used it did not overwrite every byte. Use
`alloc`, and reach for `allocUnsafe` only when you are about to fill the whole
thing immediately.

**Streams are a state machine with an event API.** A `Readable` is in flowing
or paused mode; `.pipe()`, `for await` and a `"data"` listener each put it in
flowing mode, and mixing two of those mechanisms on one stream is how chunks
get lost. Pick one consumption style per stream. `for await` is the one to
default to: it handles pause/resume, propagates errors as rejections, and
destroys the stream if you `break`.

**Backpressure is the whole design.** Every writable keeps an internal buffer
and a `highWaterMark` (64 KB for byte streams, 16 *objects* in object mode).
`write()` returns `false` once the buffer is over that mark; `"drain"` fires
when it has emptied. `.pipe()` and `pipeline()` implement this loop for you.
Doing it by hand is only necessary when you are the one generating chunks — a
loop over database rows, say — and that is exactly when people forget, which
is why "the export job used 8 GB" is such a common incident.

**Object mode.** A stream with `objectMode: true` carries arbitrary
JavaScript values instead of bytes, and its `highWaterMark` counts items, not
bytes. This is what makes streams usable as a data pipeline (rows, parsed
records, log entries) rather than only as a byte pipe — you will use it
throughout lesson 07.

**Web streams exist too.** Node supports `ReadableStream`/`WritableStream`
from the WHATWG spec (the ones `fetch` uses), and `Readable.fromWeb` /
`Readable.toWeb` convert between the two worlds. Node streams remain the
native currency of `fs`, `http` and `zlib`; know that the other family exists
and that they are convertible.

## ex1 — a header is a contract about bytes

Binary framing is how nearly every wire protocol works — HTTP/2, WebSocket,
Postgres, Redis — and they all share this shape: a fixed-size header that
tells you how much variable-size body follows. Writing the encoder and decoder
by hand once makes every protocol document readable afterwards.

Big-endian is called network byte order because that is what the internet
standardised on; `readUInt16BE`/`writeUInt16BE` are the ones you will use for
anything on a wire, and the `LE` variants for file formats that came from x86
(and for anything where a spec says so). Getting it backwards is a classic
bug: 5 written little-endian and read big-endian is 1280, and your parser will
try to read 1280 bytes of payload that are not there.

The "trailing junk" assertion is not a trick. A TCP socket gives you whatever
has arrived — half a frame, one frame, three frames and a bit — so a parser
that assumes "the buffer is exactly one message" works in tests and fails on
the network. The correct shape is exactly what review1 makes you write: a
cursor, a header read, a length-bounded slice, repeat. And in production you
also need the other half, which is buffering the *incomplete* tail until more
bytes arrive.

## ex2 — the split-character bug

This is the single most common streaming bug in Node, and it is invisible
until your input contains a non-ASCII character in an unlucky position. The
chunk boundary is decided by the kernel, the network MTU and the filesystem —
not by your data — so this failure is inherently intermittent, which is the
worst kind.

Two correct answers. Collect Buffers and `Buffer.concat` before decoding —
right when you need the whole thing anyway (a JSON body, a small file). Or use
`node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder`, which keeps incomplete multi-byte
sequences in an internal buffer and emits them once the continuation bytes
arrive — right when you want to process text as it streams. Lesson 07's line
splitter is where the second one earns its keep.

A production note on `collect`: it is exactly what a body parser does, and it
is also exactly how you accidentally hold an unbounded amount of data in
memory. Every real implementation adds a limit — count the bytes as you go and
reject with a 413 past the threshold — which is the shape you will build for
real in lesson 08.

## ex3 — being a source

Implementing `_read` teaches the contract from the other side: the stream
machinery calls it when the consumer wants data, you `push` chunks, and
`push(null)` ends it. The return value of `push` matters in bigger sources —
`false` means "the read buffer is full, stop pushing until `_read` is called
again" — which is the reading half of backpressure.

Two things worth knowing beyond the exercise. `Readable.from(iterable)` builds
a stream out of any iterable or async generator, and for most real cases it is
the better tool: an async generator is far easier to read than a `_read` state
machine, and it gets backpressure right by construction because the generator
is only pulled when the consumer wants more. And `stream.Readable` is an
`EventEmitter`, so a source that fails should `destroy(error)` rather than
throw — that emits `"error"` on the stream, which is where consumers are
listening.

## ex4 — being a sink

The `callback` in `_write` is the entire flow-control protocol, and forgetting
it produces the most confusing failure in the streams API: everything works
for exactly one chunk and then stops, silently, forever. No error, no
timeout — the stream is simply waiting for you.

Calling it with an error (`callback(err)`) is how a sink reports failure; the
stream emits `"error"` and, if you used `pipeline`, the whole chain is torn
down. There is also `_final(callback)` for flush-on-end work (close a file
handle, write a footer) and `_destroy` for cleanup — worth knowing they exist
when you write a sink that owns a resource.

`text()` being a function rather than a property is a small design lesson:
snapshot accessors that are evaluated eagerly are wrong for anything that
accumulates. The same reasoning applies to `res.locals`, to metrics counters,
and to any getter over mutable state.

## challenge — the loop `.pipe()` writes for you

The six lines you wrote are the core of `.pipe()`. Writing them explains three
things that otherwise look arbitrary.

Why `.pipe()` is better than a `"data"` listener that writes: the listener
version ignores the return value of `write`, so a slow sink buffers without
limit. Why `pipeline()` is better than `.pipe()`: `.pipe()` does *not*
propagate errors or destroy the other streams when one fails, leaving leaked
file handles and sockets — `pipeline()` cleans up, and lesson 07 makes you use
it. And why `highWaterMark` is tunable: it is the memory-versus-syscalls
trade-off, so a stream of tiny chunks over a fast link wants a bigger mark and
a memory-constrained process wants a smaller one.

The interview question this maps to is "what is backpressure and how does Node
implement it?" A strong answer names the boolean, the `"drain"` event, the
`highWaterMark`, and the observation that `pipe`/`pipeline` implement the loop
so most code never sees it — plus the case where you *do*: when you are
generating the chunks yourself.

## review1 — the parser loop, again

Reading several frames from one buffer is the shape of every length-prefixed
protocol parser, and the reason to write it twice is that the cursor
arithmetic is where the bugs live. Naming `start = offset + 3` instead of
scattering `offset + 3` through the slice call is the small discipline that
makes it right the first time.

The empty-payload case is deliberate. A frame with a zero-length body is
legitimate — a heartbeat, an acknowledgement, an end-of-stream marker — and a
loop that stops when the length is zero silently drops it. Interviewers who
ask you to write a parser tend to feed it exactly that.

The next question, which the exercise does not ask but the network will: what
do you do when the buffer ends *mid-frame*? A real parser keeps the leftover
bytes and prepends them to the next chunk, which is why a stream parser is
usually a `Transform` with an internal buffer — precisely the structure of the
line splitter in lesson 07.

## Further reading

- [`Buffer` — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html) — the whole surface, including the alloc/allocUnsafe discussion and every encoding.
- [Stream — Node.js API docs](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html) — long, and the sections on implementing `_read`/`_write` are the ones to read now.
- [Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the official essay behind the challenge exercise.
- [`string_decoder`](https://nodejs.org/api/string_decoder.html) — the correct way to decode text as it streams, and the other answer to ex2.
- [MDN: `Uint8Array`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Uint8Array) — what a Buffer actually is underneath.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — backpressure, by hand

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `writeAll(writable, chunks)`: write
every chunk in order, and whenever `write()` returns `false`, wait for the
stream's `"drain"` event before continuing. Do not call `end()` — the caller
owns the stream.

The gate builds a deliberately slow sink with a 16-byte `highWaterMark` and
records how much data was sitting in its buffer at the worst moment. Write
without checking and that number is ten times the limit; write properly and it
stays at the limit. That number is memory — in a real upload it is the
difference between a constant 64 KB and the whole file.

Honest difficulty note: the code is six lines. Understanding *why* it is six
lines and what each one prevents takes longer, and it is the point.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean, and almost every tutorial ignores
it. It means "there is still room": `false` says the stream's internal buffer
has passed its `highWaterMark` and you should stop writing until it tells you
otherwise.

The signal that it has caught up is the `"drain"` event. So the loop is:
write; if the answer was `false`, wait for `"drain"`; carry on.

## Hint 2

Waiting for an event inside an `async` function is exactly what
`events.once()` is for:

```ts
import { once } from "node:events";

await once(writable, "drain");
```

That returns a promise which resolves the next time the event fires - the
promise-flavoured version of what you built by hand in lesson 04 ex4.

Note what you are *not* doing: you are not calling `end()`. The caller owns
the lifetime of the stream; your job is only to get the chunks in.

## Hint 3

```ts
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  if (/* what condition? */) {
    await once(writable, "drain");
  }
}
```

The decision left to you is the condition, and the subtlety is that the write
itself has to happen whether or not you end up waiting - `write()` always
accepts the chunk; its return value is advice about the *next* one. If you
skip the write when the buffer is full you will lose data; if you ignore the
return value entirely, the gate's `maxBuffered` number will be roughly ten
times the highWaterMark and it will tell you so.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean, and almost every tutorial ignores
it. It means "there is still room": `false` says the stream's internal buffer
has passed its `highWaterMark` and you should stop writing until it tells you
otherwise.

The signal that it has caught up is the `"drain"` event. So the loop is:
write; if the answer was `false`, wait for `"drain"`; carry on.

## Hint 2

Waiting for an event inside an `async` function is exactly what
`events.once()` is for:

```ts
import { once } from "node:events";

await once(writable, "drain");
```

That returns a promise which resolves the next time the event fires - the
promise-flavoured version of what you built by hand in lesson 04 ex4.

Note what you are *not* doing: you are not calling `end()`. The caller owns
the lifetime of the stream; your job is only to get the chunks in.

## Hint 3

```ts
for (const chunk of chunks) {
  if (/* what condition? */) {
    await once(writable, "drain");
  }
}
```

The decision left to you is the condition, and the subtlety is that the write
itself has to happen whether or not you end up waiting - `write()` always
accepts the chunk; its return value is advice about the *next* one. If you
skip the write when the buffer is full you will lose data; if you ignore the
return value entirely, the gate's `maxBuffered` number will be roughly ten
times the highWaterMark and it will tell you so.

## Exercise 1 — read and write a binary frame

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. A "frame" in this lesson is:

```
byte 0     version (uint8)
bytes 1-2  payload length in BYTES (uint16, big-endian)
bytes 3+   the payload, UTF-8
```

Implement `encodeFrame({ version, payload })` → `Buffer`, and
`decodeFrame(buffer)` → `{ version, payload }`.

The gate encodes `"café"`, which is four characters and five bytes — if your
length field says 4, you have measured the wrong thing. It also appends junk
after a valid frame and expects `decodeFrame` to ignore it: a parser trusts
its header, not the end of the buffer it happens to be holding.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Draw the frame on paper first:

```
byte 0    byte 1    byte 2    byte 3 ...
version   length hi length lo  payload bytes
```

Then note the trap in the middle: the length is the number of **bytes** the
payload takes up in UTF-8, which is not the number of characters in the
string. `"café".length` is 4; the number of bytes is 5.

## Hint 2

For encoding: turn the payload into a `Buffer` first (`Buffer.from(text,
"utf8")`), because then its `.length` *is* the byte count you need. Allocate a
3-byte header with `Buffer.alloc(3)`, fill it with `writeUInt8` and
`writeUInt16BE`, and `Buffer.concat([header, body])`.

For decoding: `readUInt8(0)` and `readUInt16BE(1)` read the header back, and
`buffer.subarray(start, end)` gives you a view of the payload bytes to decode
with `.toString("utf8")`.

`BE` is big-endian - the most significant byte first. It is the convention for
anything on a wire, which is why it is also called network byte order.

## Hint 3

```ts
export function encodeFrame({ version, payload }: Frame): Buffer {
  const body = Buffer.from(payload, "utf8");
  const header = Buffer.alloc(3);
  header.writeUInt8(version, 0);
  header.writeUInt16BE(/* what value, at what offset? */);
  return Buffer.concat([header, body]);
}
```

Two decisions left in the encoder (the value and the offset for the length),
and one in the decoder: where the payload *ends*. The gate appends junk after
a valid frame and expects you to ignore it, so the end comes from the length
field, not from `buffer.length`. That is the difference between a parser and a
guess.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Draw the frame on paper first:

```
byte 0    byte 1    byte 2    byte 3 ...
version   length hi length lo  payload bytes
```

Then note the trap in the middle: the length is the number of **bytes** the
payload takes up in UTF-8, which is not the number of characters in the
string. `"café".length` is 4; the number of bytes is 5.

## Hint 2

For encoding: turn the payload into a `Buffer` first (`Buffer.from(text,
"utf8")`), because then its `.length` *is* the byte count you need. Allocate a
3-byte header with `Buffer.alloc(3)`, fill it with `writeUInt8` and
`writeUInt16BE`, and `Buffer.concat([header, body])`.

For decoding: `readUInt8(0)` and `readUInt16BE(1)` read the header back, and
`buffer.subarray(start, end)` gives you a view of the payload bytes to decode
with `.toString("utf8")`.

`BE` is big-endian - the most significant byte first. It is the convention for
anything on a wire, which is why it is also called network byte order.

## Hint 3

```ts
export function encodeFrame({ version, payload }: Frame): Buffer {
  const body = Buffer.from(payload, "utf8");
  const header = Buffer.alloc(3);
  header.writeUInt8(version, 0);
  header.writeUInt16BE(/* what value, at what offset? */);
  return Buffer.concat([header, body]);
}
```

Two decisions left in the encoder (the value and the offset for the length),
and one in the decoder: where the payload *ends*. The gate appends junk after
a valid frame and expects you to ignore it, so the end comes from the length
field, not from `buffer.length`. That is the difference between a parser and a
guess.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Readable` is an async iterable, so the loop you want is `for await (const
chunk of source)`. That form handles the `data`, `end` and `error` events for
you and propagates a stream error as a rejection - which is why it has almost
entirely replaced hand-wired `.on("data")` listeners in modern code.

The other half of the exercise is what you do with the chunks, and the gate is
built to catch exactly one wrong answer.

## Hint 2

The wrong answer is to decode each chunk to a string as it arrives and
concatenate the strings. UTF-8 is a variable-length encoding: `é` is two
bytes. If a chunk boundary falls between those two bytes, each half decodes to
a replacement character and the text is corrupt - permanently, because you
threw the bytes away.

So collect `Buffer`s in an array and let `Buffer.concat(chunks)` join them.
Decoding, if it happens at all, happens once at the end when every byte is
present.

## Hint 3

```ts
const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
for await (const chunk of source) {
  chunks.push(/* what, exactly? */);
}
return Buffer.concat(chunks);
```

The decision left to you is the push. Async iteration types the chunk as
`any`, so nothing warns you if a string sneaks in - `Buffer.from(chunk)` makes
the intent explicit and works either way. Check the empty-stream case in your
head: `Buffer.concat([])` gives you a zero-length Buffer, which is exactly
what the gate wants.

## Exercise 3 — build a source

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createCounter(limit)`, returning a
`Readable` that emits `"1"`, `"2"`, … up to `limit` and then ends.
`createCounter(0)` emits nothing and still ends.

Two things to get right: `this.push(value)` inside `read()` delivers a chunk,
and `this.push(null)` is the only way to say "there are no more". A stream
that never pushes `null` is a `for await` that never returns — if the gate
hangs for five seconds and then fails, that is what happened.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Readable` you build yourself has one job to implement: `_read()`, the
method the stream machinery calls when it wants more data. You supply it as
the `read` option to the constructor:

```ts
new Readable({
  read() {
    // push the next piece - or signal the end
  },
});
```

Inside `read`, `this` is the stream, so `this.push(value)` hands a chunk to
the consumer.

## Hint 2

Two rules about `push`:

- `this.push(chunk)` delivers a chunk. Strings are converted to `Buffer`s
  unless the stream is in object mode, which is why the gate can assert the
  consumer receives Buffers.
- `this.push(null)` means "that was the last one". Without it the consumer
  waits forever - and "my for-await never finished" is nearly always a missing
  `push(null)`.

The counter itself is state that has to live outside `read`, because `read` is
called many times: a `let` in the enclosing function, captured by the closure.

## Hint 3

```ts
let next = 1;

return new Readable({
  read() {
    if (/* have we run out? */) {
      this.push(null);
      return;
    }
    this.push(String(next));
    next += 1;
  },
});
```

Two decisions left: the exhaustion test (mind the boundary - `createCounter(3)`
emits 1, 2, 3 and `createCounter(0)` emits nothing at all) and whether you push
a string or a number. Push a number into a non-object-mode stream and Node
throws immediately, which is a useful thing to see once on purpose.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — build a sink

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `createCollector()`, returning
`{ writable, text() }` where `writable` is a `Writable` that keeps every chunk
written to it, and `text()` decodes all of them as UTF-8.

The rule that catches everyone once: your `write(chunk, encoding, callback)`
implementation **must call `callback()`**. That is how a writable stream says
"send me the next one". Forget it and the pipeline stalls after exactly one
chunk, with no error and no clue.

```
uv run dojo test node 06_buffers_streams ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The mirror image of ex3. A `Writable` has one method to implement, `_write`,
supplied as the `write` option:

```ts
new Writable({
  write(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    // store the chunk, then tell the stream you are ready for the next one
  },
});
```

The array of chunks lives in the closure, exactly like the counter did, so
both the stream and `text()` can see it.

## Hint 2

The `callback` argument is the whole protocol of a writable stream. Calling it
means "I am done with this chunk, send me another". Calling it with an error
(`callback(error)`) fails the stream. **Not** calling it stalls the pipeline
forever, which is the classic bug in a hand-written Writable - your test hangs
and nothing tells you why.

Store the bytes, not a decoded string, for the same reason as ex2: a chunk
boundary can land in the middle of a character. Decode once, in `text()`.

## Hint 3

```ts
const chunks: Buffer[] = [];

const writable = new Writable({
  write(chunk: Buffer, _encoding, callback) {
    chunks.push(/* ? */);
    /* and then? */
  },
});

return { writable, text: () => /* ? */ };
```

Three small decisions, and the second one is the one that hangs the gate if
you forget it. `text()` is deliberately a function rather than a property, so
it can be called at any point and report what has arrived so far - a property
would be evaluated once, at creation, when nothing has arrived at all.

lessons.briefing:
# 07 — Transforms and pipelines

Lesson 06 gave you the two ends of a stream: a source that produces chunks and
a sink that consumes them. This lesson is about the middle, which is where all
the interesting work happens. A `Transform` sits between them — bytes in,
something else out — and once you can write one, "process a file too big for
memory" stops being a special project and becomes three lines of assembly.

The other half of this lesson is `pipeline()`, and it is not a stylistic
preference. `a.pipe(b).pipe(c)` looks like a pipeline and is not one: if `b`
fails, `a` keeps reading and `c` never finds out, so you are left with a
half-written file, a socket that is never closed and a process that does not
exit. Every one of those bugs has shipped, repeatedly, which is why Node added
`pipeline` and why the streams documentation now recommends never using
`.pipe()` in production code.

By the end of this lesson you will have written a Transform with state (a line
splitter that survives chunk boundaries), a transform that is nothing but an
async generator, and a three-stage pipeline that turns a CSV stream into
filtered JSON lines while holding one line in memory at a time.

## Concept — the middle of the pipe

A `Transform` is a `Duplex` whose readable side is produced from its writable
side. You implement one method and optionally a second:

```ts
import { Transform } from "node:stream";

const doubler = new Transform({
  transform(chunk, encoding, callback) {
    callback(null, chunk.toString().repeat(2));   // push, and ask for the next
  },

  flush(callback) {
    this.push("\n--- end ---\n");                 // one last chunk, at the end
    callback();
  },
});
```

Three things to know about `transform`:

- **`callback(null, value)` is a push plus a ready signal.** You can also call
  `this.push(value)` as many times as you like and then `callback()` with no
  value — one chunk in can become zero, one, or many chunks out.
- **`callback()` with nothing means "consumed, nothing to emit yet".** That is
  how a buffering transform works: hold the partial data, emit when you have
  something complete.
- **`callback(error)` fails the stream.** Never `throw` out of `transform`;
  nothing useful catches it.

`flush(callback)` runs after the last chunk, before the readable side ends. It
is your only chance to emit whatever depends on having seen everything: the
final partial line, a closing bracket, a summary.

Then **object mode**, which is what makes transforms composable. A stream in
object mode carries JavaScript values instead of bytes, and a `Transform` can
be in different modes on each side:

```ts
new Transform({
  readableObjectMode: true,    // I emit objects
  // writable side stays in byte mode: I receive Buffers
});
```

That asymmetry is exactly what a parser is: bytes in, records out.

And the assembly:

```ts
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";

await pipeline(source, splitLines, parseJson, filterRows, sink);
```

`pipeline` connects each stage to the next with backpressure, propagates
errors, **destroys every stage** if any of them fails or the consumer goes
away, and resolves when the sink has finished. The promise version is in
`node:stream/promises`; there is a callback version in `node:stream` too.

One more form, and it is the one modern code reaches for: a stage can be an
**async generator function**.

```ts
async function* onlyErrors(source) {
  for await (const line of source) {
    if (line.includes("ERROR")) yield line;
  }
}

await pipeline(logFile, splitLines, onlyErrors, sink);
```

No class, no callbacks, no `push` — and backpressure still works, because the
generator only advances when the next stage pulls.

## Exercise 1 — a Transform with a last word

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createUppercase()`, returning a `Transform`
that uppercases every chunk that passes through it and, when the input ends,
emits one final chunk: `[N chunks]`, where N is how many chunks it saw.

`createUppercase()` on an empty stream still emits `[0 chunks]` — the flush
runs whether or not anything arrived.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — pipeline, and the thing `.pipe()` does not do

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
pipeThrough(source, transforms, sink): Promise<void>
```

Wire the source, then every transform in order, then the sink, and resolve
when it is done — or reject with the error if any stage fails.

The gate then checks something `.pipe()` cannot give you: after a failure, the
**sink and the source must both be destroyed**. That is the difference between
a pipeline that fails and a pipeline that leaks. In a real program those two
streams are a socket and a file handle, and the version that leaves them open
is the one that runs out of file descriptors at 4am on a Sunday.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — bytes in, lines out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createLineSplitter()`, a `Transform` whose
writable side takes bytes and whose readable side emits **one string per
line**, without the newline.

The rules:

- a line may be split across any number of chunks, and a chunk may hold many
  lines;
- a trailing `\r` (Windows line endings) is not part of the line;
- if the input does not end with a newline, the last partial line is still a
  line and must be emitted from `flush`;
- if the input *does* end with a newline, there is no empty extra line.

And one requirement inherited from lesson 06: the gate splits a two-byte `ü`
across two chunks. `chunk.toString()` per chunk corrupts it. Use
`node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder`, which holds an incomplete character
back until its remaining bytes arrive.

# Reading - node/07_streams_2

Transforms are where streams stop being plumbing and become a programming
model. `pipeline()` is where they stop leaking.

## Notes

**A Transform is a Duplex with a rule.** Its writable side accepts chunks, its
readable side emits chunks, and the contract is that the second is produced
from the first. Node implements `_read` for you: it calls your `_transform`
when the consumer wants more, which is why backpressure works through a chain
of transforms without you doing anything. Each stage has its own buffer and
its own `highWaterMark`, so a slow sink eventually stops the source — the
signal travels back up the chain one buffer at a time.

**One in does not mean one out.** `callback()` with no value emits nothing;
`this.push()` called three times emits three chunks. That is what lets one
transform be a splitter (one chunk in, many lines out), a batcher (many in,
one array out), or a filter (some in, fewer out). The mental model is not
"map"; it is "a function with a queue on each side".

**`flush` is the end-of-input hook.** Anything you were buffering has to come
out there, or it is silently lost — the classic bug in a hand-written parser
is a file whose last line has no trailing newline and simply vanishes. There
is also `_final` on writables (called before `"finish"`) and `_destroy` for
cleanup; `flush` is the transform-specific one.

**`.pipe()` is a footgun and the docs say so.** It does not forward errors,
and it does not destroy the other streams when one fails. The failure mode:
`source.pipe(gzip).pipe(fileStream)` where the source errors leaves `gzip` and
`fileStream` open, the file half-written, and — if the source was an HTTP
response — a socket held until it times out. `pipeline()` handles error
propagation and destruction for every stage, and the promise form makes it
`await`-able. There is also `stream.finished()` for observing a single stream's
completion.

**Async generators as stages.** Since Node 10, `pipeline` accepts async
generator functions in the middle and async functions at the end. This is the
biggest ergonomic improvement in the streams API: a `for await ... yield` loop
is readable in a way a `_transform` state machine is not, it uses ordinary
`try`/`catch` and `return`, and it participates in backpressure naturally
because the generator only runs when someone pulls. Reach for a `Transform`
class when you need `flush`, object-mode asymmetry, or to hand the stage to
something that expects a stream object; reach for a generator otherwise.

**Object mode is a different currency.** `objectMode: true` makes the
`highWaterMark` count items rather than bytes (default 16), and lets any value
travel through. A parser is asymmetric — `writableObjectMode` false,
`readableObjectMode` true — and getting that pair backwards produces the
confusing error "The 'chunk' argument must be of type string or an instance of
Buffer", which is Node telling you a byte-mode stream just received an object.

## ex1 — transform plus flush

The exercise is deliberately small so that the two callback shapes and the
flush hook are the only things to think about. The counter is closure state,
which is the normal way to give a stream memory: the `Transform` object could
hold it as a property, but a `let` in the factory function is simpler and
cannot be poked at from outside.

The caveat named in the hints is worth repeating: uppercasing chunk by chunk
is only safe for ASCII. `toUpperCase()` on half a multi-byte character
produces a replacement character exactly like the ex3 case, so a real
text-processing transform decodes with `StringDecoder` first. The reason the
gate does not test that here is that ex3 tests it properly; the reason the
hints mention it is that "this works on my ASCII test data" is how the bug
ships.

The interview-adjacent question: "what is the difference between
`callback(null, value)` and `this.push(value)`?" They are the same push;
`callback` also signals readiness. You use `push` when one input produces
several outputs, and `callback(null, value)` when it produces exactly one.

## ex2 — why pipeline exists

`.pipe()` was designed in 2010 and returns its destination so you can chain,
which is elegant and hides the fact that errors are per-stream events with no
routing. Every "pipe with error handling" utility in the ecosystem
(`pump`, and then `pipeline` in core) exists because the naive version leaks.

What `pipeline` does for you, precisely: it attaches error handlers to every
stage, calls `destroy()` on all of them when any one errors or the consumer
goes away, waits for the sink to emit `"finish"` (not merely for the source to
end), and gives you one place — a rejection — to handle all of it. That last
distinction matters: a source that has finished reading does not mean a sink
that has finished writing, and code that resolves on `"end"` rather than
`"finish"` reports success before the bytes are on disk.

The array form (`pipeline([a, ...middles, b])`) is the one to remember when the
number of stages is dynamic, which is exactly the exercise's signature.

## ex3 — the most reusable thirty lines here

Framing — turning a byte stream into records — is the fundamental job in
network and file processing, and the line splitter is its simplest instance.
The structure generalises exactly: keep a `pending` buffer, look for
delimiters, emit complete records, keep the remainder, and flush whatever is
left at the end. Swap the delimiter for a length prefix and you have the frame
parser from lesson 06 review1. Swap it for `\r\n\r\n` and you are parsing HTTP
headers.

Three details the exercise forces you to meet:

**`StringDecoder`.** Decoding per chunk is wrong; buffering all the bytes and
decoding at the end defeats streaming. The decoder is the third option: it
emits everything decodable and retains a partial character across calls. Call
`decoder.end()` in `flush` to get any final bytes.

**Carriage returns.** Files written on Windows end lines with `\r\n`. A
splitter that only splits on `\n` leaves a `\r` at the end of every line,
which then shows up as an invisible character in your parsed data and a very
confusing string comparison failure. `line.endsWith("\r")` is the whole fix.

**The last line.** `"a\nb"` has two lines; `"a\nb\n"` also has two.
`split("\n")` gives you three pieces for the second one, the last being empty
— which is why `lines.pop()` (keep the remainder) plus "emit it in flush only
if non-empty" gets both cases right without a special case.

## ex4 — the modern form

Async generators are the answer to "why is stream code so verbose". The whole
of ex1's transform, minus the flush, is three lines as a generator, and the
error handling is ordinary `try`/`catch` rather than a callback convention.

Two limitations worth knowing so you can choose deliberately. A generator
stage has no `flush` hook — though code after the `for await` loop runs at the
end, which is the same thing. And a generator is not a stream object: you
cannot attach listeners to it, pass it where a `Readable` is expected, or
`unpipe` it. `Readable.from(generator)` converts when you need an actual
stream, and `stream.compose()` (newer) builds a single stream out of several
stages.

The reason `String(item)` appears in the reference is worth a sentence: inside
a byte-mode pipeline the values arriving are `Buffer`s, and `String(buffer)`
calls `buffer.toString()`. In an object-mode pipeline they are whatever was
pushed. A stage that must work in both is a stage that converts explicitly.

## challenge — the shape of every ETL job

Read, split, parse, filter, format, write. Every batch job you will ever be
asked to write is that list with different verbs, and the reason to build it
as a pipeline rather than a loop is that the memory cost is the buffers, not
the data.

The counters are the interesting design question. They live in the closure
around the transform, mutated as rows go past, and read after `await pipeline`
resolves. That is safe here for the reason single-threaded JavaScript is
always safe: nothing else can interleave. It is also the reason returning
statistics from a stream pipeline feels awkward — the pipeline's value is
"done", not a result — and why bigger systems emit a summary event or write a
report row instead.

Two production notes the exercise skips. Real CSV is not `split(",")`: quoted
fields can contain commas and newlines, so use a parser
(`csv-parse` streams natively) unless you control the format. And a real job
needs to decide what a malformed row means — skip and count, or fail the whole
run — which is a business decision, not a technical one, and should be in the
function's signature rather than buried in a `catch`.

## review1 — failing a stream on purpose

The rule this exercise drills: **never throw out of `_transform`**. The stream
machinery calls your function from inside its own internals; an exception
there does not reach the caller's `try`, does not become an `"error"` event
reliably, and in older Node versions could take the process down. The
supported failure channel is `callback(error)`, which destroys the stream,
emits `"error"`, and — under `pipeline` — tears the chain down and rejects the
promise you awaited.

The `return` after `callback(error)` is not decoration. Calling the callback
twice for one chunk raises `ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK`, and falling through from a
`catch` into the success path is the easiest way to do it. This is the same
"exactly once" discipline as the error-first callback convention in lesson 04
— the same rule, a different API.

The last assertion in the gate is worth noticing: records that were emitted
before the failure still arrive. A stream pipeline is not a transaction. If
your job needs all-or-nothing semantics, the atomicity has to come from
somewhere else — write to a temp file and rename, or wrap the sink in a
database transaction — which is the same lesson as `buildIndex` in 05.

## Further reading

- [`stream.pipeline()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinesource-transforms-destination-callback) — including the async generator forms and the array form.
- [Implementing a Transform stream](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-transform-stream) — `_transform`, `_flush`, and the object-mode options.
- [`string_decoder`](https://nodejs.org/api/string_decoder.html) — the API ex3 turns on, with the partial-character example.
- [MDN: async generators (`for await...of`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — the language feature behind ex4.
- [Stream: Choosing an API style](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#choose-one-api-style) — the official "pick one consumption style" warning.

## Challenge — CSV in, JSON lines out

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
processCsv(source, sink, { minAmount }): Promise<{ read, written }>
```

The source is a byte stream of CSV: a header row `id,amount`, then data rows.
For every data row whose `amount` is **at least** `minAmount`, write one line
to the sink:

```
{"id":"2","amount":250}
```

— `id` as a string, `amount` as a number, `\n` at the end of each line.
Return `{ read, written }`: data rows seen (excluding the header) and rows
written.

Build it as a `pipeline` of stages. Copy your ex3 splitter into this file
rather than importing it — the exercises are deliberately isolated so a bug in
one gate never fails another.

Honest difficulty note: every individual piece is something you have already
written. The work is in the seams — the header row, blank lines, a row split
across two chunks (the gate does this on purpose), and keeping the counters
somewhere both the transform and the return statement can see.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three stages, and you have written two of them already in this lesson:

1. bytes -> lines (ex3's splitter - copy it into this file, the exercises are
   deliberately isolated),
2. lines -> JSON text, dropping the header and the rows below the threshold,
3. the sink you were handed.

Wire them with `pipeline` and return the counters afterwards. Nothing here
holds the whole input in memory, which is the point: this same function works
on a four-gigabyte export.

## Hint 2

The middle transform has `writableObjectMode: true` (strings come in from the
splitter) and a plain byte-mode readable side (text goes out to the sink).

Three rules for it:

- skip blank lines entirely - the last line of a file that ends with a newline
  is one of these;
- the first non-blank line is the header, so consume it and count nothing;
- for a data row: `split(",")`, convert the amount with `Number`, compare, and
  emit `JSON.stringify({ id, amount }) + "\n"` only when it passes.

`read` counts every data row you looked at; `written` counts the ones you
emitted.

## Hint 3

The middle stage, in outline:

```ts
transform(line: string, _encoding, callback) {
  const text = line.trim();
  if (text === "") { callback(); return; }
  if (!headerSeen) { headerSeen = true; callback(); return; }

  stats.read += 1;
  const [id, rawAmount] = text.split(",");
  const amount = Number(rawAmount);
  if (/* does it pass? */) {
    stats.written += 1;
    callback(null, /* the JSON line */);
    return;
  }
  callback();
}
```

Two decisions left: the comparison (the gate uses `minAmount: 100` and expects
the row with exactly 250 and the one with 900 - think about whether the
boundary is inclusive) and the shape of the emitted object. The gate wants
`{"id":"2","amount":250}`: the id stays a string, the amount becomes a number,
and each line ends with `\n`.

## Exercise 1 — a Transform with a last word

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createUppercase()`, returning a `Transform`
that uppercases every chunk that passes through it and, when the input ends,
emits one final chunk: `[N chunks]`, where N is how many chunks it saw.

`createUppercase()` on an empty stream still emits `[0 chunks]` — the flush
runs whether or not anything arrived.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Transform` is a `Writable` and a `Readable` welded together: what you write
in comes out the other side, changed. You implement one method,
`transform(chunk, encoding, callback)`, and optionally a second, `flush`.

`callback(null, value)` is shorthand for "push this value, and I am ready for
the next chunk". `callback()` on its own means "I consumed that chunk and have
nothing to emit for it yet" - which is how a batching or buffering transform
works.

## Hint 2

`flush(callback)` is called once, after the last chunk, before the readable
side ends. It is the only chance to emit something that depends on having seen
everything - a summary, a closing bracket, a final partial line.

Inside both methods `this` is the stream, so `this.push(value)` works in
`flush` where there is no second callback argument to use.

The chunk counter lives in the closure around the constructor call, exactly
like the counter in lesson 06 ex3.

## Hint 3

```ts
let chunks = 0;

return new Transform({
  transform(chunk: Buffer, _encoding, callback) {
    chunks += 1;
    callback(null, /* the transformed chunk */);
  },

  flush(callback) {
    this.push(/* the summary */);
    callback();
  },
});
```

Two decisions left: the transformation itself, and the exact summary text (the
gate wants `[3 chunks]`, square brackets included, and `[0 chunks]` for an
empty input - so the flush must run unconditionally). One honest caveat worth
noting: uppercasing a chunk at a time is only safe because this gate feeds
ASCII. Text transforms that must survive arbitrary UTF-8 need the decoder you
will meet in ex3.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — pipeline, and the thing `.pipe()` does not do

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

```ts
pipeThrough(source, transforms, sink): Promise<void>
```

Wire the source, then every transform in order, then the sink, and resolve
when it is done — or reject with the error if any stage fails.

The gate then checks something `.pipe()` cannot give you: after a failure, the
**sink and the source must both be destroyed**. That is the difference between
a pipeline that fails and a pipeline that leaks. In a real program those two
streams are a socket and a file handle, and the version that leaves them open
is the one that runs out of file descriptors at 4am on a Sunday.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is a promise-flavoured `pipeline` in `node:stream/promises`. It takes the
stages in order - source first, sink last - wires them together with
backpressure, and returns a promise that resolves when the last one finishes
or rejects if any of them fails.

That is the entire exercise. The interesting part is what it does that
`a.pipe(b).pipe(c)` does not, and the gate checks for it.

## Hint 2

Two forms are available:

```ts
await pipeline(source, transform, sink);      // as separate arguments
await pipeline([source, ...transforms, sink]); // as one array
```

You are handed an *array* of transforms of unknown length, so the second form
is the one that fits: spread the transforms between the source and the sink.

Do not add `.on("error")` handlers of your own, and do not wrap it in a
`try`/`catch` that swallows - the caller wants the rejection.

## Hint 3

The body is one line. The decision left to you is the assembly of the array,
and whether you `await` it or return it directly (both work - `await` inside
an `async` function that declares `Promise<void>` is the clearer of the two).

If the gate tells you the sink was not destroyed, you probably reached for
`.pipe()`: `.pipe()` returns the destination for chaining but does *not*
forward errors or clean up the other streams, which is why every modern Node
codebase uses `pipeline` instead.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a promise-flavoured `pipeline` in `node:stream/promises`. It takes the
stages in order - source first, sink last - wires them together with
backpressure, and returns a promise that resolves when the last one finishes
or rejects if any of them fails.

That is the entire exercise. The interesting part is what it does that
`a.pipe(b).pipe(c)` does not, and the gate checks for it.

## Hint 2

Two forms are available:

```ts
await pipeline(source, transform, sink);      // as separate arguments
await pipeline([source, ...transforms, sink]); // as one array
```

You are handed an *array* of transforms of unknown length, so the second form
is the one that fits: spread the transforms between the source and the sink.

Do not add `.on("error")` handlers of your own, and do not wrap it in a
`try`/`catch` that swallows - the caller wants the rejection.

## Hint 3

The body is one line. The decision left to you is the assembly of the array,
and whether you `await` it or return it directly (both work - `await` inside
an `async` function that declares `Promise<void>` is the clearer of the two).

If the gate tells you the sink was not destroyed, you probably reached for
`.pipe()`: `.pipe()` returns the destination for chaining but does *not*
forward errors or clean up the other streams, which is why every modern Node
codebase uses `pipeline` instead.

## Exercise 3 — bytes in, lines out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createLineSplitter()`, a `Transform` whose
writable side takes bytes and whose readable side emits **one string per
line**, without the newline.

The rules:

- a line may be split across any number of chunks, and a chunk may hold many
  lines;
- a trailing `\r` (Windows line endings) is not part of the line;
- if the input does not end with a newline, the last partial line is still a
  line and must be emitted from `flush`;
- if the input *does* end with a newline, there is no empty extra line.

And one requirement inherited from lesson 06: the gate splits a two-byte `ü`
across two chunks. `chunk.toString()` per chunk corrupts it. Use
`node:string_decoder`'s `StringDecoder`, which holds an incomplete character
back until its remaining bytes arrive.

This is the most useful thirty lines in this course. Log processing, CSV,
NDJSON, SMTP, HTTP header parsing — they are all this function with a
different separator.

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Chunk boundaries and line boundaries have nothing to do with each other. A
chunk can hold three lines, half a line, or one byte in the middle of a
character. So the transform needs a `pending` string: everything since the
last newline that has not been emitted yet.

Per chunk: append the new text to `pending`, split on `"\n"`, push every piece
*except the last*, and keep the last one as the new `pending`. The last piece
has no newline after it, so it might be incomplete.

## Hint 2

Two details the gate is strict about.

**Decoding.** `chunk.toString("utf8")` corrupts a character that straddles two
chunks - lesson 06 ex2, again. `node:string_decoder` exists for this:
`decoder.write(chunk)` returns the text that is safely decodable and keeps any
incomplete character back until the rest arrives; `decoder.end()` returns
whatever is left at the end.

**The output side is object mode.** You are pushing strings, one per line, so
set `readableObjectMode: true` on the constructor options. The writable side
stays in byte mode, because bytes are what arrives.

And `flush` emits the last line - but only if there is one. An input ending in
a newline leaves `pending` empty, and an empty final line is not a line.

## Hint 3

```ts
const decoder = new StringDecoder("utf8");
let pending = "";

return new Transform({
  readableObjectMode: true,

  transform(chunk: Buffer, _encoding, callback) {
    pending += decoder.write(chunk);
    const lines = pending.split("\n");
    pending = lines.pop() ?? "";
    for (const line of lines) this.push(/* what about \r? */);
    callback();
  },

  flush(callback) { /* the last line, if any */ },
});
```

Two decisions left: how you strip a trailing `\r` (Windows line endings are
`\r\n`, and the `\r` is not part of the line), and the exact contents of
`flush`. Reread the two assertions in the gate: one input ends mid-line and
one ends with a newline, and they want different numbers of lines out.

## Exercise 4 — a transform that is just a function

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `withLineNumbers(source)` as an **async
generator** that takes an async iterable and yields `` `${n}: ${item}` `` for
each item, counting from 1.

The gate uses it twice: once by iterating it directly, and once by handing the
function itself to `pipeline` as a stage. Both work, because Node's pipeline
accepts async generator functions — which means most "I need a Transform" jobs
are really "I need a small generator".

```
uv run dojo test node 07_streams_2 ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

No `Transform` subclass here, no callbacks, no `push`. An async generator
consumes with `for await` and produces with `yield`, and Node's `pipeline`
accepts one as a stage - so this is the same job as ex1 with a tenth of the
ceremony.

The counter is a plain `let` in the function body, because a generator's body
runs once per invocation and keeps its local state between yields.

## Hint 2

The shape of every generator transform:

```ts
export async function* stage(source: AsyncIterable<unknown>): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  for await (const item of source) {
    yield /* something derived from item */;
  }
}
```

`yield` is the `push`. Where the generator suspends at a `yield`, it is
waiting for the consumer to ask for the next value - which means backpressure
is built in and you never have to think about it.

Note the item type is `unknown`: inside a byte-mode pipeline the values that
arrive are `Buffer`s, and in object mode they are whatever was pushed.
`String(item)` handles both, because a Buffer stringifies to its decoded text.

## Hint 3

Three lines inside the loop at most. The decisions left to you are where the
counter starts (the gate wants the first item to be `1: ...`, not `0: ...`)
and the exact separator - a colon and a single space.

If you find yourself reaching for `source.on("data")` or `push`, stop: the
whole point of this form is that neither exists. The generator *is* the
stream stage.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

No `Transform` subclass here, no callbacks, no `push`. An async generator
consumes with `for await` and produces with `yield`, and Node's `pipeline`
accepts one as a stage - so this is the same job as ex1 with a tenth of the
ceremony.

The counter is a plain `let` in the function body, because a generator's body
runs once per invocation and keeps its local state between yields.

## Hint 2

The shape of every generator transform:

```ts
export async function* stage(source: AsyncIterable<unknown>): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  for await (const item of source) {
    yield /* something derived from item */;
  }
}
```

`yield` is the `push`. Where the generator suspends at a `yield`, it is
waiting for the consumer to ask for the next value - which means backpressure
is built in and you never have to think about it.

Note the item type is `unknown`: inside a byte-mode pipeline the values that
arrive are `Buffer`s, and in object mode they are whatever was pushed.
`String(item)` handles both, because a Buffer stringifies to its decoded text.

## Hint 3

Three lines inside the loop at most. The decisions left to you are where the
counter starts (the gate wants the first item to be `1: ...`, not `0: ...`)
and the exact separator - a colon and a single space.

If you find yourself reaching for `source.on("data")` or `push`, stop: the
whole point of this form is that neither exists. The generator *is* the
stream stage.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One chunk in, one object out, so there is no buffering and no `flush` - the
transform is four lines plus error handling.

The readable side carries objects, so `readableObjectMode: true`, exactly as
in ex3. The writable side stays in byte mode: what arrives is a `Buffer`.

## Hint 2

`JSON.parse` throws, and a `transform` implementation must never let a throw
escape - the stream machinery is calling you, and an exception there is not
routed anywhere useful. The supported way to fail is
`callback(error)`, which destroys the stream and, under `pipeline`, tears the
whole chain down and rejects.

So: `try` around the parse only, `callback(error)` in the catch, and
`callback(null, parsed)` on the success path.

## Hint 3

```ts
transform(chunk: Buffer, _encoding, callback) {
  let parsed: unknown;
  try {
    parsed = JSON.parse(chunk.toString("utf8"));
  } catch (error) {
    /* fail the stream, and then? */
  }
  callback(null, parsed);
}
```

Two decisions left: what goes in the catch, and the `return` that has to
follow it. Calling `callback` twice for one chunk is its own error
(`ERR_MULTIPLE_CALLBACK`) - falling through from the catch into the success
call is the easiest way to do it by accident.

# 08 — HTTP, without a framework

You are going to write a web server with no dependencies. Not because that is
how you should build production services — the next three lessons are express
— but because express is a thin layer over exactly what you are about to
write, and every one of its conveniences is a thing you will now recognise
rather than memorise.

Here is the whole API:

```ts
import { createServer } from "node:http";

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/plain" });
  res.end("hello");
});

server.listen(3000);
```

That callback — the *request listener* — is called once per request. `req` is
a `Readable` stream carrying the body, with the method, URL and headers hung
off it. `res` is a `Writable` stream you write the response into. There is no
router, no `req.query`, no `req.body`, no JSON parsing, no `res.json()`. Those
are all express, and by the end of this lesson you will have written each of
them yourself.

The reason this is worth a whole lesson: nearly every "why is my API doing
that" question is at this layer. Why did the request hang? Because nothing
called `res.end()`. Why 404 instead of 405? Because the router only compared
paths. Why did the upload take down the process? Because nothing bounded the
body. Frameworks answer these questions for you until the day they do not.

## Concept — request in, response out

**What arrives.** `req` is an `IncomingMessage`:

```ts
req.method;                       // "GET", "POST", ...
req.url;                          // "/search?q=node"  <- path AND query, never the host
req.headers["content-type"];      // headers, keys lowercased for you
req.headers["if-none-match"];
// req itself is a Readable stream of the body
```

Note what `req.url` is not: it is not a parsed object, and it is not just the
path. Parse it with the standard `URL` class, which needs a base because
`/search?q=node` is relative:

```ts
const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost");
url.pathname;                     // "/search"
url.searchParams.get("q");        // "node"     (first value, or null)
url.searchParams.getAll("tag");   // ["core", "io"]  (every value)
```

**What you send.** `res` is a `ServerResponse`:

```ts
res.setHeader("etag", '"abc"');            // one header, before anything is sent
res.writeHead(201, { "content-type": "application/json" });  // status + headers
res.end(JSON.stringify(body));             // body, and the response is over
```

Three rules that account for most beginner bugs. Headers can only be sent
once — a second `writeHead` throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. Nothing is sent to
the client until you call `end()`, so a handler that forgets it leaves the
request hanging until the client times out. And `writeHead` merges with
anything you set earlier via `setHeader`, with `writeHead`'s values winning.

**The body is a stream.** This is the part that surprises people coming from
other platforms: there is no `req.body`. The body may not have arrived yet, so
you read it:

```ts
const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
req.on("data", (chunk) => chunks.push(chunk));
req.on("end", () => {
  const text = Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8");
  // ...now you can answer
});
```

Which means your handler answers *later*, from a callback — and it means an
unbounded `push` is a denial-of-service waiting to happen. Every body parser
in the world takes a size limit, and this is why.

**Status codes worth knowing precisely**, because the exercises grade them:

| code | when |
|---|---|
| 200 | here it is |
| 201 | created — plus a `Location` header pointing at the new thing |
| 304 | you already have this version (a conditional GET) |
| 400 | the client sent something malformed |
| 404 | no such path |
| 405 | the path exists, that method does not — plus an `Allow` header |
| 413 | the body was too big |
| 500 | we broke |

## Exercise 1 — route by hand

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createHandler()`, returning a request
listener that answers:

- `GET /health` → 200, JSON `{"status":"ok"}`
- `GET /orders` → 200, JSON `[{"id":"1","item":"keyboard"},{"id":"2","item":"monitor"}]`
  (the `ORDERS` array already in the file)
- anything else, including `POST /health` → 404, JSON `{"error":"not found"}`

Every response carries `content-type: application/json`. Write yourself a
small `sendJson(res, status, body)` helper — you will use it in all four
exercises, and it is the seed of what express calls `res.json()`.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — parse the query string

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /search`, which reads three parameters:

- `q` — required. Missing → 400, `{"error":"q is required"}`
- `limit` — optional, **a number**, default `10`
- `tag` — optional and repeatable; collect every value into `tags`

`GET /search?q=node&limit=2` → `{"q":"node","limit":2,"tags":[]}`
`GET /search?q=streams&tag=core&tag=io` → `{"q":"streams","limit":10,"tags":["core","io"]}`

Two traps live here. `req.url` includes the query string, so ex1's exact
comparison no longer matches. And everything in a query string is a string:
`limit` arrives as `"2"` and the gate compares against the number `2`.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — read a body, and refuse a big one

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `POST /orders`:

- read the body, parse it as JSON, assign an incrementing `id` starting at 1,
  and respond **201** with the stored order and a `Location: /orders/<id>`
  header;
- a body that does not parse → **400** `{"error":"invalid json"}`;
- more than `BODY_LIMIT` (1024) bytes → **413** `{"error":"payload too large"}`;
- any other method on `/orders` → **405** with an `Allow: POST` header;
- any other path → 404.

The limit is the point of the exercise. Stop *accumulating* once you are over
it — do not buffer the whole body and check afterwards, because then the
attack has already succeeded. (Production code goes further and destroys the
connection; this exercise keeps reading and discarding so that the response is
guaranteed to reach the client.)

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — path parameters and a conditional GET

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /orders/:id` over the provided
`ORDERS` map:

- exactly two path segments, the first `orders`; anything else is a 404
  (`/orders/1/extra` included);
- an unknown id is a 404;
- a hit responds 200 with the order as JSON, plus `Cache-Control: no-cache`
  and an `ETag` header — any string that changes when the body changes;
- if the request carries `If-None-Match` equal to that ETag, respond **304**
  with no body at all.

That last part is the whole caching protocol of the web in four lines. The
client keeps the ETag it was given and offers it back; the server either says
"still valid, use your copy" or sends the new one. Every CDN, every browser
cache and every `fetch` you have ever made speaks this.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex4
```

## Challenge — write the router

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createRouter()`:

```ts
const router = createRouter();
router.get("/orders", handler);
router.get("/orders/:id", handler);       // params.id
router.get("/orders/:id/lines/:line", handler);
router.post("/orders", handler);
createServer(router.handler);
```

- a `:name` segment matches exactly one segment and its value is passed to the
  handler as `params.name`;
- match on the **pathname**, so a query string does not break the route;
- no route at all → 404;
- the path matches but the method does not → **405**, with an `Allow` header
  listing every method registered for that path.

The 405 requirement is what makes this a router rather than a lookup table:
you cannot decide it until you have checked *every* route, because the answer
depends on what else is registered.

Honest difficulty note: the matcher is twenty lines and the dispatch loop is
ten. What takes the time is the realisation that "no handler ran" has two
different causes and they deserve different answers.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core challenge
```

# Reading - node/08_http_core

The HTTP module is small, unopinionated, and the thing every Node framework is
standing on. An afternoon here saves years of framework mysteries.

## Notes

**What `http.createServer` actually gives you.** A `Server` that is an
`EventEmitter`; the callback you pass is registered as a `"request"` listener.
Node parses the request line and headers for you, hands you an
`IncomingMessage` before the body has necessarily arrived, and hands you a
`ServerResponse` you write into. It does not parse bodies, routes, cookies,
query strings, or form data, and it does not have opinions about status codes.
Everything else in the web-framework world is built from those two objects.

**`IncomingMessage` is a Readable and `ServerResponse` is a Writable.** That
is not a metaphor — everything from lessons 06 and 07 applies. You can
`pipeline(req, parser, sink)`. You can pipe a file straight into `res`. A
proxy is `pipeline(clientReq, upstreamReq)` and `pipeline(upstreamRes, res)`,
which is why a Node proxy is twenty lines and uses constant memory.

**Header handling.** Request header names arrive lowercased in `req.headers`
(HTTP header names are case-insensitive; Node normalises so you do not have to
guess). Duplicate headers are joined with `, ` except `set-cookie`, which is
always an array. On the response, `setHeader`/`getHeader`/`removeHeader` work
until the headers are flushed; after that they throw, because the bytes are
gone.

**The one-response rule.** A response is a status line, then headers, then a
body, in that order, once. `writeHead` twice throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`,
and it is nearly always caused by a missing `return` after an error response —
which is why the reference solutions in this lesson return after every
`sendJson`. Frameworks hit the same wall; express's version of this bug is
"Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client".

**Keep-alive and why `end()` matters.** Modern HTTP reuses the TCP connection
for several requests, so the client knows a response is over either from
`Content-Length` or from chunked framing. Calling `end()` is what closes the
frame; without it the client waits, holding the socket, until a timeout. This
is also why setting `Content-Length` (as the reference's `sendJson` does) is
slightly better than letting Node fall back to chunked encoding for small
bodies — one fewer thing for the client to reason about.

**The URL class is the parser.** `url.parse` from `node:url` is the legacy
API, still everywhere in old code, and deprecated. Use `new URL(req.url,
base)` — it is the same WHATWG URL you have in browsers, it decodes
percent-escapes, and `URLSearchParams` handles repeated keys properly. If you
need the real host, build the base from `req.headers.host` — and treat that
header as untrusted input, because it comes from the client.

**Bodies need limits, always.** `req` will hand you as many bytes as the
client sends. Without a cap, one request can exhaust your heap, and it costs
the attacker nothing. Every framework's body parser has a limit (express
defaults to 100 KB for JSON) and every hand-rolled parser needs one. The
correct production shape is: check `Content-Length` if present, count bytes as
they arrive, and respond `413` *and* destroy the socket the moment the limit
is passed.

## ex1 — routing is an `if`

Seeing routing as a chain of conditionals is the point. `app.get("/health",
h)` is a registration that makes the framework run the same comparison later.
When a route "does not match" in express, the cause is always one of the
things you can see in your own version: the method is different, the path has
a trailing slash, the pathname includes a query string, or an earlier
middleware already sent the response.

The 404 fallthrough is worth noticing as a design. There is no "no route
matched" event in `http` — if you send nothing, the request hangs. So every
server ends with a default, and in express that default is the built-in final
handler that produces the HTML "Cannot GET /nope" page. Yours produces JSON,
which is what an API should do: an API that answers HTML on the error path
breaks every client that assumed JSON.

The `content-type` header matters more than it looks. Without it, browsers
sniff, some proxies transform, and `fetch().json()` still works only because
it does not check. Sending it is one line and it is part of being correct.

## ex2 — the query string, and the shape of user input

`URLSearchParams` gets three things right that hand-rolled parsers get wrong:
percent-decoding (`%20`, `+` in form encoding), repeated keys, and empty
values. The repeated-key case is the one people meet in production —
`?tag=a&tag=b` is a perfectly normal way to send a list, and `get()` silently
returns only the first — which is why express's `req.query` sometimes hands
you a string and sometimes an array, a type that has caused a great deal of
grief.

The other lesson is that everything is a string. There is no type information
in a query string, so `limit=2` is `"2"`, `flag=false` is the truthy string
`"false"`, and `id=1e3` is a perfectly valid number if you `Number()` it.
Conversion and validation belong at the edge — one place, immediately — which
is exactly the argument for the zod schemas you will write in lesson 10.

The interview version: "how would you handle `?limit=abc`?" The answer worth
giving names the choice — 400 with a message, or fall back to the default —
and points out that silently coercing to `NaN` and then using it in a slice is
the one option that is definitely wrong.

## ex3 — the body, and the first security decision in this course

Three things happen in this exercise and all three are load-bearing.

**The handler answers from a callback.** Because the body arrives over time,
the response is produced inside `"end"`. This is where the "release Zalgo"
discipline from lesson 04 pays off: the request path is uniformly
asynchronous, so there is no version of the code that sometimes answers
synchronously.

**The limit protects memory.** Counting as you go and dropping bytes past the
limit means your worst case is bounded regardless of the client. Checking
`Content-Length` first is a useful optimisation — you can reject before
reading anything — but it cannot replace counting, because the header is
supplied by the client and a chunked request has no length at all.

**The status codes are a vocabulary.** 400 for malformed input, 405 with
`Allow` for a wrong method, 413 for too much data. Getting these right is what
makes an API debuggable by someone who is not you: a 500 says "the server
broke", and using it for a bad request sends the reader looking in the wrong
logs.

The follow-up question an interviewer asks here: "what happens if the client
disconnects mid-upload?" The `"end"` event never fires, `"aborted"`/`"close"`
does, and any work you started needs cancelling — which is why long-running
handlers check `req.destroyed` or listen for `"close"`.

## ex4 — conditional GETs, the cheapest optimisation in HTTP

An ETag is an opaque version identifier for a representation. The server sends
it; the client stores it; the next request offers it back in `If-None-Match`;
the server compares and either sends the whole body or a 304 with no body at
all. Same round trip, a fraction of the bytes, and the client's cache stays
correct because the server decides.

Three details worth carrying:

- **Strong vs weak.** `W/"abc"` is a *weak* ETag: the representations are
  semantically equivalent but maybe not byte-identical. Express's built-in
  ETag is weak by default, computed from a hash of the body.
- **`Cache-Control: no-cache` does not mean "do not cache".** It means "cache
  it, but revalidate before every use" — which is exactly what makes the
  conditional GET happen. The header for "never store this" is `no-store`.
- **A 304 must have no body**, and Node enforces it. It should carry the
  headers a 200 would have carried for caching purposes, which is why the
  reference sets `ETag` and `Cache-Control` before the branch.

The related mechanism, worth knowing by name: `Last-Modified` plus
`If-Modified-Since`, which is the same protocol keyed on a timestamp with
one-second resolution. ETags are strictly better when you can compute them.

## challenge — what a router is

A router is a list of (method, pattern, handler) plus a matcher. Everything
else real routers add — parameter type constraints, wildcards, regular
expressions, precedence rules, nested routers, per-route middleware — is
elaboration on that.

Two design points in the exercise are worth naming because they recur.

**Registration-time work beats request-time work.** Splitting the pattern into
segments once, at registration, is the same instinct as compiling a regex once
or preparing a SQL statement once. Express (and its path-to-regexp) goes
further and compiles each pattern into a regular expression at registration.

**"Nothing matched" is two different answers.** A path that no route claims is
a 404. A path that routes claim under other methods is a 405, and the spec
*requires* the `Allow` header so the client can discover what is possible.
Getting this right is a small thing that separates an API that feels
considered from one that does not — and it only falls out if your dispatch
loop keeps looking after the first path match fails on method.

The natural follow-up: "what about ordering and conflicts?" With `/orders/new`
and `/orders/:id` both registered, first-match-wins means registration order
decides, which is why express tells you to register specific routes before
parameterised ones. A router that scores specificity instead (like most modern
frameworks) is the alternative, and knowing that the trade-off exists is the
answer.

## Further reading

- [`node:http`](https://nodejs.org/api/http.html) — `createServer`, `IncomingMessage`, `ServerResponse`; the reference for everything in this lesson.
- [Anatomy of an HTTP transaction](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/anatomy-of-an-http-transaction) — the official walkthrough, and the best single page on the subject.
- [MDN: HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status) — the table from the Concept section, with the precise semantics of each.
- [MDN: HTTP conditional requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Conditional_requests) — ETags, `If-None-Match`, and where 304 fits.
- [MDN: `URL` and `URLSearchParams`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URL) — the parser ex2 is built on.

Three details worth carrying:

- **Strong vs weak.** `W/"abc"` is a *weak* ETag: the representations are
  semantically equivalent but maybe not byte-identical. Express's built-in
  ETag is weak by default, computed from a hash of the body.
- **`Cache-Control: no-cache` does not mean "do not cache".** It means "cache
  it, but revalidate before every use" — which is exactly what makes the
  conditional GET happen. The header for "never store this" is `no-store`.
- **A 304 must have no body**, and Node enforces it. It should carry the
  headers a 200 would have carried for caching purposes, which is why the
  reference sets `ETag` and `Cache-Control` before the branch.

The related mechanism, worth knowing by name: `Last-Modified` plus
`If-Modified-Since`, which is the same protocol keyed on a timestamp with
one-second resolution. ETags are strictly better when you can compute them.

## challenge — what a router is

A router is a list of (method, pattern, handler) plus a matcher. Everything
else real routers add — parameter type constraints, wildcards, regular
expressions, precedence rules, nested routers, per-route middleware — is
elaboration on that.

Two design points in the exercise are worth naming because they recur.

**Registration-time work beats request-time work.** Splitting the pattern into
segments once, at registration, is the same instinct as compiling a regex once
or preparing a SQL statement once. Express (and its path-to-regexp) goes
further and compiles each pattern into a regular expression at registration.

**"Nothing matched" is two different answers.** A path that no route claims is
a 404. A path that routes claim under other methods is a 405, and the spec
*requires* the `Allow` header so the client can discover what is possible.
Getting this right is a small thing that separates an API that feels
considered from one that does not — and it only falls out if your dispatch
loop keeps looking after the first path match fails on method.

The natural follow-up: "what about ordering and conflicts?" With `/orders/new`
and `/orders/:id` both registered, first-match-wins means registration order
decides, which is why express tells you to register specific routes before
parameterised ones. A router that scores specificity instead (like most modern
frameworks) is the alternative, and knowing that the trade-off exists is the
answer.

## Hint 1

Two structures and one algorithm.

The structures: a list of registered routes, each holding a method, the
pattern *already split into segments*, and the handler. Splitting at
registration time rather than per request is the small optimisation that also
makes the matching code readable.

The algorithm: for each route, does its segment list match the request's
segment list? Same length, and each pattern segment either starts with `:`
(matches anything, and records the value) or must be equal.

## Hint 2

Matching, as a function that returns the parameters or `null`:

```ts
function match(route: Route, segments: string[]): RouteParams | null {
  if (route.segments.length !== segments.length) return null;
  const params: RouteParams = {};
  for (const [index, pattern] of route.segments.entries()) {
    if (pattern.startsWith(":")) params[pattern.slice(1)] = segments[index];
    else if (pattern !== segments[index]) return null;
  }
  return params;
}
```

Then the dispatch loop has to do two things at once: find a route whose
*method and path* both match, and - if it does not find one - remember which
methods matched the path anyway. That set is the `Allow` header of the 405.

## Hint 3

```ts
const allowed = new Set<string>();

for (const route of routes) {
  const params = match(route, segments);
  if (params === null) continue;
  if (route.method === req.method) { route.handler(req, res, params); return; }
  allowed.add(route.method);
}

if (allowed.size > 0) { /* 405, with the Allow header */ return; }
/* 404 */
```

Two decisions left: what goes in the `Allow` header (the gate splits it on
commas, so `"GET, POST"` and `"GET,POST"` both pass) and where the segments
come from - remember `req.url` carries the query string, so the pathname has
to come out of a `URL` first or `/orders/42?expand=lines` will never match.
