## Exercise 1 — route by hand

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createHandler()`, returning a request
listener that answers:

- `GET /health` → 200, JSON `{"status":"ok"}`
- `GET /orders` → 200, JSON `[{"id":"1","item":"keyboard"},{"id":"2","item":"monitor"}]`
  (the `ORDERS` array already in the file)
- anything else, including `POST /health` → 404, JSON `{"error":"not found"}`

Every response carries `content-type: application/json`. Write yourself a
small `sendJson(res, status, body)` helper — you will use it in all four
exercises, and it is the seed of what express calls `res.json()`.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`createHandler()` does no work itself: it returns the function Node will call
once per request. Everything you write lives inside that returned function,
which receives `(req, res)`.

A route is two facts about the request - `req.method` and `req.url` - and one
response. Write the three cases as three `if`s and a fallthrough, in the order
the README lists them.

## Hint 2

Sending a JSON response is three steps that always go together, so write them
once as a helper and call it three times:

```ts
function sendJson(res: ServerResponse, status: number, body: unknown): void {
  const text = JSON.stringify(body);
  res.writeHead(status, { "content-type": "application/json" });
  res.end(text);
}
```

`writeHead(status, headers)` sends the status line and the headers; `end(text)`
sends the body and finishes the response. Nothing is sent until one of them
runs, and nothing may be sent after `end`.

## Hint 3

```ts
return (req, res) => {
  if (req.method === "GET" && req.url === /* which path? */) {
    sendJson(res, 200, { status: "ok" });
    return;                                  // <- do not fall through
  }
  // ...the /orders case...
  sendJson(res, 404, { error: "not found" });
};
```

Two decisions left: the paths, and the `return` after each response. Without
them every request tries to send three responses and Node throws
`ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` on the second - which is the single most common
mistake in hand-written handlers, and worth causing once on purpose so you
recognise the message.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — parse the query string

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /search`, which reads three parameters:

- `q` — required. Missing → 400, `{"error":"q is required"}`
- `limit` — optional, **a number**, default `10`
- `tag` — optional and repeatable; collect every value into `tags`

`GET /search?q=node&limit=2` → `{"q":"node","limit":2,"tags":[]}`
`GET /search?q=streams&tag=core&tag=io` → `{"q":"streams","limit":10,"tags":["core","io"]}`

Two traps live here. `req.url` includes the query string, so ex1's exact
comparison no longer matches. And everything in a query string is a string:
`limit` arrives as `"2"` and the gate compares against the number `2`.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`req.url` is not a path - it is a path *and* a query string
(`/search?q=node&limit=2`). Comparing it to `"/search"` fails the moment a
parameter is present, which is why ex1's exact match is not enough here.

Node has no `req.query`. That is an express thing. What you have is the
standard `URL` class, and the trick is that it needs a base to parse a
relative URL.

## Hint 2

```ts
const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost");
url.pathname;        // "/search"  - no query string
url.searchParams;    // a URLSearchParams
```

The base is a formality: the hostname is thrown away, you only wanted the
parsing. (`http://localhost` is the usual placeholder; some codebases build a
real one from the `Host` header.)

`URLSearchParams` gives you `get(name)` - the first value or `null` - and
`getAll(name)` - every value as an array. Percent-decoding is already done.

## Hint 3

```ts
const q = url.searchParams.get("q");
if (/* missing or empty? */) { sendJson(res, 400, { error: "q is required" }); return; }

const rawLimit = url.searchParams.get("limit");
const limit = rawLimit === null ? /* default */ : Number(rawLimit);

sendJson(res, 200, { q, limit, tags: /* which method? */ });
```

Three decisions left. Note that everything in a query string is a string:
`limit` has to be converted, and `"2"` is not `2` to the gate's `toEqual`.
And think about whether `?q=` with no value should count as present - the gate
does not test it, and a real API should decide on purpose.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`req.url` is not a path - it is a path *and* a query string
(`/search?q=node&limit=2`). Comparing it to `"/search"` fails the moment a
parameter is present, which is why ex1's exact match is not enough here.

Node has no `req.query`. That is an express thing. What you have is the
standard `URL` class, and the trick is that it needs a base to parse a
relative URL.

## Hint 2

```ts
const url = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost");
url.pathname;        // "/search"  - no query string
url.searchParams;    // a URLSearchParams
```

The base is a formality: the hostname is thrown away, you only wanted the
parsing. (`http://localhost` is the usual placeholder; some codebases build a
real one from the `Host` header.)

`URLSearchParams` gives you `get(name)` - the first value or `null` - and
`getAll(name)` - every value as an array. Percent-decoding is already done.

## Hint 3

```ts
const q = url.searchParams.get("q");
if (/* missing or empty? */) { sendJson(res, 400, { error: "q is required" }); return; }

const rawLimit = url.searchParams.get("limit");
const limit = rawLimit === null ? /* default */ : Number(rawLimit);

sendJson(res, 200, { q, limit, tags: /* which method? */ });
```

Three decisions left. Note that everything in a query string is a string:
`limit` has to be converted, and `"2"` is not `2` to the gate's `toEqual`.
And think about whether `?q=` with no value should count as present - the gate
does not test it, and a real API should decide on purpose.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — read a body, and refuse a big one

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `POST /orders`:

- read the body, parse it as JSON, assign an incrementing `id` starting at 1,
  and respond **201** with the stored order and a `Location: /orders/<id>`
  header;
- a body that does not parse → **400** `{"error":"invalid json"}`;
- more than `BODY_LIMIT` (1024) bytes → **413** `{"error":"payload too large"}`;
- any other method on `/orders` → **405** with an `Allow: POST` header;
- any other path → 404.

The limit is the point of the exercise. Stop *accumulating* once you are over
it — do not buffer the whole body and check afterwards, because then the
attack has already succeeded. (Production code goes further and destroys the
connection; this exercise keeps reading and discarding so that the response is
guaranteed to reach the client.)

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The body is not on `req`. `req` **is** the body - a `Readable` stream of the
bytes the client is still sending. So this handler cannot answer immediately:
it registers listeners and answers later, from the `"end"` callback.

Order of business: reject the wrong path (404), reject the wrong method (405,
with an `Allow` header), then read.

## Hint 2

The read loop, with the limit built in:

```ts
const chunks: Buffer[] = [];
let size = 0;
let tooLarge = false;

req.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => {
  size += chunk.length;
  if (size > BODY_LIMIT) { tooLarge = true; return; }
  chunks.push(chunk);
});

req.on("end", () => { /* decide what to send */ });
```

Note what the limit does: it stops *keeping* the bytes, so your memory is
bounded no matter what the client sends. Checking the size only at the end
would mean you had already buffered the whole thing.

`Buffer.concat(chunks).toString("utf8")` gives you the text - one decode, at
the end, for the reason lesson 06 ex2 drilled.

## Hint 3

Inside `"end"`, in order:

```ts
if (tooLarge) { /* 413 */ return; }

let parsed: { item?: string; qty?: number };
try { parsed = JSON.parse(/* the text */); }
catch { /* 400 */ return; }

const order = { id: nextId, item: parsed.item, qty: parsed.qty };
nextId += 1;
res.setHeader("location", /* what? */);
sendJson(res, 201, order);
```

Two decisions left: the `Location` value (the gate wants `/orders/1` for the
first order) and where `nextId` lives. It has to survive between requests, so
it belongs in the closure `createHandler()` creates - the same module-state
trick as lesson 01 ex3, scoped to one handler instead of one module.

## Exercise 4 — path parameters and a conditional GET

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /orders/:id` over the provided
`ORDERS` map:

- exactly two path segments, the first `orders`; anything else is a 404
  (`/orders/1/extra` included);
- an unknown id is a 404;
- a hit responds 200 with the order as JSON, plus `Cache-Control: no-cache`
  and an `ETag` header — any string that changes when the body changes;
- if the request carries `If-None-Match` equal to that ETag, respond **304**
  with no body at all.

That last part is the whole caching protocol of the web in four lines. The
client keeps the ETag it was given and offers it back; the server either says
"still valid, use your copy" or sends the new one. Every CDN, every browser
cache and every `fetch` you have ever made speaks this.

```
uv run dojo test node 08_http_core ex4
```

lessons.briefing:
# 09 — Express fundamentals

You just wrote a router, a query-string parser, a body reader and a JSON
response helper from scratch. Express is those four things, plus a
middleware stack, plus twenty years of accumulated defaults — and now that you
have built the parts, none of it is magic.

This course uses **express 5**, which became the default release in 2024 after
a decade of 4.x. Most of what you will find on the internet is written for 4,
and the differences are small but load-bearing: async handlers that reject now
reach your error handler without a `try`/`catch`, the router's path syntax got
stricter (a bare `*` is no longer a valid pattern — it must be named, like
`/*splat`), and a few long-deprecated helpers are gone. Where a difference
matters in this course, it is called out.

The mental model to carry through the next three lessons: **an express app is
a list of functions, tried in order.** Every one of them gets
`(req, res, next)`. Each either sends a response, or calls `next()` to pass
the request along, or calls `next(error)` to jump to the error handler. Routes
are just entries in that list with a method and a path attached. That is the
entire architecture, and once you see it, express stops having surprises.

## Concept — the stack, and what express adds to `req`/`res`

```ts
import express from "express";

const app = express();

app.use((req, res, next) => {          // runs for every request
  res.setHeader("x-request-id", crypto.randomUUID());
  next();                              // pass it on
});

app.get("/orders/:id", (req, res) => { // runs for GET /orders/<anything>
  res.json({ id: req.params.id });
});

export default app;                    // note: no listen() here
```

**Why a factory, not a module-level app.** Every exercise in this lesson
exports `createApp()`, and the reason is testability: the gate calls it fresh
for each test, so no state leaks between them, and nothing binds a port.
supertest takes the app object, starts a server on an ephemeral port, makes
the request and shuts it down. In a real project `createApp()` lives in
`app.ts` and `server.ts` does `createApp().listen(port)` — one line, one
place, and everything else is testable.

**What express adds to the request:**

```ts
req.params.id        // "/orders/:id" -> the matched segment, always a string
req.query.limit      // parsed query string: string | string[] | undefined
req.body             // ONLY after a body-parsing middleware (lesson 10)
req.headers["x-api-key"]
```

`req.query` deserves a warning. A client can send `?tag=a&tag=b`, so a value
you expect to be a string can arrive as an array. In express 5 `req.query` is
also a getter, computed once per request — you cannot assign to it the way
some 4.x middleware used to.

**What express adds to the response:**

```ts
res.json(value);                 // serialise + content-type + end
res.status(404).json({ ... });   // chainable
res.setHeader("x-total", "5");   // same as node's
res.send("plain text");          // content-type guessed from the argument
```

**Middleware, precisely.** Three signatures, distinguished by arity:

```ts
app.use((req, res, next) => { ... });                    // middleware
app.get("/path", (req, res) => { ... });                 // handler
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { ... });               // error handler (4 args - lesson 10)
```

Order is registration order. A `app.use` registered after your routes only
runs for requests that no route answered. A middleware that sends a response
and *also* calls `next()` causes the next handler to try to send a second one,
which is the "Cannot set headers after they are sent" error every express
developer meets exactly once.

**Routers** are mountable sub-stacks:

```ts
const api = express.Router();
api.use(authenticate);              // applies to everything in this router
api.get("/orders", listOrders);     // relative to wherever it is mounted
app.use("/api/v1", api);            // now GET /api/v1/orders
```

That is how a real app is organised: one router per resource, mounted under a
version prefix, with the middleware that applies to that area registered on
the router rather than globally.

## Exercise 1 — the smallest app that works

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` returning an express app with:

- `GET /health` → `{"status":"ok"}`
- `GET /orders` → the `ORDERS` array already in the file

Do not call `listen()`, and do not write a 404 handler — express has one, and
the gate checks that `GET /nope` and `DELETE /orders` both fall through to it.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — parameters, and validating what a client sends

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `GET /orders/:id` → the matching order, or **404** with
  `{"error":"not found"}`;
- `GET /orders` → the whole list, or the first `limit` of them when
  `?limit=n` is given;
- `?limit=abc` (or `0`, or `-1`) → **400** with
  `{"error":"limit must be a positive number"}`.

The 400 is the real exercise. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, `slice(0, NaN)`
returns an empty array, and an endpoint that answers `[]` to a malformed
request has told the client a lie. Query parameters are untrusted strings;
convert and check them at the door.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — middleware order, and stopping the line

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` with three pieces of
middleware and two routes:

- an **app-level** middleware (`app.use`) that sets an `x-request-id` header
  on every response — including responses to paths that match no route — and
  starts a trail array in `res.locals`;
- `GET /trail`, with a **route-level** middleware that adds `"route"` to the
  trail; the handler adds `"handler"` and responds with `{ trail }`. The
  result must be `["app", "route", "handler"]`;
- `GET /admin`, guarded by a middleware that requires the header
  `x-api-key: let-me-in`. Without it: **401** `{"error":"unauthorized"}` and
  the handler must not run. With it: `{"secret":"the cake is a lie"}`.

The guard is the exercise. Sending a response and then calling `next()` anyway
is the most common middleware bug there is, and the gate catches it by
checking the *body* of the 401 as well as the status.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — mount a router

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` with:

- `GET /health` registered directly on the app;
- an `express.Router()` carrying `GET /orders` and `GET /orders/:id`, plus a
  router-level middleware that sets `x-api-version: v1`;
- the router mounted at `/api/v1`.

The gate checks the scoping in both directions: `/api/v1/orders` gets the
version header, `/health` does not, and `/orders` — the unmounted path — is a
404.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex4
```

## Challenge — the collection endpoint

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /orders` over the five seeded
orders, supporting:

| parameter | meaning | default | invalid → |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status` | exact-match filter | no filter | — |
| `sort` | `id` or `amount` | `id` | 400 `{"error":"invalid sort"}` |

`total` is the number of rows **after filtering and before pagination** — the

return a million rows if asked is an endpoint that will be asked.


# Reading - node/09_express_fundamentals

Express is twelve hundred lines of routing over `node:http`. Knowing which
twelve hundred is what makes it predictable.

## Notes

**The stack is the whole design.** An express app holds an array of layers.
Each layer has an optional path pattern, an optional method, and a function.
On each request express walks the array in order; a layer whose path and
method match gets called; calling `next()` advances to the next match; sending
a response ends the walk. Routers are nested arrays with a mount path. That is
genuinely all of it — no dependency injection, no lifecycle hooks, no
decorators.

**Express 5, and what changed from 4.** The differences worth knowing:

- **Async errors are forwarded.** In express 4, a rejected promise from a
  handler was an unhandled rejection and the request hung; you needed
  `try`/`catch` plus `next(err)`, or a wrapper like `express-async-handler`.
  In express 5 a handler that returns a rejecting promise routes the error to
  your error-handling middleware automatically. Lesson 10 grades this.
- **Path syntax is stricter** (path-to-regexp v8). A bare `*` is no longer a
  pattern; wildcards must be named — `/*splat`. Optional segments are
  `{/:id}` rather than `/:id?`, and regex fragments inside a path string are
  gone. If a tutorial's route pattern throws at startup, this is why.
- `req.query` is a getter, computed once; `req.params` is not writable.
- Long-deprecated helpers (`res.sendfile`, `res.json(status, body)`,
  `app.del`) are removed.

**`res.locals` versus attaching to `req`.** Both are used in the wild for
per-request state. `res.locals` is the documented one (it is also what view
engines read) and it disappears when the response does. Attaching to `req`
works but needs TypeScript declaration merging to type properly. Either way,
per-request state must live on the request/response objects — never in a
module-level variable, because that variable is shared by every concurrent
request in the process. That is the single most dangerous mistake in a Node
server, and it is *possible* precisely because modules are singletons (lesson
01 ex3).

**Handlers are matched, not searched.** Registration order decides. `/orders/
:id` registered before `/orders/summary` means `summary` is treated as an id
forever. There is no specificity ranking like a CSS selector or a modern
framework's file-based router. Register specific routes first.

**`app.use` is not "global setup".** It is a layer at the position where you
wrote it. Registered before the routes it runs before them; registered after
it runs only for requests no route answered (which is how a custom 404 handler
works) and after `next()` is called from a route (which is how error handlers
work). Position *is* configuration.

## ex1 — the factory pattern

The most important line in this exercise is the one that is not there:
`app.listen()`. An app that listens as a side effect of being imported cannot
be tested without a port, cannot be started twice, and cannot be configured by
its caller. Splitting `createApp()` from the process that runs it is the
standard shape of a testable Node service, and supertest is built around it.

`res.json` does four things: serialises with `JSON.stringify`, sets
`content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8`, sets `Content-Length`, and
ends the response. It also applies the app's `json replacer`/`json spaces`
settings if configured, and — relevant later — sets an ETag by default, which
is why express responses support conditional GETs without you doing the work
you did in lesson 08 ex4.

The built-in 404 is worth understanding rather than replacing by reflex. When
the stack is exhausted with no response, express's final handler responds
404 with an HTML body. For an API you usually *do* want to replace it with
JSON, and the way to do that is a `app.use` **after** all routes — which is
exactly the shape lesson 10 builds.

## ex2 — the shape of untrusted input

`req.params` values are always strings, because URLs have no types. So is
everything in `req.query` — or an array, if the client repeats the key, or
`undefined` if it is absent. In TypeScript that shows up as
`string | string[] | undefined`, which is annoying and honest: it is exactly
what can arrive.

The `NaN` trap in this exercise is worth internalising because it generalises.
`Number("abc")` is `NaN`; `NaN` compares `false` against everything, including
itself; `Array.prototype.slice(0, NaN)` treats it as 0 and returns nothing.
So the naive version answers `[]` — a plausible, wrong, silent answer. The
fix is to validate the *converted* value (`Number.isInteger`,
`Number.isFinite`) rather than the raw string, and to answer 400 rather than
guess.

This is the argument for schema validation in one paragraph, and it is why
lesson 10 introduces zod: doing this by hand for four parameters is fine;
doing it by hand for forty is where the bugs live.

## ex3 — order, and the two ways to end a request

The trail array makes the stack visible. In production the same technique is
how request tracing works: a middleware at the top attaches an id, every layer
logs with it, and you can reconstruct one request's path through the system
from the logs.

The `x-request-id`-on-a-404 assertion is the structural one. A header that
appears even when no route matched can only have been set by a layer that runs
for every request — which is what `app.use` means and what a route-level
middleware cannot do. That is the gate proving *where* you registered
something, not just what it does.

The guard teaches the exit rule: **respond, or call `next()`, never both.**
After a response is sent, the response object is closed; calling `next()`
lets the next layer try to send another one, and express raises
`ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. The idiom that prevents it is `return` immediately
after every `res.*` that ends a response — which is why every reference
solution in this course does it.

Two related things worth knowing: `next("route")` skips the remaining handlers
of the *current* route and moves to the next matching route, and `next(err)`
jumps straight to the error handlers, skipping everything in between. Both are
rare; both are useful to recognise.

## ex4 — routers, and why they are how apps are organised

A router is a mini-app with its own stack, mounted at a path. The mounting is
what gives you scoping: middleware on the router runs only for requests that
matched the mount path, so `api.use(authenticate)` protects an entire area
without a single `if (req.path.startsWith("/api"))`.

Two details that come up:

- Inside a mounted router, `req.baseUrl` is the mount path and `req.path` is
  the remainder, while `req.originalUrl` is the whole thing. Useful when
  building links.
- By default a router does not inherit the parameters of its mount path —
  `express.Router({ mergeParams: true })` turns that on, which is what you
  need for nested resources like `/orders/:orderId/lines`.

The convention this leads to is one router per resource in its own file, each
exporting a factory that takes its dependencies (`createOrdersRouter(store)`),
mounted in `createApp()`. That is dependency injection without a framework,
and it is what makes each router testable on its own — you will use the shape
in lesson 11.

## challenge — everything a list endpoint owes its client

Filter, sort, paginate, and report the total. Getting the order right matters:
filter first (it decides the total), then sort (over the filtered set), then
slice (the page you actually send).

Three production notes the exercise is a scale model of:

**Cap the page size.** Without a maximum, `?perPage=1000000` is a legal way to
ask for your whole table, and someone will. Every real API has a cap, usually
50–200, and returns 400 (or silently clamps, which is worse because the client
cannot tell).

**Offset pagination has a known flaw.** `page`/`perPage` is easy and it
breaks under concurrent inserts: if a row is added while a user is reading,
page 2 can repeat a row page 1 already showed. The alternative is cursor
pagination — "give me the 20 after id X" — which is stable and cannot jump to
an arbitrary page. Knowing that trade-off by name is a good interview answer.

**Sorting on an allowlist, never on user input.** `sort=amount` is validated
against a fixed set here for the same reason it must be in SQL: interpolating
a user-supplied column name into a query is an injection. Even without SQL, an
allowlist means an unknown field is a clear 400 instead of a mysterious
`undefined` comparison that silently returns the input order.

And one JavaScript detail: `Array.prototype.sort` sorts **in place** and
returns the same array. Sorting a shared module-level fixture reorders it for
every subsequent request in the process — a bug that only appears on the
second call, and one of the reasons "why did the order change?" is such a
common report. Copy first.

## Further reading

- [Express 5: routing](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/routing.html) — route paths, parameters, `express.Router`, and the current path syntax.
- [Using middleware](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/using-middleware.html) — the five kinds of middleware and where each one goes in the stack.
- [Migrating to Express 5](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html) — the definitive list of what changed, including async error handling and path matching.
- [`req.query` and `req.params`](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#req.params) — the API reference for what arrives and in what type.
- [MDN: `Number.isInteger()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/isInteger) — the check that closes the `NaN` hole in ex2.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the collection endpoint

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `GET /orders` over the five seeded
orders, supporting:

| parameter | meaning | default | invalid → |
|---|---|---|---|
| `status` | exact-match filter | no filter | — |
| `sort` | `id` or `amount` | `id` | 400 `{"error":"invalid sort"}` |
| `order` | `asc` or `desc` | `asc` | 400 `{"error":"invalid order"}` |
| `page` | 1-based page number | `1` | 400 `{"error":"invalid pagination"}` |
| `perPage` | page size, 1–50 | `10` | 400 `{"error":"invalid pagination"}` |

The response is:

```json
{ "items": [...], "page": 2, "perPage": 2, "total": 5 }
```

`total` is the number of rows **after filtering and before pagination** — the
number the client needs to draw a pager. A page past the end is an empty
`items` array, not a 404: the collection exists, that page of it is just
empty.

Honest difficulty note: no single step is hard, and there are five of them
that have to happen in the right order (validate, filter, sort, slice,
report). The `perPage` cap is not busywork either — an endpoint that will
return a million rows if asked is an endpoint that will be asked.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One route, four query parameters, and an order of operations that matters:

1. **validate** everything first, and return the right 400 before doing any
   work;
2. **filter** (this decides `total`);
3. **sort**;
4. **slice** the page out.

Doing them in a different order gives wrong answers that look plausible: sort
before filter wastes work, paginate before filter gives a `total` that is a
lie, and validating late means an invalid page can still hit your data.

## Hint 2

Every value in `req.query` is `string | string[] | undefined` (a client can
send `?sort=a&sort=b`), so narrow with `typeof value === "string"` before you
use it. A small helper - "give me this parameter as a string, or this default"
- keeps the four reads readable.

The three validation rules from the README:

- `sort` must be `id` or `amount`, default `id`;
- `order` must be `asc` or `desc`, default `asc`;
- `page` >= 1 and `perPage` between 1 and 50, both integers.

Each has its own message, and the gate checks all three.

## Hint 3

The last two steps:

```ts
const sorted = filtered.sort((a, b) => {
  const comparison = sort === "amount" ? a.amount - b.amount : a.id.localeCompare(b.id);
  return direction === "desc" ? -comparison : comparison;
});

const start = /* which index does this page start at? */;
res.json({
  items: sorted.slice(start, start + perPage),
  page,
  perPage,
  total: /* the count of what, exactly? */,
});
```

Two decisions left: the offset arithmetic (pages are 1-based; page 1 starts at
0) and which array's length is the total. One caveat worth noticing:
`Array.prototype.sort` mutates. Sorting `ORDERS` in place would reorder the
shared fixture for every later request in the same process, which is the kind
of bug that only shows up on the second call - the reference copies with
`[...ORDERS]` when there is no filter.

## Exercise 1 — the smallest app that works

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` returning an express app with:

- `GET /health` → `{"status":"ok"}`
- `GET /orders` → the `ORDERS` array already in the file

Do not call `listen()`, and do not write a 404 handler — express has one, and
the gate checks that `GET /nope` and `DELETE /orders` both fall through to it.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`express()` builds an application object. You register routes on it and return
it - you do **not** call `listen()` here. That is the whole reason the factory
exists: the gate wants an app it can drive in-process, and a real `main.ts`
would call `createApp().listen(port)` itself.

Two routes, both GET, both answering with JSON.

## Hint 2

```ts
const app = express();

app.get("/health", (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });
});

return app;
```

`res.json(value)` serialises the value, sets `content-type: application/json`

## Exercise 2 — parameters, and validating what a client sends

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `GET /orders/:id` → the matching order, or **404** with
  `{"error":"not found"}`;
- `GET /orders` → the whole list, or the first `limit` of them when
  `?limit=n` is given;
- `?limit=abc` (or `0`, or `-1`) → **400** with
  `{"error":"limit must be a positive number"}`.

The 400 is the real exercise. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`, `slice(0, NaN)`
returns an empty array, and an endpoint that answers `[]` to a malformed
request has told the client a lie. Query parameters are untrusted strings;
convert and check them at the door.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two routes. `/orders/:id` reads `req.params.id` - always a string, because a
URL has no types. `/orders` reads `req.query.limit`, which is `undefined` when
the parameter is absent and a string when it is present.

Both routes have a failure case, and both failure cases are the client's
fault, so both are 4xx with a JSON body rather than an exception.

## Hint 2

The lookup:

```ts
const order = ORDERS.find((candidate) => candidate.id === req.params.id);
if (order === undefined) {
  res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });
  return;
}
res.json(order);
```

`res.status(code).json(body)` is the chainable form, and the `return` after it
matters exactly as much as it did in lesson 08 - express will happily let you
try to send a second response and then throw.

For `limit`: absent means "no limit". Present means convert and validate.
`Number("abc")` is `NaN`, and `NaN` passes every `<` and `>` comparison you
might think to guard with, so check with `Number.isInteger` (or
`Number.isFinite`) rather than a comparison.

## Hint 3

```ts
const raw = req.query.limit;
if (raw === undefined) { /* everything */ }

const limit = Number(raw);
if (/* not a usable limit? */) {
  res.status(400).json({ error: "limit must be a positive number" });
  return;
}
res.json(ORDERS.slice(0, limit));
```

Two decisions left: the validity test, and the order of your two route
registrations. Express matches in registration order, and `/orders/:id` will
not match `/orders` - but if you ever add `/orders/summary` alongside
`/orders/:id`, the specific one has to be registered first or `:id` swallows
it. Worth knowing before it bites you.

## Exercise 3 — middleware order, and stopping the line

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` with three pieces of
middleware and two routes:

- an **app-level** middleware (`app.use`) that sets an `x-request-id` header
  on every response — including responses to paths that match no route — and
  starts a trail array in `res.locals`;
- `GET /trail`, with a **route-level** middleware that adds `"route"` to the
  trail; the handler adds `"handler"` and responds with `{ trail }`. The
  result must be `["app", "route", "handler"]`;
- `GET /admin`, guarded by a middleware that requires the header
  `x-api-key: let-me-in`. Without it: **401** `{"error":"unauthorized"}` and
  the handler must not run. With it: `{"secret":"the cake is a lie"}`.

The guard is the exercise. Sending a response and then calling `next()` anyway
is the most common middleware bug there is, and the gate catches it by
checking the *body* of the 401 as well as the status.

```
uv run dojo test node 09_express_fundamentals ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A middleware is a handler with a third parameter: `(req, res, next)`. It can
read the request, add to it, set response headers, and then either call
`next()` to pass control on, or send a response and *not* call `next()`.

You need three of them:

- one registered with `app.use(...)`, so it runs for every request;
- one registered as an extra argument on the `/trail` route;
- one guarding `/admin`.

## Hint 2

`res.locals` is the per-request scratchpad express gives you - a plain object
that lives as long as the response. Start the trail there in the app-level
middleware, push to it in the route middleware, push again in the handler, and
send it.

Registering a route middleware is just an extra argument before the handler:

```ts
app.get("/trail", markRoute, (req, res) => { ... });
```

The header must appear even on a 404, which only happens if the middleware is
`app.use(...)` and registered **before** the routes. Express runs the stack in
registration order; anything registered after the routes only runs on the way
out.

## Hint 3

The guard:

```ts
const requireApiKey = (req, res, next) => {
  if (req.headers["x-api-key"] !== "let-me-in") {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "unauthorized" });
    return;                 // <- and this is the whole exercise
  }
  next();
};
```

Two decisions left: what the app-level middleware puts in the header, and what
happens after you send the 401. Sending a response *and* calling `next()` is
the classic middleware bug - the handler then runs anyway and tries to send a
second response, and express reports "Cannot set headers after they are sent".
The gate checks the 401 body specifically to catch it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`express.Router()` gives you an object with the same `get`/`post`/`use`
methods as an app, but it is not an app - it is a stack of routes you can
attach somewhere later:

```ts
const orders = express.Router();
orders.get("/orders", handler);
app.use("/api/v1", orders);
```

Routes inside the router are written **relative to the mount path**. The

lessons.briefing:
# 10 — Middleware, validation and error handling

An express app is a list of functions. This lesson is about the three
functions every real service has in that list and most tutorials skip: one
that reads the body, one that checks it is what you asked for, and one at the
very bottom that turns every failure in the whole application into an honest
response.

The last one deserves its own sentence. Without a central error handler, every
route needs its own `try`/`catch`, every `catch` invents its own JSON shape,
and one of them eventually forgets and sends a stack trace to a customer. With
one, a route can simply `throw` — express catches it, your handler decides
what the client is allowed to know, and the real error goes to your logs. The
same funnel handles a 404, a validation failure and a database outage, which
is why an API built this way answers consistently even on the paths nobody
tested.

Validation is the other half of the same idea. Everything arriving from
outside — body, query, params, headers — is `unknown` no matter what
TypeScript says, because types are erased before the request arrives. A schema
is the runtime check that makes the type true, and once you have parsed at the
edge, every line downstream is working with data that provably has the shape
it claims.

## Concept — parse at the edge, fail into one funnel

**Body parsing** is a middleware, not a feature:

```ts
app.use(express.json());          // JSON bodies -> req.body
app.use(express.json({ limit: "100kb" }));       // the default limit
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true })); // HTML form posts
```

Without it `req.body` is `undefined` — the body is a stream that nobody read
(lesson 08 ex3, now built in). With it, a body that will not parse produces a
400 automatically, because the parser calls `next(error)` with an error that
already carries a status.

**Validation with zod.** A schema is a value that can both check data at run
time and describe its type at compile time:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

const createOrder = z.object({
  item: z.string().min(1),
  qty: z.number().int().positive(),
});

type CreateOrder = z.infer<typeof createOrder>;   // { item: string; qty: number }

const result = createOrder.safeParse(req.body);
if (!result.success) {
  result.error.issues;      // [{ path: ["qty"], message: "..." }, ...]
} else {
  result.data;              // typed, and with unknown keys stripped
}
```

Two things to notice. `safeParse` returns a result object rather than
throwing, which makes it pleasant in a middleware. And it reports **every**
problem, so a client can fix a whole form in one round trip instead of
discovering the errors one at a time.

The phrase to remember is *parse, don't validate*. A validator says "this
looks fine" and hands you back the same untyped thing. A parser hands you a
new value that is, by construction, the shape you asked for — which is why the
exercise makes you assign `result.data` back onto `req.body`.

**Error handling.** An error handler is a middleware with **four**
parameters, registered **last**:

```ts
app.use((error: unknown, req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  // ...
});
```

Four is not a style choice; it is how express tells an error handler from an
ordinary one. Three parameters and it is never called with an error, which is
the most confusing bug in express and always looks like "my error handler does
not work".

Errors reach it three ways: a `throw` in a synchronous handler, a call to
`next(error)` from anywhere, and — **new in express 5** — a rejected promise
returned by an `async` handler. That third road is why express 5 matters:

```ts
// express 4: hangs the request, logs an unhandled rejection
// express 5: reaches the error handler
app.get("/prices", async (req, res) => {
  const prices = await fetchPrices();   // rejects
  res.json(prices);
});
```

If you have seen `express-async-handler`, `asyncHandler(fn)` wrappers, or a
`try`/`catch` in literally every route, that was the express 4 workaround, and
it is no longer needed.

**What the handler decides.** The rule from lesson 04, applied: errors you
produced deliberately carry a status and a message the client may see; errors
you did not produce get a 500 and a generic body, with the real one in your
logs. A thrown `Error` whose message contains a connection string is not
hypothetical — it is what a failed database call looks like.

## Exercise 1 — a body parser and a middleware factory

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp(log)`:

- parse JSON bodies;
- a middleware that, **after each response is finished**, calls
  `log("METHOD PATH STATUS")` — e.g. `"POST /echo 200"`, and also
  `"GET /nope 404"` for a request no route answered;
- `POST /echo` responds with the parsed body.

The logging middleware cannot log when it runs: at that point nothing has
happened yet and `res.statusCode` is still the default. Register a listener
for the response's `"finish"` event and log from there — `res` is a `Writable`
(lesson 06) and this is the same event you waited on then.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — validation as a middleware

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `validateBody(schema)` — a middleware factory. On success, replace
  `req.body` with the **parsed** value and call `next()`. On failure, respond
  400 with:

  ```json
  { "error": "validation failed",
    "details": [{ "path": "qty", "message": "..." }] }
  ```

  One detail per failing field, `path` joined with `"."`.

- `createApp()` — `POST /orders`, validated with `createOrderSchema`,
  responding 201 with the order plus an incrementing `id`.

The gate posts a body with an extra key and checks it is *gone* from the
response. That only happens if you assign the parsed value back — which is the
difference between validating and parsing.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — one error handler for the whole app

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp(logError)` with:

- `GET /orders/:id` → the order, or `throw new AppError(404, "not_found",
  "no such order")`;
- `GET /boom` → throws a plain `Error` whose message contains a database URL
  with a password in it;
- a middleware after the routes that turns "nothing matched" into
  `AppError(404, "not_found", "no such route")`;
- an error handler, registered last, that answers:
  - for an `AppError`: its status, `{ error: <code>, message: <message> }`;
  - for anything else: **500**, `{"error":"internal_error","message":"internal
    server error"}` — and calls `logError(error)` with the real error.

The gate checks that the database URL does not appear in any response, and
that `logError` was called exactly once — for the unknown error, and not for
either 404. An expected failure is not a defect; logging it as one is how a
log becomes noise nobody reads.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — async handlers that fail

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The `AppError` class, a failing dependency
(`fetchPrices`) and the error handler are provided. Implement `createApp()`
with three routes:

- `GET /ok` — an `async` handler that resolves and responds `{"status":"ok"}`;
- `GET /slow-dependency` — an `async` handler that `await`s `fetchPrices()`,
  with **no** `try`/`catch`. The rejection must reach the error handler and
  produce a 503;
- `GET /queued` — a middleware that calls `next(new AppError(409, "conflict",
  "that job is already queued"))`, followed by a handler that must never run.

…and the provided `errorHandler` registered last.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex4
```

## Challenge — a rate limiter you can actually test

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createRateLimiter({ limit, windowMs,
now })` and a `createApp(options)` that guards `GET /ping` with it.

- the key is the `x-api-key` header, or `"anonymous"` when it is absent;
- up to `limit` requests per key per fixed window of `windowMs`;
- allowed requests set `x-ratelimit-limit` and `x-ratelimit-remaining`;
- a refused request is **429** with `{"error":"too many requests"}` and a
  `Retry-After` header in **seconds**, rounded up, until the window ends;
- when the clock passes the end of a window, the count starts again.

`now` is injected, which is the whole reason this is testable: the gate moves
the clock forward 30 seconds and then 60 without a single `setTimeout`. Any
time-dependent logic you write should take its clock as an argument for
exactly this reason.

Honest difficulty note: the bookkeeping is fifteen lines. The two things that
take a second attempt are the `Retry-After` arithmetic (the gate checks both
60 and 30) and remembering that `remaining` is counted *after* the current
request.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation challenge
```

# Reading - node/10_middleware_validation

The three layers every service has: read the input, prove it is what you
asked for, and fail in one place.

## Notes

**Middleware factories are the ecosystem's shape.** `cors(options)`,
`helmet()`, `express.json({ limit })`, `rateLimit({ max })` — every
configurable middleware is a function that returns `(req, res, next)`. The
options live in a closure, which means the middleware carries its
configuration without a global and can be registered twice with different
settings (a strict body limit on one router, a generous one on another). Once
you notice the pattern, reading unfamiliar middleware source becomes easy:
find the returned function, everything above it is setup.

**Where a middleware runs is part of what it does.** Before the routes: it
sees every request on the way in. After the routes: it sees only what nothing
answered — which is how a 404 handler works. With four parameters: only errors.
On a router: only that mount path. There is no other configuration mechanism,
and "why did my middleware not run" is always answered by looking at the
registration order.

response has been fully written; `"close"` fires when the underlying
connection is closed, which also happens when a client disconnects early. A

difference is a good sign in an interview because it shows you have thought
about the failure path.

strength is that one declaration produces both the runtime check and the
static type (`z.infer`), so the two cannot drift apart — which is exactly the
failure mode of hand-written validators plus hand-written interfaces.

Alexis King. A validator answers a yes/no question and leaves you holding the
original untyped value; a parser returns a *new* value whose type encodes what
was checked. In practice that means assigning `result.data` back, not just
checking `result.success` — and it is why zod strips unknown keys by default,
so a client cannot smuggle `{ "role": "admin" }` into an object you spread
into a database row. (That attack has a name — mass assignment — and stripping
is the structural fix.)

and a stable machine-readable code; and you, who needs the stack, the inputs
and the context. Conflating them is how stack traces reach browsers and how
"something went wrong" reaches your logs. The split is exactly the
operational/programmer distinction from lesson 04, now with an HTTP response
attached.

**Express 5 changed the async story.** In express 4, a handler returning a
rejected promise was an unhandled rejection: express never saw the error, the
request hung until timeout, and (since Node 15) the process could die. The
workarounds — `express-async-handler`, a hand-rolled `asyncHandler` wrapper,
or `try { } catch (e) { next(e) }` in every route — are all over the internet
and all obsolete in 5, which awaits the handler's return value and routes a
rejection into the error pipeline.

`express.json()` is `body-parser` inlined into express. It checks the
`Content-Type`, streams the body with a size limit, parses it, and puts the
result on `req.body`; on failure it calls `next(err)` with an error carrying

default limit is 100 kb, and raising it is a decision with a memory cost —

response**. At the moment your middleware runs, the status code is not

middleware and tracing integration uses. It is also the moment to record the
duration, which is why the pattern usually starts with

request id, and be emitted once per request. A logger that writes on the way
in *and* on the way out doubles your log volume for no extra information.

## ex2 — schemas at the boundary

**One schema, two outputs.** `z.infer<typeof schema>` gives you the static
type for free. Write the schema once and use it as the source of truth for
both the runtime check and the compile-time shape; the alternative — an
`interface` next to a validator — is two declarations that drift.

form wants all of them at once; an API that stops at the first problem forces
one round trip per bad field. The `path` is an array because objects nest
(`["items", 0, "qty"]`), which is why joining it into `"items.0.qty"` is the
usual way to hand it to a form library.

you did not declare. That turns "the client sent an extra field" from a
possible privilege-escalation bug into a non-event. `.strict()` rejects
unknown keys instead, and `.passthrough()` keeps them — both are deliberate

place to convert `"2"` into `2`. And the same middleware factory works for

## ex3 — the funnel

A central error handler is the highest-leverage twenty lines in an express
app. It gives you one place to decide the response shape, one place to add a
request id, one place to translate domain errors into status codes, and one
place to make sure nothing internal escapes.

The `AppError` shape — status, code, message — is the minimum. Real ones add a
`details` field (for validation), a `cause` (lesson 04), and often follow
[RFC 9457 Problem Details](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), which
standardises `type`/`title`/`status`/`detail` and is what the .NET track's
`ProblemDetails` implements. A stable machine-readable `code` matters more
than the message: clients branch on codes, humans read messages, and messages
get rewritten.

error whose message can contain the connection string; an ORM's error can
contain the SQL and the parameters, which may be personal data. "Return
`error.message` on 500" is a one-line convenience that has put credentials in
browser dev tools more than once.

logs usable. If every not-found is an error-level log line, the real errors
are invisible by lunchtime. Operational failures belong in your request log
(with their status code); defects belong in your error log with a stack.

## ex4 — the express 5 change, and why it matters

The mechanism: express 5 calls your handler, and if the returned value is a
promise it attaches a rejection handler that funnels into `next(err)`. That is
all. But it removes an entire genre of bug — the route that silently hangs
because someone forgot a `catch` — and an entire genre of boilerplate.

Two things it does **not** do, worth knowing so you do not over-trust it:

- an error thrown inside a callback that express never sees (a `setTimeout`, an
  event listener, a stream `"error"` you did not handle) still escapes. Async
  context does not extend into callbacks you scheduled yourself.
- it does not stop the handler: `await` throws, so the lines after it do not
  run, but any side effect before the failure has already happened. Atomicity
  is your problem, not the framework's.

`next(error)` remains the explicit road, and it is the one to use from a
middleware that is not async — a guard, a permission check, a version
negotiator. Both roads end at the same handler, which is the point: one funnel,
several entrances.

## challenge — rate limiting, and testable time

Rate limiting is the simplest example of a whole category: logic whose
behaviour depends on the clock. The instinct to reach for `Date.now()` inside
the function is what makes such code untestable, and the fix is always the
same — take the clock as a dependency. The gate then moves time in whole
seconds with no `setTimeout`, no fake timers and no flakiness.

Three notes on the algorithm itself:

**Fixed windows have a burst problem.** A client can send `limit` requests in
the last millisecond of one window and `limit` more in the first millisecond
of the next — twice the intended rate. The fixes are a sliding window (count
requests in the trailing `windowMs`, usually approximated) or a token bucket
(tokens refill continuously, which also allows a controlled burst). Naming
this trade-off is a strong answer when an interviewer asks you to design one.

**In-memory state does not survive a second instance.** Two containers behind
a load balancer means two independent counters and twice the limit. Production
limiters keep the counters in Redis, which is also why the atomicity of the
increment matters (`INCR` plus `EXPIRE`, or a Lua script).

**The headers are a protocol.** `X-RateLimit-*` is the widely used convention
and there is now a standards-track `RateLimit` header. `Retry-After` is the
one that is actually specified (RFC 9110), it belongs on a 429 and on a 503,
and a client that respects it is a client that will not make your outage
worse. Sending it costs one line; omitting it makes every client guess.

- [Express: `express.json()`](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#express.json) — options, limits and what happens on a malformed body.
- [zod: basic usage and `safeParse`](https://zod.dev/) — schemas, issues, `z.infer`, and the object-stripping behaviour.
- [MDN: 429 Too Many Requests](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/429) — and `Retry-After`, the header the challenge sets.
- [MDN: `Response.status` codes overview](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status) — the vocabulary the error handler maps onto.

## Challenge — a rate limiter you can actually test

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `createRateLimiter({ limit, windowMs,
now })` and a `createApp(options)` that guards `GET /ping` with it.

- the key is the `x-api-key` header, or `"anonymous"` when it is absent;
- up to `limit` requests per key per fixed window of `windowMs`;
- allowed requests set `x-ratelimit-limit` and `x-ratelimit-remaining`;
- a refused request is **429** with `{"error":"too many requests"}` and a
  `Retry-After` header in **seconds**, rounded up, until the window ends;
- when the clock passes the end of a window, the count starts again.

`now` is injected, which is the whole reason this is testable: the gate moves
the clock forward 30 seconds and then 60 without a single `setTimeout`. Any
time-dependent logic you write should take its clock as an argument for
exactly this reason.

Honest difficulty note: the bookkeeping is fifteen lines. The two things that
take a second attempt are the `Retry-After` arithmetic (the gate checks both
60 and 30) and remembering that `remaining` is counted *after* the current
request.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

State: one bucket per key, holding a count and the moment the window started.
A `Map<string, {count, start}>` in the closure the factory creates - the same
closure-state pattern as every other factory in this course.

Per request: work out the key, read the clock **once** (call `options.now()`
one time and use that value throughout, or your comparisons can disagree with
each other), find or create the bucket, and decide.

## Hint 2

A fixed window resets when the clock has moved past `start + windowMs`:

```ts
const bucket =
  existing === undefined || time - existing.start >= options.windowMs
    ? { count: 0, start: time }   // a new window begins now
    : existing;
```

Then two paths. Over the limit: set `retry-after` (in **seconds**, rounded
up, from `start + windowMs - time`) and answer 429. Under it: increment,
set `x-ratelimit-limit` and `x-ratelimit-remaining`, and `next()`.

The key is the `x-api-key` header when it is a string, and `"anonymous"`
otherwise - remember a header can arrive as an array.

## Hint 3

```ts
if (bucket.count >= options.limit) {
  const msLeft = /* how long until this window ends? */;
  res.setHeader("retry-after", String(Math.ceil(msLeft / 1000)));
  res.status(429).json({ error: "too many requests" });
  return;
}

bucket.count += 1;
res.setHeader("x-ratelimit-remaining", String(/* how many are left? */));
next();
```

Two decisions left, and both are arithmetic the gate checks precisely: the
milliseconds remaining (60 seconds at the start of a fresh window, 30 after
half of it has passed) and the remaining count *after* this request is
counted - the first of three leaves 2, not 3.

One honest caveat about the design: a fixed window lets a client send `limit`
requests at the end of one window and `limit` more at the start of the next -
twice the intended rate in an instant. Sliding windows and token buckets fix
that, and knowing why this simple version is not enough is worth as much as
the code.

## Exercise 1 — a body parser and a middleware factory

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp(log)`:

- parse JSON bodies;
- a middleware that, **after each response is finished**, calls
  `log("METHOD PATH STATUS")` — e.g. `"POST /echo 200"`, and also
  `"GET /nope 404"` for a request no route answered;
- `POST /echo` responds with the parsed body.

The logging middleware cannot log when it runs: at that point nothing has
happened yet and `res.statusCode` is still the default. Register a listener
for the response's `"finish"` event and log from there — `res` is a `Writable`
(lesson 06) and this is the same event you waited on then.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three registrations, in order, and the order is the exercise:

1. `express.json()` - the built-in body parser. Without it `req.body` is
   `undefined`, because reading the body is a stream operation somebody has to
   perform (you did it by hand in lesson 08 ex3).
2. your logging middleware.
3. the `/echo` route.

`createApp` takes the log function as an argument rather than importing a
logger. That is dependency injection, and it is why the gate can assert on
what was logged.

## Hint 2

The logger cannot log when it runs. At that moment the status code is still
the default 200 and no handler has done anything. What you want is to register
a listener and let the request continue:

```ts
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.on("finish", () => { /* now the status is real */ });
  next();
});
```

`res` is a stream (lesson 06), and `"finish"` fires when the response has been
fully written. `req.path` is the path without the query string, and
`res.statusCode` is whatever was finally sent.

## Hint 3

```ts
res.on("finish", () => {
  log(`${req.method} ${/* which property? */} ${res.statusCode}`);
});
next();
```

## Hint 1

Three registrations, in order, and the order is the exercise:

1. `express.json()` - the built-in body parser. Without it `req.body` is
   `undefined`, because reading the body is a stream operation somebody has to
   perform (you did it by hand in lesson 08 ex3).
2. your logging middleware.
3. the `/echo` route.

`createApp` takes the log function as an argument rather than importing a
logger. That is dependency injection, and it is why the gate can assert on
what was logged.

## Hint 2

The logger cannot log when it runs. At that moment the status code is still
the default 200 and no handler has done anything. What you want is to register
a listener and let the request continue:

```ts
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.on("finish", () => { /* now the status is real */ });
  next();
});
```

`res` is a stream (lesson 06), and `"finish"` fires when the response has been
fully written. `req.path` is the path without the query string, and
`res.statusCode` is whatever was finally sent.

## Hint 3

```ts
res.on("finish", () => {
  log(`${req.method} ${/* which property? */} ${res.statusCode}`);
});
next();
```

Two decisions left: the middle field of the log line (the gate wants
`POST /echo 200`), and where in the stack this middleware goes. It has to run
for requests that match no route as well - which, as in lesson 09 ex3, means
`app.use` registered before the routes rather than after them.

## Exercise 2 — validation as a middleware

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement:

- `validateBody(schema)` — a middleware factory. On success, replace
  `req.body` with the **parsed** value and call `next()`. On failure, respond
  400 with:

  ```json
  { "error": "validation failed",
    "details": [{ "path": "qty", "message": "..." }] }
  ```

  One detail per failing field, `path` joined with `"."`.

- `createApp()` — `POST /orders`, validated with `createOrderSchema`,
  responding 201 with the order plus an incrementing `id`.

The gate posts a body with an extra key and checks it is *gone* from the
response. That only happens if you assign the parsed value back — which is the
difference between validating and parsing.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`validateBody` is a middleware *factory*: it takes a schema and returns a
middleware. The same shape as every configurable middleware in the ecosystem -
`cors(options)`, `express.json({ limit })`, `rateLimit({ max })`.

Inside the middleware there are exactly two outcomes: the body matches the
schema, in which case you replace `req.body` with the parsed value and call
`next()`, or it does not, in which case you answer 400 and stop.

## Hint 2

`schema.safeParse(value)` returns a discriminated union rather than throwing:

```ts
const result = schema.safeParse(req.body);
result.success;        // boolean - narrows the type of what follows
result.data;           // the parsed value, when success is true
result.error.issues;   // an array of problems, when it is false
```

Each issue has a `path` (an **array** of keys, because objects nest) and a
`message`. The gate wants `path` as a string, so join it with `"."`.

Note that zod reports *every* problem, not just the first. Passing them all
back is what lets a form highlight three fields at once instead of one per
round trip.

## Hint 3

```ts
const result = schema.safeParse(req.body);
if (!result.success) {
  res.status(400).json({
    error: "validation failed",
    details: result.error.issues.map((issue) => ({
      path: /* the array, as a string */,
      message: issue.message,
    })),
  });
  return;
}

req.body = /* which property? */;
next();
```

Two decisions left, and the second one is the point of the exercise. Assigning
the *parsed* value back means the handler downstream is working with data that
provably matches the schema - unknown keys stripped, types checked. Skipping
that line leaves the handler holding whatever the client sent, and the gate
notices, because the `extra` key survives.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`validateBody` is a middleware *factory*: it takes a schema and returns a
middleware. The same shape as every configurable middleware in the ecosystem -
`cors(options)`, `express.json({ limit })`, `rateLimit({ max })`.

Inside the middleware there are exactly two outcomes: the body matches the
schema, in which case you replace `req.body` with the parsed value and call
`next()`, or it does not, in which case you answer 400 and stop.

## Hint 2

`schema.safeParse(value)` returns a discriminated union rather than throwing:

```ts
const result = schema.safeParse(req.body);
result.success;        // boolean - narrows the type of what follows
result.data;           // the parsed value, when success is true
result.error.issues;   // an array of problems, when it is false
```

Each issue has a `path` (an **array** of keys, because objects nest) and a
`message`. The gate wants `path` as a string, so join it with `"."`.

Note that zod reports *every* problem, not just the first. Passing them all
back is what lets a form highlight three fields at once instead of one per
round trip.

## Hint 3

```ts
const result = schema.safeParse(req.body);
if (!result.success) {
  res.status(400).json({
    error: "validation failed",
    details: result.error.issues.map((issue) => ({
      path: /* the array, as a string */,
      message: issue.message,
    })),
  });
  return;
}

req.body = /* which property? */;
next();
```

Two decisions left, and the second one is the point of the exercise. Assigning
the *parsed* value back means the handler downstream is working with data that
provably matches the schema - unknown keys stripped, types checked. Skipping
that line leaves the handler holding whatever the client sent, and the gate
notices, because the `extra` key survives.

## Exercise 3 — one error handler for the whole app

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp(logError)` with:

- `GET /orders/:id` → the order, or `throw new AppError(404, "not_found",
  "no such order")`;
- `GET /boom` → throws a plain `Error` whose message contains a database URL
  with a password in it;
- a middleware after the routes that turns "nothing matched" into
  `AppError(404, "not_found", "no such route")`;
- an error handler, registered last, that answers:
  - for an `AppError`: its status, `{ error: <code>, message: <message> }`;
  - for anything else: **500**, `{"error":"internal_error","message":"internal
    server error"}` — and calls `logError(error)` with the real error.

The gate checks that the database URL does not appear in any response, and
that `logError` was called exactly once — for the unknown error, and not for
either 404. An expected failure is not a defect; logging it as one is how a
log becomes noise nobody reads.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Express tells an error handler apart from ordinary middleware by counting
parameters: **four** means error handler.

```ts
app.use((error, req, res, next) => { ... });
```

It must be registered **last**, after every route, because express only
reaches it by skipping forward from wherever the error happened.

Getting there happens two ways: `throw` inside a handler (express catches
synchronous throws for you), or `next(error)` from anywhere.

## Hint 2

The handler branches on what kind of error arrived:

- an `AppError` is one you produced deliberately - it already carries the
  status the client should see, a code, and a message that is safe to show.
  Use all three.
- anything else is a bug or an unknown failure. **Log it** (that is what the
  `logError` argument is for) and answer 500 with a fixed, generic body. Never
  send `error.message` from an unknown error: the `/boom` route throws one
  with a database URL and a password in it, which is exactly how credentials
  end up in a client-side error toast.

For the unmatched-path case, register a middleware after your routes that
calls `next(new AppError(404, ...))`, so 404s use the same JSON shape as
everything else.

## Hint 3

```ts
app.use((error: unknown, _req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => {
  if (error instanceof AppError) {
    res.status(/* which status? */).json({ error: /* ? */, message: /* ? */ });
    return;
  }
  logError(error);
  res.status(500).json({ error: "internal_error", message: "internal server error" });
});
```

Two decisions left: the three values from the `AppError`, and where the
`logError` call goes. Note it is only on the unknown branch - a 404 is not a
defect and logging one as an error is how a log becomes noise nobody reads.
The `_next` parameter is unused and must still be declared: remove it and
express sees a three-argument function and treats it as ordinary middleware,
which is the single most confusing failure in express error handling.

## Exercise 4 — async handlers that fail

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The `AppError` class, a failing dependency
(`fetchPrices`) and the error handler are provided. Implement `createApp()`
with three routes:

- `GET /ok` — an `async` handler that resolves and responds `{"status":"ok"}`;
- `GET /slow-dependency` — an `async` handler that `await`s `fetchPrices()`,
  with **no** `try`/`catch`. The rejection must reach the error handler and
  produce a 503;
- `GET /queued` — a middleware that calls `next(new AppError(409, "conflict",
  "that job is already queued"))`, followed by a handler that must never run.

…and the provided `errorHandler` registered last.

```
uv run dojo test node 10_middleware_validation ex4
```

## Hint 1

bottom. The whole exercise is about how an error gets from a route to that

The first road is the one that changed in express 5: an `async` handler whose
promise rejects is forwarded automatically. You write the happy path and
nothing else - no `try`, no `catch`, no `next(error)`.

## Hint 2

```ts
app.get("/slow-dependency", async (_req, res) => {
  const prices = await fetchPrices();     // this rejects
```

`next()`. Express skips every remaining handler for that request and goes
straight to the error handlers.

## Hint 3

For `/queued`, register two functions on the same route:

```ts

  "/queued",
  (_req, _res, next) => { next(/* what? */); },
  (_req, res) => { res.json({ queued: true }); },   // must NOT run
);
```

lessons.briefing:
# 11 — The REST capstone

Eleven lessons of pieces; this one is the machine. You are going to build a
small task API — list, read, create, patch, delete — with an in-memory store,
schema validation at the edge, one error handler at the bottom, and a request
id on every response. It is graded end to end with supertest, the same way you
would test it at work.

Nothing here is a new concept. The store is closure state (lesson 01) with
defensive copies. The endpoints are express routes (lesson 09). The validation
is zod in a middleware (lesson 10). The error handling is the funnel you built
in 10 ex3, and the async semantics are express 5's. What is new is that they
all have to work *at once*, on the same object, without contradicting each
other — which is a genuinely different skill from getting each one right in
isolation.

The four exercises build up in layers, each one a complete, gradeable app:
the store on its own, then reads, then writes, then the whole thing wired
together with the error funnel. You are expected to copy your own earlier code
forward. That is what a capstone is.

## Concept — the layers, and where each decision lives

```
   HTTP layer            express routes, status codes, headers
        │                  ↑ throws AppError            ↓ res.json
   validation             zod schemas at the edge
        │                  ↑ returns parsed data
   store / repository     the data, and the rules about the data
```

**The store knows nothing about HTTP.** No `req`, no `res`, no status codes.
It answers `undefined` for "not there" and lets the layer above decide that
this means 404. That separation is what lets you swap an array for Postgres
later without touching a route, and — more immediately — it is what lets ex1
be tested in microseconds with no server at all.

**The store hands out copies.** This is the rule people skip, and it is the
reason "the data changed and nothing wrote to it" bugs happen:

```ts
const task = store.get("task-1");
task.title = "whatever";          // if this is the store's own object...
store.get("task-1").title;        // ..."whatever". Your store is not in charge.
```

A `{ ...task }` on the way out costs nothing and makes the store the only
thing that can change its own data.

**The HTTP layer owns the vocabulary.** Which status, which headers, which
body shape:

| operation | success | failure |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /tasks` | 200 `{ items, total }` | 400 for a bad filter |
| `GET /tasks/:id` | 200 the task | 404 |
| `POST /tasks` | **201** + `Location` | 400 validation |
| `PATCH /tasks/:id` | 200 the new value | 400 validation, 404 |
| `DELETE /tasks/:id` | **204**, no body | 404 |

`POST` returns 201 with a `Location` header because the client did not choose
the id and needs to be told it. `DELETE` returns 204 because there is nothing
left to describe. `PATCH` is partial by definition — a body of
`{ "status": "done" }` must not blank the title, which is exactly what `PUT`
*would* mean.

**Errors go one way: up.** Routes throw; one handler converts. That is what
makes every error response in the API the same shape, including the ones from
paths nobody tested.

## Exercise 1 — the store

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createTaskStore(seed?)` returning an object
with five methods:

- `list(filter?)` — everything, in insertion order; `list({ status })`
  filters;
- `get(id)` — the task, or `undefined`;
- `create({ title, status? })` — assigns the next id (`task-1`, `task-2`, …),
  defaults the status to `"todo"`, returns the new task;
- `update(id, patch)` — merges only the fields the patch mentions, returns the
  updated task, or `undefined` if there is no such id;
- `remove(id)` — returns whether it removed anything.

And the rule that is easy to miss: **everything the store returns is a copy.**
The gate mutates a task it was handed and then checks the store is unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — the read endpoints

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `createApp()` over the provided `SEED`:

- `GET /tasks` → `{ items, total }`;
- `GET /tasks?status=done` → the filtered list, with `total` following the
  filter;
- `GET /tasks?status=elephant` → **400**
  `{"error":"invalid_status","message":"status must be one of todo, doing,
  done"}`;
- `GET /tasks/:id` → the task, or **404**
  `{"error":"not_found","message":"no such task"}`;
- any unmatched route → **404**
  `{"error":"not_found","message":"no such route"}`.

You may copy your ex1 store into this file or keep a plain array — the gate
only speaks HTTP.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the write endpoints

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. The zod schemas are provided. Implement:

- `POST /tasks` → **201**, `Location: /tasks/task-1`, the created task.
  Invalid body → **400**
  `{"error":"validation_failed","details":[{"path":"title","message":"..."}]}`;
- `PATCH /tasks/:id` → **200** with the updated task; unknown id → 404;
  invalid body → 400 in the same shape;
- `DELETE /tasks/:id` → **204** with no body; unknown id → 404.

Two details the gate checks and both are about parsing rather than
validating. A `POST` with an extra key it did not ask for comes back without
it. And a `PATCH` carrying `{"id":"hacked"}` leaves the id alone — not because
you wrote a check, but because the schema never mentioned `id` and parsing
removed it.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — the whole API

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Everything from ex2 and ex3, in one app, plus:

- an **`x-request-id` header on every response**, counted from `req-1` by a
  middleware at the top of the stack — including on error responses;
- routes that **throw** `AppError` (provided) instead of answering failures
  themselves;
- a "no such route" middleware after the routes;
- one **error handler** last, which maps:
  - a validation failure → 400 `{ error: "validation_failed", details: [...] }`
  - any other `AppError` → its status, `{ error: <code>, message: <message> }`
  - anything else → 500 `{"error":"internal_error","message":"internal server
    error"}`.

The gate runs a whole lifecycle: list, create, read back at the `Location`
URL, see it in a filtered list, patch it, delete it, and confirm it is gone —
then checks that validation still applies and that an unknown route is a JSON
404. That sequence is what "it works" actually means for an API.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex4
```
