# Reading - node/11_rest_capstone

Assembling the pieces is its own skill. This page is about the decisions that
only show up once the pieces are together.

## Notes

**Layering is not ceremony.** Three layers — HTTP, validation, store — each
with one job and one direction of dependency. The store does not know it is
being served over HTTP; the routes do not know the store is an array. That is
what makes the store testable without a server, the routes testable with a
fake store, and the database swap a change in one file. When people say a
codebase is "hard to test", they almost always mean these layers are fused.

**REST, as much of it as matters.** Resources are nouns (`/tasks`), the method
is the verb, and the status code is the outcome. `GET` is safe (no side
effects) and idempotent; `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent (doing it twice
leaves the same state); `POST` is neither. Idempotency is not academic — it is
what decides whether a client may safely retry after a timeout, which is the
retry question from lesson 03 arriving in HTTP form.

**`PATCH` versus `PUT`.** `PUT` replaces the whole resource: fields you leave
out are cleared. `PATCH` is a partial update: fields you leave out are
untouched. Most APIs that say `PUT` mean `PATCH`, and the resulting "why did
my description disappear when I renamed it?" bug is common enough to be worth
naming. The distinction shows up in your schema: the create schema requires a
title, the patch schema requires nothing.

**Status codes are an API.** 201 with `Location` says "made it, here it is".
204 says "done, nothing to say" — and must have no body. 400 is "your request
is malformed", 404 "no such thing", 409 "that conflicts with the current
state", 422 "well-formed but semantically wrong" (some teams use it for
validation; 400 is also fine as long as you are consistent). 500 is "we broke,
it is not your fault". A client can be written against those; it cannot be
written against a 200 that sometimes contains `{"error": ...}`.

**Envelopes.** Returning `{ items, total }` rather than a bare array leaves
room to add `page`, `nextCursor` or `warnings` without breaking every client,
and it keeps the top level of the JSON an object. Consistency matters more
than the specific choice: pick a collection shape and use it everywhere.

**In-memory state is a teaching device.** It is genuinely fine for a cache, a
rate-limit counter or a test double, and genuinely wrong for anything that
must survive a restart or be shared between instances. The moment there are
two containers, module-level state is two different truths. Everything above
the store in this lesson would be unchanged by a real database; that is the
point of writing it this way.

## ex1 — the repository, and defensive copying

A repository is an object that owns a collection and exposes the operations
you are allowed to perform on it. The value is not the abstraction for its own
sake; it is that all the rules about the data live in one place — id
generation, defaults, what "update" means — so no route can invent its own.

The copy rule deserves its own paragraph because it is the one that gets
skipped. JavaScript objects are references. If `get` returns the internal
object, every caller holds a live handle to your state: a route that "just
tidies up the title before rendering" has silently written to your store, and
the change is invisible in a diff because there is no assignment to the store
anywhere. A shallow `{ ...task }` fixes it here; for nested data you need
`structuredClone` (built in since Node 17) or an immutable structure.

Two design notes worth carrying:

**`undefined` versus throwing.** The store returns `undefined` for "not
found", and the HTTP layer converts that to a 404. If the store threw a
`NotFoundError`, it would be making an HTTP decision from inside the data
layer — fine in a small app, and the reason "domain errors" tend to grow their
own hierarchy in a bigger one.

**The `update` semantics.** `if (patch.title !== undefined)` is the difference
between a partial update and an accidental erasure. A spread — `{ ...task,
...patch }` — looks equivalent and is not: an explicit `undefined` in the
patch overwrites the existing value. The distinction between "absent" and
"present but undefined" is a real and annoying part of JavaScript, and this is
where it bites.

## ex2 — reads, and the shape of a collection

The interesting decision here is answering 400 for `?status=elephant` rather
than an empty list. Both are defensible and one is better: an empty list tells
the client "there are no tasks with that status", which is false — there is no
such status. Silent coercion of bad input into a plausible answer is the
category of bug that ends with a user staring at an empty screen and a support
ticket that nobody can reproduce.

The catch-all 404 middleware has a placement rule with a memorable failure. It
matches every path, so registering it *before* your routes makes every route
unreachable, and the resulting "all my endpoints 404" is confusing exactly
because the routes look correct. Registration order is the configuration
(lesson 09), and this is the sharpest instance of it.

One thing this exercise does not do, and a production API would: pagination.
An endpoint that returns every row works until the table is big, at which
point it becomes both a performance problem and a memory problem — for you and
for the client. The lesson-09 challenge built the machinery; the rule is that
any collection endpoint whose size you do not control needs a default limit.

## ex3 — writes, and parsing as a security boundary

Three separate things are being taught, and the third one is the one worth
repeating at interview.

**Status codes for writes.** 201 plus `Location` for creation is the part
people forget: the client did not choose the id, so you have to tell it where
the thing now lives. 204 for delete means "no content" and Node will not let
you send a body with it.

**Partial updates.** The patch schema makes every field optional, and the
handler applies only what is present. That is the entire difference between
`PATCH` and `PUT`, expressed as two schemas.

**Mass assignment, and why stripping fixes it.** The gate patches with
`{"id":"hacked"}`. Nothing in the handler checks for it; the schema simply
never mentioned `id`, so zod removed it before the handler ran. Spread that
raw body into a database row instead and the client picks its own primary key
— or, in the classic version of this vulnerability, sets `"role": "admin"` on
a user-update endpoint. Rails had this exact bug famously in 2012; it recurs
in every ecosystem where objects are spread without being parsed. "Parse,
don't validate" is a security posture, not just a typing convenience.

## ex4 — the assembly, and the two things it adds

Everything in ex4 exists in an earlier lesson except the composition, and
composition is where two habits become visible.

**Routes throw, one handler answers.** Once errors go up rather than out, the
routes get shorter (a `find()` helper that throws is one line at the call
site), the error shape is uniform by construction, and adding a field to every
error response — a request id, a documentation URL, a trace id — is a change
in one function. The ordering detail the hint warns about is real: a
`ValidationError` extending `AppError` matches both `instanceof` checks, so
the specific branch must come first. That is a general rule for any
error-handling chain.

**Observability costs four lines.** A per-request id, set by the first
middleware, echoed on every response including errors, and logged with every
log line. When a user says "it failed at 14:32", an id in the error body turns
an archaeology exercise into a single log query. Real systems go further —
`traceparent` headers, OpenTelemetry spans, propagating the id to downstream
calls — but the first four lines deliver most of the value.

The natural interview follow-up to this exercise: "what would you add before

limits, authentication and authorisation, request logging with the id, metrics

limit (lesson 08/10), CORS if browsers call it, and an OpenAPI description so
clients can be generated. Naming that list is often worth more than any single
implementation detail.

## Notes

with one job and one direction of dependency. The store does not know it is
being served over HTTP; the routes do not know the store is an array. That is
what makes the store testable without a server, the routes testable with a
fake store, and the database swap a change in one file. When people say a
codebase is "hard to test", they almost always mean these layers are fused.

**REST, as much of it as matters.** Resources are nouns (`/tasks`), the method
is the verb, and the status code is the outcome. `GET` is safe (no side
effects) and idempotent; `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent (doing it twice
leaves the same state); `POST` is neither. Idempotency is not academic — it is
what decides whether a client may safely retry after a timeout, which is the
retry question from lesson 03 arriving in HTTP form.

title, the patch schema requires nothing.

## Exercise 1 — the store

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `createTaskStore(seed?)` returning an object
with five methods:

- `list(filter?)` — everything, in insertion order; `list({ status })`
  filters;
- `get(id)` — the task, or `undefined`;
- `create({ title, status? })` — assigns the next id (`task-1`, `task-2`, …),
  defaults the status to `"todo"`, returns the new task;
- `update(id, patch)` — merges only the fields the patch mentions, returns the
  updated task, or `undefined` if there is no such id;
- `remove(id)` — returns whether it removed anything.

And the rule that is easy to miss: **everything the store returns is a copy.**
The gate mutates a task it was handed and then checks the store is unchanged.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two routes and a fallback, in that order. The data can be a plain array
seeded from `SEED` (copy it - mutating the exported constant would leak state
between apps), or your ex1 store copied into this file. Either is fine; the
gate only talks HTTP.

Write `GET /tasks/:id` first: find, 404 if missing, `res.json` if found. Then
the collection, which has the interesting part.

## Hint 2

The collection response is an *envelope*: `{ items, total }` rather than a
bare array. Two reasons, and both come up in code review. It leaves room to
add pagination fields later without breaking clients, and it is not a
top-level JSON array, which used to be an XSS vector and is still a habit
worth keeping.

`?status=` needs validating against the allowed set before you use it.
Remember `req.query.status` is `string | string[] | undefined`, so check
`typeof status === "string"` before comparing, and answer 400 with the exact
body the gate asks for when it is not one of the three.

## Hint 3

```ts
app.get("/tasks", (req, res) => {
  const status = req.query.status;
  if (status !== undefined && /* not an allowed status? */) {
    res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid_status", message: /* ? */ });
    return;
  }
  const items = /* all of them, or the filtered ones */;
  res.json({ items, total: /* which length? */ });
});
```

Two decisions left: the validation test, and where the final "no such route"
middleware goes. It must be registered *after* both routes - a catch-all
registered first answers everything, which is a mistake that produces a
gloriously confusing "all my routes 404" bug.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the write endpoints

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. The zod schemas are provided. Implement:

- `POST /tasks` → **201**, `Location: /tasks/task-1`, the created task.
  Invalid body → **400**
  `{"error":"validation_failed","details":[{"path":"title","message":"..."}]}`;
- `PATCH /tasks/:id` → **200** with the updated task; unknown id → 404;
  invalid body → 400 in the same shape;
- `DELETE /tasks/:id` → **204** with no body; unknown id → 404.

Two details the gate checks and both are about parsing rather than
validating. A `POST` with an extra key it did not ask for comes back without
it. And a `PATCH` carrying `{"id":"hacked"}` leaves the id alone — not because
you wrote a check, but because the schema never mentioned `id` and parsing
removed it.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three routes, and each one is the same three steps: parse the input, find the
row (or not), answer with the right status code.

Do not forget `app.use(express.json())` at the top, or `req.body` is
`undefined` and every schema fails with an unhelpful message about expecting
an object.

The schemas are provided. Note there are two of them: creating requires a
title, patching requires nothing at all - which is exactly what makes PATCH
different from PUT.

## Hint 2

The status codes carry meaning and the gate checks each one:

- **201** for a create, with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource
  (`/tasks/task-1`). The body is the created task, including the id the server
  chose.
- **200** for a successful patch, with the *new* value of the resource.
- **204** for a successful delete: no body at all (`res.status(204).end()`),
  because there is nothing left to describe.
- **404** when the id does not exist - for both patch and delete.

Since both write endpoints validate, a small helper that either returns the
parsed value or answers 400 and returns `null` will save you writing the same
eight lines twice.

## Hint 3

```ts
const input = parseOr400(createTaskSchema, req.body, res);
if (input === null) return;      // the helper already answered
```

Two decisions left. First, the order inside PATCH: validate before you look
the task up, or look it up first? Either passes the gate - but think about
which error a client would rather see when they send a bad body *and* a bad
id, and be able to defend your answer.

Second, the forged-id case. The gate patches with `{ id: "hacked" }` and
expects the id to be untouched. You do not need a check for it: the schema
does not mention `id`, so parsing removes it before your code runs. That is
"parse, don't validate" doing security work for free.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three routes, and each one is the same three steps: parse the input, find the
row (or not), answer with the right status code.

Do not forget `app.use(express.json())` at the top, or `req.body` is
`undefined` and every schema fails with an unhelpful message about expecting
an object.

The schemas are provided. Note there are two of them: creating requires a
title, patching requires nothing at all - which is exactly what makes PATCH
different from PUT.

## Hint 2

The status codes carry meaning and the gate checks each one:

- **201** for a create, with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource
  (`/tasks/task-1`). The body is the created task, including the id the server
  chose.
- **200** for a successful patch, with the *new* value of the resource.
- **204** for a successful delete: no body at all (`res.status(204).end()`),
  because there is nothing left to describe.
- **404** when the id does not exist - for both patch and delete.

Since both write endpoints validate, a small helper that either returns the
parsed value or answers 400 and returns `null` will save you writing the same
eight lines twice.

## Hint 3

```ts
const input = parseOr400(createTaskSchema, req.body, res);
if (input === null) return;      // the helper already answered
```

Two decisions left. First, the order inside PATCH: validate before you look
the task up, or look it up first? Either passes the gate - but think about
which error a client would rather see when they send a bad body *and* a bad
id, and be able to defend your answer.

Second, the forged-id case. The gate patches with `{ id: "hacked" }` and
expects the id to be untouched. You do not need a check for it: the schema
does not mention `id`, so parsing removes it before your code runs. That is
"parse, don't validate" doing security work for free.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the whole API

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Everything from ex2 and ex3, in one app, plus:

- an **`x-request-id` header on every response**, counted from `req-1` by a
  middleware at the top of the stack — including on error responses;
- routes that **throw** `AppError` (provided) instead of answering failures
  themselves;
- a "no such route" middleware after the routes;
- one **error handler** last, which maps:
  - a validation failure → 400 `{ error: "validation_failed", details: [...] }`
  - any other `AppError` → its status, `{ error: <code>, message: <message> }`
  - anything else → 500 `{"error":"internal_error","message":"internal server
    error"}`.

The gate runs a whole lifecycle: list, create, read back at the `Location`
URL, see it in a filtered list, patch it, delete it, and confirm it is gone —
then checks that validation still applies and that an unknown route is a JSON
404. That sequence is what "it works" actually means for an API.

```
uv run dojo test node 11_rest_capstone ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is assembly, not invention: every piece exists in a file you have already
written. What is new is that the routes stop answering errors themselves and
start *throwing* them, and one handler at the bottom turns every throw into a
response.

Build it in this order and run the gate after each step:

1. the request-id middleware, first in the stack;
2. `express.json()`;
3. the four routes from ex2 and ex3;
4. the "no such route" middleware;
5. the error handler, last.

## Hint 2

The shape that makes the routes short: a helper that finds a task or throws.

```ts
function find(tasks: Task[], id: string): Task {
  const task = tasks.find((candidate) => candidate.id === id);
  if (task === undefined) throw new AppError(404, "not_found", "no such task");
  return task;
}
```

Now `GET /tasks/:id` is one line, and the 404 rule lives in exactly one place.

Validation failures need a *different* body from other errors -
`{ error: "validation_failed", details: [...] }` rather than
`{ error, message }` - so either subclass `AppError` with the details attached
(the reference does this) or check for a `ZodError` in the handler. Both are
respectable; pick one and make the handler read cleanly.

## Hint 3

The error handler:

```ts
app.use((error: unknown, _req: Request, res: Response, _next: NextFunction) => {
  if (/* a validation failure? */) { /* 400 + details */ return; }
  if (error instanceof AppError) { /* its status, code and message */ return; }
  res.status(500).json({ error: "internal_error", message: "internal server error" });
});
```

Two decisions left: how you recognise a validation failure, and the order of
the branches (a subclass matches `instanceof AppError` too, so the specific
test has to come first - get this backwards and your details silently
disappear). Check the request-id header on an error response before you call
it done: it is set by the first middleware in the stack, so it should be there
whatever happens afterwards.

lessons.briefing:
# d01 — ESM and CommonJS

Eight problems on the seam between the two module systems — lesson **01_modules**
is where this was taught, and if the first three feel like guessing, reread it
before you carry on. Nothing here is a trick question: every one of them is a
thing you will actually be asked to do the week you inherit a codebase that was
half-migrated in 2021.

## Problem 1 — a module URL is not a path

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `resolveSibling(metaUrl, ...segments)` returns the
absolute filesystem path of `segments` resolved against the directory the module
at `metaUrl` lives in. With no segments it returns that directory itself. It has
to survive a URL containing a percent-encoded space.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a path is not a specifier

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `specifierFor(absolutePath)` returns a string that
`import()` will accept on every platform. A space must come back as `%20`, a `#`
as `%23`, and the result must round-trip through `fileURLToPath` to the exact
path you were given.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex2
```

## Problem 3 — call the CommonJS module you cannot rewrite

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `ex3/legacy-rules.cjs` exports `{ VERSION, RULES, apply }`
and you may not touch it. Export `legacyVersion()` (its `VERSION`), `ruleNames()`
(the keys of its `RULES`, sorted) and `applyRule(name, value)` (a call into its
`apply`, so an unknown rule fails with its message, `unknown rule: triple`).

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex3
```

## Problem 4 — the require cache, and evicting from it

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `ex4/registry.cjs` keeps a list. `sharedRegistry()`
returns the cached instance — the same object on every call. `freshRegistry()`
evicts that module from the cache and loads it again, returning a brand-new
object with an empty list, without disturbing the object anybody already holds.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex4
```

## Problem 5 — live bindings versus copied values

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `ex5/tally.ts` and `ex5/tally.cjs` hold the same counter
in the two module systems. `readTwice()` reads the total three ways — through the
ESM import, through a name destructured out of the `require()`, and as a property
of the `require()`d object — then adds 5 through **both** modules and reads all
three again, returning `{ esm, cjsCopy, cjsProperty }` as `[before, after]` pairs.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex5
```

## Problem 6 — what order do module bodies run in

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Four fixtures sit next to it: `trace.ts` holds a shared
array, `alpha.ts` and `beta.ts` push a label as their bodies run, and `entry.ts`
imports them. The listings are in the file. `predictEvaluationOrder()` returns
the labels in the order they land in `trace`. The gate imports `entry` for real
and reports the first position you got wrong — never what belonged there.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex6
```

## Problem 7 — implement the CommonJS lookup

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `resolveSpecifier(dir, specifier)` resolves a relative
specifier inside one directory the way `require()` does: the path exactly as
written, then `.js`, `.json`, `.cjs`, then `index.js` and `index.json` inside it
if it names a directory. It returns the absolute path, or `null`. A file beats a
directory of the same name.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex7
```

## Problem 8 — implement the modern replacement

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `resolveExports(field, subpath)` resolves a subpath
against a `package.json` `exports` field. A bare string publishes only `.`. An
object may hold exact keys, `*` patterns (which match slashes), and `null`
targets meaning *blocked*. An exact key beats any pattern; among patterns, the
longest literal prefix wins. Anything unmatched is `null`.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d01_esm_cjs

What each of the eight problems was really asking, the mistake that costs
people the question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill this set drills is a single distinction with many faces: **a name, a
path and a URL are three different things, and Node uses all three at once.**
`import "./util"` is a specifier; what it resolves to is a path; what the ESM
loader actually fetches is a URL. Every problem here lives at one of those
conversion points, or at the older seam beside it — CommonJS, where the unit of
identity is a resolved filename in a cache and an export is a property on a
mutable object rather than a binding into a live module. Two systems, two
notions of identity, and the bugs all come from assuming one while standing in
the other. Answer these eight cold and you can walk into a half-migrated
codebase without flinching.

## ex1 — the URL you were handed is not the path you want

**What it tested:** whether you know that `import.meta.url` is a URL string and
that converting it is a library call, not string surgery.

**The classic mistake:** `metaUrl.replace("file://", "")`. It works on your
Linux laptop, produces `/C:/Users/...` on Windows, and turns `two words` into
`two%20words` on everybody's machine. The bug reaches production because the
happy path has no spaces in it.

**Model answer:** `fileURLToPath` decodes the percent-escapes and strips the
Windows drive prefix, so the whole exercise is that one call plus
`path.dirname`, and `path.join` handles the `..` in the third assertion for
free.

## ex2 — the path you have is not a specifier

**What it tested:** the reverse conversion, and the reason it exists. Dynamic
`import()` takes a *specifier*: a relative path, a bare package name, or a URL.
An absolute Windows path is none of those — `C:\plugins\x.mjs` starts with what
a URL parser reads as a scheme.

**The classic mistake:** `"file://" + absolutePath`. On Windows that yields
`file://C:/...`, where `C:` is parsed as the *host*, and the import fails with a
message about an unsupported URL. Everything after a `#` silently disappears
too.

**Model answer:** `pathToFileURL(p).href` — one call that adds the third slash,
percent-encodes the reserved characters, and gives back a string rather than a
`URL` object, which is what `import()` and the gate both want.

## ex3 — you cannot rewrite everything

**What it tested:** the `createRequire` escape hatch, and the discipline to
*call* the legacy module rather than copy what it does.

**The classic mistake:** two of them. Reimplementing the rules in TypeScript,
which passes today and drifts from the real module next quarter; and
maintaining `["double", "half", "negate"]` as a hand-written list, which is the
same drift in miniature. The gate checks both by asking for the version and the
sorted keys straight off the exports object.

**Model answer:** build the `require` once at module scope from
`import.meta.url`, require once, and delegate — `applyRule` calls the module's
`apply`, so the unknown-rule message belongs to the module that owns the rules.

## ex4 — the cache is the module system

**What it tested:** that `require()` is memoised on the *resolved filename*, so
"the module" and "the object require gives you" are the same thing, and that
the cache is an ordinary object you can delete from.

**The classic mistake:** believing the eviction rewrites what callers already
hold. It does not: `delete require.cache[id]` only changes what the *next*
require returns. A long-lived reference keeps pointing at the old instance, and
two halves of an app can end up talking to different copies of the same module

What each of the eight problems was really asking, the mistake that costs
people the question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill this set drills is a single distinction with many faces: **a name, a

the other. Answer these eight cold and you can walk into a half-migrated
codebase without flinching.

## Problem 1 — a module URL is not a path

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `resolveSibling(metaUrl, ...segments)` returns the

`import.meta.url` is a URL string (`file:///C:/…` or `file:///home/…`), not a
filesystem path. Two things are wrong with treating it as one: the characters
are percent-encoded, and on Windows the path is prefixed with an extra slash
before the drive letter. `node:url` has one function whose entire job is
undoing both.

## Hint 2

Three steps, in this order: URL to path, path to directory, directory joined
with the segments.

```ts
const file = /* the node:url function */ (metaUrl);
const dir = path.dirname(file);
```

Then join. `path.join` normalises `..` for you, which is why the third
assertion in the gate works without any special handling — and note what
`path.join(dir)` with no extra segments returns, because that is the no-segment
case handled for free (or not, if you decide it needs a branch).

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a path is not a specifier

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `specifierFor(absolutePath)` returns a string that
`import()` will accept on every platform. A space must come back as `%20`, a `#`
as `%23`, and the result must round-trip through `fileURLToPath` to the exact
path you were given.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex1 run backwards, and `node:url` has the matching function. Do not
build the string yourself: `"file://" + p` is wrong on Windows (one slash
short), wrong for spaces, and wrong for `#`, `?` and `%`.

## Hint 2

The function you want returns a `URL` object, not a string. The gate compares
strings, so decide which property of a `URL` is the one an `import()` call
wants — `href`, `pathname` and `toString()` are not interchangeable here, and
only one of them survives the round-trip back through `fileURLToPath`.

## Problem 4 — the require cache, and evicting from it

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `ex4/registry.cjs` keeps a list. `sharedRegistry()`
returns the cached instance — the same object on every call. `freshRegistry()`
evicts that module from the cache and loads it again, returning a brand-new

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`require()` is memoised. The key is not the specifier you typed, it is the
*resolved absolute filename* — which is why two different relative specifiers
pointing at the same file share one entry. `sharedRegistry()` therefore needs
no caching of its own: just require it and return.

## Hint 2

The cache is an ordinary object hanging off the require function, keyed by that
resolved filename. Two pieces fit together:

```ts
require.resolve("./registry.cjs"); // the key
require.cache;                     // the object it is a key of
```

Delete the entry, then require again. Note what that means for the object you
handed out a moment ago — nobody rewrites it, it simply stops being the one the
cache will serve, which is exactly what the gate checks last.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`require()` is memoised. The key is not the specifier you typed, it is the
*resolved absolute filename* — which is why two different relative specifiers
pointing at the same file share one entry. `sharedRegistry()` therefore needs
no caching of its own: just require it and return.

## Hint 2

The cache is an ordinary object hanging off the require function, keyed by that
resolved filename. Two pieces fit together:

```ts
require.resolve("./registry.cjs"); // the key
require.cache;                     // the object it is a key of
```

Delete the entry, then require again. Note what that means for the object you
handed out a moment ago — nobody rewrites it, it simply stops being the one the
cache will serve, which is exactly what the gate checks last.

## Problem 5 — live bindings versus copied values

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `ex5/tally.ts` and `ex5/tally.cjs` hold the same counter
in the two module systems. `readTwice()` reads the total three ways — through the
ESM import, through a name destructured out of the `require()`, and as a property
of the `require()`d object — then adds 5 through **both** modules and reads all
three again, returning `{ esm, cjsCopy, cjsProperty }` as `[before, after]` pairs.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three readers, three mechanisms:

- `import { total } from "./tally"` gives you a *binding*, not a value. Reading
  `total` later re-reads the exporting module variable.
- `const { total } = require("./tally.cjs")` runs an ordinary property read at
  the moment the line executes, and stores the number in a local.
- `legacy.total` is a property read every time you write it.

Only one of the three can change under you, and only one of the three can go
stale.

## Hint 2

Structure the body as: take all three "before" readings, call both `add`
functions, then take all three "after" readings — except that one of the three
cannot be re-read at all, because the local you copied it into is the only
thing you have.

That last sentence is the answer to why `cjsCopy` looks the way it does in the
gate. Write it so it falls out of the mechanism rather than typing the number.

## Problem 7 — implement the CommonJS lookup

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `resolveSpecifier(dir, specifier)` resolves a relative
specifier inside one directory the way `require()` does: the path exactly as
written, then `.js`, `.json`, `.cjs`, then `index.js` and `index.json` inside it
if it names a directory. It returns the absolute path, or `null`. A file beats a
directory of the same name.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The algorithm is a list of candidates tried in a fixed order, and the first one
that exists **as a file** wins. Write the list out before you write any code:
the bare path, the three extensions, the two index files. Now the function is a
loop over that list.

## Hint 2

Two traps live in the details.

`existsSync`-style checks answer "is there something here", not "is there a
*file* here" — and the directory case needs the difference, or `./lib` matches
the directory `lib` itself and stops. `stat()` gives you `isFile()`.

`stat()` on a missing path rejects, so the candidate test has to swallow that
rejection and answer `false`. That is one of the rare places a bare `catch`
with no rethrow is the right call — say out loud why, because an interviewer
will ask.

## Hint 3

Build the base path with `path.resolve(dir, specifier)` rather than string
concatenation: it makes the result absolute, normalises the separators for the
platform, and removes the leading `./` in one step.

The remaining decision is what to do when a candidate exists but is a
directory: you have to keep going rather than return it, and the order in which
you keep going is what the last two assertions in the gate are about.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The algorithm is a list of candidates tried in a fixed order, and the first one
that exists **as a file** wins. Write the list out before you write any code:
the bare path, the three extensions, the two index files. Now the function is a
loop over that list.

## Hint 2

Two traps live in the details.

`existsSync`-style checks answer "is there something here", not "is there a
*file* here" — and the directory case needs the difference, or `./lib` matches
the directory `lib` itself and stops. `stat()` gives you `isFile()`.

`stat()` on a missing path rejects, so the candidate test has to swallow that
rejection and answer `false`. That is one of the rare places a bare `catch`
with no rethrow is the right call — say out loud why, because an interviewer
will ask.

## Hint 3

Build the base path with `path.resolve(dir, specifier)` rather than string
concatenation: it makes the result absolute, normalises the separators for the
platform, and removes the leading `./` in one step.

The remaining decision is what to do when a candidate exists but is a
directory: you have to keep going rather than return it, and the order in which
you keep going is what the last two assertions in the gate are about.

## Problem 8 — implement the modern replacement

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `resolveExports(field, subpath)` resolves a subpath
against a `package.json` `exports` field. A bare string publishes only `.`. An
object may hold exact keys, `*` patterns (which match slashes), and `null`
targets meaning *blocked*. An exact key beats any pattern; among patterns, the
longest literal prefix wins. Anything unmatched is `null`.

```
uv run dojo test node d01_esm_cjs ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four cases, and getting them in the right order is most of the work:

1. the whole field is a string — only `.` resolves;
2. an exact key exists — use it, even if its value is `null`;
3. some pattern keys match — pick one and substitute;
4. nothing matches — `null`.

Case 2 before case 3 is what makes `./features/legacy` beat `./features/*`.

## Hint 2

A pattern is a key containing one `*`. Split it there into a prefix and a
suffix; it matches when the subpath starts with the prefix, ends with the
suffix, and is long enough to have both without them overlapping. Whatever sits
between them is the captured text, and it goes into the `*` in the target.

Note that `*` is not a glob: it matches slashes happily, which is why
`./features/deep/nested` resolves.

## Hint 3

For the tie-break, keep a running best while you loop and only replace it when
the new pattern has a strictly longer prefix. Two decisions are left to you: at
what point you check for a `null` target (before or after choosing the winner
changes the answer for `./internal/secret`), and how you substitute — `*` may
appear only once in a target, so the simplest string replacement is enough.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four cases, and getting them in the right order is most of the work:

1. the whole field is a string — only `.` resolves;
2. an exact key exists — use it, even if its value is `null`;
3. some pattern keys match — pick one and substitute;
4. nothing matches — `null`.

Case 2 before case 3 is what makes `./features/legacy` beat `./features/*`.

## Hint 2

A pattern is a key containing one `*`. Split it there into a prefix and a
suffix; it matches when the subpath starts with the prefix, ends with the
suffix, and is long enough to have both without them overlapping. Whatever sits
between them is the captured text, and it goes into the `*` in the target.

Note that `*` is not a glob: it matches slashes happily, which is why
`./features/deep/nested` resolves.

## Hint 3

For the tie-break, keep a running best while you loop and only replace it when
the new pattern has a strictly longer prefix. Two decisions are left to you: at
what point you check for a `null` target (before or after choosing the winner
changes the answer for `./internal/secret`), and how you substitute — `*` may
appear only once in a target, so the simplest string replacement is enough.

# d02 — Module patterns

Eight problems on what you build *out of* modules once you know how they load —
lesson **01_modules** again, this time the second half of it: module state,
singletons and the seams that keep a module testable. No filesystem, no clock,
no network; every answer is a closure and a decision about who owns what.

## Problem 1 — the lazy singleton

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `once(factory)` returns a wrapper that runs `factory` at
most once and hands back the same value ever after. A factory returning
`undefined` counts as having run; a factory that **throws** is not remembered,
and the next call tries again.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a registry that refuses to be ambiguous

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createRegistry<T>()` returns `{ register, get, has,
names }`. `register` throws `duplicate registration: <name>` on a name already
taken; `get` throws `nothing registered under: <name>`; `names()` is sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex2
```

## Problem 3 — defaults in, frozen out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `defineConfig(overrides)` merges onto the defaults
`{ port: 3000, host: "0.0.0.0", limits: { maxBodyBytes: 1000000, timeoutMs:
5000 }, tags: [] }`. `limits` merges key by key; `tags` is replaced wholesale.
The result is frozen all the way down, and two calls share no objects at all.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex3
```

## Problem 4 — a namespace that builds on demand

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createNamespace(factories)` returns an object with one
enumerable property per key. `Object.keys()` lists them all without evaluating
anything; reading one property runs that one factory, once; reading it again
returns the same instance; an unknown property is `undefined`.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex4
```

## Problem 5 — the dependency seam

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createService(overrides?)` builds a service over
`{ now, ids, store }`, taking anything not overridden from a **fresh** set of
defaults — real `Date.now`, ids counting `e-1`, `e-2`, …, and an in-memory
store. `record(event)` returns and saves `{ id, event, at }`; `history()`
returns the saved entries. Two services must never share a store.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a plugin host with a lifecycle

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createPluginHost()` returns `{ use, start, run, stop,
started }`. `use` is chainable and registers only; `start()` calls each plugin's
`setup(api)` once in registration order; `api.addCommand(name, run)` makes
`run(name)` work. `start` twice throws `already started`, `use` after start
throws `cannot add plugins after start`, `run` before start or after stop throws
`not started`, an unknown command throws `unknown command: <name>`. `stop()`
calls the teardown functions plugins returned, in **reverse** order.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a container that detects its own loops

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createContainer()` returns `{ register, resolve }`.
A factory is handed the container so it can resolve its own dependencies, and
runs at most once — `resolve` is a singleton lookup. An unregistered name throws
`nothing registered under: <name>`; a loop throws
`circular dependency: left -> right -> left`, and the container keeps working
afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex7
```

## Problem 8 — order the graph, deterministically

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `orderPlugins(plugins)` returns every `name` exactly
once, each after everything in its `after` list, breaking ties alphabetically so
the input order is irrelevant. An `after` naming an absent plugin throws
`unknown dependency: <name> needs <missing>`; a loop throws
`circular dependency among: a, b` listing only the stuck names, sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex8
```

# Reading - node/d02_module_patterns

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **ownership**: for every piece of state in a module,
who creates it, when, and how many of it exist. A module body runs once per
process, so anything you write at module scope is a singleton whether you meant
it or not — which is the source of the shared-store bug in ex5, the frozen
defaults bug in ex3, and half the "works alone, fails in the suite" reports you
will ever triage. The pattern that unites all eight answers is the same move:
push creation into a **function** and hand the result to the caller, so the
module exports a way to build one rather than the one. Lazy (ex1, ex4),
validated (ex2), copied (ex3), injected (ex5), staged (ex6), graphed (ex7, ex8)
— all of them are that move applied at a different scale.

## ex1 — the flag is not the value

**What it tested:** whether your memo distinguishes "has not run" from "ran and
produced nothing", and whether a failure is a state you can recover from.

**The classic mistake:** `if (value === undefined) value = factory()`. A factory
that legitimately returns `undefined` re-runs on every call, which turns a lazy
singleton into an eager multiplier — and if the factory has side effects, into a
bug you find in production.

**Model answer:** a separate boolean, set *after* the factory returns, so a
throw leaves the flag false and the retry is free. That is exactly what
`require()` does with a module whose body threw, and saying so is the sentence
an interviewer is listening for.

## ex2 — errors at the boundary

**What it tested:** that a lookup table is a place to *refuse* things. Two
plugins registering `csv` is a bug; returning `undefined` for `xml` moves the
crash three frames away from the cause.

**The classic mistake:** a plain object as the store. `{}` inherits
`toString`, `constructor` and friends, so `has("constructor")` is `true` on an
empty registry and `get("constructor")` hands out a function. `Map` has no
prototype chain to trip over and no coercion of keys.

**Model answer:** `Map` plus two guards, and `names()` returning a fresh sorted
array rather than the live key iterator — the same instinct that makes
`history()` copy in ex5.

## ex3 — shallow is the default, twice

**What it tested:** two independent depths that both default to shallow. Object
spread merges one level; `Object.freeze` freezes one level. The exercise needs
both to go one deeper, and needs you to notice they are separate problems.

**The classic mistake:** module-level `const DEFAULTS`. `{ ...DEFAULTS }` copies
the top level but every call then shares the *same* `limits` object, so the
first `Object.freeze` freezes it for the whole process and the second call
inherits a frozen nested object it did not create. The symptom is a test that
passes alone and throws in the suite.

**Model answer:** a `defaults()` function returning a fresh graph, an explicit
spread for the nested object, and freezing the children before the parent —
because after the parent is frozen you can still reach the children, which is
precisely the hole being closed.

## ex4 — the shape before the contents

**What it tested:** getters, and the reason a lazy namespace beats a lazy
function: callers can enumerate what exists without paying to build it.

**The classic mistake:** `Object.defineProperty` defaults `enumerable` to
`false`, so a correct-looking implementation returns an object whose
`Object.keys` is empty — the namespace becomes invisible to every tool that
introspects it. The other mistake is one shared memo cell for all properties,
which happens the moment the `built` flag is hoisted above the loop.

**Model answer:** one `defineProperty` per entry, `enumerable: true` stated
explicitly, and the `let` pair declared *inside* the loop body so each getter
closes over its own.

## ex5 — the module that takes what it needs

**What it tested:** inversion of control at the smallest useful scale. A service
that imports its clock cannot be tested without freezing time globally; a
service that takes `now` can be tested with a two-line fake, which is exactly
what the gate does.

**The classic mistake:** `const defaultDeps = { store: createMemoryStore() }` at
module scope. Every service in the process then appends to one array — and
because the first test to run is usually the one that passes, the failure shows
up somewhere else entirely.

**Model answer:** `{ ...createDefaultDeps(), ...overrides }`, where the defaults
are built per call. Shallow merge is the right depth here: a dependency is
replaced whole or not at all.

## ex6 — a lifecycle is a contract about time

**What it tested:** staging. Registration, setup and teardown are three
different moments, and the value of the pattern comes from refusing to blur
them — which means the interesting code is the guards, not the happy path.

**The classic mistake:** tearing down in registration order. Plugins are
normally built on the ones before them, so shutting down the logger before the
router that logs its shutdown is how you lose the last, most useful lines of a
crash. The mirror mistake is running `setup` at `use()` time, which makes plugin
order depend on import order.

**Model answer:** one `running` flag guarding all four transitions, one `api`
object shared by every `setup`, teardowns collected in order and replayed
backwards.

## ex7 — a stack is what turns a hang into a message

**What it tested:** singleton resolution plus loop detection, and the discipline
to keep the bookkeeping balanced on the error path.

**The classic mistake:** detecting the cycle but leaving the name on the
resolution stack, because the pop sits after the `return` instead of in a
`finally`. Everything resolved afterwards then reports a phantom circular
dependency, and the second bug hides the first. The other classic is using a
`Set` for the stack, which detects the loop but cannot print the path — and the
path is the only part a human needs.

**Model answer:** an array as the stack, `slice` from the first occurrence to
build the message, and `try`/`finally` around the factory call so the pop
happens whatever the factory does.

## ex8 — deterministic is a requirement, not a nicety

**What it tested:** Kahn's algorithm, plus the observation that a topological
sort has many valid answers and a build system needs exactly one of them.

**The classic mistake:** draining every unblocked node in a batch. Removing one
node can unblock another that sorts earlier than the rest of the batch, so
batching produces a valid order that is not the *stable* one — and a plugin
order that changes when someone reorders an array is a bug report nobody can
reproduce. Skipping the up-front validation is the other one: a typo in `after`
then surfaces as "circular dependency", which sends the reader hunting for a
loop that does not exist.

**Model answer:** validate all `after` names first, then loop: sort the
currently-ready names, take exactly one, delete it from every remaining
blocker set, and report whatever is left over if a pass finds nothing ready.

## Further reading

- [MDN: Closures](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Closures) — the mechanism every one of these eight answers is built on.
- [MDN: `Object.defineProperty()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/defineProperty) — property descriptors, getters, and why `enumerable` defaults to `false`.
- [MDN: `Object.freeze()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/freeze) — including the explicit note that the freeze is shallow.
- [MDN: `Map`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map) — key handling and the comparison with plain objects that ex2 turns on.
- [Node.js: Modules — caching](https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html#caching) — why module scope is process-wide singleton scope, which is the premise of this whole set.

## Problem 1 — the lazy singleton

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `once(factory)` returns a wrapper that runs `factory` at
most once and hands back the same value ever after. A factory returning
`undefined` counts as having run; a factory that **throws** is not remembered,
and the next call tries again.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`once` builds nothing itself — it returns a closure over two variables that
outlive each call. Sketch those two variables before you write the body, and
ask what each one is for.

## Hint 2

The tempting single variable is the cached value, tested with
`if (value === undefined)`. The gate has a factory that returns `undefined` on
purpose, because that shortcut re-runs it forever.

The other half is the ordering inside the `if`: the line that records "we have
run" has to sit somewhere relative to the line that calls the factory, and only
one of the two placements lets a throwing factory be retried.

## Problem 2 — a registry that refuses to be ambiguous

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createRegistry<T>()` returns `{ register, get, has,
names }`. `register` throws `duplicate registration: <name>` on a name already
taken; `get` throws `nothing registered under: <name>`; `names()` is sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Closure over one collection, four methods returned in an object literal. The
only real decision is what the collection is — and a plain object brings
inherited keys with it, so `has("toString")` answers `true` on an empty
registry unless you are careful.

## Hint 2

Both error paths are the same shape: check membership, throw a `new Error` with
a template string that includes the name, otherwise proceed. Write the messages
exactly as the gate quotes them.

`names()` returns a **new sorted array** every call. Handing out the live key
list would let a caller sort it, splice it, or hold it and be surprised later —
a registry that leaks its internals is not a registry.

## Hint 1

Closure over one collection, four methods returned in an object literal. The
only real decision is what the collection is — and a plain object brings
inherited keys with it, so `has("toString")` answers `true` on an empty
registry unless you are careful.

## Hint 2

Both error paths are the same shape: check membership, throw a `new Error` with
a template string that includes the name, otherwise proceed. Write the messages
exactly as the gate quotes them.

`names()` returns a **new sorted array** every call. Handing out the live key
list would let a caller sort it, splice it, or hold it and be surprised later —
a registry that leaks its internals is not a registry.

## Problem 3 — defaults in, frozen out

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `defineConfig(overrides)` merges onto the defaults
`{ port: 3000, host: "0.0.0.0", limits: { maxBodyBytes: 1000000, timeoutMs:
5000 }, tags: [] }`. `limits` merges key by key; `tags` is replaced wholesale.
The result is frozen all the way down, and two calls share no objects at all.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex3
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent requirements, and people usually get one of them:

- **merge depth.** `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }` replaces `limits` entirely,
  so an override of `timeoutMs` alone silently drops `maxBodyBytes`. The nested
  object needs its own spread.
- **freeze depth.** `Object.freeze` is shallow. `config.limits.timeoutMs = 1`
  still works after freezing `config`.

## Hint 2

The third requirement is the one that bites in production. If your defaults are
a module-level `const`, then `{ ...DEFAULTS }` copies the top level but every
call shares the *same* `limits` object — so the first `Object.freeze` freezes
it for the whole process, and the second call quietly inherits whatever the
first one did to it.

Make the defaults a function that returns a fresh object graph, and the problem
disappears. Freeze the nested pieces before the outer object, and decide for
yourself whether `tags` needs copying as well as freezing (ask what happens if
a caller keeps a reference to the array they passed in).

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two independent requirements, and people usually get one of them:

- **merge depth.** `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }` replaces `limits` entirely,
  so an override of `timeoutMs` alone silently drops `maxBodyBytes`. The nested
  object needs its own spread.
- **freeze depth.** `Object.freeze` is shallow. `config.limits.timeoutMs = 1`
  still works after freezing `config`.

## Hint 2

The third requirement is the one that bites in production. If your defaults are
a module-level `const`, then `{ ...DEFAULTS }` copies the top level but every
call shares the *same* `limits` object — so the first `Object.freeze` freezes
it for the whole process, and the second call quietly inherits whatever the
first one did to it.

Make the defaults a function that returns a fresh object graph, and the problem
disappears. Freeze the nested pieces before the outer object, and decide for
yourself whether `tags` needs copying as well as freezing (ask what happens if
a caller keeps a reference to the array they passed in).

## Problem 5 — the dependency seam

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createService(overrides?)` builds a service over
`{ now, ids, store }`, taking anything not overridden from a **fresh** set of
defaults — real `Date.now`, ids counting `e-1`, `e-2`, …, and an in-memory
store. `record(event)` returns and saves `{ id, event, at }`; `history()`
returns the saved entries. Two services must never share a store.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The seam is one line: `const deps = { ...someDefaults, ...overrides }`. Spread
is a shallow merge, which is exactly right here — a caller either replaces a
whole dependency or does not mention it. Everything the service does afterwards
goes through `deps`, never through an import.

## Hint 2

The trap is where `someDefaults` comes from. Written as a module-level constant,
the store inside it is created once when the module is first imported, so every
service in the process appends to the same array — invisible until a second
test runs and finds the first one's data.

Make it a function that builds the defaults fresh, and call it inside
`createService`. The same reasoning applies to the default id counter: it has to
count per service, which means the `let` lives inside that function too.

`history()` returning a copy rather than the live array is the last decision,
and the reason is the same one as ex2's `names()`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The seam is one line: `const deps = { ...someDefaults, ...overrides }`. Spread
is a shallow merge, which is exactly right here — a caller either replaces a
whole dependency or does not mention it. Everything the service does afterwards
goes through `deps`, never through an import.

## Hint 2

The trap is where `someDefaults` comes from. Written as a module-level constant,
the store inside it is created once when the module is first imported, so every
service in the process appends to the same array — invisible until a second
test runs and finds the first one's data.

Make it a function that builds the defaults fresh, and call it inside
`createService`. The same reasoning applies to the default id counter: it has to
count per service, which means the `let` lives inside that function too.

`history()` returning a copy rather than the live array is the last decision,
and the reason is the same one as ex2's `names()`.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — a plugin host with a lifecycle

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createPluginHost()` returns `{ use, start, run, stop,
started }`. `use` is chainable and registers only; `start()` calls each plugin's
`setup(api)` once in registration order; `api.addCommand(name, run)` makes
`run(name)` work. `start` twice throws `already started`, `use` after start
throws `cannot add plugins after start`, `run` before start or after stop throws
`not started`, an unknown command throws `unknown command: <name>`. `stop()`
calls the teardown functions plugins returned, in **reverse** order.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four pieces of state in the closure: the registered plugins, the commands they
add, the teardowns they return, and one boolean for whether the host is
running. Every method is then a guard plus two lines.

For `use` to be chainable it has to return the host object — which means
building the object into a named `const` first, so the method has something to
return.

## Hint 2

`start()` is where the `api` object comes from: build it once, pass the same one
to every `setup`, and collect the return values. `setup` may return nothing, so
check the return is a function before pushing it.

Reverse teardown is a backwards `for` loop, or `[...teardowns].reverse()` —
mutating the array you are iterating is a way to get this subtly wrong.

## Hint 3

Decide what `stop()` leaves behind. The gate calls `run` afterwards and expects
`not started`, which the running flag alone already gives you — but think about
whether the commands from the previous run should still be sitting in the map
if someone calls `start()` again on a host they have restarted.

There is no single right answer to that; there is a right answer to "does your
code say which one you chose".

Four pieces of state in the closure: the registered plugins, the commands they
add, the teardowns they return, and one boolean for whether the host is
running. Every method is then a guard plus two lines.

return.

## Hint 2

`start()` is where the `api` object comes from: build it once, pass the same one
to every `setup`, and collect the return values. `setup` may return nothing, so
check the return is a function before pushing it.

Reverse teardown is a backwards `for` loop, or `[...teardowns].reverse()` —
mutating the array you are iterating is a way to get this subtly wrong.

## Hint 3

Decide what `stop()` leaves behind. The gate calls `run` afterwards and expects
`not started`, which the running flag alone already gives you — but think about
whether the commands from the previous run should still be sitting in the map
if someone calls `start()` again on a host they have restarted.

There is no single right answer to that; there is a right answer to "does your
code say which one you chose".

## Problem 7 — a container that detects its own loops

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createContainer()` returns `{ register, resolve }`.
A factory is handed the container so it can resolve its own dependencies, and
runs at most once — `resolve` is a singleton lookup. An unregistered name throws

afterwards.

## Problem 8 — order the graph, deterministically

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `orderPlugins(plugins)` returns every `name` exactly
once, each after everything in its `after` list, breaking ties alphabetically so
the input order is irrelevant. An `after` naming an absent plugin throws
`unknown dependency: <name> needs <missing>`; a loop throws
`circular dependency among: a, b` listing only the stuck names, sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d02_module_patterns ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is a topological sort, and the readable version is Kahn's algorithm: keep
a map from each name to the set of names still blocking it, repeatedly take a
name with nothing blocking it, and remove it from everybody else's set.

Validate the `after` names against the full set of plugin names **before** the
loop starts, or a typo turns into a phantom cycle instead of the message the
gate asks for.

## Hint 2

The determinism requirement lands in one place: at each step there may be
several unblocked names, and you must take the alphabetically first. Collect the
candidates, sort, take one — not all of them at once, because removing one can
unblock another that sorts earlier than the rest of the batch.

## Hint 3

The cycle case is what is left when a pass finds **no** unblocked name and the
map is not yet empty. Everything still in the map is stuck, and the message
wants those names sorted — which is why deleting resolved names from the map as
you go matters: it is what keeps `z` out of the cycle report.

The remaining decision is whether you sort the candidate list every pass or keep
a sorted structure; both pass, and only one of them is worth defending in an
interview for a graph of ten plugins.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is a topological sort, and the readable version is Kahn's algorithm: keep
a map from each name to the set of names still blocking it, repeatedly take a
name with nothing blocking it, and remove it from everybody else's set.

Validate the `after` names against the full set of plugin names **before** the
loop starts, or a typo turns into a phantom cycle instead of the message the
gate asks for.

## Hint 2

The determinism requirement lands in one place: at each step there may be
several unblocked names, and you must take the alphabetically first. Collect the
candidates, sort, take one — not all of them at once, because removing one can
unblock another that sorts earlier than the rest of the batch.

## Hint 3

The cycle case is what is left when a pass finds **no** unblocked name and the
map is not yet empty. Everything still in the map is stuck, and the message
wants those names sorted — which is why deleting resolved names from the map as
you go matters: it is what keeps `z` out of the cycle report.

The remaining decision is whether you sort the candidate list every pass or keep
a sorted structure; both pass, and only one of them is worth defending in an
interview for a graph of ten plugins.

# d03 — Event loop order

Five predictions and three pieces of code, all drilling one skill: knowing which
queue a callback is in and when that queue runs. This is lesson **02_event_loop**
made automatic — if problem 1 is not instant, go back and reread it, because
problems 3 and 7 assume you can do problem 1 in your head.

Every snippet is scheduled from inside a **timer callback**, the ordinary
context for server code, because the ordering at the top level of an ES module
is subtly different. The gate never prints the right answer: it tells you the
first position where your prediction and reality parted company.

## Problem 1 — the four queues

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `predictOrder()` returns the five labels `./snippet.ts`
logs, in order. The snippet is reproduced in the file.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex1
```

## Problem 2 — callbacks that schedule more callbacks

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Six labels this time, and two of them are queued from
inside another callback — one onto a queue that has not run yet, one onto a
queue that has already been drained.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex2
```

## Problem 3 — an async function is a scheduling instruction

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Seven labels: two nested async functions and a two-link
`.then` chain. Count the microtask hops rather than reading it as a program.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex3
```

## Problem 4 — one label per queue

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `scheduleLabels(log)` logs `sync` immediately, then
arranges for `tick`, `micro`, `check` and `timer` to come out in that order. The
gate queues a microtask of its own *before* calling you, and expects it to land
between `tick` and `micro` — which is what proves which queue each label went
into.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex4
```

## Problem 5 — starvation, and the cure

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Both functions handle every item in order and resolve
when done, one item per scheduled callback. `drainQueue` uses the queue that
re-enters the checkpoint, so a `setImmediate` queued before the call gets no
turn until the drain finishes. `drainQueueFairly` uses the one that completes a
turn of the loop between items, so it does.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a queue that refills itself

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Six labels. A `process.nextTick` callback re-arms itself
twice; a microtask and a timer are waiting.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a chain is not a block

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Nine labels: a three-link `.then` chain, two bare
microtasks and an async function with two awaits, all queued during the same
synchronous run. This is the hard one; do it with a written-out queue.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex7
```

## Problem 8 — map a list without blocking the loop

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `yieldingMap(items, size, fn)` maps in chunks of `size`,
handing the event loop a full turn **between** chunks and not after the last,
and resolves to `{ results, yields }` with results in input order. Five items in
chunks of two is three chunks and two yields.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex8
```

# Reading - node/d03_event_loop_order

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is a single mental object: **the checkpoint**. Between
any two callbacks the runtime runs, it does the same thing — drain the
`nextTick` queue completely, drain the microtask queue completely, and if either
refilled, go round again. Only when both are empty does the event loop advance
to a phase: timers, then poll, then check. Every prediction here is that
sentence applied carefully, and every piece of code here is a choice about which
queue to put work in. The pattern that unites them: a microtask is *not* a turn
of the loop. Anything that only ever queues microtasks — `await`,
`process.nextTick`, `.then` — is still holding the thread, and nothing else in
the process can happen. That is why ex5 and ex8 exist next to five prediction
problems.

## ex1 — the order, without any complications

**What it tested:** the base case. Synchronous code, then `nextTick`, then
microtasks, then the loop's own phases.

**The classic mistake:** putting the timer before the microtask because
`setTimeout(..., 0)` reads like "right now", or putting `queueMicrotask` before
`process.nextTick` because microtasks are the standard and `nextTick` is the
Node oddity. Node drains its own queue first, deliberately, and that is one of
the few places Node departs from the browser.

**Model answer:** both synchronous logs first — nothing scheduled can start
while the function that scheduled it is still running — then C, D, B.

## ex2 — the checkpoint is a loop, not a sequence

**What it tested:** what happens when a callback adds to a queue while the
checkpoint is running, and whether you know which queues have already been
drained at that moment.

**The classic mistake:** expecting `micro-from-tick` to run immediately after
`tick-1`, as though queueing a microtask from inside a `nextTick` callback
interrupted the drain. It does not: the tick queue empties first, and the
microtask joins the ones already waiting, behind `micro-1`.

**Model answer:** sync, both ticks, both microtasks in queueing order, and then
the tick queued from a microtask — which only runs because the checkpoint goes
round again after finding its queue refilled.

## ex3 — awaiting a promise costs an extra hop

**What it tested:** the translation from `async`/`await` to microtasks, and the
one detail almost nobody has right: `await` on a plain value resumes in one
microtask, but `await` on a *promise* has to adopt that promise first, and
adoption costs an extra hop.

**The classic mistake:** predicting `outer-end` immediately after `inner-end`.
It reads that way — `inner()` finished, so `outer` continues — but `then-1` was
queued during the synchronous run and gets there first, because `outer` is still
one hop behind.

**Model answer:** three synchronous labels, then `inner-end`, then `then-1`,
then `outer-end`, then `then-2`. If your model predicted six labels in the right
order and one in the wrong place, your model is one hop off, and it is worth
fixing rather than memorising.

## ex4 — writing into a queue on purpose

**What it tested:** the inverse of the prediction problems. Given a required
order, choose the mechanism — which is the form the question actually takes at
work.

**The classic mistake:** treating `setImmediate` and `setTimeout(fn, 0)` as
interchangeable. They race unpredictably at the top level of a program, which is
why everybody has seen both orders and concluded it is random. It is not: from
inside an I/O or timer callback, the check phase of *this* turn comes before the
timers phase of the *next* one, so `setImmediate` wins every time.

**Model answer:** five lines, one per mechanism, and the ability to say why the
last two are deterministic in this context and not in general.

## ex5 — the difference that matters in production

**What it tested:** whether "yield to the event loop" means something specific
to you. A recursive `process.nextTick` loop is the classic accidental denial of
service: the process is not blocked in the CPU sense, yet no timer fires, no
socket is read, and no health check is answered.

**The classic mistake:** believing `await` fixes it. Awaiting an
already-resolved promise queues a microtask, which the checkpoint drains before
the loop advances — so an `await`-per-item loop starves exactly as thoroughly as
a `nextTick`-per-item loop, just with nicer syntax.

**Model answer:** one driver parameterised by the scheduler, `process.nextTick`
for the starving version and `setImmediate` for the fair one — and the first
item handled synchronously, so the yields land between items rather than in
front of them.

## ex6 — a queue with no fixed length

**What it tested:** that the `nextTick` drain is `while (queue.length)`, not a
pass over a snapshot. Everything pushed during the drain is drained in the same
pass.

**The classic mistake:** predicting `tick-1`, `micro`, `tick-2`, … — imagining
the queues alternate one entry at a time. They do not; each is emptied before
the next is touched, and "emptied" includes whatever arrived in the meantime.

**Model answer:** the three ticks run back to back with nothing between them,
then the microtask, then the timer. Three is a demo; a few thousand is an
incident, and that is the entire content of the warning in Node's docs.

## ex7 — one microtask per link

**What it tested:** the bookkeeping. Nine labels, four schedulers, and no rule
you have not already used — which is exactly what makes it the interview
version.

**The classic mistake:** treating `.then(a).then(b).then(c)` as a block of three
microtasks queued together. Only `a` is queued up front; `b` is queued when `a`
returns and the intermediate promise settles. Everything else waiting in the
queue runs in between, which is why `q1`, `q2` and `a-1` all land inside the
chain.

**Model answer:** write the queue as a list, append as you go, and process it
front to back. The moment you stop trying to hold it in your head, the problem
becomes mechanical.

## ex8 — chunking, with the yield in the right place

**What it tested:** ex5's lesson applied to a real shape — processing a large
array without making the process unresponsive — plus an off-by-one that the
gate pins down precisely.

**The classic mistake:** two of them. Yielding with `await Promise.resolve()`,
which does not yield at all; and yielding after every chunk including the last,
which adds a pointless turn of the loop before resolving and makes the count
wrong. The gate catches the first with a probe position and the second with a
number.

**Model answer:** yield at the top of every iteration except the first. That
places the gaps between chunks by construction, so the count is just the number
of gaps and there is nothing to adjust at the end.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: The event loop, timers, and `process.nextTick()`](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick) — the phases, and the official explanation of why `nextTick` is drained first.
- [Node.js: Dont block the event loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop) — the production framing of ex5 and ex8.
- [MDN: In depth — microtasks and the JavaScript runtime](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_DOM_API/Microtask_guide/In_depth) — the microtask queue as the specification defines it.
- [MDN: `queueMicrotask()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/queueMicrotask) — when to reach for it instead of `Promise.resolve().then`.
- [MDN: `await`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/await) — including the note about how many ticks resuming costs, which is the whole of ex3.

## Hint 1

Read the snippet twice. The first pass collects only the lines that *run* as you
read them; the second pass collects the callbacks, in the order the runtime will
reach them.

Nothing scheduled can run until the function has returned, because there is only
one thread and it is busy running this function.

## Hint 2

After the synchronous code, the order of the queues is fixed and worth
memorising:

1. `process.nextTick` — the Node-specific queue, drained first;
2. microtasks — `queueMicrotask` and promise handlers;
3. the loop phases — timers, then poll, then check.

That is three of the four positions. The remaining decision is which of `A` and
`E` is first, and whether either of the deferred callbacks can sneak between
them.

## Hint 1

Translate each `await` into the thing it is shorthand for: everything before it
runs now, everything after it is a callback attached to whatever was awaited.
So an `async` function is really "run this bit, then queue the rest".

Start by writing down only the labels that appear before any `await` in the call
chain. That is your synchronous prefix, and there are three lines in it.

## Hint 2

The two `.then` handlers are not queued at the same time. Registering
`.then(a).then(b)` queues only `a`; `b` is queued when `a` returns, because only
then does the intermediate promise settle. One microtask per link.

## Hint 3

Now the interesting part, and the reason this snippet exists.
`await null` resumes on the next microtask — one hop. `await somePromise` has to
*adopt* that promise first, and adopting costs an extra hop.

So count carefully: `inner` finishes on hop 1, and `outer` is waiting on
`inner`'s promise. Does `outer` resume on hop 2, or does something else that was
queued at hop 1 get there first? Write both orders down and pick the one your
model of adoption predicts — then run it and find out whether your model was
right.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Translate each `await` into the thing it is shorthand for: everything before it
runs now, everything after it is a callback attached to whatever was awaited.
So an `async` function is really "run this bit, then queue the rest".

Start by writing down only the labels that appear before any `await` in the call
chain. That is your synchronous prefix, and there are three lines in it.

## Hint 2

The two `.then` handlers are not queued at the same time. Registering
`.then(a).then(b)` queues only `a`; `b` is queued when `a` returns, because only
then does the intermediate promise settle. One microtask per link.

## Hint 3

Now the interesting part, and the reason this snippet exists.
`await null` resumes on the next microtask — one hop. `await somePromise` has to
*adopt* that promise first, and adopting costs an extra hop.

So count carefully: `inner` finishes on hop 1, and `outer` is waiting on
`inner`'s promise. Does `outer` resume on hop 2, or does something else that was
queued at hop 1 get there first? Write both orders down and pick the one your
model of adoption predicts — then run it and find out whether your model was
right.

## Problem 4 — one label per queue

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `scheduleLabels(log)` logs `sync` immediately, then
arranges for `tick`, `micro`, `check` and `timer` to come out in that order. The
gate queues a microtask of its own *before* calling you, and expects it to land
between `tick` and `micro` — which is what proves which queue each label went
into.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five labels, five different mechanisms, and each requirement in the doc comment
names exactly one of them. Two are easy (`sync` is just a call; `micro` can be
`queueMicrotask` or `Promise.resolve().then`). The interesting pair is `check`
and `timer`.

## Hint 2

`setImmediate` runs in the **check** phase; `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs in the
**timers** phase. At the top level of a program the race between them is
genuinely unpredictable — but you are being called from inside a timer callback,
which means the timers phase for this turn is already in progress.

So a `setTimeout(0)` you register now cannot run until the loop comes all the
way round again, while the check phase of *this* turn is still ahead of you.
That is why the gate can assert an order that would be flaky anywhere else, and
it is worth being able to say that sentence out loud.

## Hint 1

Five labels, five different mechanisms, and each requirement in the doc comment
names exactly one of them. Two are easy (`sync` is just a call; `micro` can be
`queueMicrotask` or `Promise.resolve().then`). The interesting pair is `check`
and `timer`.

## Hint 2

`setImmediate` runs in the **check** phase; `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs in the
**timers** phase. At the top level of a program the race between them is
genuinely unpredictable — but you are being called from inside a timer callback,
which means the timers phase for this turn is already in progress.

So a `setTimeout(0)` you register now cannot run until the loop comes all the
way round again, while the check phase of *this* turn is still ahead of you.
That is why the gate can assert an order that would be flaky anywhere else, and
it is worth being able to say that sentence out loud.
