## Hint 1

Both functions are the same recursive step: handle one item, then schedule
yourself again for the next one, and resolve when there are none left. Only the

The two schedulers are `process.nextTick` and `setImmediate`.

`process.nextTick` puts you back in the checkpoint, and the checkpoint runs

## Hint 1

The question is not "in what order do the queues run" — you know that from ex1.
It is "when does the nextTick queue count as empty", given that draining it adds
to it.

## Hint 2

Node drains that queue with a `while` loop, not a fixed-length pass: it keeps
taking the front entry until there is nothing left, including entries added
while it is running. Three callbacks therefore run consecutively with no gap.

That is the mechanism behind the warning you have read about `process.nextTick`
recursion, and this snippet is the smallest possible demonstration of it. The
only thing left for you to decide is where `micro` and `timer` end up relative
to that block — and whether either of them can get in between.

## Problem 7 — a chain is not a block

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Nine labels: a three-link `.then` chain, two bare
microtasks and an async function with two awaits, all queued during the same
synchronous run. This is the hard one; do it with a written-out queue.

```
uv run dojo test node d03_event_loop_order ex7
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write out the microtask queue as an actual list and process it one entry at a
time, appending to the end as callbacks queue more work. Nine labels is too many
to hold in your head, and the whole skill being drilled is the bookkeeping.

Start by filling in the queue as it stands the moment the synchronous code
finishes. Three of the four initial entries come from the three schedulers in
the snippet; the fourth comes from the `await`.

## Hint 2

The rule that makes this snippet interesting: `.then(a).then(b)` queues only
`a`. `b` is queued when `a` returns, because that is when the promise `b` is
attached to settles.

So the chain is not three consecutive microtasks — it is one, then a gap, then
one, then a gap. Whatever was already waiting fills the gaps.

## Hint 3

`await Promise.resolve()` behaves the same way: the code after it is queued as
one microtask, at the moment the await is reached — so it goes to the *back* of
the queue, behind everything queued during the synchronous run.

You now have every rule you need. The only judgement left is where `a-2` lands
relative to `p2` and `p3`, and that is decided purely by the order you appended
things in step 1. Trust the list.

## Hint 1

Write out the microtask queue as an actual list and process it one entry at a
time, appending to the end as callbacks queue more work. Nine labels is too many
to hold in your head, and the whole skill being drilled is the bookkeeping.

Start by filling in the queue as it stands the moment the synchronous code
finishes. Three of the four initial entries come from the three schedulers in
the snippet; the fourth comes from the `await`.

## Hint 2

The rule that makes this snippet interesting: `.then(a).then(b)` queues only
`a`. `b` is queued when `a` returns, because that is when the promise `b` is
attached to settles.

So the chain is not three consecutive microtasks — it is one, then a gap, then
one, then a gap. Whatever was already waiting fills the gaps.

## Hint 3

`await Promise.resolve()` behaves the same way: the code after it is queued as
one microtask, at the moment the await is reached — so it goes to the *back* of
the queue, behind everything queued during the synchronous run.

You now have every rule you need. The only judgement left is where `a-2` lands
relative to `p2` and `p3`, and that is decided purely by the order you appended
things in step 1. Trust the list.

lessons.briefing:
# d04 — Timers and microtasks

Eight problems on the two ways to make something happen later: put it in the
microtask queue, or hand it to a timer. Lesson **02_event_loop** is where the
queues were taught; this set is about the tools built on top of them, and about
writing them so they can be tested without anybody waiting.

Everything runs under vitest fake timers, and where an implementation needs to
know the wall clock it is **handed** one. If that pairing is new, read problem 7
first — it is the reason the rest of the set is instant.

## Problem 1 — the two waits

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `delay(ms)` resolves after `ms`, leaving no timer
behind. `immediate()` resolves on the microtask queue and must arm **no timer at
all** — the gate counts them.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex1
```

## Problem 2 — an interval you can actually stop

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createTicker({ intervalMs, onTick })` returns
`{ start, stop, ticks, running }`. Constructing arms nothing; `onTick` gets 1,
2, 3 …; `start()` on a running ticker and `stop()` on a stopped one are both
no-ops; `stop()` leaves no timer armed; the count survives a restart.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex2
```

## Problem 3 — debounce

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `debounce(fn, waitMs)` returns a function that runs `fn`
once, `waitMs` after the **last** call, with that call's arguments. Every call
restarts the wait and there is never more than one timer. It also carries
`cancel()` and `pending()`.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex3
```

## Problem 4 — throttle

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `throttle(fn, waitMs)` runs `fn` immediately, then at
most once per `waitMs`. Calls inside a window are suppressed; the last of them
runs when the window closes, and that run opens a new window. A window that
closes with nothing suppressed runs nothing and arms nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex4
```

## Problem 5 — poll with a budget

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `pollUntil(check, { intervalMs, timeoutMs })` checks
immediately, then every `intervalMs`. It resolves with the number of checks made
as soon as one returns true, or rejects with `timed out after 250ms`. Either
way it stops checking and leaves no timer armed.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex5
```

## Problem 6 — virtual time, no timers

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createScheduler()` starts at time 0 and offers
`at(time, run)`, `advanceTo(time)` (returns how many callbacks ran), `now()` and
`pending()`. Due callbacks run in time order, ties in insertion order, and
anything a callback schedules inside the window you are advancing through runs
in the same advance. Going backwards throws `time cannot go backwards`.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex6
```

## Problem 7 — an interval that does not drift

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createSelfCorrectingInterval({ intervalMs, now,
onTick })` puts tick *n* at `startedAt + n * intervalMs` whatever the handler
cost: a handler that burns 30ms is followed by a 70ms wait, not another 100ms
one. The delay is computed from `now()` every time and never goes negative.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex7
```

## Problem 8 — many deadlines, one timer

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createDelayQueue(now)` returns `{ enqueue, size }`.
`enqueue(delayMs, run)` returns a cancel function that is safe to call twice.
However many entries are waiting, the queue holds **exactly one** underlying
timer aimed at the earliest deadline — and none when it is empty. Entries run in
deadline order, ties in insertion order.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d04_timers_micro

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **making time an input**. Every one of these eight
utilities is trivial to write and horrible to test if it reads the clock itself
and sleeps for real; every one of them becomes a two-line test the moment the
clock is either faked by the runner (`vi.useFakeTimers`) or handed in as a
`now()` function. The pattern that unites the set: hold a *handle* for anything
you armed, compute delays from absolute deadlines rather than from elapsed gaps,
and make sure that when the work is finished nothing is left armed — because in
Node a live timer is a live handle, and a live handle is a process that will not
exit. Half the bugs here are the same bug at different scales: two timers where
there should have been one.

## ex1 — a microtask is not a zero-length timer

**What it tested:** that you can tell the two deferral mechanisms apart, and
that "as soon as possible" has two very different meanings.

**The classic mistake:** implementing `immediate` as `setTimeout(resolve, 0)`.
It looks equivalent and behaves completely differently: a timer is a whole turn
of the event loop away, it can be starved, and — the part the gate checks — it
registers a handle. In a CLI that means the process cannot exit until it fires.

**Model answer:** `Promise.resolve()` is already settled, so a handler attached
to it is a microtask by definition; there is nothing to schedule and nothing to
clear.

## ex2 — the handle is the state

**What it tested:** the smallest possible resource lifecycle. Arm, hold the
handle, clear it, forget it.

**The classic mistake:** a separate `running` boolean beside the handle. The two
drift — most often when `start()` is called twice, which arms a second interval
and overwrites the handle, so the first one can never be cleared and ticks
forever. That is a leak with a heartbeat, and it survives every code review that
only reads the happy path.

**Model answer:** let `handle !== undefined` be the running flag, guard both
transitions with an early return, and keep the counter in the closure so a
restart continues rather than resets.

## ex3 — the reset is the whole idea

**What it tested:** whether you clear before you arm. A debounce that arms a new
timer without clearing the old one fires once per call, `waitMs` after each —
which is not a debounce, it is a delay.

**The classic mistake:** capturing the arguments at schedule time in a way that
keeps the *first* call's arguments rather than the last. Storing them in a
closure variable that every call overwrites is the fix, and it is why the gate
passes `"a"` then `"b"` and expects `"b"`.

**Model answer:** `clearTimeout` then `setTimeout` on every call, arguments
stashed in a shared variable, and the handle cleared inside the callback before
`fn` runs so `pending()` tells the truth.

## ex4 — leading, trailing, and the timer that never dies

**What it tested:** the shape of a rate limiter you would actually ship. The
leading call is what makes it feel instant; the trailing call is what stops the
last event of a burst from being lost.

**The classic mistake:** re-arming unconditionally when the window closes. The
throttle then holds a timer forever, ticking every `waitMs` for the lifetime of
the process, and a CLI using it simply never exits. The gate catches it by
advancing a full second and demanding a timer count of zero.

**Model answer:** one variable for "window open", stash-or-run in the returned
function, and a closing callback that only opens a new window if it actually ran
something.

**What it tested:** polling with a deadline, and the cleanup discipline that
makes both exits safe.

**The classic mistake:** clearing only the timer belonging to the path you took.
Resolving without clearing the deadline leaves a timer that will fire on a
settled promise — harmless in behaviour, fatal for process exit. Rejecting
without clearing the poll leaves a `check()` running forever against a caller
that has already given up, which is how a load test turns a 500ms timeout into a
permanent background workload.

**Model answer:** one `cleanup()` closing over both handles, called from both
exits, and the first check made directly rather than through the first interval.

**What it tested:** that "virtual time" is not magic. It is a sorted list, a
number, and a loop — the same thing `vi.useFakeTimers()` is doing for the other
seven problems.

**The classic mistake:** sorting the due entries once and then walking the
snapshot. A callback that schedules something inside the window you are
advancing through is invisible to a pre-computed list, so `e` never runs. The
other one is forgetting the insertion-order tie-break, which makes the output
depend on array churn and therefore irreproducible.

the next pass.

second one.

measured handler duration, which is nearly right and accumulates rounding, or

when the handler overran; `setTimeout` treats anything below 1 as 1, so the
symptom is a schedule that is silently one millisecond off forever.

**What it tested:** the timer-wheel idea in miniature, and the discipline of a
single `rearm()` that every mutating operation ends with.

# Reading - node/d04_timers_micro

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **making time an input**. Every one of these eight
utilities is trivial to write and horrible to test if it reads the clock itself
and sleeps for real; every one of them becomes a two-line test the moment the
clock is either faked by the runner (`vi.useFakeTimers`) or handed in as a
`now()` function. The pattern that unites the set: hold a *handle* for anything
you armed, compute delays from absolute deadlines rather than from elapsed gaps,
and make sure that when the work is finished nothing is left armed — because in
Node a live timer is a live handle, and a live handle is a process that will not
exit. Half the bugs here are the same bug at different scales: two timers where
there should have been one.

## ex1 — a microtask is not a zero-length timer

**What it tested:** that you can tell the two deferral mechanisms apart, and
that "as soon as possible" has two very different meanings.

**The classic mistake:** implementing `immediate` as `setTimeout(resolve, 0)`.
It looks equivalent and behaves completely differently: a timer is a whole turn
of the event loop away, it can be starved, and — the part the gate checks — it
registers a handle. In a CLI that means the process cannot exit until it fires.

**Model answer:** `Promise.resolve()` is already settled, so a handler attached
to it is a microtask by definition; there is nothing to schedule and nothing to
clear.

## ex2 — the handle is the state

**What it tested:** the smallest possible resource lifecycle. Arm, hold the
handle, clear it, forget it.

**The classic mistake:** a separate `running` boolean beside the handle. The two
drift — most often when `start()` is called twice, which arms a second interval
and overwrites the handle, so the first one can never be cleared and ticks
forever. That is a leak with a heartbeat, and it survives every code review that
only reads the happy path.

**Model answer:** let `handle !== undefined` be the running flag, guard both
transitions with an early return, and keep the counter in the closure so a
restart continues rather than resets.

## ex3 — the reset is the whole idea

**What it tested:** whether you clear before you arm. A debounce that arms a new
timer without clearing the old one fires once per call, `waitMs` after each —
which is not a debounce, it is a delay.

**The classic mistake:** capturing the arguments at schedule time in a way that

stashed in a shared variable, and the handle cleared inside the callback before

## Problem 1 — the two waits

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `delay(ms)` resolves after `ms`, leaving no timer
behind. `immediate()` resolves on the microtask queue and must arm **no timer at
all** — the gate counts them.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`delay` is the `new Promise` constructor with a `setTimeout` inside it, and the
resolver is the timer callback. Note that `setTimeout(resolve, ms)` passes
`resolve` directly — there is nothing to wrap.

Once the timer has fired it is finished, so there is nothing to clear: the
"leaves no timer behind" requirement is satisfied automatically as long as you
armed exactly one.

## Hint 2

`immediate` is the shorter of the two and the one people over-engineer.
"Resolve on the microtask queue" is the default behaviour of every already
settled promise — a `.then` on one is a microtask by definition.

So the question is not how to schedule a microtask; it is which single
expression is already a promise that has settled. `setTimeout(resolve, 0)` and
`setImmediate(resolve)` are both wrong here, and the gate proves it by counting
timers.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`delay` is the `new Promise` constructor with a `setTimeout` inside it, and the
resolver is the timer callback. Note that `setTimeout(resolve, ms)` passes
`resolve` directly — there is nothing to wrap.

Once the timer has fired it is finished, so there is nothing to clear: the
"leaves no timer behind" requirement is satisfied automatically as long as you
armed exactly one.

## Hint 2

`immediate` is the shorter of the two and the one people over-engineer.
"Resolve on the microtask queue" is the default behaviour of every already
settled promise — a `.then` on one is a microtask by definition.

So the question is not how to schedule a microtask; it is which single
expression is already a promise that has settled. `setTimeout(resolve, 0)` and
`setImmediate(resolve)` are both wrong here, and the gate proves it by counting
timers.

## Problem 2 — an interval you can actually stop

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createTicker({ intervalMs, onTick })` returns
`{ start, stop, ticks, running }`. Constructing arms nothing; `onTick` gets 1,
2, 3 …; `start()` on a running ticker and `stop()` on a stopped one are both
no-ops; `stop()` leaves no timer armed; the count survives a restart.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: the interval handle and the tick count. Note that you do
not need a separate `running` boolean — the handle already is one, as long as
you set it back to `undefined` when you clear it.

Keeping both a boolean and a handle is how they drift apart, and a `running`
flag that says `false` while a timer is still armed is the bug the gate's
`getTimerCount()` assertions are hunting for.

## Hint 2

Both `start` and `stop` need an early return, and they are mirror images: start
does nothing if the handle exists, stop does nothing if it does not.

The count is incremented inside the interval callback, before `onTick` is
called, so the first tick is 1 rather than 0 — and because it lives in the
closure rather than in `start`, restarting continues where it left off.

## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: the interval handle and the tick count. Note that you do
not need a separate `running` boolean — the handle already is one, as long as
you set it back to `undefined` when you clear it.

Keeping both a boolean and a handle is how they drift apart, and a `running`
flag that says `false` while a timer is still armed is the bug the gate's
`getTimerCount()` assertions are hunting for.

## Hint 2

Both `start` and `stop` need an early return, and they are mirror images: start
does nothing if the handle exists, stop does nothing if it does not.

The count is incremented inside the interval callback, before `onTick` is
called, so the first tick is 1 rather than 0 — and because it lives in the
closure rather than in `start`, restarting continues where it left off.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — throttle

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `throttle(fn, waitMs)` runs `fn` immediately, then at
most once per `waitMs`. Calls inside a window are suppressed; the last of them
runs when the window closes, and that run opens a new window. A window that
closes with nothing suppressed runs nothing and arms nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A throttle has two states, and one variable can hold both: either a window is
open (a timer is armed) or it is not. The returned function is therefore an
`if` with two arms — run now and open a window, or stash the arguments.

Compare that with ex3, where *every* call re-armed the timer. Here a call inside
the window must leave the timer completely alone, or the window never closes.

## Hint 2

The window-closing callback is where the interesting decisions are. It has to:

- mark the window closed;
- run `fn` with the stashed arguments **if** there were any;
- decide whether that trailing run opens a new window.

## Hint 3

That last decision is what the gate's `getTimerCount()` assertions pin down. If
the trailing call opens a new window, a burst followed by silence leaves exactly
one more window that closes empty — and closing empty must arm nothing, or the
throttle keeps a timer alive forever and the process never exits.

If it does not open a new window, a call arriving one millisecond after the
trailing run gets a leading edge it should not have had. Pick the version that
matches "at most once per `waitMs`" and make the empty close terminate.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A throttle has two states, and one variable can hold both: either a window is
open (a timer is armed) or it is not. The returned function is therefore an
`if` with two arms — run now and open a window, or stash the arguments.

Compare that with ex3, where *every* call re-armed the timer. Here a call inside
the window must leave the timer completely alone, or the window never closes.

## Hint 2

The window-closing callback is where the interesting decisions are. It has to:

- mark the window closed;
- run `fn` with the stashed arguments **if** there were any;
- decide whether that trailing run opens a new window.

## Hint 3

That last decision is what the gate's `getTimerCount()` assertions pin down. If
the trailing call opens a new window, a burst followed by silence leaves exactly
one more window that closes empty — and closing empty must arm nothing, or the
throttle keeps a timer alive forever and the process never exits.

If it does not open a new window, a call arriving one millisecond after the
trailing run gets a leading edge it should not have had. Pick the version that
matches "at most once per `waitMs`" and make the empty close terminate.

## Problem 5 — poll with a budget

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `pollUntil(check, { intervalMs, timeoutMs })` checks
immediately, then every `intervalMs`. It resolves with the number of checks made
as soon as one returns true, or rejects with `timed out after 250ms`. Either
way it stops checking and leaves no timer armed.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two timers, two jobs: one re-arming poll and one deadline that fires once. The
`new Promise` executor is the natural home for both, because both need `resolve`
and `reject` in scope.

Write the recursive `attempt` first — count, check, either settle or arm the
next one — and call it directly at the end so the first check costs nothing.

## Hint 2

A re-arming `setTimeout` and a `setInterval` both work, but only one of them
gives you a handle you can be sure is the current one. If you use `setInterval`
you clear the same handle at the end; if you re-arm with `setTimeout` you have
to keep the latest handle in a variable.

## Hint 3

One `cleanup()` used by both exit paths is what makes the last two assertions
pass. Success has to clear the *deadline* (otherwise it fires later, on a
promise that has already settled — harmless here, but it holds the process open
for the rest of the budget), and the timeout has to clear the *poll* (otherwise
the check keeps running forever on work nobody is waiting for).

The remaining decision: what happens if `check()` itself throws. The gate does
not test it; a reviewer will ask.

## Problem 7 — an interval that does not drift

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createSelfCorrectingInterval({ intervalMs, now,
onTick })` puts tick *n* at `startedAt + n * intervalMs` whatever the handler
cost: a handler that burns 30ms is followed by a 70ms wait, not another 100ms
one. The delay is computed from `now()` every time and never goes negative.

```
uv run dojo test node d04_timers_micro ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`setInterval` cannot do this, and that is the point of the exercise. It measures
each gap from when the previous callback *finished*, so a handler that takes
30ms pushes every future tick 30ms further out — a minute of one-second ticks
ends up half a tick late, and an hour ends up minutes late.

So: `setTimeout`, re-armed from inside the callback, with the delay recomputed
each time.

## Hint 2

Keep the *grid* rather than the gap. Record the start time once, count the ticks,
and the deadline for the next tick is

```
startedAt + (count + 1) * intervalMs
```

The delay you hand `setTimeout` is that deadline minus `now()`. Nothing about
the handler's cost appears in the formula — it falls out of the clock reading.

## Hint 3

Two guards finish it.

The delay must not go negative: if the handler overran the whole interval, the
next tick is already due and the right answer is zero, not a negative number
that `setTimeout` will quietly reinterpret.

And `stop()` has to clear the pending timeout and forget the handle, so a
`start()` after it does not end up with two chains running — which is the same
mistake as ex2, one level of indirection further in.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`setInterval` cannot do this, and that is the point of the exercise. It measures
each gap from when the previous callback *finished*, so a handler that takes
30ms pushes every future tick 30ms further out — a minute of one-second ticks
ends up half a tick late, and an hour ends up minutes late.

So: `setTimeout`, re-armed from inside the callback, with the delay recomputed
each time.

## Hint 2

Keep the *grid* rather than the gap. Record the start time once, count the ticks,
and the deadline for the next tick is

```
startedAt + (count + 1) * intervalMs
```

The delay you hand `setTimeout` is that deadline minus `now()`. Nothing about
the handler's cost appears in the formula — it falls out of the clock reading.

## Hint 3

Two guards finish it.

The delay must not go negative: if the handler overran the whole interval, the
next tick is already due and the right answer is zero, not a negative number
that `setTimeout` will quietly reinterpret.

And `stop()` has to clear the pending timeout and forget the handle, so a
`start()` after it does not end up with two chains running — which is the same
mistake as ex2, one level of indirection further in.

## Problem 8 — many deadlines, one timer

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createDelayQueue(now)` returns `{ enqueue, size }`.
`enqueue(delayMs, run)` returns a cancel function that is safe to call twice.
However many entries are waiting, the queue holds **exactly one** underlying
timer aimed at the earliest deadline — and none when it is empty. Entries run in
deadline order, ties in insertion order.


exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Store deadlines, not delays. Convert `delayMs` to an absolute `now() + delayMs`
the moment the entry is created, and every later comparison is a plain number
comparison — no arithmetic about how much of a delay has already elapsed.

The invariant to hold on to: **one timer, aimed at the earliest deadline**.
Every operation that could change which deadline is earliest ends with the same
`rearm()` call — enqueue, cancel, and the firing itself.

## Hint 2

`rearm()` is: clear whatever is armed, and if anything is left, arm one timer
for `earliest.at - now()`, clamped at zero. Writing it once and calling it from
three places is what keeps the invariant true; inlining it three times is how
one of the three drifts.

When the timer fires, more than one entry may be due — the gate advances 200ms
over two deadlines on purpose. Collect everything due, sort it by deadline then
insertion order, and run the batch.

## Hint 3

Remove the due entries from the queue **before** running any of them. A callback
is allowed to enqueue more work, and if you splice while iterating over the live
array you will either skip an entry or run one twice.

Two decisions are left to you. What `size()` counts while a batch is running,
and whether `cancel` on an entry that already ran should re-arm — the gate calls
a cancel twice, so whatever you decide has to be idempotent.

the moment the entry is created, and every later comparison is a plain number
comparison — no arithmetic about how much of a delay has already elapsed.

The invariant to hold on to: **one timer, aimed at the earliest deadline**.
Every operation that could change which deadline is earliest ends with the same
`rearm()` call — enqueue, cancel, and the firing itself.

## Hint 2

`rearm()` is: clear whatever is armed, and if anything is left, arm one timer
for `earliest.at - now()`, clamped at zero. Writing it once and calling it from
three places is what keeps the invariant true; inlining it three times is how
one of the three drifts.

When the timer fires, more than one entry may be due — the gate advances 200ms
over two deadlines on purpose. Collect everything due, sort it by deadline then
insertion order, and run the batch.

## Hint 3

Remove the due entries from the queue **before** running any of them. A callback
is allowed to enqueue more work, and if you splice while iterating over the live
array you will either skip an entry or run one twice.

Two decisions are left to you. What `size()` counts while a batch is running,
and whether `cancel` on an entry that already ran should re-arm — the gate calls
a cancel twice, so whatever you decide has to be idempotent.

# d05 — Promise basics

Eight problems on the promise state machine itself, drawn from lesson
**03_async_patterns** — the first half of it, before `async`/`await` hides the
machinery. Write these with `.then` and `.catch`; the point is to see what the
syntax you normally use is doing on your behalf.

If problem 2 makes you reach for `new Promise` around a promise you already
have, reread lesson 03 before going on.

## Problem 1 — the deferred

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `deferred<T>()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject,
settled }`. The first settlement wins and every later one is **ignored**, not
thrown. Handlers never run synchronously, including ones attached after it has
settled.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex1
```

## Problem 2 — what `.then` actually does

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `mapPromise(promise, fn)` transforms the fulfilled
value. A mapper that throws rejects the result; a mapper returning a promise is
flattened; a rejected input never reaches the mapper.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex2
```

## Problem 3 — recovering, and failing to recover

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `orElse(promise, fallback)` passes a fulfilled promise
through without calling `fallback` at all. On a rejection it calls `fallback`
with the reason and **fulfils** with the result — unless `fallback` itself
fails, in which case that error is the one the caller gets.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex3
```

## Problem 4 — observing without interfering

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `tap(promise, onSettle)` calls
`onSettle("fulfilled", value)` or `onSettle("rejected", reason)` and then passes
the original outcome through unchanged — the same value **by identity**, or the
same rejection. If `onSettle` throws, that error replaces the outcome on both
paths.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a snapshot of a state you cannot ask for

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `inspect(promise)` resolves to `{ state: "pending" }`,
`{ state: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ state: "rejected", reason }` describing the
promise as it is now — without waiting for it and without changing it.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex5
```

## Problem 6 — one at a time, on purpose

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `chainSequential(items, step)` runs `step(item, index)`
strictly in sequence: item *n+1* does not **start** until item *n* has settled.
Results come back in input order. A failing step stops the chain and rejects
with `step 1 failed`, carrying the original error as `cause`.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex6
```

## Problem 7 — adopting a thenable, by the book

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `adoptThenable(value)` does what `Promise.resolve` does:
a non-thenable is wrapped; otherwise `then` is **read once**, called once, with
two settle callbacks. The first settlement wins. A throw while reading or
calling `then` rejects — unless it had already settled, in which case the throw
is ignored.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex7
```

## Problem 8 — build one from the other side

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createSettleable<T>()` returns `{ thenable, resolve,
reject }`, where `thenable` is a hand-built promise-like — no `Promise` holding
the state. `then` works before or after settling, handlers always run
asynchronously and in registration order, and the first settlement wins. A
native `Promise.resolve()` must be able to adopt it.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex8
```

# Reading - node/d05_promise_basics

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is reading `.then` as a **specification** rather than as
a method call. A promise has three states, one transition, and one guarantee:
pending becomes fulfilled or rejected exactly once, and every handler runs
asynchronously no matter when it was attached. Almost everything in this set
falls out of two consequences of that. First, `.then` already does more than
people credit it with — it returns a new promise, converts a thrown handler into
a rejection, adopts a returned promise, and passes an unhandled rejection
along — so four of the eight answers are one line and the work is being certain
enough to write one line. Second, the guarantees you get for free from a native
promise are exactly the guarantees you have to *implement* the moment you build
one by hand, which is what the last two problems are for.

## ex1 — the executor is synchronous

**What it tested:** the one structural fact that makes a deferred possible.
`new Promise(executor)` calls the executor immediately, so `resolve` and
`reject` are available before the constructor returns.

**The classic mistake:** believing the handler will run right after `resolve()`
on the next line. It never does — and that is the point. A function that
sometimes calls back synchronously and sometimes not ("releasing Zalgo") creates
ordering bugs that only appear under load, and promises structurally cannot do
it.

**Model answer:** capture both functions out of the executor, add one boolean so
`settled()` can be answered, and guard both methods with it — even though the
native promise would ignore the second settlement anyway.

## ex2 — four guarantees in one method

**What it tested:** whether you can enumerate what `.then` gives you. New
promise, throw-to-rejection, promise flattening, rejection pass-through.

**The classic mistake:** the explicit construction antipattern — wrapping a
promise you already have in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`. The
hand-rolled version nearly always drops one of the four rules, most often the
flattening, and the caller ends up awaiting a promise of a promise.

**Model answer:** `promise.then(fn)`. Being able to defend that as complete is
the exercise.

## ex3 — a catch that returns is a recovery

**What it tested:** what a *rejection* handler's return value means. Returning
normally from `.catch` produces a **fulfilled** promise; that is why
`try`/`catch` around an `await` recovers rather than rethrowing.

**The classic mistake:** assuming `.catch` re-raises unless you tell it not to.
It is the opposite: it swallows unless you rethrow, which is the single most
common source of "the error disappeared" in promise code — and the reason ex4
has to rethrow explicitly.

**Model answer:** `promise.catch(fallback)`, and the observation that the
fallback throwing produces a new rejection with no extra work.

## ex4 — observe, then put it back

**What it tested:** the two-handler form of `.then`, and the discipline of
restoring the outcome on both branches.

**The classic mistake:** the rejection handler that logs and returns. It looks
symmetric with the success handler and quietly converts every failure into a
fulfilment of `undefined` — a monitoring wrapper that eats the errors it was
added to report. The other one is wrapping `onSettle` in a `try`/`catch` "to be
safe", which hides a broken logger forever.

**Model answer:** `.then(onOk, onErr)`, return the value on one side, `throw
reason` on the other, and no protective `try` anywhere.

## ex5 — you cannot ask, so you race

**What it tested:** that promise state is deliberately unreadable, and the
standard trick for approximating it.

**The classic mistake:** attaching the success and failure handlers in separate
`.then().catch()` links. The catch then sits one microtask further down the
chain and loses the race with the marker, so every rejected promise reports
"pending". The other one is racing against a timer, which turns an exact answer
into a flaky one.

**Model answer:** one `.then(onOk, onErr)` attached first, one
`Promise.resolve().then(...)` marker attached second, `Promise.race` between
them — the marker settles one hop later, which is exactly the window that
separates "already settled" from "not settled".

## ex6 — creating is starting

**What it tested:** the distinction between calling an async function and
awaiting its promise. `map` calls everything immediately; awaiting afterwards
changes when you look, not when the work began.

**The classic mistake:** `const promises = items.map(step); for (const p of
promises) results.push(await p);` — which reads as sequential, runs as fully
parallel, and passes any test that only checks the results. The gate defeats it
by holding each step open and asserting that only one has *started*.

**Model answer:** `reduce` with a promise accumulator, so the call to `step` for
item n+1 happens inside a handler attached to item n. The index comes free from
`reduce`, which is what makes the error message cheap to build.

## ex7 — the specification is made of edge cases

**What it tested:** the thenable-adoption rules from Promises/A+, which exist
because a "thenable" can be any object anybody wrote, including a hostile one.

**The classic mistake:** `if (typeof value.then === "function") value.then(...)`
— two separate reads of a property that might be a getter. The A+ spec
explicitly requires one read, and the gate counts. Close behind: putting the
`try` around only the *call*, which misses a getter that throws, and forgetting
that `typeof null === "object"`.

**Model answer:** one read into a local, everything inside the `try`, a `settled`
flag so a throw after settling can be distinguished from a throw before, and
`then.call(value, ...)` so the thenable keeps its `this`.

## ex8 — the guarantees, from the implementer's chair

**What it tested:** everything the first seven problems took for granted, now
that nothing gives it to you: asynchronous delivery, ordering, register-before
and register-after, settle-once.

**The classic mistake:** calling the handlers directly from `resolve()`. It
passes a naive test and breaks the guarantee that makes promises composable —
which is why the gate checks the synchronous case first, before it checks
anything useful. The second is delivering handlers registered after settling
*synchronously* from `then`, which is the same bug on the other branch.

**Model answer:** a state variable, a waiting list, and one `deliver` helper
that always goes through `queueMicrotask`. Because microtasks are FIFO,
scheduling in registration order is delivering in registration order, and
nothing more is needed.

## Further reading

- [MDN: Promise](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise) — states, settling rules, and every method used here.
- [MDN: `Promise.prototype.then()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/then) — the four guarantees ex2 and ex3 are made of, stated explicitly.
- [Promises/A+ specification](https://promisesaplus.com/) — short, readable, and the source of every rule in ex7 and ex8.
- [MDN: Using promises](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Using_promises) — including the composition patterns behind ex6.
- [MDN: `queueMicrotask()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/queueMicrotask) — how ex8 keeps its asynchrony guarantee without a timer.

## Problem 1 — the deferred

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `deferred<T>()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject,
settled }`. The first settlement wins and every later one is **ignored**, not
thrown. Handlers never run synchronously, including ones attached after it has
settled.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `Promise` executor runs **synchronously**, before the constructor returns.
That is the fact the whole pattern rests on: you can assign `resolve` and
`reject` to variables declared outside it and be certain they are populated by
the time you use them.

TypeScript will not believe that on its own — `let resolve: (v: T) => void;` is
"used before assigned". The definite assignment assertion (`let resolve!: ...`)
is how you tell it you know something it does not.

## Hint 2

A native promise already ignores a second settlement, so `settled()` is the only
part that needs a flag of your own — and once you have the flag, guarding the
two methods with it costs one line each and makes the intent explicit rather
than relying on the platform.

Nothing here needs to *do* anything asynchronous. The "handlers never run
synchronously" requirement is a guarantee the promise gives you for free; the
gate checks it to make sure you did not build the thing out of callbacks.

## Problem 2 — what `.then` actually does

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `mapPromise(promise, fn)` transforms the fulfilled
value. A mapper that throws rejects the result; a mapper returning a promise is
flattened; a rejected input never reaches the mapper.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex2
```

## Hint 1

Go through the four requirements one at a time and ask, for each: is this
something I have to implement, or something `.then` already guarantees?

- returns a new promise rather than mutating the old one

All four are `.then`. The answer is one line, and the exercise is being sure
enough of the semantics to write one line instead of fifteen.

already have, that is the "explicit construction antipattern" — worth being able
to name, because interviewers ask about it and because the hand-rolled version
almost always drops one of the four rules above.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Go through the four requirements one at a time and ask, for each: is this
something I have to implement, or something `.then` already guarantees?

- returns a new promise rather than mutating the old one
- a handler that throws produces a rejection
- a handler that returns a promise is adopted rather than nested
- with no rejection handler, a rejected input passes through

## Hint 2

All four are `.then`. The answer is one line, and the exercise is being sure
enough of the semantics to write one line instead of fifteen.

If you reached for `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)` around a promise you
already have, that is the "explicit construction antipattern" — worth being able
to name, because interviewers ask about it and because the hand-rolled version
almost always drops one of the four rules above.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 3 — recovering, and failing to recover

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `orElse(promise, fallback)` passes a fulfilled promise
through without calling `fallback` at all. On a rejection it calls `fallback`
with the reason and **fulfils** with the result — unless `fallback` itself
fails, in which case that error is the one the caller gets.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The mirror image of ex2. `.catch(fn)` is sugar for `.then(undefined, fn)`, and
the key fact is what a *rejection handler* does with its return value: returning
normally means "handled", and the promise `.catch` gives back is **fulfilled**
with that value.

That is why `try`/`catch` around an `await` recovers rather than rethrowing, and
it is the answer to the interview question "does `.catch` swallow errors?" — it
does, and that is the point.

## Hint 2

Once you see that, three of the four requirements are free: the fulfilled input
never reaches the handler, a returned promise is adopted, and a throw inside the
handler becomes a new rejection.

The fourth — the fallback receiving the reason — is just the handler's argument.
Decide whether you want `.catch` or the two-argument `.then`, and be ready to
say why one of them can accidentally catch an error thrown by its own success
handler while the other cannot.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The mirror image of ex2. `.catch(fn)` is sugar for `.then(undefined, fn)`, and
the key fact is what a *rejection handler* does with its return value: returning
normally means "handled", and the promise `.catch` gives back is **fulfilled**
with that value.

That is why `try`/`catch` around an `await` recovers rather than rethrowing, and
it is the answer to the interview question "does `.catch` swallow errors?" — it
does, and that is the point.

## Hint 2

Once you see that, three of the four requirements are free: the fulfilled input
never reaches the handler, a returned promise is adopted, and a throw inside the
handler becomes a new rejection.

The fourth — the fallback receiving the reason — is just the handler's argument.
Decide whether you want `.catch` or the two-argument `.then`, and be ready to
say why one of them can accidentally catch an error thrown by its own success
handler while the other cannot.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is no `promise.state` — deliberately, because reading it would tempt
people into polling. The only way to observe a promise is to attach a handler,
and the only way to observe *absence* is to race it against something you know
will settle.

So: build a promise that reports the outcome, build a second one that reports
"pending", and race them.

## Hint 2

The "pending" marker must settle **after** an already-settled promise would have
delivered, and **before** a genuinely pending one could. One microtask hop is
exactly that window: `Promise.resolve().then(...)`.

Order matters. Attach the handlers to the input promise *first*, so on a settled
promise its microtask is queued ahead of the marker's.

## Hint 3

Both handlers on the input have to be attached in the same `.then(onOk, onErr)`
call rather than as a `.then().catch()` chain — otherwise the catch sits one hop
further down and loses the race with the marker.

That same attachment is also what stops a rejected input becoming an unhandled
rejection just because somebody inspected it. Whether that is a feature or a
footgun is worth an opinion: `inspect` quietly marks the rejection as handled,
which is convenient in a test and hides a real problem in production code.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is no `promise.state` — deliberately, because reading it would tempt
people into polling. The only way to observe a promise is to attach a handler,
and the only way to observe *absence* is to race it against something you know
will settle.

So: build a promise that reports the outcome, build a second one that reports
"pending", and race them.

## Hint 2

The "pending" marker must settle **after** an already-settled promise would have
delivered, and **before** a genuinely pending one could. One microtask hop is
exactly that window: `Promise.resolve().then(...)`.

Order matters. Attach the handlers to the input promise *first*, so on a settled
promise its microtask is queued ahead of the marker's.

## Hint 3

Both handlers on the input have to be attached in the same `.then(onOk, onErr)`
call rather than as a `.then().catch()` chain — otherwise the catch sits one hop
further down and loses the race with the marker.

That same attachment is also what stops a rejected input becoming an unhandled
rejection just because somebody inspected it. Whether that is a feature or a
footgun is worth an opinion: `inspect` quietly marks the rejection as handled,
which is convenient in a test and hides a real problem in production code.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — one at a time, on purpose

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `chainSequential(items, step)` runs `step(item, index)`
strictly in sequence: item *n+1* does not **start** until item *n* has settled.
Results come back in input order. A failing step stops the chain and rejects
with `step 1 failed`, carrying the original error as `cause`.

```
uv run dojo test node d05_promise_basics ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The trap is starting the work too early. `items.map((item) => step(item))` calls
every `step` immediately — you now have N promises in flight and awaiting them
in a loop only changes when you *look* at them, not when they *ran*.

Sequential means the call to `step` for item n + 1 must happen **inside** a
handler attached to item n's promise.

## Hint 2

`reduce` over the items, carrying a promise as the accumulator:

```ts
items.reduce(
  (chain, item, index) => chain.then(() => step(item, index).then(/* ... */)),
  Promise.resolve(),
);
```

Each link's `.then` callback is where the next `step` is called, so nothing can
start early. Collect the values into an array declared outside the reduce, or
carry the array through the chain — either is fine, and one of them is much
easier to read.

## Hint 3

For the error, wrap rather than replace: `new Error(msg, { cause: original })`
keeps the real failure reachable, and the gate checks both the message and the
cause.

Wrapping at the inner `.then`'s rejection handler is what gives you the index
for free. Wrapping at the outer end of the chain would mean carrying the index
along separately — and the last decision left to you is whether an already
wrapped error should be wrapped twice when a later step fails, which cannot
happen here and absolutely can in production code.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The trap is starting the work too early. `items.map((item) => step(item))` calls
every `step` immediately — you now have N promises in flight and awaiting them
in a loop only changes when you *look* at them, not when they *ran*.

Sequential means the call to `step` for item n + 1 must happen **inside** a
handler attached to item n's promise.

## Hint 2

`reduce` over the items, carrying a promise as the accumulator:

```ts
items.reduce(
  (chain, item, index) => chain.then(() => step(item, index).then(/* ... */)),
  Promise.resolve(),
);
```

Each link's `.then` callback is where the next `step` is called, so nothing can
start early. Collect the values into an array declared outside the reduce, or
carry the array through the chain — either is fine, and one of them is much
easier to read.

## Hint 3

For the error, wrap rather than replace: `new Error(msg, { cause: original })`
keeps the real failure reachable, and the gate checks both the message and the
cause.

Wrapping at the inner `.then`'s rejection handler is what gives you the index
for free. Wrapping at the outer end of the chain would mean carrying the index
along separately — and the last decision left to you is whether an already
wrapped error should be wrapped twice when a later step fails, which cannot
happen here and absolutely can in production code.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `adoptThenable(value)` does what `Promise.resolve` does:
a non-thenable is wrapped; otherwise `then` is **read once**, called once, with
two settle callbacks. The first settlement wins. A throw while reading or
calling `then` rejects — unless it had already settled, in which case the throw
is ignored.

## Hint 1

Structure first: `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`, and inside it

## Problem 8 — build one from the other side

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createSettleable<T>()` returns `{ thenable, resolve,
reject }`, where `thenable` is a hand-built promise-like — no `Promise` holding
the state. `then` works before or after settling, handlers always run
asynchronously and in registration order, and the first settlement wins. A
native `Promise.resolve()` must be able to adopt it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state and one list: the state (`pending` / `fulfilled` /
`rejected`), the value, the reason, and the handlers registered while it was
still pending.

`then` is then an `if`: pending means push onto the list, settled means deliver
now. `resolve` and `reject` are the same function with a different label, so
write one `settle(state, payload)` and have both call it.

## Hint 2

"Deliver now" cannot mean "call the handler now". The asynchrony guarantee is
the single most load-bearing property of a promise — an API that is sometimes
synchronous and sometimes not creates races that only show up under load — and
the gate checks it twice: once for handlers registered before `resolve`, once
for handlers registered after.

`queueMicrotask` is exactly the right tool. Wrap the *delivery* in it, not the
whole of `then`, or you lose the ordering.

## Hint 3

Two details finish it.

Ordering: schedule the waiting handlers in the order they were registered, one
microtask each. Because microtasks are FIFO, scheduling in order is delivering
in order — you do not need to do anything cleverer.

Idempotence: `settle` returns immediately if the state is not `pending`. That
one line is what makes "the first settlement wins" true, and it is the same
guard as ex1 and ex7.

The remaining decision is what happens to the waiting list after settling. Ask
whether keeping the entries around could hold a large captured value alive
longer than anybody wanted.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state and one list: the state (`pending` / `fulfilled` /
`rejected`), the value, the reason, and the handlers registered while it was
still pending.

`then` is then an `if`: pending means push onto the list, settled means deliver
now. `resolve` and `reject` are the same function with a different label, so
write one `settle(state, payload)` and have both call it.

## Hint 2

"Deliver now" cannot mean "call the handler now". The asynchrony guarantee is
the single most load-bearing property of a promise — an API that is sometimes
synchronous and sometimes not creates races that only show up under load — and
the gate checks it twice: once for handlers registered before `resolve`, once
for handlers registered after.

`queueMicrotask` is exactly the right tool. Wrap the *delivery* in it, not the
whole of `then`, or you lose the ordering.

## Hint 3

Two details finish it.

Ordering: schedule the waiting handlers in the order they were registered, one
microtask each. Because microtasks are FIFO, scheduling in order is delivering
in order — you do not need to do anything cleverer.

Idempotence: `settle` returns immediately if the state is not `pending`. That
one line is what makes "the first settlement wins" true, and it is the same
guard as ex1 and ex7.

The remaining decision is what happens to the waiting list after settling. Ask
whether keeping the entries around could hold a large captured value alive
longer than anybody wanted.

lessons.briefing:
# d06 — async / await

Eight problems on the syntax half of lesson **03_async_patterns**: what `await`
actually does to control flow, when sequential is right and when it is a
performance bug, and how `try`/`catch`/`finally` behave once promises are
involved. Problems 5 and 7 pull in async iteration from the same lesson's
neighbourhood — if `for await` is unfamiliar, read problem 5's hints first.

## Problem 1 — when sequential is right

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `loadProfile(id, deps)` calls `deps.findUser(id)`, then
`deps.findTeam(user.teamId)`, and returns `{ id, name, team }` where `team` is
the team's **name**. A failure in the first call propagates unchanged and the
second call never happens.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex1
```

## Problem 2 — when sequential is wrong

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `startBoth(first, second)` starts both pieces of work
before waiting for either and returns `[a, b]` in **argument** order, whatever
order they settled in. One rejection rejects the pair.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex2
```

## Problem 3 — failure as a value

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `attempt(fn)` resolves to `[null, value]` or
`[error, null]` and never rejects. `fn` may throw **synchronously**, before it
returns a promise, and anything at all may be thrown — the first slot is always
`null` or a real `Error`.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex3
```

## Problem 4 — cleanup that does not lie

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `withCleanup(run, cleanup)` runs the cleanup on both
paths and **awaits** it before the caller resumes. If only the cleanup failed,
its error is the result; if both failed, the **original** error is the result.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex4
```

## Problem 5 — consume a stream, and let go of it

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `sumUntil(source, stopAt)` adds up values from an
`AsyncIterable<number>` until one equals `stopAt` — the sentinel is not counted.
Leaving early must close the iterator; the gate counts the `return()` calls.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex5
```

## Problem 6 — map the values of an object

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `mapValuesAsync(record, fn)` applies `fn(value, key)` to
every value **all at once** and returns an object with the same keys. An empty
object gives an empty object; one rejection rejects the call.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex6
```

## Problem 7 — an async generator

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `chunked(source, size)` yields arrays of `size` items;
the last one may be short and an empty source yields nothing at all. A consumer
that breaks out early must end up closing the source.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex7
```

## Problem 8 — run it, and be able to undo it

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `runStages(stages)` runs each stage in order and returns
the names that ran. On a failure it rolls back the stages that **completed**, in
reverse order, and rejects with the original error — with any rollback failures
attached to it as `rollbackErrors`.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex8
```

# Reading - node/d06_async_await

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is reading `await` as **two separate events**: a call
that starts work, and a suspension that waits for it. Written as `await f()`
they look like one thing, and almost every mistake in this set comes from that
blurring — sequential where parallel was free (ex2, ex6), a call outside the
`try` that was supposed to protect it (ex3), a cleanup that was not waited for
(ex4). The other half of the set is about what `await` does to control-flow
constructs you thought you knew: `try`/`finally` swallows the error you cared
about (ex4), `break` in a `for await` closes a resource for you (ex5, ex7), and
an ordinary `for` loop plus an array is all a transaction unwinder needs (ex8).
Separate calling from waiting, and every one of these becomes obvious.

## ex1 — the await that has to be there

**What it tested:** recognising a genuine data dependency. `findTeam` needs
`user.teamId`; there is no arrangement of these two calls that overlaps them.

**The classic mistake:** none, in the code — this is the calibration problem. Its
job is to fix the shape in your head *before* ex2 asks you to break it, so that
"await one at a time" stops being a habit and becomes a decision you can defend.

**Model answer:** two awaits and a returned literal, with no `try`/`catch` at
all: an un-caught rejection inside an `async` function is already a rejection of
the promise it returns.

## ex2 — calling is starting

**What it tested:** that a promise begins its work when it is *created*, not
when it is awaited — so hoisting the calls above the awaits is the whole fix.

**The classic mistake:** `const a = await first(); const b = await second();`.
Both round trips are now end to end, and on anything network-shaped that is
double the latency for no reason. The gate catches it by counting how many were
in flight at the same moment.

**Model answer:** call both, then `Promise.all`. Not `[await a, await b]` —
that also overlaps the work, but leaves the second promise unobserved while the
first is being awaited, so a rejection there is briefly an unhandled rejection.

## ex3 — the call belongs inside the try

**What it tested:** that a function returning `Promise<T>` can still throw
*synchronously*, and that `catch` in TypeScript hands you `unknown` for a
reason.

**The classic mistake:** `const p = fn(); try { return [null, await p] } catch
{...}`. Argument validation typically throws at the call, which is now outside
the protected region, so the helper that exists to never throw... throws. The
second mistake is assuming the caught value is an `Error` — `throw "nope"` is
legal and libraries do it.

**Model answer:** call and await inside the same `try`, and normalise in the
catch so the caller can always read `.message`.

## ex4 — finally is the wrong tool when cleanup can fail

**What it tested:** the interaction between `finally` and an in-flight
exception. A `throw` from `finally` **replaces** the original — so the tidy
version of this function destroys the only error worth reading.

**The classic mistake:** exactly that, plus its quieter cousin: calling
`cleanup()` without awaiting it. The function then resolves while the cleanup is
still running, and the next thing the caller does races it. In fs code the
symptom is a temp directory that disappears mid-test.

**Model answer:** two paths written separately — a defensive cleanup then a
rethrow on the failure path, a plain awaited cleanup on the success path — so
the "which error wins" rule is visible in the structure rather than implied.

## ex5 — break closes things

**What it tested:** that `for await` is a resource-management construct, not
just sugar. Leaving it early calls the iterator's `return()`, which is how a
source releases its file handle, socket or cursor.

**The classic mistake:** driving the iterator by hand —
`while (true) { const { value, done } = await it.next(); ... }` — and breaking
out of that. Nothing calls `return()`, and a database cursor stays open until
the process ends. The gate counts the `return()` calls precisely so the two
loops are distinguishable.

**Model answer:** `for await`, sentinel checked before the addition, `break`. And
the observation that a loop which ends naturally does *not* get a `return()`,
because the iterator closed itself.

## ex6 — the same lesson as ex2, N wide

**What it tested:** the object-shaped version of the sequential-await bug, plus
keeping keys aligned with values across the round trip.

**The classic mistake:** `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(record)) result[k]
= await fn(v, k);` — perfectly readable, and N times slower than it needs to be.
The other one is rebuilding the object from a `Promise.all` result without
holding onto the key order, which silently transposes values between keys when
the input has more than a couple of entries.

**Model answer:** keys once, `keys.map(...)` into `Promise.all`, then zip back by
index — relying on `Promise.all` preserving input order, which is a guarantee
worth being able to quote.

## ex7 — three links in a cleanup chain

**What it tested:** writing an async generator, and understanding what happens
to it when the consumer walks away.

**The classic mistake:** reusing the chunk array (`chunk.length = 0`) after
yielding it. The consumer is holding that exact array, so it empties under them
— a bug that looks like data loss and is really aliasing. Close behind:
yielding an empty trailing chunk when the source length divides evenly.

**Model answer:** accumulate, yield, replace the array, and a final `if` for the
remainder. The cleanup requirement needs no code at all: breaking the outer loop
closes the generator, which unwinds the `for await` inside it, which closes the
source.

## ex8 — unwind in reverse, and tell the truth

**What it tested:** the saga/compensation pattern, and error hygiene under a
failing cleanup.

**The classic mistake:** rolling back the stage that threw. It did not complete,
so undoing it is at best a no-op and at worst a second failure. Nearly as
common: letting a rollback failure escape, which replaces the real error with a
message about the cleanup — so the incident report says "rollback a failed" and
nobody ever learns what caused the rollback.

**Model answer:** push onto the completed list only after `run()` returns, unwind
backwards with a `try` per rollback, collect the rollback failures onto the
original error, and throw the original. The caller then has both facts: what
broke, and that the undo was incomplete.

## Further reading

- [MDN: `async function`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function) — what the syntax compiles to, and how throws become rejections.
- [MDN: `await`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/await) — including the note that the expression is evaluated before the suspension, which is the whole of ex2.
- [MDN: `for await...of`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — the closing behaviour ex5 and ex7 depend on.
- [MDN: async generators](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function*) — the construct ex7 is built from.
- [Node.js: Discover promises in Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/discover-promises-in-nodejs) — the platform-level tour, callbacks through async/await.

still running, and the next thing the caller does races it. In fs code the
symptom is a temp directory that disappears mid-test.

**Model answer:** two paths written separately — a defensive cleanup then a
rethrow on the failure path, a plain awaited cleanup on the success path — so
the "which error wins" rule is visible in the structure rather than implied.

## ex5 — break closes things

**What it tested:** that `for await` is a resource-management construct, not
just sugar. Leaving it early calls the iterator's `return()`, which is how a
source releases its file handle, socket or cursor.

**The classic mistake:** driving the iterator by hand —
`while (true) { const { value, done } = await it.next(); ... }` — and breaking
out of that. Nothing calls `return()`, and a database cursor stays open until
the process ends. The gate counts the `return()` calls precisely so the two
loops are distinguishable.

**Model answer:** `for await`, sentinel checked before the addition, `break`. And
the observation that a loop which ends naturally does *not* get a `return()`,
because the iterator closed itself.

## ex6 — the same lesson as ex2, N wide

**What it tested:** the object-shaped version of the sequential-await bug, plus
keeping keys aligned with values across the round trip.

**The classic mistake:** `for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(record)) result[k]
= await fn(v, k);` — perfectly readable, and N times slower than it needs to be.
The other one is rebuilding the object from a `Promise.all` result without
holding onto the key order, which silently transposes values between keys when
the input has more than a couple of entries.

**Model answer:** keys once, `keys.map(...)` into `Promise.all`, then zip back by
index — relying on `Promise.all` preserving input order, which is a guarantee
worth being able to quote.

## ex7 — three links in a cleanup chain

**What it tested:** writing an async generator, and understanding what happens
to it when the consumer walks away.

**The classic mistake:** reusing the chunk array (`chunk.length = 0`) after
yielding it. The consumer is holding that exact array, so it empties under them
— a bug that looks like data loss and is really aliasing. Close behind:
yielding an empty trailing chunk when the source length divides evenly.

**Model answer:** accumulate, yield, replace the array, and a final `if` for the
remainder. The cleanup requirement needs no code at all: breaking the outer loop
closes the generator, which unwinds the `for await` inside it, which closes the
source.

## ex8 — unwind in reverse, and tell the truth

**What it tested:** the saga/compensation pattern, and error hygiene under a
failing cleanup.

**The classic mistake:** rolling back the stage that threw. It did not complete,
so undoing it is at best a no-op and at worst a second failure. Nearly as
common: letting a rollback failure escape, which replaces the real error with a
message about the cleanup — so the incident report says "rollback a failed" and
nobody ever learns what caused the rollback.

**Model answer:** push onto the completed list only after `run()` returns, unwind
backwards with a `try` per rollback, collect the rollback failures onto the
original error, and throw the original. The caller then has both facts: what
broke, and that the undo was incomplete.

- [MDN: `async function`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function) — what the syntax compiles to, and how throws become rejections.
- [MDN: `await`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/await) — including the note that the expression is evaluated before the suspension, which is the whole of ex2.
- [MDN: `for await...of`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — the closing behaviour ex5 and ex7 depend on.
- [MDN: async generators](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/async_function*) — the construct ex7 is built from.
- [Node.js: Discover promises in Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/discover-promises-in-nodejs) — the platform-level tour, callbacks through async/await.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — when sequential is right

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `loadProfile(id, deps)` calls `deps.findUser(id)`, then
`deps.findTeam(user.teamId)`, and returns `{ id, name, team }` where `team` is
the team's **name**. A failure in the first call propagates unchanged and the
second call never happens.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three lines: await the user, await the team using something from the user,
return the combined shape. Read the second call's argument carefully — it is the
reason these two cannot be parallel, and being able to say that out loud is the
whole point of starting the set here.

## Hint 2

You do not need a `try`/`catch`. "The rejection propagates unchanged" is what an
un-caught `await` already does: the rejection becomes a throw inside your
function, and an uncaught throw inside an `async` function becomes a rejection
of the promise it returned.

Watch the shape of the result: the profile's `team` is the team's **name**, not
the team object and not the id.

## Hint 1

Three lines: await the user, await the team using something from the user,
return the combined shape. Read the second call's argument carefully — it is the
reason these two cannot be parallel, and being able to say that out loud is the
whole point of starting the set here.

## Hint 2

You do not need a `try`/`catch`. "The rejection propagates unchanged" is what an
un-caught `await` already does: the rejection becomes a throw inside your
function, and an uncaught throw inside an `async` function becomes a rejection
of the promise it returned.

Watch the shape of the result: the profile's `team` is the team's **name**, not
the team object and not the id.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`await first()` does two things on one line: it calls, and it waits. Separate
them. Call both functions first, keeping the promises in variables, and only
then wait.

That single change is the difference between two round trips and one, and it is
the most common performance review comment there is on async code.

## Hint 2

`[await a, await b]` works and passes the concurrency check — but think about
what happens if `b` rejects while you are still waiting on `a`: for that moment
nobody is listening to `b`, which is how a legitimate failure becomes an
unhandled rejection warning.

`Promise.all` attaches to both immediately and returns the tuple you want. Two
decisions are left: whether the argument-order requirement needs any work from
you (it does not, and knowing why is the point), and what `Promise.all` does the
instant one input rejects.

## Problem 3 — failure as a value

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `attempt(fn)` resolves to `[null, value]` or
`[error, null]` and never rejects. `fn` may throw **synchronously**, before it
returns a promise, and anything at all may be thrown — the first slot is always
`null` or a real `Error`.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The body is a `try`/`catch` with a `return` in each arm. What matters is what
sits *inside* the try.

`const promise = fn(); try { return [null, await promise]; } catch { ... }`
looks equivalent and is not: a function that validates its arguments and throws
does so at the call, which is now outside the try.

## Hint 2

In TypeScript, `catch (error)` gives you `unknown` (the project has
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` on), which is honest — a `throw` can carry a
string, a number, `undefined`, or an object that merely looks like an error.

So the catch arm has to *produce* an `Error`: keep it if it already is one,
otherwise build one from it. `String(thrown)` is a reasonable message, and the
gate checks exactly that case.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The body is a `try`/`catch` with a `return` in each arm. What matters is what
sits *inside* the try.

`const promise = fn(); try { return [null, await promise]; } catch { ... }`
looks equivalent and is not: a function that validates its arguments and throws
does so at the call, which is now outside the try.

## Hint 2

In TypeScript, `catch (error)` gives you `unknown` (the project has
`useUnknownInCatchVariables` on), which is honest — a `throw` can carry a
string, a number, `undefined`, or an object that merely looks like an error.

So the catch arm has to *produce* an `Error`: keep it if it already is one,
otherwise build one from it. `String(thrown)` is a reasonable message, and the
gate checks exactly that case.

## Problem 4 — cleanup that does not lie

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `withCleanup(run, cleanup)` runs the cleanup on both
paths and **awaits** it before the caller resumes. If only the cleanup failed,
its error is the result; if both failed, the **original** error is the result.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing it with `try`/`finally` and then read the last requirement
again. A `throw` inside `finally` **replaces** the exception that was already in
flight — so a cleanup that fails while the work was also failing destroys the
only useful error in the whole call.

`finally` is right when the cleanup cannot fail. Here it can.

## Hint 2

Two paths, written separately:

- **failure**: run the cleanup defensively, ignore whatever it does, rethrow the
  original;
- **success**: run the cleanup normally, and let it fail loudly if it wants to.

That is a `try`/`catch` around the work rather than a `try`/`finally`, with the
success-path cleanup after the block.

## Hint 3

Two details left.

`await cleanup()` rather than `cleanup()`: the gate makes the cleanup itself
asynchronous and checks it has finished before the caller's next line. An
unawaited cleanup is a race with whatever runs next, and the usual symptom is a
temp directory deleted halfway through the next test.

And in the swallow, decide what an empty `catch` block owes the reader. A bare
`catch {}` with no comment is the line a reviewer will stop on every time — say
in the code why this one is deliberate.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing it with `try`/`finally` and then read the last requirement
again. A `throw` inside `finally` **replaces** the exception that was already in
flight — so a cleanup that fails while the work was also failing destroys the
only useful error in the whole call.

`finally` is right when the cleanup cannot fail. Here it can.

## Hint 2

Two paths, written separately:

- **failure**: run the cleanup defensively, ignore whatever it does, rethrow the
  original;
- **success**: run the cleanup normally, and let it fail loudly if it wants to.

That is a `try`/`catch` around the work rather than a `try`/`finally`, with the
success-path cleanup after the block.

## Hint 3

Two details left.

`await cleanup()` rather than `cleanup()`: the gate makes the cleanup itself
asynchronous and checks it has finished before the caller's next line. An
unawaited cleanup is a race with whatever runs next, and the usual symptom is a
temp directory deleted halfway through the next test.

And in the swallow, decide what an empty `catch` block owes the reader. A bare
`catch {}` with no comment is the line a reviewer will stop on every time — say
in the code why this one is deliberate.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An object is not iterable, so step one is turning it into something that is:
`Object.keys`, `Object.values` or `Object.entries`. Pick the one that keeps the
key available, because `fn` is given it.

Then it is ex2 again with N instead of 2: build the array of promises first,
wait once.

## Hint 2

The mistake this is guarding against is `for (const [key, value] of
Object.entries(record)) { result[key] = await fn(value, key); }`. It is
readable, it is correct, and it turns three 50ms calls into 150ms — the gate
detects it by counting how many were in flight at once.

## Hint 3

Rebuilding the object is where the keys can drift. `Promise.all` preserves input
order, so the values line up with `keys` by index — pair them back up with
`Object.fromEntries` or a plain loop.

Two things fall out for free and are worth noticing rather than coding around:
an empty object produces an empty array, and `Promise.all([])` resolves
immediately rather than hanging; and one rejection rejecting the whole call is
`Promise.all`'s own behaviour, not something you add.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An object is not iterable, so step one is turning it into something that is:
`Object.keys`, `Object.values` or `Object.entries`. Pick the one that keeps the
key available, because `fn` is given it.

Then it is ex2 again with N instead of 2: build the array of promises first,
wait once.

## Hint 2

The mistake this is guarding against is `for (const [key, value] of
Object.entries(record)) { result[key] = await fn(value, key); }`. It is
readable, it is correct, and it turns three 50ms calls into 150ms — the gate
detects it by counting how many were in flight at once.

## Hint 3

Rebuilding the object is where the keys can drift. `Promise.all` preserves input
order, so the values line up with `keys` by index — pair them back up with
`Object.fromEntries` or a plain loop.

Two things fall out for free and are worth noticing rather than coding around:
an empty object produces an empty array, and `Promise.all([])` resolves
immediately rather than hanging; and one rejection rejecting the whole call is
`Promise.all`'s own behaviour, not something you add.
