## Problem 7 — an async generator

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `chunked(source, size)` yields arrays of `size` items;
the last one may be short and an empty source yields nothing at all. A consumer
that breaks out early must end up closing the source.

```
uv run dojo test node d06_async_await ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`async function*` gives you `yield` and `for await` in the same body. Accumulate
into an array, `yield` it when it is full, and deal with the leftovers after the
loop.

The `if` after the loop is what makes the last chunk short rather than lost —
and the same `if` is what stops an empty source yielding one empty array.

## Hint 2

After yielding a full chunk, replace the array rather than emptying it. The
consumer now holds a reference to the array you just handed over; clearing it in
place mutates *their* value, and the bug shows up as chunks that are empty by
the time anybody looks at them.

## Hint 3

The cleanup requirement needs no code, but it does need you to see why it works.

When the consumer breaks out of `for await (const chunk of chunked(...))`, the
generator's `return()` is called, which resumes the generator at the paused
`yield` with a return completion. That unwinds the `for await` inside your
generator abruptly, which calls the **source's** `return()`.

Break, generator, source: three links, all automatic — as long as the middle one
is a `for await` and not a hand-driven `.next()` loop.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`async function*` gives you `yield` and `for await` in the same body. Accumulate
into an array, `yield` it when it is full, and deal with the leftovers after the
loop.

The `if` after the loop is what makes the last chunk short rather than lost —
and the same `if` is what stops an empty source yielding one empty array.

## Hint 2

After yielding a full chunk, replace the array rather than emptying it. The
consumer now holds a reference to the array you just handed over; clearing it in
place mutates *their* value, and the bug shows up as chunks that are empty by
the time anybody looks at them.

## Hint 3

The cleanup requirement needs no code, but it does need you to see why it works.

When the consumer breaks out of `for await (const chunk of chunked(...))`, the
generator's `return()` is called, which resumes the generator at the paused
`yield` with a return completion. That unwinds the `for await` inside your
generator abruptly, which calls the **source's** `return()`.

Break, generator, source: three links, all automatic — as long as the middle one
is a `for await` and not a hand-driven `.next()` loop.

lessons.briefing:
# d07 — Concurrency control

Eight problems on the one question every async service eventually asks: **how
many at once?** Lesson **03_async_patterns** taught the limiter; this set drills
the family it belongs to — permits, de-duplication, queues, batches, keyed
locks, pools and cancellation. If problem 5 feels unfamiliar rather than
mechanical, go back to lesson 03 ex3 first.

Nothing here is graded by timing. The gate holds each unit of work open and
releases it by hand, so every claim about concurrency is an exact count.

## Problem 1 — the primitive underneath

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createSemaphore(limit)` returns `{ acquire, available,
waiting }`. `acquire()` resolves with a **release function** once a permit is
free; waiters are served FIFO; each release function is idempotent, so calling
it twice returns one permit rather than two.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex1
```

## Problem 2 — de-duplicate, do not cache

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `singleFlight(fn)` returns a wrapper: while a call is in
flight, further calls join it and share its outcome. Once it settles — either
way — the next call starts a **new** one. Nothing is remembered between flights,
including failures.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a queue you keep pushing into

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createTaskQueue({ concurrency })` returns `{ push,
size, active, onIdle }`. `push(task)` returns a promise for **that task's**
outcome, and a failing task rejects only its own promise while the queue carries
on. `onIdle()` resolves when nothing is queued and nothing is running.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex3
```

## Problem 4 — batches, which are not limits

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `batched(items, size, worker)` processes in groups:
everything in a group starts together, and group *n+1* does not start until
every member of group *n* has settled. Results are flat and in input order; one
failure fails the call and no later group starts.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a limiter that reports instead of failing

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `mapSettledLimit(items, limit, worker)` keeps at most
`limit` workers in flight, freeing a slot the moment one settles either way. It
returns one `{ status, value }` / `{ status, reason }` record per input, in
input order, and never rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex5
```

## Problem 6 — lock the row, not the table

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createKeyedLock()` returns `{ withLock, held }`. Calls
on the same key run one at a time in call order; calls on different keys do not
wait for each other. The lock is released whatever `fn` does, and `fn`'s outcome
reaches its caller unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a resource pool

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createPool({ create, max })` returns `{ acquire,
release, size, waiting }`. Resources are created lazily and never more than
`max` of them; a release goes straight to the longest waiter; releasing the same
resource twice must not put two copies in the free list.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a limiter you can call off

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `mapLimitAbortable(items, limit, worker, signal)` is an
ordinary limiter until the signal aborts. Then: nothing further is started, the
call rejects with `signal.reason` immediately rather than waiting for the work
in flight, and an already-aborted signal starts nothing at all. The worker is
handed the signal as its third argument.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d07_concurrency_control

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **choosing the right amount of parallelism and
enforcing it exactly**. All eight answers are variations on one structure: a
counter or a set of permits, a FIFO queue of parked `resolve` functions, and a
release path that must run on every outcome. What changes between them is the
unit being limited — permits (ex1), identical calls (ex2), submissions (ex3),
groups (ex4), array items (ex5), keys (ex6), objects (ex7) — and what happens on
failure or cancellation. The single most common bug across the whole family is a
release that only runs on the success path: the limit silently shrinks with
every error until the system stops entirely, and the stack trace when it does
points at nothing. Every one of these gates has an assertion for it.

## ex1 — permits, and the double release

**What it tested:** the primitive itself, plus the ownership question: who is
allowed to give a permit back, and how many times?

**The classic mistake:** a single shared `release` per semaphore, or a release
with no guard. A caller that releases in both a `.then` and a `finally` — an
easy mistake, and a common one after a refactor — hands back two permits for one
acquire, and the limit is silently raised for the rest of the process.

**Model answer:** a factory that builds a fresh release closure per acquire,
each with its own `returned` flag, and a release that hands the permit straight
to the next waiter rather than incrementing and re-checking.

## ex2 — the stampede, and why this is not a cache

**What it tested:** single-flight de-duplication, and the discipline to clear
the slot on *both* outcomes.

**The classic mistake:** clearing only on success, which turns a transient
failure into a permanently cached rejection — every caller for the rest of the
process gets an error from a request that happened once. The opposite mistake is
keeping the value after it settles, which is a cache, and a cache needs an
invalidation story this function does not have.

**Model answer:** hold the promise, share it, and clear it in a `.finally` —
guarded by `inFlight === flight` so a landing flight cannot cancel the one that
replaced it.

## ex3 — one bad task must not stop the pipeline

**What it tested:** a queue whose callers own their own outcomes. The queue is
infrastructure; a task's failure is the submitter's problem, not the queue's.

**The classic mistake:** releasing the concurrency slot only when a task
succeeds. Each failure permanently reduces the effective concurrency by one, so
a service degrades over hours and eventually stops processing anything — with no
error at the moment it wedges. Almost as common: letting the task's rejection
propagate into the queue's own bookkeeping promise, which makes the whole queue
unusable after the first error.

**Model answer:** route each task's settlement to its own `resolve`/`reject`, and
hang the slot release on `.finally` so it runs whatever happened.

## ex4 — a batch is a barrier

**What it tested:** the thing a limiter is often mistaken for, asked for on
purpose. Sometimes the group *is* the unit — one bulk insert, one multi-get —
and then the barrier is the feature.

**The classic mistake:** starting the next group when the first member of the
current one finishes. That is a limiter, not a batch, and it breaks the
guarantee callers rely on: that everything in group *n* has landed before
anything in group *n+1* begins.

**Model answer:** `slice`, `map` into `Promise.all`, `await`, append. And the
matching sentence: this wastes capacity whenever the items are independent,
because every group takes as long as its slowest member.

## ex5 — the pool, with failures as data

**What it tested:** the limiter pattern proper — a shared cursor, `limit`
runners, results by index — with `allSettled` semantics bolted on.

**The classic mistake:** putting the `try`/`catch` around the whole runner or
around the final `Promise.all`. Either turns "keep going and report" back into
"stop on the first error". The catch belongs around the single `await
worker(...)` inside the loop, which is exactly what lets the loop take another
index.

**Model answer:** `const index = next; next += 1;` with no `await` between the
two lines — safe here precisely because JavaScript is single threaded, which is
the sentence an interviewer is listening for.

## ex6 — chaining onto a tail

**What it tested:** per-key serialisation, which is what you actually want
almost every time somebody asks for "a lock" — a global one would serialise
unrelated work and destroy your throughput.

**The classic mistake:** storing the caller's own result promise as the tail. If
`fn` rejects, the tail is a rejected promise, and the next waiter either
inherits the previous caller's error or never runs at all — the key is locked
forever. The other mistake is never deleting the map entry, so `held` is true
for every key ever seen and the map is a memory leak.

**Model answer:** store a promise that settles the same way for both outcomes,
return the real one to the caller, and delete the entry only if the tail you are
holding is still the current one.

## ex7 — a semaphore that remembers what it lent you

**What it tested:** lazy creation, a hard ceiling, and FIFO hand-off.

**The classic mistake:** creating a resource for every acquire until `max`, even
when idle ones are sitting right there — the reuse that makes it a pool never
happens. And the serious one: no double-release guard, so the same connection
ends up lent to two callers, who interleave statements on it and produce a bug
report about the database.

**Model answer:** idle list first, then create-if-under-max, then queue; and on
release, hand straight to a waiter rather than via the idle list, because a
round trip through the list is a chance for somebody else to take it.

## ex8 — cancellation has three separate jobs

**What it tested:** that "abortable" is not one behaviour. Refusing to start when
already aborted, refusing to start *more* once aborted, and unblocking the
caller immediately are three requirements, and an implementation can satisfy any
two of them and still be useless.

**The classic mistake:** checking the signal only at the top. The call then runs
to completion after the user has cancelled, and the rejection — if any — arrives
whenever the last worker happens to finish. Nearly as common: forgetting to
remove the abort listener, which accumulates one per call on a long-lived signal
until Node prints `MaxListenersExceededWarning`.

**Model answer:** the ex5 pool with `while (!signal.aborted)` as the loop
condition, raced against a promise that rejects on the abort event, with the
listener removed in a `finally` — and the signal handed to the worker, because
stopping the scheduling does not stop the requests already in flight.

- [MDN: `Promise.all()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) — the ordering and fail-fast guarantees ex4 and ex5 lean on.
- [MDN: `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController) — the cancellation model of ex8, including `AbortSignal.abort()` and `signal.reason`.
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) — `aborted`, the `abort` event, and `throwIfAborted()`.
- [Node.js: Dont block the event loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop) — why unbounded concurrency is a problem even when nothing is CPU bound.
- [`p-limit`](https://github.com/sindresorhus/p-limit) — the library version of ex5, worth reading now that you have written it.

# Reading - node/d07_concurrency_control

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **choosing the right amount of parallelism and
enforcing it exactly**. All eight answers are variations on one structure: a
counter or a set of permits, a FIFO queue of parked `resolve` functions, and a
release path that must run on every outcome. What changes between them is the
unit being limited — permits (ex1), identical calls (ex2), submissions (ex3),
groups (ex4), array items (ex5), keys (ex6), objects (ex7) — and what happens on
failure or cancellation. The single most common bug across the whole family is a
release that only runs on the success path: the limit silently shrinks with
every error until the system stops entirely, and the stack trace when it does
points at nothing. Every one of these gates has an assertion for it.

allowed to give a permit back, and how many times?

easy mistake, and a common one after a refactor — hands back two permits for one
acquire, and the limit is silently raised for the rest of the process.

**Model answer:** a factory that builds a fresh release closure per acquire,
each with its own `returned` flag, and a release that hands the permit straight
to the next waiter rather than incrementing and re-checking.

## ex2 — the stampede, and why this is not a cache

**What it tested:** single-flight de-duplication, and the discipline to clear
the slot on *both* outcomes.

**The classic mistake:** clearing only on success, which turns a transient
failure into a permanently cached rejection — every caller for the rest of the
process gets an error from a request that happened once. The opposite mistake is
keeping the value after it settles, which is a cache, and a cache needs an
invalidation story this function does not have.

**Model answer:** hold the promise, share it, and clear it in a `.finally` —
guarded by `inFlight === flight` so a landing flight cannot cancel the one that
replaced it.

## ex3 — one bad task must not stop the pipeline

**What it tested:** a queue whose callers own their own outcomes. The queue is
infrastructure; a task's failure is the submitter's problem, not the queue's.

unusable after the first error.

hang the slot release on `.finally` so it runs whatever happened.

current one finishes. That is a limiter, not a batch, and it breaks the

anything in group *n+1* begins.

## Problem 1 — the primitive underneath

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createSemaphore(limit)` returns `{ acquire, available,
waiting }`. `acquire()` resolves with a **release function** once a permit is
free; waiters are served FIFO; each release function is idempotent, so calling
it twice returns one permit rather than two.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: a count of free permits and a FIFO queue of waiting
`resolve` functions. `acquire` is an `if`: take a permit if there is one,
otherwise park a `resolve` on the queue and return the promise.

## Hint 2

The release is where it gets interesting. When a permit comes back there are
two cases, and only one of them touches the counter:

- somebody is waiting: hand the permit **straight to them**. The count never
  changes, because the permit went from one holder to the next.
- nobody is waiting: put it back on the count.

Incrementing first and then checking the queue works too, as long as you
remember to decrement again — which is exactly the sort of bookkeeping that
drifts.

## Hint 3

The idempotence requirement needs one boolean **per release function**, not one
per semaphore. Build the release inside a factory so each call to `acquire`
closes over its own flag.

Without it, a caller that releases in both a `.then` and a `finally` — which is
a very easy mistake to make — quietly raises your limit by one, permanently. The

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: a count of free permits and a FIFO queue of waiting
`resolve` functions. `acquire` is an `if`: take a permit if there is one,
otherwise park a `resolve` on the queue and return the promise.

## Hint 2

The release is where it gets interesting. When a permit comes back there are
two cases, and only one of them touches the counter:

- somebody is waiting: hand the permit **straight to them**. The count never
  changes, because the permit went from one holder to the next.
- nobody is waiting: put it back on the count.

Incrementing first and then checking the queue works too, as long as you
remember to decrement again — which is exactly the sort of bookkeeping that
drifts.

## Hint 3

The idempotence requirement needs one boolean **per release function**, not one
per semaphore. Build the release inside a factory so each call to `acquire`
closes over its own flag.

Without it, a caller that releases in both a `.then` and a `finally` — which is
a very easy mistake to make — quietly raises your limit by one, permanently. The
remaining decision is what a release should do if it is called by somebody who
never acquired; the gate does not test it, and a reviewer will ask.

## Problem 2 — de-duplicate, do not cache

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `singleFlight(fn)` returns a wrapper: while a call is in
flight, further calls join it and share its outcome. Once it settles — either
way — the next call starts a **new** one. Nothing is remembered between flights,
including failures.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One variable: the promise currently in flight, or nothing. The returned function
is "if there is one, return it; otherwise start one, remember it, return it".

Note what is being shared — the **promise**, not the value. Every caller that
joins gets the same promise object, so they all settle together with the same
outcome.

## Hint 2

Clearing the variable when the flight lands is the whole difference between
this and a cache. It has to happen on *both* outcomes, which is what `.finally`
is for — and it must not swallow the rejection, which `.finally` also gets
right: it passes the settlement through untouched.

## Hint 3

`if (inFlight === flight) inFlight = undefined;` rather than an unconditional
clear. Consider the sequence where flight A settles, a new caller starts flight
B, and only then A's `finally` gets its turn on the microtask queue: an
unconditional clear would throw away B while it was still running, and the next
caller would start a third flight for work already underway.

That cannot quite happen with the ordering here, and it can in every variation
of this function you will write later. Guard it now.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One variable: the promise currently in flight, or nothing. The returned function
is "if there is one, return it; otherwise start one, remember it, return it".

Note what is being shared — the **promise**, not the value. Every caller that
joins gets the same promise object, so they all settle together with the same
outcome.

## Hint 2

Clearing the variable when the flight lands is the whole difference between
this and a cache. It has to happen on *both* outcomes, which is what `.finally`
is for — and it must not swallow the rejection, which `.finally` also gets
right: it passes the settlement through untouched.

## Hint 3

`if (inFlight === flight) inFlight = undefined;` rather than an unconditional
clear. Consider the sequence where flight A settles, a new caller starts flight
B, and only then A's `finally` gets its turn on the microtask queue: an
unconditional clear would throw away B while it was still running, and the next
caller would start a third flight for work already underway.

That cannot quite happen with the ordering here, and it can in every variation
of this function you will write later. Guard it now.

## Problem 3 — a queue you keep pushing into

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createTaskQueue({ concurrency })` returns `{ push,
size, active, onIdle }`. `push(task)` returns a promise for **that task's**
outcome, and a failing task rejects only its own promise while the queue carries
on. `onIdle()` resolves when nothing is queued and nothing is running.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The shape is: a list of not-yet-started runners, a count of running ones, and a
`pump()` that starts runners while there is room. `push` builds a runner, puts it
on the list, and calls `pump()`.

The runner is a closure over `resolve` and `reject` from the promise `push`
returned — that is how each caller gets its own outcome.

## Hint 2

The critical difference from an array-in / array-out limiter: the queue must
never *observe* a task's rejection as its own failure. Route the settlement to
the caller (`.then(resolve, reject)`) and hook the slot release onto `.finally`,
which runs on both outcomes.

If the slot release is only on the success path, one failing task permanently
shrinks your concurrency by one — a queue that quietly grinds to a halt after a
few errors, which is a genuinely hard bug to see.

## Hint 3

`onIdle` needs a list of waiters, resolved when a task finishes and both
counters reach zero. Return an already-resolved promise if the queue is idle
when it is asked, or the caller waits for an event that has already happened.

The remaining decision is where the idle check goes. Putting it inside the same
callback that releases the slot is simplest — but make sure `pump()` has had its
chance to start the next task first, or a queue with work still waiting will
briefly declare itself idle.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — batches, which are not limits

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `batched(items, size, worker)` processes in groups:
everything in a group starts together, and group *n+1* does not start until
every member of group *n* has settled. Results are flat and in input order; one
failure fails the call and no later group starts.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is the shape people write when they *mean* a concurrency limiter and get
it wrong — and here it is what was asked for, because sometimes a batch really
is the unit of work (one bulk insert, one multi-get, one API call that takes a
hundred ids).

Outer loop stepping `size` at a time, `slice` the group, start them all, await
them all, append.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all` gives you three of the four requirements for free: it starts
nothing itself (the `map` already did), it preserves input order, and it rejects
on the first failure. Awaiting it is what stops the next group.

Two details: the worker is given its **absolute** index, not its offset within
the group — so add the group's start. And an empty input has to fall out
naturally, which it does if the loop condition is written against the length
rather than a computed batch count.

Be ready to say why this is the wrong tool when the items are independent: every
group takes as long as its slowest member, and the fast slots sit idle. That is
what ex5 is for.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the shape people write when they *mean* a concurrency limiter and get
it wrong — and here it is what was asked for, because sometimes a batch really
is the unit of work (one bulk insert, one multi-get, one API call that takes a
hundred ids).

Outer loop stepping `size` at a time, `slice` the group, start them all, await
them all, append.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all` gives you three of the four requirements for free: it starts
nothing itself (the `map` already did), it preserves input order, and it rejects
on the first failure. Awaiting it is what stops the next group.

Two details: the worker is given its **absolute** index, not its offset within
the group — so add the group's start. And an empty input has to fall out
naturally, which it does if the loop condition is written against the length
rather than a computed batch count.

Be ready to say why this is the wrong tool when the items are independent: every
group takes as long as its slowest member, and the fast slots sit idle. That is
what ex5 is for.

## Problem 5 — a limiter that reports instead of failing

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `mapSettledLimit(items, limit, worker)` keeps at most
`limit` workers in flight, freeing a slot the moment one settles either way. It
returns one `{ status, value }` / `{ status, reason }` record per input, in
input order, and never rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The pool shape: start `limit` runners, each looping "claim the next index, do
it, repeat" until the indexes run out. Nothing is batched, so a slot frees the
instant one worker settles rather than when a group does.

Results go into a pre-sized array **by index**, which is what keeps input order
without any sorting.

## Hint 2

The shared cursor is the trick worth naming:

```ts
const index = next;
next += 1;
```

There is no `await` between those two lines, so no two runners can ever claim
the same index. JavaScript being single threaded is doing real work for you
here — the identical code in Java or Go needs an atomic increment.

## Hint 3

The `try`/`catch` goes **inside** the runner loop, around the single `await
worker(...)`. That is what turns a failure into a record and lets the loop carry
on to the next index.

Wrapping the whole runner, or the final `Promise.all`, gets you a limiter that
stops on the first error — a different function with different semantics. Two
decisions are left: how many runners to start when there are fewer items than
`limit` (starting `limit` of them works, and think about what the extra ones
do), and whether `reason` should be normalised to an `Error` the way `attempt`
did in d06.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The pool shape: start `limit` runners, each looping "claim the next index, do
it, repeat" until the indexes run out. Nothing is batched, so a slot frees the
instant one worker settles rather than when a group does.

Results go into a pre-sized array **by index**, which is what keeps input order
without any sorting.

## Hint 2

The shared cursor is the trick worth naming:

```ts
const index = next;
next += 1;
```

There is no `await` between those two lines, so no two runners can ever claim
the same index. JavaScript being single threaded is doing real work for you
here — the identical code in Java or Go needs an atomic increment.

## Hint 3

The `try`/`catch` goes **inside** the runner loop, around the single `await
worker(...)`. That is what turns a failure into a record and lets the loop carry
on to the next index.

Wrapping the whole runner, or the final `Promise.all`, gets you a limiter that
stops on the first error — a different function with different semantics. Two
decisions are left: how many runners to start when there are fewer items than
`limit` (starting `limit` of them works, and think about what the extra ones
do), and whether `reason` should be normalised to an `Error` the way `attempt`
did in d06.

## Hint 1

A `Map` from key to *a promise*, not to a boolean. The promise represents "the
current holder of this key is finished", and the queue for a key is just a chain
built on it:

```ts
const previous = tails.get(key) ?? Promise.resolve();
const result = previous.then(fn);
```

Different keys have different chains, so they never wait for one another. That
is the whole design.

## Hint 2

The tail you store must not be `result` itself. If `fn` rejects, `result` is a
rejected promise, and chaining the next caller onto it would either skip them or
hand them the previous caller's error.

`held(key)` is `map.has(key)`, which means you have to delete the entry when the
chain empties, or every key ever used stays "held" forever and the map grows

```ts
if (tails.get(key) === tail) tails.delete(key);
```

the second is still running, and the fourth caller starts immediately alongside
it. The remaining decision is whether `held` should be true for a key that has
waiters but no active holder — say what your answer is and why.

## Problem 7 — a resource pool

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createPool({ create, max })` returns `{ acquire,
release, size, waiting }`. Resources are created lazily and never more than
`max` of them; a release goes straight to the longest waiter; releasing the same
resource twice must not put two copies in the free list.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state: the idle resources, the queue of waiting `resolve`
functions, and a count of how many have been created.

`acquire` is a three-way decision in this exact order: reuse an idle one, create
a new one if you are under `max`, otherwise queue. Getting the order wrong is
how a pool ends up creating `max` resources on the first `max` acquires even
when they are all coming back immediately.

## Hint 2

`release` is the mirror: if somebody is waiting, hand it straight to them —
never via the idle list, because a round trip through the list is a chance for
another caller to take it. Otherwise put it back.

This is ex1 with objects instead of permits, which is a good sentence to have
ready: a pool *is* a semaphore that remembers what it lent you.

## Hint 3

The double-release guard is the assertion most implementations miss. If the same
resource can be pushed onto the idle list twice, two later callers each get what
they think is an exclusive connection and start interleaving statements on it —
which produces a bug report about the database, not about your pool.

Checking membership before pushing is enough here. Two decisions are left: what
to do with a released resource nobody in this pool ever created, and whether
`size()` should count resources that have been created and thrown away — this
pool has no eviction, and a real one would.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state: the idle resources, the queue of waiting `resolve`
functions, and a count of how many have been created.

`acquire` is a three-way decision in this exact order: reuse an idle one, create
a new one if you are under `max`, otherwise queue. Getting the order wrong is
how a pool ends up creating `max` resources on the first `max` acquires even
when they are all coming back immediately.

## Hint 2

`release` is the mirror: if somebody is waiting, hand it straight to them —
never via the idle list, because a round trip through the list is a chance for
another caller to take it. Otherwise put it back.

This is ex1 with objects instead of permits, which is a good sentence to have
ready: a pool *is* a semaphore that remembers what it lent you.

## Hint 3

The double-release guard is the assertion most implementations miss. If the same
resource can be pushed onto the idle list twice, two later callers each get what
they think is an exclusive connection and start interleaving statements on it —
which produces a bug report about the database, not about your pool.

Checking membership before pushing is enough here. Two decisions are left: what
to do with a released resource nobody in this pool ever created, and whether
`size()` should count resources that have been created and thrown away — this
pool has no eviction, and a real one would.

## Problem 8 — a limiter you can call off

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `mapLimitAbortable(items, limit, worker, signal)` is an
ordinary limiter until the signal aborts. Then: nothing further is started, the
call rejects with `signal.reason` immediately rather than waiting for the work
in flight, and an already-aborted signal starts nothing at all. The worker is
handed the signal as its third argument.

```
uv run dojo test node d07_concurrency_control ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from ex5's pool: `limit` runners, a shared cursor, results by index. Then
add cancellation in three places, because "abortable" means three different
things and the gate checks each one.

1. Before anything starts: if `signal.aborted` already, throw `signal.reason`.
2. In the runner's loop condition: stop claiming new indexes once aborted.
3. In the return: reject as soon as the abort happens, rather than after the
   in-flight work finishes.

## Hint 2

The third one needs a promise that rejects on the abort event:

```ts
const aborted = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
  signal.addEventListener("abort", () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true });
});
```

Then `Promise.race([Promise.all(runners), aborted])`. On the happy path that
promise simply never settles — which is fine, and is also why it needs a
`.catch(() => {})` of its own so an abort with nobody racing it is not an
unhandled rejection.

## Hint 3

Two details separate this from a version that passes today and leaks tomorrow.

Remove the abort listener when you are done. A long-lived `AbortSignal` — a
request signal, say — accumulates one listener per call, and at eleven of them
Node starts printing `MaxListenersExceededWarning`.

And pass the signal to the worker. A limiter that only stops *scheduling* leaves
the requests already in flight running to completion, which is not what the user
who pressed cancel meant. What the worker does with it is its business; your
job is to hand it over.

The remaining decision is what to do with the results collected before the
abort. This version throws them away; an alternative returns the partial array.
Be able to say which one a caller would rather have.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from ex5's pool: `limit` runners, a shared cursor, results by index. Then
add cancellation in three places, because "abortable" means three different
things and the gate checks each one.

1. Before anything starts: if `signal.aborted` already, throw `signal.reason`.
2. In the runner's loop condition: stop claiming new indexes once aborted.
3. In the return: reject as soon as the abort happens, rather than after the
   in-flight work finishes.

## Hint 2

The third one needs a promise that rejects on the abort event:

```ts
const aborted = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
  signal.addEventListener("abort", () => reject(signal.reason), { once: true });
});
```

Then `Promise.race([Promise.all(runners), aborted])`. On the happy path that
promise simply never settles — which is fine, and is also why it needs a
`.catch(() => {})` of its own so an abort with nobody racing it is not an
unhandled rejection.

## Hint 3

Two details separate this from a version that passes today and leaks tomorrow.

Remove the abort listener when you are done. A long-lived `AbortSignal` — a
request signal, say — accumulates one listener per call, and at eleven of them
Node starts printing `MaxListenersExceededWarning`.

And pass the signal to the worker. A limiter that only stops *scheduling* leaves
the requests already in flight running to completion, which is not what the user
who pressed cancel meant. What the worker does with it is its business; your
job is to hand it over.

The remaining decision is what to do with the results collected before the
abort. This version throws them away; an alternative returns the partial array.
Be able to say which one a caller would rather have.

# d08 — Promise combinators

Eight problems on combining promises — the four built-ins written from scratch,
and four that are not built in and that you will end up needing anyway. Lesson
**03_async_patterns** is the source; if the difference between `race` and `any`
is not instant, reread its review section before starting.

Do not call the built-in you are reimplementing. Every input in the gate is a
deferred it settles by hand, so several of these tests contain a promise that
never settles at all — on purpose.

## Problem 1 — write `Promise.all`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `allInOrder(promises)` resolves with every value in
**input** order. An empty array resolves immediately with `[]`; the first
rejection rejects the result with that reason, without waiting for the rest.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex1
```

## Problem 2 — write `Promise.race`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `raceFirst(promises)` settles with the first input to
settle, fulfilled or rejected. An empty array **never settles at all**.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex2
```

## Problem 3 — write `Promise.any`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `anyOf(promises)` resolves with the first input to
*fulfil*, ignoring rejections. If every input rejects it rejects with an
`AggregateError` whose `.errors` holds every reason in **input** order. An empty
array rejects immediately with an empty `.errors`.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex3
```

## Problem 4 — all, with a progress bar

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `allWithProgress(promises, onProgress)` behaves like
`Promise.all` and additionally calls `onProgress(done, total)` once per
fulfilment, in **completion** order, with the running count. An empty input
reports nothing at all — not even `(0, 0)`.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex4
```

## Problem 5 — allSettled, with a deadline

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `settleWithin(promises, ms)` waits at most `ms` and
returns one record per input in input order: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }`,
`{ status: "rejected", reason }` or `{ status: "timedout" }`. It never rejects,
resolves early if everything settles early, and leaves no timer armed either
way.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex5
```

## Problem 6 — the first answer that is any good

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `firstMatching(promises, predicate)` resolves with the
first value to arrive that satisfies the predicate. Rejections and values that
fail the predicate are ignored; when every input has settled without a match it
rejects with `no result matched`.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex6
```

## Problem 7 — results as they land

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `settledStream(promises)` is an async generator yielding
`{ index, result }` — one entry per input, in **completion** order, tagged with
the input it came from. It never throws: a rejection is an entry. An empty input
yields nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a combinator that thinks ahead

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `firstQuorum(promises, quorum)` resolves as soon as
`quorum` inputs have fulfilled with the **same** value (`Object.is`). Rejections
are lost votes. It rejects with `no quorum` as soon as a quorum becomes
*impossible*, which is not the same as waiting for everything to settle.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex8
```

# Reading - node/d08_promise_combinators

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **choosing a settling rule and implementing it
exactly**. Every combinator here is the same three lines of scaffolding — a
`new Promise`, a results array written by index, and a counter — with one
question answered differently: *what makes this settle, and what makes it give
up?* `all` settles on the last success or the first failure; `race` on the first
of anything; `any` on the first success or the last failure; and the four
hand-written ones settle on a deadline, a predicate, each arrival, or an
arithmetic proof that no answer is coming. Two facts do most of the work
throughout: a promise silently ignores every settlement after the first, so you
almost never need a `done` flag of your own; and writing results **by index**
rather than pushing is what keeps input order separate from completion order —
which several of these problems need to track at the same time.

## ex1 — index for order, counter for completion

**What it tested:** the two mechanisms every combinator is built from, and the
empty-array case.

**The classic mistake:** `results.push(value)` in the handler. It passes any
test where the inputs settle in order and silently scrambles the output when
they do not — which is to say, in production. Close behind: forgetting that an
empty array must resolve immediately, because a counter that starts at zero
never reaches zero by decrementing.

**Model answer:** a pre-sized array written at `index`, a `remaining` counter,
and `reject` passed straight through as the second `.then` argument — the first
rejection settles the promise and every later one is a no-op.

## ex2 — the shortest one is the one people overthink

**What it tested:** whether you trust the settle-once rule enough to write four
lines.

**The classic mistake:** adding a `settled` boolean and checking it in both
handlers. It is harmless and it is a tell: it means you are not sure what a
second `resolve` does. (Nothing. It does nothing.)

**Model answer:** attach `resolve` and `reject` to every input. The empty case
needs no branch — nothing is attached, so nothing settles, which is exactly what
`Promise.race([])` specifies.

## ex3 — the mirror image, and an error type most people have never constructed

**What it tested:** inverting ex1's logic, and knowing that `AggregateError` is a
real built-in with an `.errors` array rather than something you fake with a
joined message.

**The classic mistake:** collecting the reasons with `push`, so `.errors` comes
back in completion order. A caller trying to work out which of five replicas
failed now has to guess. The other one: treating `anyOf([])` like
`raceFirst([])` and leaving it pending. `any` resolves on a success, and with no
inputs there can never be one, so the outcome is already decided — the two empty
cases differ for a reason worth being able to state.

**Model answer:** `resolve` straight through, reasons stored by index,
`new AggregateError(errors, message)` when the outstanding count hits zero.

## ex4 — two orders at once

**What it tested:** holding input order and completion order in the same
function without confusing them.

**The classic mistake:** reporting progress with the index (`onProgress(index +
1, total)`), which produces a progress bar that jumps backwards whenever an
early input finishes late. Progress is a count of arrivals; the index is a
position. They are different numbers and both are in scope.

**Model answer:** write `results[index]`, increment a separate `done`, and call
`onProgress(done, total)` from the fulfilment handler — with the empty case
returning before any of it is wired up, so nothing is reported at all.

## ex5 — pre-fill, then overwrite

**What it tested:** combining `allSettled` semantics with a deadline, and timer
hygiene.

**The classic mistake:** working out at deadline time which inputs are still
missing. That needs a second structure — a set of settled indexes, usually — and
it is where the off-by-ones live. Filling the array with `timedout` up front
makes the deadline handler a one-liner. The other mistake is not clearing the
timeout on the early-completion path: the result is correct and the process
stays alive for the rest of the budget.

**Model answer:** `promises.map(() => ({ status: "timedout" }))`, overwrite each
slot as it settles, `clearTimeout` when the counter empties.

## ex6 — count the chances, not the failures

**What it tested:** a settle rule with three outcomes per input — match, no
match, rejection — where two of the three mean the same thing.

**The classic mistake:** counting only rejections towards giving up. When every
input fulfils with something the predicate turns down, nothing ever counts, and
the call hangs forever — which is the case the gate feeds it with `1` and `2`
against `> 10`.

**Model answer:** one `giveUp()` helper used by both the rejection handler and
the predicate's `else`, so "a chance was used up" is expressed once.

## ex7 — push meets pull

**What it tested:** the adapter between a callback-shaped world and a
pull-shaped one, which is what every async iterator over an event source is.

**The classic mistake:** attaching the handlers lazily, one per `yield`, which
serialises inputs that are already in flight and can miss settlements that
happen while the consumer is away. The subtler one is a wake-up resolver that is
not cleared before being called: a later settlement then resolves a promise that
has already been used, and the consumer sleeps through it forever.

**Model answer:** attach everything up front, buffer arrivals in a queue, and
loop — sleep on a fresh wake promise only when the queue is empty, then drain
the whole queue, because several inputs can land in one microtask checkpoint.

## ex8 — settle when the answer is decided, not when the work is done

**What it tested:** forward-looking failure detection. Every other problem here
gives up when the inputs run out; this one has to give up when the *arithmetic*
runs out.

**The classic mistake:** waiting for every input before deciding there is no
quorum. With two voters, a quorum of two and one rejection, the answer is
already known and the call sits there waiting for a vote that cannot change
anything — which in a real quorum read means holding a request open on a replica
that will never reply.

**Model answer:** after every settlement, compare `leader + undecided` with the
quorum and reject the moment it falls short. That one expression covers the
all-settled case, the early-impossible case and the empty-input case, which is
why none of them needs a branch of its own.

## Further reading

- [MDN: `Promise.all()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) — the ordering and fail-fast rules ex1 reimplements.
- [MDN: `Promise.any()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/any) — including the `AggregateError` contract from ex3.
- [MDN: `AggregateError`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/AggregateError) — how to construct one and what `.errors` holds.
- [MDN: `Promise.allSettled()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/allSettled) — the record shape ex5 and ex7 borrow.
- [MDN: `Object.is()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/is) — the equality `Map` keys use, which is what makes ex8's tally behave.

## Problem 1 — write `Promise.all`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `new Promise` constructor is the right tool here — you are building a
promise out of N others, not wrapping one you already have. Inside it you need
two pieces of state: a results array and a count of how many are still
outstanding.

Attach a handler to each input with its index captured, write the value at that
index, decrement, and resolve when the count reaches zero.

## Hint 2

Two cases people miss.

The empty array has to resolve **immediately**. A count that starts at zero
never reaches zero by decrementing, so the promise hangs forever unless you
check up front.

And the rejection path is simply `reject` passed straight through as the second
argument to every `.then`. The first one to fire settles the promise; the rest
are no-ops, because a settled promise ignores later settlements — which is why
you do not need a `done` flag of your own.

## Hint 3

Counting rather than checking `results.length` matters: an array written by
index is *sparse* until the last hole is filled, and `results.length` is the
full length from the moment it is constructed. `Object.keys(results).length`
would work and is slower and stranger than a counter.

The remaining decision is whether to accept plain values mixed in with the
promises the way the real `Promise.all` does. The gate only passes promises;
adding it is one line, and knowing which line is the point.

Attach a handler to each input with its index captured, write the value at that
index, decrement, and resolve when the count reaches zero.

## Hint 2

Two cases people miss.

The empty array has to resolve **immediately**. A count that starts at zero
never reaches zero by decrementing, so the promise hangs forever unless you
check up front.

And the rejection path is simply `reject` passed straight through as the second
argument to every `.then`. The first one to fire settles the promise; the rest
are no-ops, because a settled promise ignores later settlements — which is why
you do not need a `done` flag of your own.

## Hint 3

Counting rather than checking `results.length` matters: an array written by
index is *sparse* until the last hole is filled, and `results.length` is the
full length from the moment it is constructed. `Object.keys(results).length`
would work and is slower and stranger than a counter.

The remaining decision is whether to accept plain values mixed in with the
promises the way the real `Promise.all` does. The gate only passes promises;
adding it is one line, and knowing which line is the point.

## Problem 3 — write `Promise.any`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `anyOf(promises)` resolves with the first input to
*fulfil*, ignoring rejections. If every input rejects it rejects with an
`AggregateError` whose `.errors` holds every reason in **input** order. An empty

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The mirror of ex1: there, one rejection ended it and the successes were
counted; here one success ends it and the *rejections* are counted.

So `resolve` goes straight through as the first argument to every `.then`, and
the second argument does the bookkeeping.

## Hint 2

`AggregateError` is a real built-in: `new AggregateError(errors, message)`, with
the array readable afterwards as `.errors`. Collect the reasons **by index**
rather than pushing, or the array ends up in completion order and a caller
trying to work out which source failed has to guess.

## Hint 3

The empty case rejects rather than hanging, and the reasoning is worth having
ready: `any` resolves on the first success, and with no inputs there can never
be one — so the outcome is already decided, and it is failure. Compare with
`race([])`, which stays pending forever because nothing has *happened*.

Two rules, two different answers to the same-looking question, and being able to
explain the difference is what the interviewer is listening for.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The mirror of ex1: there, one rejection ended it and the successes were
counted; here one success ends it and the *rejections* are counted.

So `resolve` goes straight through as the first argument to every `.then`, and
the second argument does the bookkeeping.

## Hint 2

`AggregateError` is a real built-in: `new AggregateError(errors, message)`, with
the array readable afterwards as `.errors`. Collect the reasons **by index**
rather than pushing, or the array ends up in completion order and a caller
trying to work out which source failed has to guess.

## Hint 3

The empty case rejects rather than hanging, and the reasoning is worth having
ready: `any` resolves on the first success, and with no inputs there can never
be one — so the outcome is already decided, and it is failure. Compare with
`race([])`, which stays pending forever because nothing has *happened*.

Two rules, two different answers to the same-looking question, and being able to
explain the difference is what the interviewer is listening for.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from your ex1 and add three lines. The counter you already have is the
`done` number; the total is the input length; the callback goes in the
fulfilment handler.

The interesting part is that this function deals in **two orders at once**, and
each has its own mechanism: the results are written by index, and the progress
is reported as things arrive.

## Hint 2

Watch the direction of the counter. ex1 counted *down* to zero; a progress
report wants to count *up*, so either flip it or derive one from the other.
Reporting `total - remaining` works and is one more place for an off-by-one to
live.

## Hint 3

Two edge decisions the gate pins down.

An empty input reports nothing — not even `onProgress(0, 0)`. The natural
implementation gives you that for free as long as the empty case returns before
any callback is wired up.

And the callback is *not* wrapped in a `try`. If a progress reporter throws, the
whole call should fail: it is your code, and a broken progress bar that silently
eats its own exception is worse than one that stops. The remaining decision is
whether a rejection should also count as progress — the specification here says
no, and there is a reasonable argument for yes.

## Problem 5 — allSettled, with a deadline

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `settleWithin(promises, ms)` waits at most `ms` and
returns one record per input in input order: `{ status: "fulfilled", value }`,
`{ status: "rejected", reason }` or `{ status: "timedout" }`. It never rejects,
resolves early if everything settles early, and leaves no timer armed either
way.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The move that makes this easy: fill the results array with `{ status:
"timedout" }` up front, one per input, and overwrite each slot as its answer
arrives. The deadline handler then has nothing to compute — it just resolves
with whatever the array currently holds.

The alternative, working out at deadline time which indexes are still missing,

## Problem 6 — the first answer that is any good

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `firstMatching(promises, predicate)` resolves with the
first value to arrive that satisfies the predicate. Rejections and values that
fail the predicate are ignored; when every input has settled without a match it
rejects with `no result matched`.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex6
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is ex3 with one extra condition. There, any fulfilment resolved; here, only
a fulfilment that passes the predicate does. Everything else — a rejection, or a
value the predicate turns down — is a lost chance, and lost chances are counted.

So: one counter, one `resolve` guarded by the predicate, and one "that was our
last chance" check.

## Hint 2

Note what the counter must **not** be. Counting only rejections would leave the
call hanging when every input fulfils with something unsuitable — the gate has
exactly that case, with `1` and `2` against a predicate of `> 10`.

Count every settlement that failed to produce an answer, whichever kind it was.
Both paths reaching the same helper is the tidy way to guarantee that.

## Hint 3

The empty case cannot match, so it fails immediately for the same reason ex3's
does — there is no chance left.

The remaining decision, and it is a real one: what if the predicate throws? This
version lets it escape into the `.then` handler, which rejects the promise the
handler belongs to and quietly loses that input rather than failing the call.
Decide whether you want that, and say so in the code.

## Hint 1

This is ex3 with one extra condition. There, any fulfilment resolved; here, only
a fulfilment that passes the predicate does. Everything else — a rejection, or a
value the predicate turns down — is a lost chance, and lost chances are counted.

So: one counter, one `resolve` guarded by the predicate, and one "that was our
last chance" check.

## Hint 2

Note what the counter must **not** be. Counting only rejections would leave the
call hanging when every input fulfils with something unsuitable — the gate has
exactly that case, with `1` and `2` against a predicate of `> 10`.

Count every settlement that failed to produce an answer, whichever kind it was.
Both paths reaching the same helper is the tidy way to guarantee that.

## Hint 3

The empty case cannot match, so it fails immediately for the same reason ex3's
does — there is no chance left.

The remaining decision, and it is a real one: what if the predicate throws? This
version lets it escape into the `.then` handler, which rejects the promise the
handler belongs to and quietly loses that input rather than failing the call.
Decide whether you want that, and say so in the code.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `settledStream(promises)` is an async generator yielding
`{ index, result }` — one entry per input, in **completion** order, tagged with

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A generator is pulled, and promises push — so you need a small buffer between
them. Three pieces: a queue of entries that have landed, a "wake me up"
resolver for when the consumer is waiting and the queue is empty, and a count of
how many entries are still to come.

## Hint 2

Attach the handlers to **all** the inputs before the first `yield`. A generator
body does not start running until the first `next()`, so this happens on the
consumer's first pull — but it must all happen at once, not one input at a time,
or you would be serialising work that is already in flight and could miss
settlements that happen while the consumer is away.

Each handler pushes `{ index, result }` and wakes the consumer if it is waiting.

## Hint 3

The loop is: while entries remain, if the queue is empty await a fresh "wake"
promise, then drain everything in the queue with `yield`.

Two details. Clear the `wake` reference *before* calling it, or a later
settlement resolves an already-used promise and the consumer sleeps forever.
And drain the whole queue each time round rather than yielding one entry per
wake — several inputs can land inside a single microtask checkpoint, and you do
not want a wake-up for each.

The remaining decision is what should happen if the consumer breaks out early:
the generator is closed, its state is dropped, and the handlers still fire into
a queue nobody reads. That is harmless here and would not be if the entries were
large.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — a combinator that thinks ahead

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `firstQuorum(promises, quorum)` resolves as soon as
`quorum` inputs have fulfilled with the **same** value (`Object.is`). Rejections
are lost votes. It rejects with `no quorum` as soon as a quorum becomes
*impossible*, which is not the same as waiting for everything to settle.

```
uv run dojo test node d08_promise_combinators ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: a tally from value to vote count, and how many inputs have
not settled yet. A `Map` compares its keys the way `Object.is` does, which is
exactly the comparison asked for.

Every fulfilment increments its value's count and checks it against the quorum;
every settlement of either kind decrements the undecided count.

## Hint 2

The hard half is knowing when to give up. "Everything has settled and nothing
reached the quorum" is one case, and it is not the only one — the gate has a
run with two voters, a quorum of two, one rejection and one input that never
settles at all.

So ask the forward-looking question after every settlement: **could any value
still reach the quorum?**

## Hint 3

Formally: take the current leader's count, add the number of votes still to be
cast, and compare with the quorum. If even the best case falls short, reject
now.

That single expression covers all three failure shapes — everything settled and
nobody won, a rejection that makes the arithmetic hopeless, and an empty input
list where the leader is 0 and there are no votes left. Which is why the empty
case needs no branch of its own beyond running the check once.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces of state: a tally from value to vote count, and how many inputs have
not settled yet. A `Map` compares its keys the way `Object.is` does, which is
exactly the comparison asked for.

Every fulfilment increments its value's count and checks it against the quorum;
every settlement of either kind decrements the undecided count.

## Hint 2

The hard half is knowing when to give up. "Everything has settled and nothing
reached the quorum" is one case, and it is not the only one — the gate has a
run with two voters, a quorum of two, one rejection and one input that never
settles at all.

So ask the forward-looking question after every settlement: **could any value
still reach the quorum?**

## Hint 3

Formally: take the current leader's count, add the number of votes still to be
cast, and compare with the quorum. If even the best case falls short, reject
now.

That single expression covers all three failure shapes — everything settled and
nobody won, a rejection that makes the arithmetic hopeless, and an empty input
list where the leader is 0 and there are no votes left. Which is why the empty
case needs no branch of its own beyond running the check once.

The remaining decision is what to do about the inputs that are still pending
when you settle. Nothing in this exercise stops them, and a real quorum read
would want an `AbortSignal` so the losers can be called off.

lessons.briefing:
# d09 — Emitters

Eight problems on `EventEmitter` and the adapters people build around it —
lesson **04_events_errors** is the source. The recurring theme is *who owns the
listener*: almost every bug here is a listener that outlived its purpose, or one
that was removed along with somebody else's.

The gate checks listener counts after every helper settles, for exactly that
reason.

## Problem 1 — a class that announces what it did

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `Store extends EventEmitter` with `set`, `get`, `delete`
and `size`. `set` emits `"change"` with `(key, value, previous)` — but **only**
when the value really changed. `delete` emits `"delete"` with `(key, value)` and
returns whether anything was removed; deleting a missing key says nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex1
```

## Problem 2 — whichever happens first

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `firstOf(emitter, names)` resolves with
`{ event, args }` for whichever named event fires first. An `"error"` event
rejects with that error. Every listener it added is removed once it settles,
whichever way.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex2
```

## Problem 3 — pipe events across

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `forward(source, target, { events, prefix })` re-emits
the named events on the target under the prefixed name, arguments untouched. It
returns an unsubscribe that removes **exactly** what it added — the gate puts an
unrelated listener on the same event and checks it survives — and is safe to
call twice.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex3
```

## Problem 4 — an emitter that remembers what it missed

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createStickyEmitter()` returns `{ emit, on, off,
buffered }`. An event emitted with no listener is buffered and `emit` returns
`false`. The **first** listener for an event receives the whole backlog
immediately, in order, and the backlog is then spent — a second listener gets
nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex4
```

## Problem 5 — events as an async iterable

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `iterateEvents(emitter, name)` yields the first argument
of each `name` event in order. `"end"` finishes the iteration and `"error"`
throws into the loop — after anything already queued has been delivered. Events
emitted faster than they are read are buffered, and the listeners go when the
iteration finishes.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex5
```

## Problem 6 — the error event is not an ordinary event

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createStrictEmitter()` returns `{ on, once, off, emit,
listenerCount }`. `emit` returns whether anybody was listening — except for
`"error"` with no listener, which **throws**. A `once` listener counts until it
fires and is gone afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex6
```

## Problem 7 — one delivery per window

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createCoalescingEmitter({ windowMs })` returns
`{ push, on, flush, pending }`. The first push opens a window; later pushes join
it **without extending it**; when it closes, listeners get the whole batch in
push order. `flush()` delivers now and cancels the window. An empty buffer
delivers nothing, and an idle emitter arms no timer.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex7
```

## Problem 8 — waiting for an event, with a way out

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `onceWithSignal(emitter, name, signal)` resolves with
the first argument of the next `name` event, or rejects with `signal.reason` if
the caller gives up first. An already-aborted signal rejects without attaching
anything, and every path removes **both** listeners.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex8
```

# Reading - node/d09_emitters

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **listener ownership**. An `EventEmitter` is a shared
object with no notion of scope: whoever attaches a listener owns it forever
unless they remove it, and whoever removes listeners can remove somebody else's.
Nearly every problem here turns on that — keeping the exact function reference so
it can be removed (ex2, ex3, ex8), cleaning up on the failure path as well as the
success path (ex2, ex5), copying the list before dispatching so a listener can
unsubscribe itself mid-call (ex4, ex6). The second theme is the seam between
**push and pull**: an emitter pushes whenever it likes, while promises and
iterators are pulled, and every adapter between them needs a buffer, a way to
wake a sleeping consumer, and a decision about what happens to events nobody was
there to hear (ex4, ex5, ex7).

## ex1 — an event for something that did not happen

**What it tested:** subclassing `EventEmitter`, and the discipline of emitting
only on real transitions.

**The classic mistake:** emitting `"change"` on every `set`. A config poller
writing the same value every ten seconds then re-renders the UI every ten
seconds, and the fix always arrives as a diff somewhere downstream instead of
here, where the information is. The other mistake is reading the previous value
after overwriting it, which quietly reports the new value twice.

**Model answer:** capture `previous`, compare, and return early — being careful
that "the key was never set" is different from "the key holds `undefined`",
which is what `Map.has` is for.

## ex2 — cleanup on both paths

**What it tested:** turning several events into one promise, and removing every
listener afterwards.

**The classic mistake:** attaching inline arrow functions and having nothing to
pass to `off`. The listeners then live as long as the emitter does — and because
a settled promise ignores later settlements, everything still *works*, which is
why this leak survives review. Node's `MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven
listeners is the only thing that will ever tell you.

**Model answer:** collect `[event, listener]` pairs, one `cleanup()` walking
them, called from every settling path — including the `"error"` handler, which
exists mainly to stop the emitter throwing.

## ex3 — remove exactly what you added

**What it tested:** whether "unsubscribe" means what you think it means.

**The classic mistake:** `source.removeAllListeners(event)`. It passes the
obvious test and destroys unrelated subscriptions belonging to code you have
never read — the gate registers one on purpose and checks it is still there. Its
sibling: calling `off` with a newly written arrow function that looks identical
to the one registered. Different function, no removal, no error.

**Model answer:** build each listener into a variable, keep the pairs, and have
the returned closure remove precisely those.

## ex4 — the subscribe-too-late race

**What it tested:** the sticky/replay pattern, which exists because "ready" often
fires before the thing that cares about it has finished constructing.

**The classic mistake:** replaying the backlog to *every* new listener. That is a
log, not an emitter, and the second subscriber gets a burst of ancient events it
has no context for. The other one is dispatching over the live listener array,
so a listener that unsubscribes itself makes the loop skip the next one.

**Model answer:** buffer whole argument lists while the listener list is empty,
detect "I am the first" by checking the length before pushing, delete the backlog
before replaying it, and always iterate a copy.

## ex5 — attach eagerly, iterate lazily

**What it tested:** the push-to-pull adapter, and one specific trap about
generators.

**The classic mistake:** writing `iterateEvents` as an `async function*`. Its
body does not run until the consumer's first `next()`, so the listeners are
attached late and every event emitted in between is gone — which the gate
catches by emitting twice before the consumer gets a turn. The second mistake is
checking the error flag before draining the queue, which throws away values that
had already arrived.

**Model answer:** an ordinary function that attaches the three listeners and
returns an object whose `[Symbol.asyncIterator]` is the generator — with the
loop draining the queue first, and cleanup in a `finally` so an early `break`
releases the emitter too.

## ex6 — the one event that throws

**What it tested:** the `"error"` special case, which is the single most
consequential rule in the whole `EventEmitter` API.

**The classic mistake:** treating `"error"` like any other event and returning
`false` when nobody is listening. Node deliberately throws instead, because a
failure nobody is watching should be loud — it is exactly why an unhandled
stream error crashes the process rather than leaving it wedged. Second mistake:
removing a `once` registration *after* calling it, so a listener that re-emits
its own event finds itself still registered and runs twice.

**Model answer:** one registry of `{ listener, once }`, dispatch over a copy,
remove `once` entries before invoking them, and on `"error"` with an empty list
throw the argument itself when it is an `Error` so the stack trace stays real.

## ex7 — a window, not a debounce

**What it tested:** the distinction between "wait until things go quiet" and
"deliver at most once per window".

**The classic mistake:** re-arming the timer on every push. That is a debounce,
and under a producer that never pauses it never delivers at all — the batching
window exists precisely to bound how long a value can sit unsent. The other
mistake is `flush()` that delivers without cancelling the timer, so the batch
goes out twice.

**Model answer:** arm the timer only when none is armed, one `deliver()` shared
by the timer and `flush()`, an empty-buffer guard, and a fresh array rather than
emptying the one the listeners are holding.

## ex8 — two listeners, one promise, two removals

**What it tested:** combining an emitter with an `AbortSignal`, and cleaning up
both sides.

**The classic mistake:** removing the emitter listener and forgetting the abort
listener. Request-scoped signals outlive dozens of these calls, so one leak per
call is how the warning appears in production. Nearly as common: attaching
listeners before checking `signal.aborted`, so an already-cancelled caller still
touches the emitter.

**Model answer:** early return on an aborted signal, two named handlers sharing
one `cleanup()`, and `signal.reason` as the rejection on both abort paths.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: Events](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html) — the whole API, including the `"error"` rule and `captureRejections`.
- [Node.js: The Node.js event emitter](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/the-nodejs-event-emitter) — the short introduction, worth rereading after ex6.
- [Node.js: `events.on()` and `events.once()`](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html#eventsonemitter-eventname-options) — the built-in versions of ex5 and ex8, including their `signal` options.
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) — `aborted`, `reason`, and the `abort` event ex8 listens for.
- [MDN: `Symbol.asyncIterator`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/asyncIterator) — the protocol ex5 implements by hand.
