it can be removed (ex2, ex3, ex8), cleaning up on the failure path as well as the
success path (ex2, ex5), copying the list before dispatching so a listener can
unsubscribe itself mid-call (ex4, ex6). The second theme is the seam between
**push and pull**: an emitter pushes whenever it likes, while promises and
iterators are pulled, and every adapter between them needs a buffer, a way to
wake a sleeping consumer, and a decision about what happens to events nobody was
there to hear (ex4, ex5, ex7).

## ex1 — an event for something that did not happen

**What it tested:** subclassing `EventEmitter`, and the discipline of emitting
only on real transitions.

**The classic mistake:** emitting `"change"` on every `set`. A config poller
writing the same value every ten seconds then re-renders the UI every ten
seconds, and the fix always arrives as a diff somewhere downstream instead of
here, where the information is. The other mistake is reading the previous value
after overwriting it, which quietly reports the new value twice.

**Model answer:** capture `previous`, compare, and return early — being careful
that "the key was never set" is different from "the key holds `undefined`",
which is what `Map.has` is for.

## ex2 — cleanup on both paths

**What it tested:** turning several events into one promise, and removing every
listener afterwards.

**The classic mistake:** attaching inline arrow functions and having nothing to
pass to `off`. The listeners then live as long as the emitter does — and because
a settled promise ignores later settlements, everything still *works*, which is
why this leak survives review. Node's `MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven
listeners is the only thing that will ever tell you.

**Model answer:** collect `[event, listener]` pairs, one `cleanup()` walking
them, called from every settling path — including the `"error"` handler, which
exists mainly to stop the emitter throwing.

## ex3 — remove exactly what you added

**What it tested:** whether "unsubscribe" means what you think it means.

**The classic mistake:** `source.removeAllListeners(event)`. It passes the
obvious test and destroys unrelated subscriptions belonging to code you have
never read — the gate registers one on purpose and checks it is still there. Its
sibling: calling `off` with a newly written arrow function that looks identical
to the one registered. Different function, no removal, no error.

**Model answer:** build each listener into a variable, keep the pairs, and have
the returned closure remove precisely those.

## ex4 — the subscribe-too-late race

**What it tested:** the sticky/replay pattern, which exists because "ready" often
fires before the thing that cares about it has finished constructing.

**The classic mistake:** replaying the backlog to *every* new listener. That is a
log, not an emitter, and the second subscriber gets a burst of ancient events it
has no context for. The other one is dispatching over the live listener array,
so a listener that unsubscribes itself makes the loop skip the next one.

**Model answer:** buffer whole argument lists while the listener list is empty,
detect "I am the first" by checking the length before pushing, delete the backlog
before replaying it, and always iterate a copy.

## ex5 — attach eagerly, iterate lazily

**What it tested:** the push-to-pull adapter, and one specific trap about
generators.

**The classic mistake:** writing `iterateEvents` as an `async function*`. Its
body does not run until the consumer's first `next()`, so the listeners are
attached late and every event emitted in between is gone — which the gate
catches by emitting twice before the consumer gets a turn. The second mistake is
checking the error flag before draining the queue, which throws away values that
had already arrived.

**Model answer:** an ordinary function that attaches the three listeners and
returns an object whose `[Symbol.asyncIterator]` is the generator — with the
loop draining the queue first, and cleanup in a `finally` so an early `break`
releases the emitter too.

## ex6 — the one event that throws

**What it tested:** the `"error"` special case, which is the single most
consequential rule in the whole `EventEmitter` API.

**The classic mistake:** treating `"error"` like any other event and returning
`false` when nobody is listening. Node deliberately throws instead, because a
failure nobody is watching should be loud — it is exactly why an unhandled
stream error crashes the process rather than leaving it wedged. Second mistake:
removing a `once` registration *after* calling it, so a listener that re-emits
its own event finds itself still registered and runs twice.

**Model answer:** one registry of `{ listener, once }`, dispatch over a copy,
remove `once` entries before invoking them, and on `"error"` with an empty list
throw the argument itself when it is an `Error` so the stack trace stays real.

## ex7 — a window, not a debounce

**What it tested:** the distinction between "wait until things go quiet" and
"deliver at most once per window".

**The classic mistake:** re-arming the timer on every push. That is a debounce,
and under a producer that never pauses it never delivers at all — the batching
window exists precisely to bound how long a value can sit unsent. The other
mistake is `flush()` that delivers without cancelling the timer, so the batch
goes out twice.

**Model answer:** arm the timer only when none is armed, one `deliver()` shared
by the timer and `flush()`, an empty-buffer guard, and a fresh array rather than
emptying the one the listeners are holding.

## ex8 — two listeners, one promise, two removals

**What it tested:** combining an emitter with an `AbortSignal`, and cleaning up
both sides.

**The classic mistake:** removing the emitter listener and forgetting the abort
listener. Request-scoped signals outlive dozens of these calls, so one leak per
call is how the warning appears in production. Nearly as common: attaching
listeners before checking `signal.aborted`, so an already-cancelled caller still
touches the emitter.

**Model answer:** early return on an aborted signal, two named handlers sharing
one `cleanup()`, and `signal.reason` as the rejection on both abort paths.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: Events](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html) — the whole API, including the `"error"` rule and `captureRejections`.
- [Node.js: The Node.js event emitter](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/the-nodejs-event-emitter) — the short introduction, worth rereading after ex6.
- [Node.js: `events.on()` and `events.once()`](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html#eventsonemitter-eventname-options) — the built-in versions of ex5 and ex8, including their `signal` options.
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) — `aborted`, `reason`, and the `abort` event ex8 listens for.
- [MDN: `Symbol.asyncIterator`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/asyncIterator) — the protocol ex5 implements by hand.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — a class that announces what it did

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `Store extends EventEmitter` with `set`, `get`, `delete`
and `size`. `set` emits `"change"` with `(key, value, previous)` — but **only**
when the value really changed. `delete` emits `"delete"` with `(key, value)` and
returns whether anything was removed; deleting a missing key says nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`extends EventEmitter` gives you `on`, `once`, `off`, `emit` and the rest for
free — you write none of them. The only new state is the map holding the data.

`emit(name, ...args)` is synchronous: by the time it returns, every listener has
already run. That is worth remembering, because it means a listener that throws
takes your `set()` call down with it.

## Hint 2

Read the previous value **before** you overwrite it: the whole point of the
third argument is that the listener can see what changed, and once the map is
updated that information is gone.

The no-change rule needs care with a key that was never set. `previous ===
value` is not enough on its own to decide "unchanged" — think about what
`get` returns for a missing key and what that means if somebody legitimately
stores the same thing twice.

## Hint 3

`delete` has the same shape: capture the value, then remove, then decide whether
to announce anything. `Map.prototype.delete` already returns whether it removed
something, which is exactly the boolean you owe the caller.

The remaining decision is whether `set` should emit before or after the map is
updated. A listener that calls `get()` will see different things in the two
orders — pick one deliberately, because the answer to "is the store consistent
during the event" is something callers will build on.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`extends EventEmitter` gives you `on`, `once`, `off`, `emit` and the rest for
free — you write none of them. The only new state is the map holding the data.

`emit(name, ...args)` is synchronous: by the time it returns, every listener has
already run. That is worth remembering, because it means a listener that throws
takes your `set()` call down with it.

## Hint 2

Read the previous value **before** you overwrite it: the whole point of the
third argument is that the listener can see what changed, and once the map is
updated that information is gone.

The no-change rule needs care with a key that was never set. `previous ===
value` is not enough on its own to decide "unchanged" — think about what
`get` returns for a missing key and what that means if somebody legitimately
stores the same thing twice.

## Hint 3

`delete` has the same shape: capture the value, then remove, then decide whether
to announce anything. `Map.prototype.delete` already returns whether it removed
something, which is exactly the boolean you owe the caller.

The remaining decision is whether `set` should emit before or after the map is
updated. A listener that calls `get()` will see different things in the two
orders — pick one deliberately, because the answer to "is the store consistent
during the event" is something callers will build on.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `new Promise` with one listener per name plus one for `"error"`. Each listener
settles the promise — and because a promise ignores every settlement after the
first, you do not need a flag to work out who won.

What you *do* need is the ability to remove the listeners afterwards, which
means keeping a reference to every one you attached. An inline arrow function
you did not save cannot be removed.

## Hint 2

Collect them as pairs of `[eventName, listener]` and write one `cleanup()` that
walks the list calling `emitter.off`. Call it from every settling path.

Do not reach for `removeAllListeners()`. The emitter is not yours: the gate
proves the point in ex3 by putting somebody else's listener on the same event.

## Hint 3

The `"error"` listener earns its place twice over. It rejects the promise, and —
more importantly — its mere existence stops the emitter throwing.

An `EventEmitter` that emits `"error"` with no listener throws the argument
synchronously, which in Node means an uncaught exception and a dead process.
Attaching a handler is how you convert that into a rejection you can `await`.

The remaining decision: what if `"error"` is one of the `names` the caller
passed? Say what your implementation does, and whether that is the behaviour you
would document.

passed? Say what your implementation does, and whether that is the behaviour you
would document.

## Problem 4 — an emitter that remembers what it missed

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createStickyEmitter()` returns `{ emit, on, off,
buffered }`. An event emitted with no listener is buffered and `emit` returns
`false`. The **first** listener for an event receives the whole backlog
immediately, in order, and the backlog is then spent — a second listener gets
nothing.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two maps: event to listeners, and event to the backlog of argument lists that
arrived while nobody was there. `emit` is an `if` on whether the listener list
is empty — deliver, or buffer.

Note that the backlog stores the **whole argument list** per emit, not a single
value, so it is an array of arrays.

## Hint 2

`on` has to notice that it is the *first* listener for this event, which means
checking the list length before pushing rather than after. If it is, take the
backlog and call the new listener once per buffered entry, in order.

Delete the backlog entry before you replay it. A listener that emits the same
event during its own replay would otherwise be appending to the very list you
are iterating.

## Hint 3

When you dispatch to several listeners, iterate over a **copy** of the list. A
listener is allowed to call `off` on itself mid-dispatch, and splicing the array
you are walking makes the loop skip whoever came next — a bug that only appears
when two listeners are registered and the first one unsubscribes.

The remaining design decision is the sticky policy itself: this one spends the
backlog on the first subscriber. Replaying it to everyone forever would be a
log; dropping it after a while would be a buffer with a TTL. Know which you
built.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two maps: event to listeners, and event to the backlog of argument lists that
arrived while nobody was there. `emit` is an `if` on whether the listener list
is empty — deliver, or buffer.

Note that the backlog stores the **whole argument list** per emit, not a single
value, so it is an array of arrays.

## Hint 2

`on` has to notice that it is the *first* listener for this event, which means
checking the list length before pushing rather than after. If it is, take the
backlog and call the new listener once per buffered entry, in order.

Delete the backlog entry before you replay it. A listener that emits the same
event during its own replay would otherwise be appending to the very list you
are iterating.

## Hint 3

When you dispatch to several listeners, iterate over a **copy** of the list. A
listener is allowed to call `off` on itself mid-dispatch, and splicing the array
you are walking makes the loop skip whoever came next — a bug that only appears
when two listeners are registered and the first one unsubscribes.

The remaining design decision is the sticky policy itself: this one spends the
backlog on the first subscriber. Replaying it to everyone forever would be a
log; dropping it after a while would be a buffer with a TTL. Know which you
built.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The push/pull adapter again, and it wants four pieces of state: a queue, a
"finished" flag, a place to keep an error, and a "wake me" resolver for when the
consumer is waiting on an empty queue.

Three listeners feed them — one for `name`, one for `"end"`, one for
`"error"` — and each ends by waking the consumer if it is asleep.

## Hint 2

Where the listeners are attached matters enormously. If `iterateEvents` is
itself an `async function*`, its body does not run until the consumer's first
`next()` — and every event emitted before that is gone.

So attach eagerly in an ordinary function, and return an object with a
`[Symbol.asyncIterator]` method that *is* the generator. The gate emits two
events before the consumer gets a turn, precisely to catch this.

## Hint 3

The loop: drain the queue with `yield`, then check the terminal states, then
sleep on a fresh wake promise. That order is what makes the error case deliver
the buffered values first, which the gate checks.

Cleanup goes in a `finally` around the whole loop. It then runs on all three
exits — the natural end, the thrown error, and a consumer that breaks out early
— and only that last one is easy to forget, because it never appears in the
happy path.

The remaining decision is what to do about an unbounded queue. A producer faster
than its consumer will grow this forever, and the real answer is backpressure.

## Problem 6 — the error event is not an ordinary event

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createStrictEmitter()` returns `{ on, once, off, emit,
listenerCount }`. `emit` returns whether anybody was listening — except for
`"error"` with no listener, which **throws**. A `once` listener counts until it
fires and is gone afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One map from event name to a list of registrations, where a registration is the
listener plus a flag saying whether it is a `once`. `on` and `once` are the same
code with that flag flipped, so write one private `add`.

`emit` walks a **copy** of the list — dispatch is exactly when listeners tend to
add and remove listeners.

## Hint 2

Remove a `once` registration **before** calling it, not after. A listener that
re-emits the same event during its own call would otherwise be found still
registered and run again — and the two orders differ in exactly the case that is
hardest to debug.

`off` has to find the registration by the function the caller originally passed,
which is why the registration keeps a reference to it rather than only to a
wrapper.

## Hint 3

The `"error"` rule is the point of the exercise. An emitter with no listener for
`"error"` throws rather than silently dropping it — that is why an unhandled
stream error crashes a Node process instead of leaving it wedged, and it is
deliberate: a failure nobody is watching should be loud.

Throw the argument itself when it is an `Error`, so the stack trace is the real
one. When it is not, wrap it, because throwing a bare string helps nobody.

The remaining decision: should `emit` return `true` or `false` for an `"error"`
that threw? It never returns at all — say why that is not a cop-out.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One map from event name to a list of registrations, where a registration is the
listener plus a flag saying whether it is a `once`. `on` and `once` are the same
code with that flag flipped, so write one private `add`.

`emit` walks a **copy** of the list — dispatch is exactly when listeners tend to
add and remove listeners.

## Hint 2

Remove a `once` registration **before** calling it, not after. A listener that
re-emits the same event during its own call would otherwise be found still
registered and run again — and the two orders differ in exactly the case that is
hardest to debug.

`off` has to find the registration by the function the caller originally passed,
which is why the registration keeps a reference to it rather than only to a
wrapper.

## Hint 3

The `"error"` rule is the point of the exercise. An emitter with no listener for
`"error"` throws rather than silently dropping it — that is why an unhandled
stream error crashes a Node process instead of leaving it wedged, and it is
deliberate: a failure nobody is watching should be loud.

Throw the argument itself when it is an `Error`, so the stack trace is the real
one. When it is not, wrap it, because throwing a bare string helps nobody.

The remaining decision: should `emit` return `true` or `false` for an `"error"`
that threw? It never returns at all — say why that is not a cop-out.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — one delivery per window

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createCoalescingEmitter({ windowMs })` returns
`{ push, on, flush, pending }`. The first push opens a window; later pushes join
it **without extending it**; when it closes, listeners get the whole batch in
push order. `flush()` delivers now and cancels the window. An empty buffer
delivers nothing, and an idle emitter arms no timer.

```
uv run dojo test node d09_emitters ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state: the listeners, the buffer, and the timer handle for the
open window. `push` appends and then arms a timer **only if one is not already
armed**.

That "only if" is the whole difference between this and d04's debounce. A
debounce restarts its timer on every call, so a producer that never pauses can
delay a value indefinitely. A coalescing window is measured from the first push,
so every value is delivered within `windowMs` of arriving no matter how busy
things get.

## Hint 2

Write one `deliver()` and use it for both the timer callback and `flush()`. It
has to: clear any armed timer, do nothing at all if the buffer is empty, and
otherwise take the buffer, replace it with a fresh array, and hand the old one
to every listener.

Replacing rather than emptying matters for the same reason as d06's chunked
generator: the listeners are holding the array you just gave them.

## Hint 3

Two timer facts the gate checks by counting.

After a window closes, nothing is re-armed — the next push opens the next
window. An emitter that always keeps a timer alive stops a Node process from
exiting.

And `flush()` cancels the pending window as well as delivering, or the batch
goes out twice: once now and once when the timer catches up to an empty buffer.
The empty-buffer guard covers you there too, which is a good example of two
correct defences making the code obviously right rather than merely right.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state: the listeners, the buffer, and the timer handle for the
open window. `push` appends and then arms a timer **only if one is not already
armed**.

That "only if" is the whole difference between this and d04's debounce. A
debounce restarts its timer on every call, so a producer that never pauses can
delay a value indefinitely. A coalescing window is measured from the first push,
so every value is delivered within `windowMs` of arriving no matter how busy
things get.

## Hint 2

Write one `deliver()` and use it for both the timer callback and `flush()`. It
has to: clear any armed timer, do nothing at all if the buffer is empty, and
otherwise take the buffer, replace it with a fresh array, and hand the old one
to every listener.

Replacing rather than emptying matters for the same reason as d06's chunked
generator: the listeners are holding the array you just gave them.

## Hint 3

Two timer facts the gate checks by counting.

After a window closes, nothing is re-armed — the next push opens the next
window. An emitter that always keeps a timer alive stops a Node process from
exiting.

And `flush()` cancels the pending window as well as delivering, or the batch
goes out twice: once now and once when the timer catches up to an empty buffer.
The empty-buffer guard covers you there too, which is a good example of two
correct defences making the code obviously right rather than merely right.

lessons.briefing:
# d10 — Error patterns

Eight problems on the shapes you put around a failure — lesson
**04_events_errors** is the source. Not error *classes* (that is d11), but the
wrappers, guards and walks: normalising what was thrown, adding context without
losing the cause, catching narrowly, and deciding where a failure finally goes.

Every one of these is a function you will end up writing in any codebase that
runs unattended.

## Problem 1 — anything can be thrown

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `asError(thrown)` returns a real `Error`. An `Error` (or
subclass) comes back as the **same object**. A string becomes the message, with
no cause. An object with a string `message` donates that message and is kept as
the cause. Anything else is stringified and kept as the cause.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a callback that cannot be called twice

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `onceCallback(cb)` returns a wrapper that passes the
first call through and refuses the rest, plus `calls()` and `suppressed()`
counters.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex2
```

## Problem 3 — never release Zalgo

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `ensureAsync(fn)` returns a wrapper that **always**
returns a promise and **never** throws synchronously — including when `fn`
validates its arguments and throws before any promise exists. A function that
already returns a promise is adopted, not double-wrapped.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex3
```

## Problem 4 — reading a cause chain

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `explain(error)` returns `{ chain, root, depth }` —
messages outermost first, the last error reached, and the number of links. Only
an `Error` cause is another link; anything else is data and the walk stops. A
chain that loops back on itself stops at the repeat.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex4
```

## Problem 5 — say what you were doing

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `withContext(fn, context)` wraps an async function so
every rejection becomes a **new** error reading `<context>: <original message>`
with the original as `cause`. Anything thrown is normalised first, a success
passes through by identity, and the original is never mutated.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex5
```

## Problem 6 — catch narrowly

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `swallow(fn, { when, fallback })` returns the fallback
for a rejection the predicate accepts and rethrows everything else **exactly as
it was thrown** — same object, same stack. The predicate is always handed a real
`Error`.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex6
```

## Problem 7 — the leaves of a failure tree

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `flattenErrors(error)` collects the errors at the bottom
of a tree built from `AggregateError.errors` arrays and `cause` links. Leaves
come back in first-seen order without duplicates; a cycle terminates; anything
that is not an `Error` has no leaves.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the last place a failure can go

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createErrorBoundary({ classify, onOperational,
onFatal })` normalises, classifies and routes. If `classify` throws, the
**original** error is treated as fatal. If `onOperational` throws, that failure
is itself fatal. If `onFatal` throws, it escapes.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d10_error_patterns

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **handling a failure without destroying the evidence**.
JavaScript lets you throw anything, so the first job of any error-handling code
is to get back to a real `Error` (ex1) — and the second is to stop there, because
everything past that point is a temptation to lose something. The three things
worth protecting, and the three things these problems keep taking away from a
careless implementation, are: the original object (rethrow it, do not rebuild
it), the stack trace on it (do not construct a new error where you meant to
forward one), and the `cause` chain (wrap, never overwrite). The other half of
the set is about the *timing* of failures — a callback called twice, a throw that
escapes before a promise exists, a handler that fails while handling — because
those are the failures that never show up in a stack trace at all.

## ex1 — anything can be thrown

**What it tested:** that `catch (e)` gives you `unknown` for a real reason, and
that normalising it is a four-branch decision rather than a cast.

**The classic mistake:** `new Error(String(thrown))` for everything, including
things that already *were* errors. The stack trace then points at your
normaliser instead of at the failure, and every error in the system looks like it
originated in one file. Second: forgetting `typeof null === "object"` and
reading `.message` off `null`.

**Model answer:** `instanceof Error` first and return the same object; a string
becomes the message; a `{ message: string }` object donates its message and is
kept as `cause`; everything else is `String()`-ed and kept as `cause`.

## ex2 — calling back twice runs everything twice

**What it tested:** the callback-era hazard that promises made impossible.
Settling a promise twice is a silent no-op; calling a callback twice runs the
entire continuation twice.

**The classic mistake:** incrementing the "already called" flag *after* invoking
the callback. A callback that re-enters the API it was passed to then finds the
guard still open. The other one is throwing on the second call — satisfying, and
usually wrong, because the offender is somebody else's library and crashing it
does not fix their bug.

**Model answer:** flag set before the call, later calls counted rather than
thrown, and the counter exposed so a nonzero value is a diagnostic instead of a
mystery.

## ex3 — sometimes-sync is worse than always-slow

**What it tested:** whether you can name the guarantee and produce it in one
line. A function that usually returns a promise but occasionally throws
synchronously cannot be used safely: the caller's `.catch()` never sees the
throw.

**The classic mistake:** `try { return fn(...) } catch (e) { return
Promise.reject(e) }`, which works and is four times as long, or
`Promise.resolve(fn(...))`, which does **not** work — `fn` is called before
`Promise.resolve` gets a chance, so a synchronous throw still escapes.

**Model answer:** an `async` arrow. `async` converts every throw in the body into
a rejection of the promise it has already returned, and adopts a returned
promise rather than nesting it.

## ex4 — walking a chain that might be a circle

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **handling a failure without destroying the evidence**.
JavaScript lets you throw anything, so the first job of any error-handling code
is to get back to a real `Error` (ex1) — and the second is to stop there, because
everything past that point is a temptation to lose something. The three things
worth protecting, and the three things these problems keep taking away from a
careless implementation, are: the original object (rethrow it, do not rebuild
it), the stack trace on it (do not construct a new error where you meant to
forward one), and the `cause` chain (wrap, never overwrite). The other half of
the set is about the *timing* of failures — a callback called twice, a throw that
escapes before a promise exists, a handler that fails while handling — because
those are the failures that never show up in a stack trace at all.

normaliser instead of at the failure, and every error in the system looks like it
originated in one file. Second: forgetting `typeof null === "object"` and
reading `.message` off `null`.

**Model answer:** `instanceof Error` first and return the same object; a string
becomes the message; a `{ message: string }` object donates its message and is
kept as `cause`; everything else is `String()`-ed and kept as `cause`.

## ex2 — calling back twice runs everything twice

**What it tested:** the callback-era hazard that promises made impossible.

entire continuation twice.

## Problem 1 — anything can be thrown

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `asError(thrown)` returns a real `Error`. An `Error` (or
subclass) comes back as the **same object**. A string becomes the message, with
no cause. An object with a string `message` donates that message and is kept as
the cause. Anything else is stringified and kept as the cause.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four branches, in a deliberate order: already an `Error`, a string, an
object with a string `message`, everything else.

The first branch returns the **same object**. Rebuilding it would give you a
stack trace pointing at this function instead of at the code that failed, which
is the single most useful thing an error carries.

## Hint 2

`typeof null === "object"`, so the duck-typing branch needs a null check before

## Hint 1

Two counters in a closure and one early return. The returned function is
callable *and* has methods, so build the arrow function first, assert it to the
interface type, then attach `calls` and `suppressed` to it.

## Hint 2

Increment the "real call" counter **before** invoking the callback, not after. A
callback that calls itself — directly or through the API it drives — would
otherwise find the guard still open and run twice, which is the exact bug the
guard exists to prevent.

Counting the suppressed calls rather than throwing is a deliberate choice worth
being able to defend: this wrapper usually sits between you and somebody else's
library, and a nonzero count is a diagnostic you can log without turning their
bug into your crash.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 4 — reading a cause chain

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `explain(error)` returns `{ chain, root, depth }` —
messages outermost first, the last error reached, and the number of links. Only
an `Error` cause is another link; anything else is data and the walk stops. A
chain that loops back on itself stops at the repeat.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `while` walking `current = current.cause`, pushing the message each time. The
loop ends when the cause is not another `Error` — which covers both "no cause at
all" and "a cause holding some data", because `undefined instanceof Error` is
`false` and so is `{ row: 3 } instanceof Error`.

`root` is whatever `current` is holding when the loop stops, and `depth` is the
length of the array you built.

## Hint 2

`cause` is not in TypeScript's `Error` type in every configuration, so you may
need `(current as Error & { cause?: unknown }).cause` to read it. That cast is
also a good moment to notice that `cause` is typed `unknown` on purpose: it is
allowed to hold literally anything.

## Hint 3

The loop guard is a `Set` of the errors already visited, keyed by **identity**
rather than by message — two genuinely different errors are allowed to say the
same thing.

Cycles are not hypothetical: any wrapper that attaches a caught error as the
cause of a new one, inside a retry loop that re-wraps, can build one. Without
the guard `explain` hangs the process, which is a spectacular way for an error
reporter to fail.

The remaining decision is where `root` should point when a loop is detected.
This version says "the last error reached before the repeat" — say why that is
more useful than throwing.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `while` walking `current = current.cause`, pushing the message each time. The
loop ends when the cause is not another `Error` — which covers both "no cause at
all" and "a cause holding some data", because `undefined instanceof Error` is
`false` and so is `{ row: 3 } instanceof Error`.

`root` is whatever `current` is holding when the loop stops, and `depth` is the
length of the array you built.

## Hint 2

`cause` is not in TypeScript's `Error` type in every configuration, so you may
need `(current as Error & { cause?: unknown }).cause` to read it. That cast is
also a good moment to notice that `cause` is typed `unknown` on purpose: it is
allowed to hold literally anything.

## Hint 3

The loop guard is a `Set` of the errors already visited, keyed by **identity**
rather than by message — two genuinely different errors are allowed to say the
same thing.

Cycles are not hypothetical: any wrapper that attaches a caught error as the
cause of a new one, inside a retry loop that re-wraps, can build one. Without
the guard `explain` hangs the process, which is a spectacular way for an error
reporter to fail.

The remaining decision is where `root` should point when a loop is detected.
This version says "the last error reached before the repeat" — say why that is
more useful than throwing.

## Problem 5 — say what you were doing

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `withContext(fn, context)` wraps an async function so
every rejection becomes a **new** error reading `<context>: <original message>`
with the original as `cause`. Anything thrown is normalised first, a success
passes through by identity, and the original is never mutated.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex5
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An `async` wrapper with a `try`/`catch`, returning a new arrow function that
takes the same arguments and passes them straight through with `...args`.

The catch builds a **new** `Error` — `` new Error(`${context}: ${message}`, {
cause: error }) `` — rather than touching the one it caught. That object may be
held by a retry loop, a logger, or three other frames, and rewriting its message
under them is a genuinely unpleasant bug.

## Hint 2

`return await fn(...args)` inside the `try`, not `return fn(...args)`.

Without the `await`, the function returns the pending promise immediately, the
`try` block ends, and the rejection arrives when nothing is watching — so the
caller gets the original error with no context at all. Most linters flag `return
await` as redundant; inside a `try` it is load bearing, and this is the
canonical counterexample.

## Hint 3

The message has to survive a non-Error rejection, because a `throw "..."` two
libraries down is not your choice. Read `.message` when it is an `Error` and
`String(thrown)` otherwise.

The remaining decision is what to do when the same wrapper is applied at three
levels of a call stack. You get `a: b: c: ECONNREFUSED`, which is genuinely
useful — and `cause` gives a reader the structured version of the same thing.
Decide whether you would ever want to collapse it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An `async` wrapper with a `try`/`catch`, returning a new arrow function that
takes the same arguments and passes them straight through with `...args`.

The catch builds a **new** `Error` — `` new Error(`${context}: ${message}`, {
cause: error }) `` — rather than touching the one it caught. That object may be
held by a retry loop, a logger, or three other frames, and rewriting its message
under them is a genuinely unpleasant bug.

## Hint 2

`return await fn(...args)` inside the `try`, not `return fn(...args)`.

Without the `await`, the function returns the pending promise immediately, the
`try` block ends, and the rejection arrives when nothing is watching — so the
caller gets the original error with no context at all. Most linters flag `return
await` as redundant; inside a `try` it is load bearing, and this is the
canonical counterexample.

## Hint 3

The message has to survive a non-Error rejection, because a `throw "..."` two
libraries down is not your choice. Read `.message` when it is an `Error` and
`String(thrown)` otherwise.

The remaining decision is what to do when the same wrapper is applied at three
levels of a call stack. You get `a: b: c: ECONNREFUSED`, which is genuinely
useful — and `cause` gives a reader the structured version of the same thing.
Decide whether you would ever want to collapse it.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — the leaves of a failure tree

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `flattenErrors(error)` collects the errors at the bottom
of a tree built from `AggregateError.errors` arrays and `cause` links. Leaves
come back in first-seen order without duplicates; a cycle terminates; anything
that is not an `Error` has no leaves.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A depth-first walk with a `Set` of visited errors. Write the "what is below
this error" helper first, on its own: an `AggregateError` contributes every
`Error` in its `errors` array, and *any* error contributes its `cause` when the
cause is an `Error`.

Note that both can apply to the same node — an `AggregateError` is allowed to
have a cause as well.

## Hint 2

The visit is: if already seen, stop; mark it seen; ask what is below it; if
nothing, record it as a leaf; otherwise recurse.

The `Set` does double duty. It deduplicates — one underlying failure commonly
appears in several branches of a fan-out — and it is the loop guard.

## Hint 3

The cycle case needs one extra thought, and it is the interesting one.

If you recurse into links you have already seen, the recursion terminates but
the node that closed the loop is left with children and therefore never counts
as a leaf — so a two-error cycle reports **nothing at all**, which is a useless
answer.

Filter the links to the *unvisited* ones first, then ask whether any remain. An
error whose only link points back at something already visited has nothing new
underneath it, so it is the bottom of that branch. Order the recursion so the
result is first-seen order, and remember the non-Error input returns an empty
array rather than throwing.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A depth-first walk with a `Set` of visited errors. Write the "what is below
this error" helper first, on its own: an `AggregateError` contributes every
`Error` in its `errors` array, and *any* error contributes its `cause` when the
cause is an `Error`.

Note that both can apply to the same node — an `AggregateError` is allowed to
have a cause as well.

## Hint 2

The visit is: if already seen, stop; mark it seen; ask what is below it; if
nothing, record it as a leaf; otherwise recurse.

The `Set` does double duty. It deduplicates — one underlying failure commonly
appears in several branches of a fan-out — and it is the loop guard.

## Hint 3

The cycle case needs one extra thought, and it is the interesting one.

If you recurse into links you have already seen, the recursion terminates but
the node that closed the loop is left with children and therefore never counts
as a leaf — so a two-error cycle reports **nothing at all**, which is a useless
answer.

Filter the links to the *unvisited* ones first, then ask whether any remain. An
error whose only link points back at something already visited has nothing new
underneath it, so it is the bottom of that branch. Order the recursion so the
result is first-seen order, and remember the non-Error input returns an empty
array rather than throwing.

## Problem 8 — the last place a failure can go

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createErrorBoundary({ classify, onOperational,
onFatal })` normalises, classifies and routes. If `classify` throws, the
**original** error is treated as fatal. If `onOperational` throws, that failure
is itself fatal. If `onFatal` throws, it escapes.

```
uv run dojo test node d10_error_patterns ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four steps in `handle`, and each of the last three has a failure mode of its
own:

1. normalise whatever arrived into an `Error` (ex1 again);
2. classify it — inside a `try`, because the classifier is code too;
3. route it;
4. deal with a routing handler that fails.

Write the happy path first, then add one guard at a time and check it against
the gate's four scenarios.

## Hint 2

Two of the three guards are asymmetric on purpose, and being able to say why is
the exercise.

A `classify` that throws means you do not know what you are looking at, and the
safe assumption is the worse one — but the error you report is the **original**,
not the classifier's complaint, because the original is what somebody has to
fix.

An `onOperational` that throws is a failure of your error handling, which is
itself a fatal problem: send *that* error to `onFatal`.

## Hint 3

`onFatal` is deliberately **not** wrapped. When the last handler in the chain
fails there is nowhere left to send anything, and catching it would lose both
errors silently. Letting it escape is what makes a process-level handler behave
the way an operator expects — loudly.

The remaining decision is whether `onFatal` receiving a handler failure should
also get the original error attached, say as `cause`. The gate does not require
it; an on-call engineer would thank you for it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four steps in `handle`, and each of the last three has a failure mode of its
own:

1. normalise whatever arrived into an `Error` (ex1 again);
2. classify it — inside a `try`, because the classifier is code too;
3. route it;
4. deal with a routing handler that fails.

Write the happy path first, then add one guard at a time and check it against
the gate's four scenarios.

## Hint 2

Two of the three guards are asymmetric on purpose, and being able to say why is
the exercise.

A `classify` that throws means you do not know what you are looking at, and the
safe assumption is the worse one — but the error you report is the **original**,
not the classifier's complaint, because the original is what somebody has to
fix.

An `onOperational` that throws is a failure of your error handling, which is
itself a fatal problem: send *that* error to `onFatal`.

## Hint 3

`onFatal` is deliberately **not** wrapped. When the last handler in the chain
fails there is nowhere left to send anything, and catching it would lose both
errors silently. Letting it escape is what makes a process-level handler behave
the way an operator expects — loudly.

The remaining decision is whether `onFatal` receiving a handler failure should
also get the original error attached, say as `cause`. The gate does not require
it; an on-call engineer would thank you for it.

lessons.briefing:
# d11 — Custom errors

Eight problems on error *classes* — lesson **04_events_errors** taught the first
one; this set drills the family that grows out of it. Subclassing, hierarchies,
serialising across a wire and back, aggregates, and the two places `instanceof`
stops being enough.

Everything here is synchronous. What is being checked throughout is that the
things a subclass is supposed to inherit — `instanceof`, the stack, the name
that ends up in a log — actually survived.

## Problem 1 — the smallest useful error class

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `new NotFoundError(resource, id)` has the message
`<resource> not found: <id>`, `name` `"NotFoundError"`, `status` 404, and both
pieces kept as fields. It is an `Error`, it is a `NotFoundError`, and it has a
stack that names the class.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a family, not a flag

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `HttpError(status, message, options?)` sets `status`,
sets `expose` (true for a 4xx, false for a 5xx), names itself after the class
actually constructed, and passes `options` through so `cause` works.
`BadRequestError` (400) and `ConflictError` (409) extend it.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex2
```

## Problem 3 — an error you can put in a log line

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `serialiseError(error)` returns `{ name, message }` plus
`code` when it is a string, `status` when it is a number, and `cause` recursed
when it is an `Error`. Absent keys are **omitted**, the stack is never included,
and a cause chain that loops must terminate.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex3
```

## Problem 4 — the other side of the wire

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `reviveError(json, registry)` rebuilds an error: a name
the registry knows becomes an instance of that class, anything else becomes a
plain `Error` that **keeps the original name anyway**. `code` and `status` go
back on, and `cause` is revived recursively.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a class that carries its own guard

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `RetryableError(message, code, options?)`, plus two
statics: `is(value)` as a type guard, and `wrap(thrown, code)` which keeps the
original message, puts the original in `cause`, and returns something already
retryable **unchanged**.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex5
```

## Problem 6 — extend the aggregate the platform already has

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `new BatchError(operation, errors)` extends
`AggregateError`. Message `<operation>: <n> failed`, name `"BatchError"`,
`operation` kept as data, `errors` a **copy** of the input, and `codes()`
returning the distinct string `code` values, sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex6
```

## Problem 7 — identity when instanceof cannot help

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `isErrorOfType(value, name)` is true for anything with a
string `name` matching and a string `message` — including an error-shaped object
from another realm. `ErrorLike` uses `Symbol.hasInstance` so
`x instanceof ErrorLike` answers the same structural question.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex7
```

## Problem 8 — one error carrying every problem

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `validate(input, rules)` runs **every** rule for every
path — path order, then rule order — and throws `ValidationFailed` with all the
issues if there are any. The class exposes `issues` and a `toJSON()` returning
`{ name, message, issues }` and no stack.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex8
```

# Reading - node/d11_custom_errors

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **making a failure identifiable without reading its
message**. A custom error class exists so that a `catch` block can branch on
what happened rather than on an English sentence somebody will reword next
sprint — which means the identity has to survive everything the error goes
through: a `throw` and a `catch` (ex1), a subclass boundary (ex2), a JSON round
trip (ex3, ex4), being one of many (ex6), and even a realm boundary where
`instanceof` stops working entirely (ex7). Two lines do most of the work in this
set and are the two people forget: `this.name = ...` in the constructor, because
otherwise every log says `Error`; and passing the options object to `super`,
because otherwise `cause` is silently dropped and every chain in the system
stops at your class.

## ex1 — the two lines that make a class worth having

**What it tested:** that a subclass of `Error` is an ordinary class, and that
two of its four lines are not optional.

**The classic mistake:** omitting `this.name`. The class works, `instanceof`
works, and every log line, every `console.log`, every stack trace says `Error` —
so the one place the name would have helped is the one place it is missing.
Second: keeping the resource and id only inside the message, which forces every
handler to parse a sentence.

**Model answer:** `super` with the composed message, then `name`, then the two
fields — and `name` set before anything reads `.stack`, since the stack is
formatted from `name` and `message`.

## ex2 — narrowing in two directions

**What it tested:** a two-level hierarchy, so one middleware can catch
`HttpError` while a specific handler catches `ConflictError`. That is what a
class hierarchy buys you over a `status` field: you can be broad *or* precise at
the point of catching.

**The classic mistake:** `super(message)` without the options object. `cause` is
then never set, and every chain that passes through your error class loses
everything below it — a bug that only shows up when somebody tries to debug a
production incident through three layers of wrapping.

**Model answer:** `super(message, options)`, `this.name = new.target.name` so
each subclass names itself without repeating the line, and `expose` derived from
the status rather than passed in.

## ex3 — what you actually want in a log

**What it tested:** turning an error into something JSON-shaped, and the
judgement about what to leave out.

**The classic mistake:** building the object as one literal, so absent fields
become `code: undefined` keys. It survives `JSON.stringify` (which drops them)
and fails everything that inspects the object, which is why the gate checks
`Object.keys`. Second: including the stack, which is enormous, does not survive a
round trip usefully, and leaks absolute build paths.

**Model answer:** two required keys, conditional assignment for the rest with a
`typeof` check on each, recursion into an `Error` cause only, and a visited set —
because serialising is often the last thing a dying process does and a hang
there loses the whole report.

## ex4 — a registry is an allow list

**What it tested:** reconstructing a class from a name, and the security
instinct that goes with it.

**The classic mistake:** looking the name up with a bare `registry[json.name]`.
The payload came off a wire, so `"constructor"` and `"toString"` find things on
`Object.prototype` — `hasOwnProperty` is the fix. The far worse version, and one
you will see, is resolving the name against a global scope or an `eval`, which
lets a remote payload construct anything at all in your process.

**Model answer:** an own-property lookup into the registry, a plain `Error`
fallback, `name` reassigned unconditionally so the original survives even
without a class, and recursion for the cause.

## ex5 — a guard that lives with the class

**What it tested:** static helpers, TypeScript type guards
(`value is RetryableError`), and idempotent wrapping.

**The classic mistake:** `wrap` that always wraps. A retry loop typically wraps
whatever it caught before deciding whether to retry, so after five attempts the
error is five identical `cause` links deep and the useful root is buried. The
early return costs one line.

**Model answer:** `static is` returning `value is RetryableError` so callers get
narrowing for free, and `wrap` reusing `is` rather than repeating the
`instanceof` — one definition of what retryable means.

## ex6 — do not reinvent AggregateError

**What it tested:** that the platform already has a class for "several things
failed", and extending it keeps every tool that knows about it working.

**The classic mistake:** a custom class with a `failures` array and a message
built by joining four other messages together. Nothing recognises it, and the
message is unreadable at exactly the moment you need it. The argument order
catches people too: `AggregateError(errors, message)` is the reverse of `Error`.

**Model answer:** `super([...errors], summary)`, `name`, the operation kept as
data, and a `codes()` that de-duplicates and sorts so its output is stable enough
to use as an alert key.

## ex7 — when instanceof lies

**What it tested:** that `instanceof` compares prototype identity, and that
identity is per-realm. An error from a worker thread, a `vm` context or a
deserialised payload has a different `Error` constructor entirely, so
`instanceof` says no about something that is, for every practical purpose, that
error.

**The classic mistake:** checking one field. `value.name === "NotFoundError"`
alone makes every config object with a `name` an error. And `typeof value ===
"object"` alone lets `null` through to a property read.

**Model answer:** one shared structural predicate — object, not null, string
`name`, string `message` — used by both the function and the
`Symbol.hasInstance` static, which is the hook `instanceof` consults on its
right-hand side.

## ex8 — every problem, in one round trip

**What it tested:** collecting rather than short-circuiting, and the `toJSON`
that error classes almost always need and almost never have.

**The classic mistake:** returning on the first failure. The user fixes one
field, resubmits, and is told about the next one — four times. The other, and it
is the one that surprises people: `JSON.stringify(someError)` returns `{}`.
`message`, `name` and `stack` are all non-enumerable, so the default serialiser
finds nothing and the entire report vanishes on the way to the client.

**Model answer:** two loops with no `break`, issues stored as a copy, and a
`toJSON` that names exactly what crosses the wire — which is also the place to
decide that the stack does not.

## Further reading

- [MDN: `Error`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error) — the constructor, `cause`, and the non-enumerable properties behind ex8's `toJSON`.
- [MDN: `AggregateError`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/AggregateError) — the base class ex6 extends, including the argument order.
- [MDN: `Symbol.hasInstance`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/hasInstance) — how ex7 changes what `instanceof` means.
- [MDN: `JSON.stringify()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify) — the `toJSON` protocol ex8 relies on.
- [Node.js: Errors](https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html) — the platform's own error classes, the `code` convention, and `Error.captureStackTrace`.

## Problem 1 — the smallest useful error class

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `new NotFoundError(resource, id)` has the message
`<resource> not found: <id>`, `name` `"NotFoundError"`, `status` 404, and both
pieces kept as fields. It is an `Error`, it is a `NotFoundError`, and it has a
stack that names the class.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`class NotFoundError extends Error`, a constructor taking the two pieces, and
`super(...)` with the composed message as the very first statement — the
language requires `super` before any use of `this`.

Everything else is three assignments.

## Hint 2

`this.name = "NotFoundError"` is the line people leave out, and it is the one
that matters most in practice. `name` is inherited as `"Error"`, and it is what
`console.log`, `util.inspect` and the first line of `.stack` all print — so
without it your carefully named class is invisible in every log you will ever
read.

Set it in the constructor, after `super`. Setting it before the stack is first
read is what makes the stack say `NotFoundError:` too.

Keeping `resource` and `id` as fields rather than only in the message is the
other half: a handler deciding what to do should never have to run a regular
expression over an English sentence.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a family, not a flag

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `HttpError(status, message, options?)` sets `status`,
sets `expose` (true for a 4xx, false for a 5xx), names itself after the class
actually constructed, and passes `options` through so `cause` works.
`BadRequestError` (400) and `ConflictError` (409) extend it.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three classes, two levels. The base takes the status; each subclass is a
constructor that calls `super` with its own number and passes the message and
options straight through.

`expose` is a comparison, not a field the caller sets: a 4xx is the client's
fault and its message is safe to return, a 5xx is yours and its message is an
internal detail.

## Hint 2

Two things have to reach `Error` itself.

The message, obviously. And the **options object** — `super(message, options)` —
because that is the only way `cause` gets set. Dropping it is easy to do and
silently breaks every cause chain that passes through your class.

## Hint 3

For `name`, the tidy version is `this.name = new.target.name` in the base
constructor: `new.target` is the constructor that was actually invoked, so each
subclass names itself and no subclass repeats the line.

Writing `this.name = "BadRequestError"` in each subclass also works and drifts
the first time somebody renames a class without renaming the string.

The remaining decision is whether `expose` should be overridable — some
frameworks let a 5xx opt in to exposing its message for a specific case. Say
what you would do and why the default is the safe direction.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three classes, two levels. The base takes the status; each subclass is a
constructor that calls `super` with its own number and passes the message and
options straight through.

`expose` is a comparison, not a field the caller sets: a 4xx is the client's
fault and its message is safe to return, a 5xx is yours and its message is an
internal detail.

## Hint 2

Two things have to reach `Error` itself.

The message, obviously. And the **options object** — `super(message, options)` —
because that is the only way `cause` gets set. Dropping it is easy to do and
silently breaks every cause chain that passes through your class.

## Hint 3

For `name`, the tidy version is `this.name = new.target.name` in the base
constructor: `new.target` is the constructor that was actually invoked, so each
subclass names itself and no subclass repeats the line.

Writing `this.name = "BadRequestError"` in each subclass also works and drifts
the first time somebody renames a class without renaming the string.

The remaining decision is whether `expose` should be overridable — some
frameworks let a 5xx opt in to exposing its message for a specific case. Say
what you would do and why the default is the safe direction.

## Problem 3 — an error you can put in a log line

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `serialiseError(error)` returns `{ name, message }` plus
`code` when it is a string, `status` when it is a number, and `cause` recursed
when it is an `Error`. Absent keys are **omitted**, the stack is never included,
and a cause chain that loops must terminate.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A recursive helper over the cause chain, building a plain object. `name` and
`message` go in unconditionally; the other three are conditional.

Build the object with the two required keys and then **assign** the optional
ones inside `if`s. Writing `{ name, message, code: error.code }` in one literal
gives you a `code: undefined` key, and the gate checks `Object.keys`.

## Hint 2

Type-check the optional fields rather than truth-checking them. `code` is
meaningful only when it is a string; `status` only when it is a number. Both are
`unknown` as far as the type system is concerned, because anybody can attach
anything to an error.

The stack is not on the list, deliberately: it is enormous, it does not
round-trip through JSON well, and it leaks absolute paths from your build
machine into whatever you send this to.

## Hint 3

The loop guard is the same `Set` as d10's `explain`, and it matters more here.
Serialising is often the last thing a dying process does — a hang at that point
loses the entire report, which is the one thing you needed.

The remaining decision: when the walk stops at an already-seen cause, this
version simply omits it. The alternative is a marker like
`{ name: "Circular", message: "..." }`. One of those is easier for a reader to
interpret; pick deliberately.

## Hint 1

A recursive helper over the cause chain, building a plain object. `name` and
`message` go in unconditionally; the other three are conditional.

Build the object with the two required keys and then **assign** the optional
ones inside `if`s. Writing `{ name, message, code: error.code }` in one literal
gives you a `code: undefined` key, and the gate checks `Object.keys`.

## Hint 2

Type-check the optional fields rather than truth-checking them. `code` is
meaningful only when it is a string; `status` only when it is a number. Both are
`unknown` as far as the type system is concerned, because anybody can attach
anything to an error.

The stack is not on the list, deliberately: it is enormous, it does not
round-trip through JSON well, and it leaks absolute paths from your build
machine into whatever you send this to.

## Hint 3

The loop guard is the same `Set` as d10's `explain`, and it matters more here.
Serialising is often the last thing a dying process does — a hang at that point
loses the entire report, which is the one thing you needed.

The remaining decision: when the walk stops at an already-seen cause, this
version simply omits it. The alternative is a marker like
`{ name: "Circular", message: "..." }`. One of those is easier for a reader to
interpret; pick deliberately.

## Problem 5 — a class that carries its own guard

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `RetryableError(message, code, options?)`, plus two
statics: `is(value)` as a type guard, and `wrap(thrown, code)` which keeps the
original message, puts the original in `cause`, and returns something already
retryable **unchanged**.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The constructor is ex1 again with an extra field and the options object passed
through to `super` so `cause` works.

`static is` is one `instanceof`. The `value is RetryableError` return type is
what makes it a **type guard**: after `if (RetryableError.is(e))` TypeScript
knows `e.code` exists, which is the whole reason to put it on the class instead
of writing the `instanceof` at each call site.

## Hint 2

`wrap` has three cases and only one of them is obvious:

- already a `RetryableError` — return it **as it is**;
- an `Error` — take its `message`, keep it as `cause`;
- anything else — `String(thrown)` for the message, still keep it as `cause`.

## Hint 3

The idempotence rule is the one worth understanding. A retry loop typically
wraps whatever it caught before deciding whether to retry — so without the early
return, attempt five produces an error five `cause` links deep, all saying the
same thing, and the useful root is buried.

Reuse your own `is` inside `wrap` rather than repeating the `instanceof`: one
definition of what "retryable" means, in one place.

The remaining decision: `wrap` keeps the original message rather than composing
a new one. Compare with d10's `withContext`, which composes. Both are right for
different jobs — be able to say which job is which.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The constructor is ex1 again with an extra field and the options object passed
through to `super` so `cause` works.

`static is` is one `instanceof`. The `value is RetryableError` return type is
what makes it a **type guard**: after `if (RetryableError.is(e))` TypeScript
knows `e.code` exists, which is the whole reason to put it on the class instead
of writing the `instanceof` at each call site.

## Hint 2

`wrap` has three cases and only one of them is obvious:

- already a `RetryableError` — return it **as it is**;
- an `Error` — take its `message`, keep it as `cause`;
- anything else — `String(thrown)` for the message, still keep it as `cause`.

## Hint 3

The idempotence rule is the one worth understanding. A retry loop typically
wraps whatever it caught before deciding whether to retry — so without the early
return, attempt five produces an error five `cause` links deep, all saying the
same thing, and the useful root is buried.

Reuse your own `is` inside `wrap` rather than repeating the `instanceof`: one
definition of what "retryable" means, in one place.

The remaining decision: `wrap` keeps the original message rather than composing
a new one. Compare with d10's `withContext`, which composes. Both are right for
different jobs — be able to say which job is which.

## Problem 6 — extend the aggregate the platform already has

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `new BatchError(operation, errors)` extends
`AggregateError`. Message `<operation>: <n> failed`, name `"BatchError"`,
`operation` kept as data, `errors` a **copy** of the input, and `codes()`
returning the distinct string `code` values, sorted.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex6
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`AggregateError`'s constructor is `(errors, message)` — the opposite order from
`Error`, which catches everyone once. Everything else is the same pattern as
ex1: `super(...)` first, then `name`, then your own field.

The summarising message matters more than it looks. Concatenating four failure
messages into one line produces something nobody reads; a count plus the list on
`.errors` produces something a log aggregator can group.

## Hint 2

Copy the array on the way in. `AggregateError` builds its own array from the
iterable, so a spread is belt and braces — but say it anyway, because "the
errors I reported changed after I reported them" is a genuinely awful debugging
session and the guarantee should be visible in the code.

## Hint 3

`codes()` is a `Set` for distinctness, a `typeof` check because `code` is
`unknown` on an arbitrary error, and a `sort()` so the output does not depend on
the order the failures happened to arrive in — which is what makes it usable as
an alert key.

The remaining decision is what `codes()` should do about an error whose `code` is
a number, which some libraries do. This version ignores it. Decide whether
ignoring or coercing is more honest.

## Hint 1

`AggregateError`'s constructor is `(errors, message)` — the opposite order from
`Error`, which catches everyone once. Everything else is the same pattern as
ex1: `super(...)` first, then `name`, then your own field.

The summarising message matters more than it looks. Concatenating four failure
messages into one line produces something nobody reads; a count plus the list on
`.errors` produces something a log aggregator can group.

## Hint 2

Copy the array on the way in. `AggregateError` builds its own array from the
iterable, so a spread is belt and braces — but say it anyway, because "the
errors I reported changed after I reported them" is a genuinely awful debugging
session and the guarantee should be visible in the code.

## Hint 3

`codes()` is a `Set` for distinctness, a `typeof` check because `code` is
`unknown` on an arbitrary error, and a `sort()` so the output does not depend on
the order the failures happened to arrive in — which is what makes it usable as
an alert key.

The remaining decision is what `codes()` should do about an error whose `code` is
a number, which some libraries do. This version ignores it. Decide whether
ignoring or coercing is more honest.

## Problem 8 — one error carrying every problem

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `validate(input, rules)` runs **every** rule for every
path — path order, then rule order — and throws `ValidationFailed` with all the
issues if there are any. The class exposes `issues` and a `toJSON()` returning
`{ name, message, issues }` and no stack.

```
uv run dojo test node d11_custom_errors ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two nested loops and no `break` anywhere. The outer walks
`Object.entries(rules)`; the inner walks that path's rules; each rule that
returns an issue contributes one entry.

That ordering — path order then rule order — falls out for free, which is why
the gate can assert an exact array.

## Hint 2

The class is ex1 with a list: `super` with the counted message, `this.name`, and
the issues stored as a copy so the array the caller passed cannot change under
the error afterwards.

## Hint 3

`toJSON` is the part people have never needed until the day they do.

`JSON.stringify(new Error("boom"))` produces `{}`. An `Error`'s `message`,
`stack` and `name` are all non-enumerable, so the default serialiser finds
nothing — and a validation error that arrives at the client as an empty object
takes every issue with it. Defining `toJSON` fixes it and, at the same time,
lets you decide exactly what leaves the process. The stack does not.

The remaining decision is what `validate` should do about keys present in the
input but absent from the rules. This version ignores them; a stricter validator
would reject unknown fields, and which one you want depends on whether you are
writing an API or a config loader.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two nested loops and no `break` anywhere. The outer walks
`Object.entries(rules)`; the inner walks that path's rules; each rule that
returns an issue contributes one entry.

That ordering — path order then rule order — falls out for free, which is why
the gate can assert an exact array.

## Hint 2

The class is ex1 with a list: `super` with the counted message, `this.name`, and
the issues stored as a copy so the array the caller passed cannot change under
the error afterwards.

## Hint 3

`toJSON` is the part people have never needed until the day they do.

`JSON.stringify(new Error("boom"))` produces `{}`. An `Error`'s `message`,
`stack` and `name` are all non-enumerable, so the default serialiser finds
nothing — and a validation error that arrives at the client as an empty object
takes every issue with it. Defining `toJSON` fixes it and, at the same time,
lets you decide exactly what leaves the process. The stack does not.

The remaining decision is what `validate` should do about keys present in the
input but absent from the rules. This version ignores them; a stricter validator
would reject unknown fields, and which one you want depends on whether you are
writing an API or a config loader.

# d12 — Filesystem operations

Eight problems on `node:fs/promises` — lesson **05_fs_path** is the source, and
this set is the part of it that runs unattended: writes that cannot be caught
half-finished, trees walked in the right order, and cleanup that happens even
when the work failed.

Every gate builds its own directory under the OS temp dir and removes it
afterwards. Nothing here is ever written inside the repository, every path a
solution **returns** uses forward slashes, and every path the gate builds comes
from `node:path` — so these run the same on Windows and on Linux.

## Problem 1 — a write nobody can catch half-finished

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `writeTextAtomic(file, text)` creates parent directories,
writes to a temporary name in the **same directory**, and renames it into place.
The temporary name must be unique per call, and nothing may be left behind —
including when the write fails.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex1
```

## Problem 2 — copy a tree, minus the parts you do not want

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `copyTree(src, dest, { skip })` copies recursively and
returns the relative paths of the files copied, forward slashes, sorted. `skip`
is called with every entry's relative path; returning true for a **directory**
prunes the whole subtree and does not even create it.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex2
```

## Problem 3 — how big is that directory

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `dirStats(dir)` returns `{ files, bytes }` for the whole
subtree. Directories are traversed, never counted, and their own size on disk is
not part of the answer.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex3
```

## Problem 4 — prune from the bottom

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `removeEmptyDirs(root)` removes every empty directory
under `root`, **including ones that only become empty once their children are
gone**, and returns the removed paths relative to `root`, sorted. `root` itself
is never removed.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex4
```

## Problem 5 — an append-only log

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `appendJsonl(file, record)` appends one compact JSON
object and a newline, creating parents as needed. `readJsonl(file)` reads them
back: a missing file is an empty log, blank lines are skipped, and a line that
will not parse rejects with `invalid JSON on line 3` — counting every line from
one.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex5
```

## Problem 6 — borrow a directory, give it back

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `withTempWorkspace(run)` creates a fresh directory under
the OS temp dir, hands it to `run`, and removes it afterwards on **both** paths.
The value comes back to the caller; so does a rejection, unchanged. Two calls
never produce the same directory.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex6
```

## Problem 7 — make one directory look like another

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `syncDirectories(src, dest)` returns `{ copied, updated,
deleted }` — files only, compared by **size**. New files are copied, differing
files overwritten, files the source no longer has removed, and matching files
left alone and reported in none of the lists. All three are relative, forward
slashes, sorted. Running it twice must do nothing the second time.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the same file under different names

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `findDuplicates(dir)` groups the files under `dir` by
their **contents** and returns only groups of two or more: members sorted,
groups ordered by their first member, paths relative with forward slashes.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex8
```
