# Reading - node/d12_fs_ops

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **filesystem work that survives being interrupted**.
A disk is shared, slow and mutable: another process can read your file halfway
through the write (ex1), your own recursion can be looking at a directory whose
contents you are changing (ex4, ex7), and any of it can throw at any point,
which is where the temporary files and orphaned directories come from (ex1,
ex6). Three habits run through all eight answers. Walk trees with `readdir(dir,
{ withFileTypes: true })` and carry the **relative** path as a forward-slash
string, converting to a real path only at the syscall — that is what makes the
returned values portable by construction. Sort at the end, because `readdir`
promises no order. And treat `ENOENT` as the one error that means "nothing is
there yet", rethrowing everything else, because a permissions failure reported
as an empty result is how real damage goes unnoticed.

## ex1 — rename is the atomic operation

**What it tested:** that "write a file safely" means write elsewhere and rename,
and that both properties of "elsewhere" matter.

**The classic mistake:** a fixed temporary name like `config.json.tmp`. Two
concurrent writers share it: the first rename succeeds, the second fails with
`ENOENT` on a file that has already been moved. The other mistake is putting the
temporary in `os.tmpdir()`, which is usually a different filesystem — `rename`
across filesystems is not a rename, Node falls back to copy-then-delete, and the
atomicity you were buying is gone.

**Model answer:** `mkdir` the parent, a unique temporary name in the *same*
directory, `writeFile`, `rename`, and a `catch` that removes the temporary
before rethrowing.

## ex2 — pruning is not filtering

**What it tested:** a recursive copy with an exclusion predicate, and the
distinction between skipping a directory's *contents* and skipping the directory
itself.

**The classic mistake:** creating the destination directory and then filtering
its children, which leaves an empty `node_modules/` in the output. Second, and
more portable-looking than it is: building native paths during the walk and
converting to forward slashes at the end. Do it the other way round — carry the
portable form and convert at the syscall — and there is nothing left to forget.

**Model answer:** `readdir` with `withFileTypes`, a relative forward-slash string
threaded through the recursion, `continue` before the `mkdir` when `skip` says
so, and one `sort()` at the end.

## ex3 — the recursion returns the answer

**What it tested:** the simplest possible tree fold, and two things that are not
files.

**The classic mistake:** counting directories, whose `size` from `stat` is a
real number and means nothing anybody wants. Or using `else` rather than
`else if (entry.isFile())`, which sweeps sockets, FIFOs and symlinks into the
file count.

**Model answer:** return `{ files, bytes }` from the recursive call and add the
totals up — no accumulator parameter, and the empty-directory case handled by
the loop simply not running.

## ex4 — bottom up, because emptiness propagates

**What it tested:** that this cannot be done top down in one pass. `outer/`
containing `inner/` is not empty when you first look at it; it becomes empty
only after `inner` is removed.

**The classic mistake:** checking emptiness before recursing, which finds
`outer` non-empty and moves on — so the caller has to run the function
repeatedly until it stops changing anything. The other one is `rm(dir, {
recursive: true })` instead of `rmdir`, which happily deletes a directory full
of files if your emptiness check was wrong.

**Model answer:** a helper that returns "am I empty *after* my children were
pruned", recursing first and removing from the parent's loop — which is also
what keeps the root itself safe.

## ex5 — one line, one record

**What it tested:** the JSONL format and two pieces of error hygiene.

**The classic mistake:** returning `[]` for any read failure. `ENOENT` means the
log has not been written yet; `EACCES` means somebody has a permissions problem
they will never find out about if you hide it behind an empty array. The second:
reporting the position of a `JSON.parse` failure by counting *records* rather
than *lines*, so one blank line puts every number after it out by one — and the
number is the only reason you added it.

**Model answer:** `appendFile` with a trailing newline, `ENOENT` caught by code
and nothing else, blank lines skipped by `trim()`, and the line number taken
from the index of the split array plus one.

## ex6 — finally, and the resource you did not own

**What it tested:** the scoped-resource pattern applied to a directory, and
`mkdtemp` — which creates and names in one step, so two callers cannot collide.

**The classic mistake:** cleaning up after the call rather than in a `finally`,
so the failure path — precisely the one with a half-written workspace on it —
leaks. The subtler one is `return run(dir)` instead of `return await run(dir)`:
the function returns the pending promise, `finally` runs at once, and the
directory is deleted while the work is still using it.

**Model answer:** `mkdtemp` under `os.tmpdir()`, `try { return await run(dir) }
finally { await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true }) }`, and no `catch`, so
the caller's failure passes through untouched.

## ex7 — index first, then act

**What it tested:** a three-way diff over two trees, and the discipline of not
mutating what you are still reading.

**The classic mistake:** walking the source and writing as you go, then walking
the destination to find extras — the second walk now sees the files the first
one just created, and every one of them looks like a match, which is correct by
luck rather than by design. Build both indexes first and the arithmetic is
obvious. The other mistake is letting `ENOENT` escape when the destination does
not exist yet, when what it means is "the destination is empty".

**Model answer:** two `Map`s from relative path to size, three loops over set
membership, and a note that comparing by size alone misses an edit that keeps
the length — which is why real tools also compare mtime or a hash.

## ex8 — hash, do not compare

**What it tested:** grouping by content, and choosing a representation that does
not scale with file size.

**The classic mistake:** comparing every pair of files, which is O(n squared)
reads for an answer a single pass can produce. Or using the file contents
themselves as the `Map` key, which holds every byte of every file in memory at
once. A digest is 64 characters regardless.

**Model answer:** one `sha256` per file into a `Map<string, string[]>`, filter
to groups of two or more, sort members and then groups — and the honest caveat
that a serious deduplicator compares the bytes before deleting anything, because
a hash match is evidence and not proof.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: File system promises API](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#promises-api) — everything used here, including `mkdtemp`, `rename` and `rm`.
- [Node.js: `fs.Dirent`](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#class-fsdirent) — what `withFileTypes: true` gives you, and why it beats a `stat` per entry.
- [Node.js: `path`](https://nodejs.org/api/path.html) — `join`, `relative`, `sep`, and the `path.posix` variants when you want forward slashes on purpose.
- [Node.js: Errors — common system errors](https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html#common-system-errors) — `ENOENT`, `EACCES`, `EXDEV` and the rest of the codes ex5 and ex7 branch on.
- [Node.js: `crypto.createHash()`](https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#cryptocreatehashalgorithm-options) — the digest ex8 groups by, and the streaming interface a large-file version would use.

**Model answer:** one `sha256` per file into a `Map<string, string[]>`, filter
to groups of two or more, sort members and then groups — and the honest caveat
that a serious deduplicator compares the bytes before deleting anything, because
a hash match is evidence and not proof.

- [Node.js: `path`](https://nodejs.org/api/path.html) — `join`, `relative`, `sep`, and the `path.posix` variants when you want forward slashes on purpose.
- [Node.js: Errors — common system errors](https://nodejs.org/api/errors.html#common-system-errors) — `ENOENT`, `EACCES`, `EXDEV` and the rest of the codes ex5 and ex7 branch on.

## Problem 1 — a write nobody can catch half-finished

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `writeTextAtomic(file, text)` creates parent directories,
writes to a temporary name in the **same directory**, and renames it into place.
The temporary name must be unique per call, and nothing may be left behind —
including when the write fails.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three calls: `mkdir` with `{ recursive: true }` on the parent, `writeFile` to a
temporary name, `rename` onto the target.

`rename` is the whole point. On a single filesystem it is atomic: at every
instant the target is either entirely the old file or entirely the new one.
`writeFile` straight onto the target is not — a reader arriving mid-write gets
whatever has been flushed so far, which is how a config file ends up truncated
after a crash.

## Hint 2

Two properties the temporary name must have, and the gate checks both.

**Same directory as the target.** A temp file in the OS temp dir usually sits on
a different filesystem, and `rename` across filesystems is not a rename at all —
Node falls back to copy-then-delete, and the atomicity is gone.

**Unique per call.** With a fixed name like `file.tmp`, two concurrent writers
share one temporary file: the first rename succeeds and the second fails with
`ENOENT` on a file the other writer already moved. `randomUUID()` or a counter
solves it.

## Hint 3

Clean up on the failure path. If `writeFile` fails halfway, the temporary is
still there — and a directory that slowly fills with `.q1.txt.<uuid>.tmp` files
is exactly what this pattern is famous for when nobody wrote the `catch`.

The remaining decision is durability. This version is atomic but not durable: a
power cut immediately after the rename can still lose the data, because neither
the file nor the directory entry has been `fsync`ed. Know that the grown-up
version opens the file handle, calls `sync()`, and syncs the directory too — and
know why most code does not bother.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three calls: `mkdir` with `{ recursive: true }` on the parent, `writeFile` to a
temporary name, `rename` onto the target.

`rename` is the whole point. On a single filesystem it is atomic: at every
instant the target is either entirely the old file or entirely the new one.
`writeFile` straight onto the target is not — a reader arriving mid-write gets
whatever has been flushed so far, which is how a config file ends up truncated
after a crash.

## Hint 2

Two properties the temporary name must have, and the gate checks both.

**Same directory as the target.** A temp file in the OS temp dir usually sits on
a different filesystem, and `rename` across filesystems is not a rename at all —
Node falls back to copy-then-delete, and the atomicity is gone.

**Unique per call.** With a fixed name like `file.tmp`, two concurrent writers
share one temporary file: the first rename succeeds and the second fails with
`ENOENT` on a file the other writer already moved. `randomUUID()` or a counter
solves it.

## Hint 3

Clean up on the failure path. If `writeFile` fails halfway, the temporary is
still there — and a directory that slowly fills with `.q1.txt.<uuid>.tmp` files
is exactly what this pattern is famous for when nobody wrote the `catch`.

The remaining decision is durability. This version is atomic but not durable: a
power cut immediately after the rename can still lose the data, because neither
the file nor the directory entry has been `fsync`ed. Know that the grown-up
version opens the file handle, calls `sync()`, and syncs the directory too — and
know why most code does not bother.

## Hint 1

A recursive walk carrying the **relative** path as it goes. `readdir(dir, {
withFileTypes: true })` gives you entries that know whether they are a directory,
which saves a `stat` per entry and is the difference between a walk that is fast
and one that is not.

Create the destination directory before recursing into it, and let `copyFile` do
the actual copying.

## Hint 2

Keep the relative path as a **forward-slash string** all the way through, and
build a real filesystem path from it only when you need one
(`path.join(root, ...relative.split("/"))`).

Doing it the other way round — carrying native paths and converting at the end —
means remembering to convert, and the day somebody forgets, the function returns
`nested\b.txt` on Windows and every test comparing paths breaks on one machine
out of three.

## Hint 3

`skip` is consulted on directories as well as files, and returning true prunes
the whole subtree: `continue` before you `mkdir` it, so the empty directory is
not even created.

That distinction — pruning versus filtering — is worth naming. A filter that
copies the directory and then skips its contents leaves `node_modules/` sitting
empty in the output, and somebody will file a bug about it.

Sorting once at the end is simpler than trying to walk in order, because
`readdir` makes no promises about the order it returns entries in.

## Hint 1

The shape of the answer is the shape of the recursion: `dirStats` returns
`{ files, bytes }`, so the recursive call returns the same thing and the totals

directory, which is why the `else if` is `isFile()` rather than a bare `else`.

the kind of edge case worth *noticing* is already handled rather than adding a
branch for.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The shape of the answer is the shape of the recursion: `dirStats` returns
`{ files, bytes }`, so the recursive call returns the same thing and the totals
simply add up. No accumulator parameter needed.

`readdir` with `withFileTypes: true`, then a branch on `isDirectory()` and
`isFile()`.

## Hint 2

`stat(file).size` is the byte count. Note the two things that are *not* counted:
directories themselves — they have a size on disk and it is not what anybody
means by "how big is this folder" — and anything that is neither a file nor a
directory, which is why the `else if` is `isFile()` rather than a bare `else`.

An empty directory returns zeros because the loop simply does not run, which is
the kind of edge case worth *noticing* is already handled rather than adding a
branch for.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The recursion has to answer a question, not just do work: **is this directory
empty once I have finished with its children?** Have the helper return a boolean
and the whole thing falls out.

For each entry: a file means "not empty, and nothing to do". A directory means
"recurse, and if the answer is yes, remove it and record it — otherwise I am not
empty either".

## Hint 2

The order is the entire exercise. `outer/` contains `inner/`, so at the moment
you first look at `outer` it is *not* empty — it only becomes empty after
`inner` is removed. A top-down walk therefore sees a non-empty directory and
moves on, and one pass is not enough.

Recursing before deciding is what makes a single pass correct.

## Hint 3

Use `rmdir`, not `rm(dir, { recursive: true })`. `rmdir` refuses to delete a
directory that is not empty, which turns your "I believe this is empty" into a
check the operating system performs for you — and this is a function that
deletes things, so a second opinion is worth having.

Two details: the root is visited but never removed, which falls out of removing
directories from the *parent's* loop rather than at the top of `visit`. And the
returned paths are relative with forward slashes, for the same reason as ex2.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The recursion has to answer a question, not just do work: **is this directory
empty once I have finished with its children?** Have the helper return a boolean
and the whole thing falls out.

For each entry: a file means "not empty, and nothing to do". A directory means
"recurse, and if the answer is yes, remove it and record it — otherwise I am not
empty either".

## Hint 2

The order is the entire exercise. `outer/` contains `inner/`, so at the moment
you first look at `outer` it is *not* empty — it only becomes empty after
`inner` is removed. A top-down walk therefore sees a non-empty directory and
moves on, and one pass is not enough.

Recursing before deciding is what makes a single pass correct.

## Hint 3

Use `rmdir`, not `rm(dir, { recursive: true })`. `rmdir` refuses to delete a
directory that is not empty, which turns your "I believe this is empty" into a
check the operating system performs for you — and this is a function that
deletes things, so a second opinion is worth having.

Two details: the root is visited but never removed, which falls out of removing
directories from the *parent's* loop rather than at the top of `visit`. And the
returned paths are relative with forward slashes, for the same reason as ex2.

## Hint 1

## Problem 6 — borrow a directory, give it back

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `withTempWorkspace(run)` creates a fresh directory under
the OS temp dir, hands it to `run`, and removes it afterwards on **both** paths.
The value comes back to the caller; so does a rejection, unchanged. Two calls
never produce the same directory.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`mkdtemp(path.join(tmpdir(), "some-prefix-"))` creates the directory and gives
you its path in one call, appending random characters to the prefix. That is why
two calls back to back can never collide — and why you should not roll your own
name from `Date.now()`.

## Hint 2

`try { return await run(dir) } finally { await rm(...) }`.

`finally` rather than a line after the call, because the failure path is exactly
the one where a half-written workspace is lying around. And `return await`
rather than `return`, or the function returns the pending promise, `finally`
runs immediately, and the directory is deleted while the work is still using it.

`rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })` — recursive because the work put
things in there, force so an already-missing directory is not an error.

## Hint 3

Note what this helper does *not* do: it does not swallow the failure. The `try`
has no `catch`, so a rejection from `run` passes straight through while the
cleanup still happens. That is d06's `withCleanup` again, and it is worth
noticing that the pattern is the same one.

The remaining decision is what should happen if the *cleanup* fails — a Windows
antivirus holding a handle open is the usual culprit. As written, that failure
replaces whatever `run` was reporting. Decide whether you would rather it did
not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`mkdtemp(path.join(tmpdir(), "some-prefix-"))` creates the directory and gives
you its path in one call, appending random characters to the prefix. That is why
two calls back to back can never collide — and why you should not roll your own
name from `Date.now()`.

## Hint 2

`try { return await run(dir) } finally { await rm(...) }`.

`finally` rather than a line after the call, because the failure path is exactly
the one where a half-written workspace is lying around. And `return await`
rather than `return`, or the function returns the pending promise, `finally`
runs immediately, and the directory is deleted while the work is still using it.

`rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true })` — recursive because the work put
things in there, force so an already-missing directory is not an error.

## Hint 3

Note what this helper does *not* do: it does not swallow the failure. The `try`
has no `catch`, so a rejection from `run` passes straight through while the
cleanup still happens. That is d06's `withCleanup` again, and it is worth
noticing that the pattern is the same one.

The remaining decision is what should happen if the *cleanup* fails — a Windows
antivirus holding a handle open is the usual culprit. As written, that failure
replaces whatever `run` was reporting. Decide whether you would rather it did
not.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — make one directory look like another

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `syncDirectories(src, dest)` returns `{ copied, updated,
deleted }` — files only, compared by **size**. New files are copied, differing
files overwritten, files the source no longer has removed, and matching files
left alone and reported in none of the lists. All three are relative, forward
slashes, sorted. Running it twice must do nothing the second time.

```
uv run dojo test node d12_fs_ops ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do not try to do this in one walk. Build **two indexes** first — a map from
relative path to size, one per side — and then the whole problem becomes set
arithmetic over two maps:

- in src, not in dest → copy
- in both, sizes differ → overwrite
- in dest, not in src → delete

Indexing both sides before writing anything also means you are comparing against
a consistent picture rather than against a directory your own loop is halfway
through changing.

## Hint 2

Reuse the walk from ex2 or ex4, but have it collect into a `Map` instead of
copying. One detail it needs that the others did not: a destination that does
not exist yet should index as **empty**, not throw — so catch `ENOENT` from
`readdir` and return.

Creating parent directories is only needed on the copy path, and only for files
that are new.

## Hint 3

Comparing by size is a deliberate simplification, and you should be ready to say
what it costs: a file edited without changing its length looks identical, and a
real sync tool therefore compares modification time as well, or a content hash
when it can afford one. Size alone is fast, deterministic, and wrong in exactly
one interesting way.

Two decisions left. This version does not remove directories that become empty
in the destination — you have ex4 for that if you want it. And it says nothing
about what happens when a path is a file on one side and a directory on the
other, which is the case a production sync spends most of its code on.

## Hint 1

Do not try to do this in one walk. Build **two indexes** first — a map from
relative path to size, one per side — and then the whole problem becomes set
arithmetic over two maps:

- in src, not in dest → copy
- in both, sizes differ → overwrite
- in dest, not in src → delete

Indexing both sides before writing anything also means you are comparing against
a consistent picture rather than against a directory your own loop is halfway
through changing.

## Hint 2

Reuse the walk from ex2 or ex4, but have it collect into a `Map` instead of
copying. One detail it needs that the others did not: a destination that does
not exist yet should index as **empty**, not throw — so catch `ENOENT` from
`readdir` and return.

Creating parent directories is only needed on the copy path, and only for files
that are new.

## Hint 3

Comparing by size is a deliberate simplification, and you should be ready to say
what it costs: a file edited without changing its length looks identical, and a
real sync tool therefore compares modification time as well, or a content hash
when it can afford one. Size alone is fast, deterministic, and wrong in exactly
one interesting way.

Two decisions left. This version does not remove directories that become empty
in the destination — you have ex4 for that if you want it. And it says nothing
about what happens when a path is a file on one side and a directory on the
other, which is the case a production sync spends most of its code on.

lessons.briefing:
# d13 — Path portability

Eight problems on `node:path`, drawn from lesson **05_fs_path** — the half of it
that has nothing to do with the disk. Nothing here reads or writes a file: these
are pure functions over path strings, and every one of them is a bug somebody
has shipped because the string happened to look right on their machine.

Two rules run through the whole set. Paths that live on a filesystem are built
and taken apart with `node:path`, never with `split("/")`. Paths that leave the
filesystem — into a URL, a manifest, a log line, a glob — are forward-slash
strings, and converting between the two is a deliberate step you write down. If
that distinction feels blurry, reread lesson 05 ex1 before you start.

## Problem 1 — the same path, for a browser

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `relativeUrlPath(fromDir, toFile)` returns the path from
`fromDir` to `toFile` with forward slashes, relative, never absolute — and `"."`
when the two are the same place.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex1
```

## Problem 2 — swap the extension, touch nothing else

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `changeExtension(file, ext)` replaces the **last**
extension. `ext` may arrive with or without its dot, and `""` removes one level.
The directory in front of the file is preserved exactly as it was given.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a join a stranger gets to influence

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `safeJoin(root, ...segments)` returns the absolute path
the segments name under `root`, or `null` if it would land outside. `root`
itself counts as inside. A `..` that cancels out is fine; a `..` that climbs
out, and an absolute segment, are not.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex3
```

## Problem 4 — the deepest directory they all agree on

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `commonAncestor(paths)` resolves every entry and returns
the longest path all of them are equal to or below. An empty list is `null`; one
path is its own answer.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex4
```

## Problem 5 — from a link in a document to a file on disk

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `resolveDocLink(fromFile, link)` returns the absolute
path a relative link inside `fromFile` points at — fragment and query stripped,
percent-escapes decoded — or `null` when the link is external (`https:`,
`mailto:`), protocol-relative (`//host`), site-absolute (`/x`) or a bare `#`
fragment.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex5
```

## Problem 6 — where the build puts it

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `outputPathFor(file, { srcRoot, outRoot, ext })` mirrors
`file`'s position under `srcRoot` into `outRoot`, optionally changing the
extension. A file that is not **strictly** below `srcRoot` returns `null`.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex6
```

## Problem 7 — the pattern language in every config file

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `matchesGlob(pattern, filePath)` matches forward-slash
relative paths. `*` matches any run of characters **inside one segment**; `**`
stands in for any number of whole segments, including none. No other
metacharacters.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the shortest name that is still unambiguous

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `shortestUniqueLabels(paths)` maps each path to the
shortest suffix of **whole segments** that no other path in the list shares.
Each path is decided independently, so two paths in the same list can need
different lengths.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d13_path_portability

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **knowing which kind of path you are holding**. There
are only two, and every bug in this set is a confusion between them: a
*filesystem* path, whose separator is `path.sep` and whose meaning depends on
the platform and the working directory, and a *portable* path — the forward
-slash string you put in a URL, a manifest, a glob or a log line. `node:path`
converts between them and nothing else does. Four of the eight answers are the
same three lines — resolve, take the relative path, look at its first segment —
because "is this path inside that one" is the question underneath containment,
relocation and traversal defence alike. The other four are about the difference
between a string operation that usually works and a segment operation that
always does.

## ex1 — path.sep is not a slash

**What it tested:** that you convert on purpose at the boundary, rather than
hoping the platform separator is the one the consumer wants.

**The classic mistake:** `path.relative(...).replace(/\\/g, "/")`, which is
correct and also unfalsifiable — on Linux it is a no-op, so a mistake in it
survives every CI run and surfaces only when a colleague on Windows opens the
generated site and every link is dead. Splitting on `path.sep` and joining with
`/` says what you mean on both platforms.

**Model answer:** one `path.relative`, one split-join, and a named case for the
empty string, because "the same directory" is a real answer and `href=""` is not.

## ex2 — parse and format are inverses, with one trap

**What it tested:** that the extension rule (last dot onwards, and a leading dot
is not an extension) belongs to `node:path`, not to your regular expression.

**The classic mistake:** `path.format({ ...path.parse(file), ext: ".md" })`.
`format` prefers `base` over `name` + `ext`, so the spread quietly wins and the
function returns its input unchanged — a bug that looks like the build cache
misbehaving. The other one is `file.replace(/\.[^.]+$/, ext)`, which mangles a
directory called `v1.2` on a file with no extension.

**Model answer:** parse, rebuild from `dir` + `name` + `ext` explicitly, and
normalise the caller's dot before formatting rather than during.

## ex3 — the traversal defence, in the constructive direction

**What it tested:** the one security-relevant function in the set. Lesson 05
asked you to *judge* whether a path was inside a base; this asks you to *build*
one that is, from segments a client controls.

**The classic mistake:** filtering the segments — rejecting anything containing
`..` — instead of resolving and then judging. Encodings, doubled dots and
absolute segments all get past a filter, and `path.resolve` throws away
everything to the left of an absolute argument, so a single `/etc/passwd`
segment defeats it entirely. The subtler one is `relative.startsWith("..")`,
which also rejects the perfectly ordinary directory `..config`.

**Model answer:** resolve to one normalised absolute path, then ask
`path.relative` where it landed and look at its **first segment** — never at its
first two characters.

## ex4 — segments, not characters

**What it tested:** longest common prefix, on the right alphabet.

**The classic mistake:** comparing the strings character by character. It gives
`/var/log` as the common ancestor of `/var/log` and `/var/logging`, which is not
an ancestor of the second one at all — and the caller then chdirs into it, or
watches it, or deletes it.

**Model answer:** `path.resolve` everything first, because two relative paths
have no relationship until they do; split on `path.sep`; fold the running prefix
down; and remember that an absolute POSIX path's first segment is the empty
string, so the join needs a fallback for the root.

## ex5 — a link is not a path

**What it tested:** the boundary in the other direction. The document is a file
and the link is a URL, and the two obey different rules for separators,
escaping, and what "absolute" means.

**The classic mistake:** `path.resolve(fromFile, link)` — resolving against the
file rather than its directory, so every link lands one level too deep. Close
behind: forgetting that `#anchor` and `?raw=1` are not part of the filename, and
treating `/downloads/report.pdf` as a local path when it is relative to a web
root this function has never heard of.

**Model answer:** reject by prefix first (scheme, `//`, `/`, `#`), then strip
the fragment and query, then `decodeURIComponent`, then resolve against
`path.dirname(fromFile)` with the segments split on `/`.

## ex6 — relative first, always

**What it tested:** the ex3 containment test and the ex2 extension swap in the
same function, which is exactly how a build tool uses them.

# Reading - node/d13_path_portability

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **knowing which kind of path you are holding**. There
are only two, and every bug in this set is a confusion between them: a
*filesystem* path, whose separator is `path.sep` and whose meaning depends on
the platform and the working directory, and a *portable* path — the forward
-slash string you put in a URL, a manifest, a glob or a log line. `node:path`
converts between them and nothing else does. Four of the eight answers are the
same three lines — resolve, take the relative path, look at its first segment —
because "is this path inside that one" is the question underneath containment,
relocation and traversal defence alike. The other four are about the difference
between a string operation that usually works and a segment operation that
always does.

## ex1 — path.sep is not a slash

**What it tested:** that you convert on purpose at the boundary, rather than
hoping the platform separator is the one the consumer wants.

**The classic mistake:** `path.relative(...).replace(/\\/g, "/")`, which is
correct and also unfalsifiable — on Linux it is a no-op, so a mistake in it
survives every CI run and surfaces only when a colleague on Windows opens the
generated site and every link is dead. Splitting on `path.sep` and joining with
`/` says what you mean on both platforms.

**Model answer:** one `path.relative`, one split-join, and a named case for the
empty string, because "the same directory" is a real answer and `href=""` is not.

## ex2 — parse and format are inverses, with one trap

**What it tested:** that the extension rule (last dot onwards, and a leading dot
is not an extension) belongs to `node:path`, not to your regular expression.

directory called `v1.2` on a file with no extension.

normalise the caller's dot before formatting rather than during.

## ex3 — the traversal defence, in the constructive direction

first two characters.

string, so the join needs a fallback for the root.

## ex5 — a link is not a path

## Hint 1

There is a function in `node:path` that answers exactly the question "how do I
get from A to B" — you are not meant to compare the two strings yourself.

## Hint 2

That function answers in the **platform** separator, and this one has to answer
in the URL separator. Split on `path.sep` and join with `/` rather than
replacing characters — a `replaceAll("\\", "/")` is a no-op on Linux, so the bug
it hides never shows up until somebody on Windows runs the build.

One case comes back as the empty string. Decide what that should be before you
look at the gate.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`path.parse()` and `path.format()` are inverses. Parse gives you `{ root, dir,
base, name, ext }`; format builds a path back out of the parts you hand it.

## Hint 2

`path.format()` has a precedence rule that catches everybody: if you give it
`base`, it ignores `name` and `ext` entirely. So

```ts
path.format({ ...path.parse(file), ext: ".md" }); // unchanged - base wins
```

does nothing at all. Pass `dir`, `name` and `ext` and leave `base` out.

Normalising the caller's `ext` (dot or no dot, empty or not) is a two-line
concern; do it before you format, not inside it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`path.parse()` and `path.format()` are inverses. Parse gives you `{ root, dir,
base, name, ext }`; format builds a path back out of the parts you hand it.

## Hint 2

`path.format()` has a precedence rule that catches everybody: if you give it
`base`, it ignores `name` and `ext` entirely. So

```ts
path.format({ ...path.parse(file), ext: ".md" }); // unchanged - base wins
```

does nothing at all. Pass `dir`, `name` and `ext` and leave `base` out.

Normalising the caller's `ext` (dot or no dot, empty or not) is a two-line
concern; do it before you format, not inside it.

## Hint 1

Two paths cannot be compared until they mean the same thing, so `path.resolve()`
every entry before you look at any of them. After that the problem is a longest
common prefix — of **segments**, not of characters.

Split each resolved path on `path.sep`, then fold: start with the first path's

deploy script into the wrong directory. The gate has that exact pair in it.

Joining the segments back together needs one moment of care on POSIX, where the
first segment of an absolute path is the empty string.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two paths cannot be compared until they mean the same thing, so `path.resolve()`
every entry before you look at any of them. After that the problem is a longest
common prefix — of **segments**, not of characters.

## Hint 2

Split each resolved path on `path.sep`, then fold: start with the first path's
segments and, for every other path, cut the running answer down to the point
where the two arrays first disagree.

The character-prefix version passes every test you would think to write by hand
and then reports `/var/log` as an ancestor of `/var/logging`, which sends a
deploy script into the wrong directory. The gate has that exact pair in it.

Joining the segments back together needs one moment of care on POSIX, where the
first segment of an absolute path is the empty string.

## Problem 5 — from a link in a document to a file on disk

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `resolveDocLink(fromFile, link)` returns the absolute
path a relative link inside `fromFile` points at — fragment and query stripped,
percent-escapes decoded — or `null` when the link is external (`https:`,
`mailto:`), protocol-relative (`//host`), site-absolute (`/x`) or a bare `#`
fragment.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs, in this order: decide whether the link names a local file at
all, and only then turn it into a path. The rejections are all prefix tests —
a scheme (`https:`, `mailto:`), a leading `//`, a leading `/`, a leading `#`.

## Hint 2

A link is relative to the **directory** the document sits in, so
`path.dirname(fromFile)` is where the resolve starts from. Everything after a
`#` or a `?` belongs to the browser, not to the filesystem, so strip it before
you resolve.

And a link is percent-encoded while a filename is not: `my%20diagram.png` is a
file with a space in it. `decodeURIComponent` is the one-liner, and the decision
left to you is what to do when it throws on a malformed escape.

## Hint 1

Two separate jobs, in this order: decide whether the link names a local file at
all, and only then turn it into a path. The rejections are all prefix tests —
a scheme (`https:`, `mailto:`), a leading `//`, a leading `/`, a leading `#`.

## Hint 2

A link is relative to the **directory** the document sits in, so
`path.dirname(fromFile)` is where the resolve starts from. Everything after a
`#` or a `?` belongs to the browser, not to the filesystem, so strip it before
you resolve.

And a link is percent-encoded while a filename is not: `my%20diagram.png` is a
file with a space in it. `decodeURIComponent` is the one-liner, and the decision
left to you is what to do when it throws on a malformed escape.

## Problem 7 — the pattern language in every config file

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `matchesGlob(pattern, filePath)` matches forward-slash
relative paths. `*` matches any run of characters **inside one segment**; `**`
stands in for any number of whole segments, including none. No other
metacharacters.

```
uv run dojo test node d13_path_portability ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split both sides on `/` and match segment against segment. The whole difficulty
is that `**` does not consume one segment — it consumes an unknown number of
them, so this is a search with backtracking, not a walk with two cursors.

## Hint 2

Write it as a recursive `match(patternIndex, fileIndex)`:

- pattern exhausted → true only if the file is exhausted too;
- pattern segment is `**` → try every number of file segments it could swallow,
  **starting at zero**, and succeed if any of them lets the rest match;
- otherwise → the segment has to match this one file segment, and then recurse
  on the pair after it.

## Hint 3

A `*` inside a segment is a small regular expression: escape everything that is
special, then turn the escaped `\*` back into `[^/]*`. The `[^/]` is the part
that matters — a `.*` there would let `*.md` match `docs/readme.md`, and an
ignore rule written like that silently swallows your whole tree.

The remaining decision is what a pattern like `a**b` inside one segment should
mean. The gate does not ask; a reviewer might.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split both sides on `/` and match segment against segment. The whole difficulty
is that `**` does not consume one segment — it consumes an unknown number of
them, so this is a search with backtracking, not a walk with two cursors.

## Hint 2

Write it as a recursive `match(patternIndex, fileIndex)`:

- pattern exhausted → true only if the file is exhausted too;
- pattern segment is `**` → try every number of file segments it could swallow,
  **starting at zero**, and succeed if any of them lets the rest match;
- otherwise → the segment has to match this one file segment, and then recurse
  on the pair after it.

## Hint 3

A `*` inside a segment is a small regular expression: escape everything that is
special, then turn the escaped `\*` back into `[^/]*`. The `[^/]` is the part
that matters — a `.*` there would let `*.md` match `docs/readme.md`, and an
ignore rule written like that silently swallows your whole tree.

The remaining decision is what a pattern like `a**b` inside one segment should
mean. The gate does not ask; a reviewer might.

## Hint 1

Every path is decided on its own: grow its suffix one segment at a time and stop
at the first length no other path can produce. The answer for one path says
nothing about the answer for another — in the gate, one needs two segments and
its neighbour needs three.

For a candidate of `take` segments, the question is whether any *other* path's

this question runs out of interview time.

Two edges to get right. A path with fewer than `take` segments has to compare as
its whole self rather than throwing or wrapping around — `slice(-take)` on a

say so on purpose. And a path that is still ambiguous at full length needs a
last resort; deciding what that is (the whole path? a numbered suffix?) is left
to you, because the gate only feeds it distinct paths.

lessons.briefing:
# d14 — Buffers

Eight problems on `Buffer`, drawn from lesson **06_buffers_streams** — the half
of it that never touches a stream. Lesson 06 taught you to encode a frame and to
concatenate bytes rather than strings; this set drills the family that lives
around that skill: encodings with names, numbers whose width you choose, fixed
layouts, and text that arrives in the wrong places.

One rule runs through all eight. A `Buffer` is a sequence of **bytes**, and a
string is a sequence of **characters**; the conversion between them is lossy in
one direction and expensive in the other, so you do it exactly once, at a
boundary you chose. Every trap in this set is a solution that reached for
`toString()` a step too early.

## Problem 1 — the encoding that survives a URL

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `toBase64Url(buffer)` encodes with the url-safe alphabet
(`-` and `_` instead of `+` and `/`) and no `=` padding.
`fromBase64Url(text)` is the inverse, and also accepts an ordinary padded
base64 string, because half the tokens in the world are encoded by somebody else.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a number that costs what it is worth

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `writeVarInt(value)` encodes an unsigned LEB128 varint:
seven bits of number per byte, least significant group first, top bit set while
more bytes follow. `readVarInt(buffer, offset)` reads one starting at `offset`
and returns `{ value, bytesRead }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a fixed layout, read field by field

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `parseRecordHeader(buffer)` reads a 19-byte header —
magic `"DOJO"` (4 bytes) | `flags` uint8 | `count` uint32 **LE** | `id` uint16
**BE** | `name`, 8 bytes of ASCII padded with NUL — and returns
`{ flags, count, id, name }` with the padding stripped. A buffer too short, or
with the wrong magic, throws a message that says which.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex3
```

## Problem 4 — split, without ever decoding

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `splitBuffer(buffer, delimiter)` cuts at every
occurrence of a multi-byte `delimiter` and returns **Buffers**. Empty pieces are
kept, including at either end, and a delimiter that never occurs yields one
piece: the whole input.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex4
```

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createUtf8Decoder()` returns `{ push, end }`.
`push(chunk)` returns the complete characters that chunk finished and **holds**
any partial one; `end()` returns whatever is left when no more bytes are coming.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a whole file inlined in a string

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `parseDataUrl(text)` returns `{ mediaType, data }` for a
`data:` URL, or `null`. The payload is base64 when the metadata ends `;base64`
and percent-encoded otherwise; an omitted media type is
`text/plain;charset=US-ASCII`, and `data` is always a Buffer.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex6
```

## Problem 7 — frames out of chunks that do not line up

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createFrameReader()` returns `{ push, pending }` for a
stream of `uint32BE length` + payload. `push(chunk)` returns every whole frame
that chunk completed — none, one, or several — and keeps the leftover bytes;
`pending()` reports how many are held. Chunks split anywhere, including inside a
length prefix.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex7
```

## Problem 8 — where the text ends and the bytes begin

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `splitHeadersAndBody(buffer)` splits at the **first**
`CRLF CRLF`. The head is CRLF-separated `Name: value` lines: names lower-cased,
values trimmed, a repeated header joined with `", "`, and only the first colon
on a line is a separator. The body stays raw bytes. No terminator, or a line
with no colon, throws a message naming the problem.

```

```

# Reading - node/d14_buffers

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **staying in bytes until you have decided to leave
them**. A Buffer is a fixed-width sequence of octets; a JavaScript string is a
sequence of UTF-16 code units. Converting between them is a decision with two
costs: it is lossy in one direction (any byte that is not valid UTF-8 becomes
`U+FFFD` and never comes back) and it changes the length, which quietly
invalidates every offset you had computed. Six of these eight answers are the
same shape — find a boundary with `indexOf` or arithmetic, slice with
`subarray`, and decode only the range you know is text. The other two are about
knowing what the platform already ships: `base64url` is an encoding name, and
`StringDecoder` is the module that holds a half-arrived character for you.

## ex1 — the encoding has a name

**What it tested:** whether you look up the encoding list before you write a
transformation. base64url is not a variant you implement on top of base64; it is
a value `Buffer` has accepted since Node 14.

**The classic mistake:** the four-step hand roll —
`toString("base64").replace(/\+/g, "-").replace(/\//g, "_").replace(/=+$/, "")` —
and then a decoder that has to compute the padding back from `length % 4`. That
padding arithmetic is where it breaks, and it breaks on one input in four, so
the bug reaches production with a passing test suite behind it.

**Model answer:** `buffer.toString("base64url")` and
`Buffer.from(text, "base64url")` — and the decoder is liberal for free, because
Node's base64 decoder accepts both alphabets and missing padding.

## ex2 — seven bits at a time, little end first

**What it tested:** a variable-length integer, which is the encoding underneath
Protocol Buffers, DWARF, WebAssembly and half the binary formats you will meet.
The point of it is that a small number costs one byte.

**The classic mistake:** two of them, and both are silent. A `while` loop with
the test at the top encodes `0` as an empty buffer, because the body never runs.
And `value |= (byte & 0x7f) << shift` truncates to 32 bits, so the fifth group
of seven bits contributes nothing at all and a large varint decodes to a
plausible smaller number.

**Model answer:** `do/while` for the write; multiply by a running `scale` rather
than shifting for the read; and return `bytesRead` so the caller can find the
next field, since a varint is almost never the only thing in the buffer.

## ex3 — the layout is the specification

**What it tested:** reading a fixed record with `readUInt32LE` / `readUInt16BE`
and friends, where the width **and** the byte order are part of the contract and
neither is guessable from the data.

**The classic mistake:** assuming one endianness for the whole structure. Mixed
layouts are ordinary — a format that stores its own fields little-endian and its
network identifiers big-endian is not being perverse, it is being two formats
that grew together. Reading `count` big-endian here gives 1880096512, a number
that looks like a number and passes straight through your validation. Second
mistake: leaving the NUL padding on the fixed-width name, producing a string
that prints correctly and compares equal to nothing.

**Model answer:** check the length before any read, check the magic before you
believe anything, then read each field at its offset in its declared order — and
strip the padding, because the field is fixed width and the value is not.

## ex4 — indexOf takes a Buffer

**What it tested:** that splitting is a byte operation with a byte engine.
`Buffer#indexOf` accepts a Buffer needle and a start offset, which is the entire
algorithm.

**The classic mistake:** `buffer.toString().split(delimiter).map(Buffer.from)`.
It works on ASCII and destroys everything else: the gate splits on `0xa9`, the
*second* byte of a two-byte character, which no string-level search can find
because by then those two bytes are one character. Close behind: dropping the
final piece when the buffer ends on a delimiter, which is how a blank line stops
terminating a header block.

**Model answer:** a cursor and `indexOf(delimiter, start)` in a loop, with the
tail pushed unconditionally after it — `subarray`, not `slice`-and-copy, because
staying in bytes is the point.

## ex5 — somebody already wrote this

**What it tested:** that "a character can be split across chunks" has a core
module devoted to it, and that you recognise the problem before you start
counting lead bytes.

**The classic mistake:** handling a one-byte remainder and calling it done. A
four-byte character can be split **three** times, so the hand-rolled version
passes every test until an emoji arrives at a chunk boundary. The other mistake
is dropping the held bytes at end of stream instead of reporting them: a
truncated sequence that vanishes is a bug nobody can see.

**Model answer:** `new StringDecoder("utf8")`, `write` for push and `end` for
end — the same object a Readable in string mode is already using underneath you.

## ex6 — the first comma is the boundary

**What it tested:** parsing a small grammar where the interesting decision (how
is the payload encoded?) is carried by a suffix on the metadata rather than by
the payload itself.

**The classic mistake:** `text.split(",")`, which corrupts any payload
containing a comma — and base64 payloads do not contain commas, so this passes
the test you wrote and fails on the percent-encoded JSON somebody inlines later.
Second: reporting the media type as `text/plain;base64`, leaving the encoding
marker inside the type, so every content-type comparison downstream misses.

**Model answer:** `indexOf(",")` and two slices; strip `;base64` from the
metadata before reporting it; substitute the spec's default when the type is
empty; and decode to a Buffer either way, because the payload is bytes even when
those bytes happen to be text.

## ex7 — the chunk boundary is not the frame boundary

**What it tested:** stateful reassembly. Lesson 06 handed you a complete buffer
and asked for the frames in it; the network does not do that, and the difference
between the two is the entire exercise.

**The classic mistake:** reading the length before checking that four bytes are
actually there — `readUInt32BE` on a two-byte buffer throws `ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE`
and takes the connection with it. Then: handling one frame per `push` instead of
looping, which works perfectly until traffic gets busy enough for two frames to
share a packet, at which point you drop every frame after the first and the
symptom is "messages go missing under load".

**Model answer:** concatenate onto the leftover, then loop with two separate
guards — enough bytes for the header, then enough bytes for the payload — and
copy each payload out, because a `subarray` is a view over a buffer that is
about to be replaced.

## ex8 — decode the head, keep the body

**What it tested:** the boundary decision itself. Half of this buffer is text
and half of it is not, and the whole job is to find the line between them
without decoding across it.

**The classic mistake:** `buffer.toString()` on the whole message, split on the
blank line, and `Buffer.from()` the second half back. Every byte that was not
valid UTF-8 is now a replacement character, the body is a different length than
it was, and the `content-length` you already sent is a lie. The other one is
`line.split(":")`, which turns `Location: https://example.com:8443/x` into a
header whose value is `https`.

**Model answer:** `indexOf` the CRLF CRLF as bytes, decode only `[0, at)`, keep
`[at + 4, end)` as a Buffer, and cut each header line at its **first** colon —
joining a repeated name with `", "` rather than letting the last one win.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `Buffer`](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html) — the supported encoding names (including `base64url`), the `read*` family, and the difference between `subarray` and a copy.
- [Node.js: `buf.indexOf()`](https://nodejs.org/api/buffer.html#bufindexofvalue-byteoffset-encoding) — the byte search ex4, ex7 and ex8 are all built on.
- [Node.js: `node:string_decoder`](https://nodejs.org/api/string_decoder.html) — ex5, and what a Readable in string mode does for you already.
- [MDN: `data:` URLs](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/URI/Reference/Schemes/data) — the grammar of ex6, including the default media type.
- [MDN: UTF-8](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/UTF-8) — why a character can be one to four bytes, and what a lead byte looks like.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a number that costs what it is worth

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `writeVarInt(value)` encodes an unsigned LEB128 varint:
seven bits of number per byte, least significant group first, top bit set while
more bytes follow. `readVarInt(buffer, offset)` reads one starting at `offset`
and returns `{ value, bytesRead }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Seven bits of number per byte, and the eighth bit means "there is another byte
after this one". Least significant group first — which looks backwards until you
realise it is what lets a reader stop without knowing the length in advance.

## Hint 2

Writing: take the low seven bits, shift the number down by seven, and set the
continuation bit on the byte you just produced **if there is anything left**.
The loop has to run at least once or zero encodes as an empty buffer, so
`do { ... } while (rest > 0)`.

Reading: accumulate `(byte & 0x7f) * scale` and multiply `scale` by 128 each
time. Use multiplication rather than `<<`: JavaScript's bitwise operators
truncate to 32 bits, so the fifth byte of a large varint silently contributes
zero. Returning `bytesRead` is not decoration — it is how the caller finds the
next field.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Seven bits of number per byte, and the eighth bit means "there is another byte
after this one". Least significant group first — which looks backwards until you
realise it is what lets a reader stop without knowing the length in advance.

## Hint 2

Writing: take the low seven bits, shift the number down by seven, and set the
continuation bit on the byte you just produced **if there is anything left**.
The loop has to run at least once or zero encodes as an empty buffer, so
`do { ... } while (rest > 0)`.

Reading: accumulate `(byte & 0x7f) * scale` and multiply `scale` by 128 each
time. Use multiplication rather than `<<`: JavaScript's bitwise operators
truncate to 32 bits, so the fifth byte of a large varint silently contributes
zero. Returning `bytesRead` is not decoration — it is how the caller finds the
next field.

## Problem 3 — a fixed layout, read field by field

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `parseRecordHeader(buffer)` reads a 19-byte header —
magic `"DOJO"` (4 bytes) | `flags` uint8 | `count` uint32 **LE** | `id` uint16
**BE** | `name`, 8 bytes of ASCII padded with NUL — and returns
`{ flags, count, id, name }` with the padding stripped. A buffer too short, or
with the wrong magic, throws a message that says which.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex3
```

## Hint 1

Write the layout down as offsets before you write any code:

```
0  magic  4 bytes ascii
4  flags  uint8
5  count  uint32 LE
9  id     uint16 BE

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Node ships the answer as a core module. It is the thing a Readable in string
mode uses internally, and its two methods are exactly the two methods this
interface asks for. Look for it in the module list before you start counting
lead bytes.

## Hint 2

The module is `node:string_decoder`; the class is `StringDecoder`; the methods
are `write(chunk)` and `end()`.

Writing it by hand means recognising a lead byte (`0b110xxxxx` is two bytes,
`0b1110xxxx` three, `0b11110xxx` four), holding the tail, and remembering that a
four-byte character can be split **three** times — which is why the hand-rolled
version that only handles a one-byte remainder passes every test until an emoji
arrives.

What `end()` should do with a sequence that can never be completed is a real
decision. The platform picks the replacement character; a stricter caller might
want an error.

## Hint 1

Node ships the answer as a core module. It is the thing a Readable in string
mode uses internally, and its two methods are exactly the two methods this
interface asks for. Look for it in the module list before you start counting
lead bytes.

## Hint 2

The module is `node:string_decoder`; the class is `StringDecoder`; the methods
are `write(chunk)` and `end()`.

Writing it by hand means recognising a lead byte (`0b110xxxxx` is two bytes,
`0b1110xxxx` three, `0b11110xxx` four), holding the tail, and remembering that a
four-byte character can be split **three** times — which is why the hand-rolled
version that only handles a one-byte remainder passes every test until an emoji
arrives.

What `end()` should do with a sequence that can never be completed is a real
decision. The platform picks the replacement character; a stricter caller might
want an error.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — frames out of chunks that do not line up

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createFrameReader()` returns `{ push, pending }` for a
stream of `uint32BE length` + payload. `push(chunk)` returns every whole frame
that chunk completed — none, one, or several — and keeps the leftover bytes;
`pending()` reports how many are held. Chunks split anywhere, including inside a
length prefix.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One piece of state: the bytes that arrived but did not add up to a whole frame.
Every `push` concatenates the new chunk onto that leftover and then takes as
many complete frames off the front as it can.

## Hint 2

Two guards, and they are separate:

- fewer than four bytes available → you cannot even read the length. `readUInt32BE`
  on a two-byte buffer throws, so this check has to come first;
- fewer than `length` bytes after the header → the frame is not finished; stop
  and keep everything.

Both are `break`, and both leave the cursor where it was, which is what makes
the leftover correct.

## Hint 3

The loop is what the test with three frames in one chunk is checking: an `if`
instead of a `for` returns the first frame and silently drops the rest, and the
bug does not appear until traffic gets busy enough for two frames to share a
packet.

Slice the payload out with `subarray` and then **copy** it — a subarray is a
view over the leftover buffer, and the leftover buffer is about to be replaced.
Whether `pending()` should also cap how much you are willing to hold before
giving up is not tested here, and is the first thing a reviewer will ask about a
reader facing the network.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One piece of state: the bytes that arrived but did not add up to a whole frame.
Every `push` concatenates the new chunk onto that leftover and then takes as
many complete frames off the front as it can.

## Hint 2

Two guards, and they are separate:

- fewer than four bytes available → you cannot even read the length. `readUInt32BE`
  on a two-byte buffer throws, so this check has to come first;
- fewer than `length` bytes after the header → the frame is not finished; stop
  and keep everything.

Both are `break`, and both leave the cursor where it was, which is what makes
the leftover correct.

## Hint 3

The loop is what the test with three frames in one chunk is checking: an `if`
instead of a `for` returns the first frame and silently drops the rest, and the
bug does not appear until traffic gets busy enough for two frames to share a
packet.

Slice the payload out with `subarray` and then **copy** it — a subarray is a
view over the leftover buffer, and the leftover buffer is about to be replaced.
Whether `pending()` should also cap how much you are willing to hold before
giving up is not tested here, and is the first thing a reviewer will ask about a
reader facing the network.

## Problem 8 — where the text ends and the bytes begin

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `splitHeadersAndBody(buffer)` splits at the **first**
`CRLF CRLF`. The head is CRLF-separated `Name: value` lines: names lower-cased,
values trimmed, a repeated header joined with `", "`, and only the first colon
on a line is a separator. The body stays raw bytes. No terminator, or a line
with no colon, throws a message naming the problem.

```
uv run dojo test node d14_buffers ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Find the boundary before you decode anything. `buffer.indexOf(Buffer.from("\r\n\r\n"))`
gives you one number, and that number splits the buffer into a part that is text
and a part that is not.

## Hint 2

Only the head is text. `buffer.toString("utf8", 0, at)` decodes exactly that
range; the body is `subarray(at + 4)` and stays a Buffer for the rest of its
life. The moment you write `buffer.toString()` on the whole thing, every byte
that is not valid UTF-8 becomes a replacement character, the length changes, and
the content-length you already sent is a lie.

Then it is line handling: split the head on CRLF, skip empties, and cut each
line at its **first** colon.

## Hint 3

`indexOf` on the whole line finds the first colon, which is what you want:
`Location: https://example.com:8443/x` has three of them and only the first is a
separator. `line.split(":")` throws away the rest of that URL.

A repeated header is not an error and not a last-one-wins: the field value is
the list, joined with a comma and a space. Whether you should keep the original
order (you should) and what to do with a header whose name has spaces around it
are the two things left for you to decide.

Then it is line handling: split the head on CRLF, skip empties, and cut each
line at its **first** colon.

## Hint 3

`indexOf` on the whole line finds the first colon, which is what you want:
`Location: https://example.com:8443/x` has three of them and only the first is a
separator. `line.split(":")` throws away the rest of that URL.

A repeated header is not an error and not a last-one-wins: the field value is
the list, joined with a comma and a space. Whether you should keep the original
order (you should) and what to do with a header whose name has spaces around it
are the two things left for you to decide.

# d15 — Readable and Writable

Eight problems on building and consuming streams, drawn from lesson
**06_buffers_streams** — the stream half. Lesson 06 had you write one source and
one sink; this set drills the shapes those two come in: ranges, drains, budgets,
early stops, concatenation, pagination, merging, and the in-memory socket pair.
Transforms and `pipeline()` chains belong to lesson 07 and to **d16**;
backpressure proper belongs to **d17**. If `push(null)` does not feel like
second nature yet, redo lesson 06 ex3 first.

Everything here is in memory and driven by hand. The gate pushes into sources it
controls, settles the event loop a fixed number of turns, and grades laziness
with flags planted inside `read()` implementations — never with a clock.

## Problem 1 — a source you build yourself

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createRangeStream(from, to, step)` is an **object-mode**
Readable producing `from`, `from + step`, ... up to and including `to` when the
step lands on it. An empty range (`from > to`) ends immediately rather than
hanging.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex1
```

## Problem 2 — the whole stream, or the real error

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `toArray(readable)` collects any object-mode Readable
into an array, in order. An empty stream is `[]`. A stream that errors part way
through **rejects** with that error — never resolves with a partial array.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a sink with a budget

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createBoundedSink(limit)` returns `{ writable, bytes }`.
The sink accepts chunks until one would take the total **past** `limit` bytes —
landing exactly on it is fine — then fails that write with an error naming the
limit. `bytes()` reports what was actually accepted, and a `pipeline()` feeding
the sink rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex3
```

## Problem 4 — take what you need, stop the rest

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `takeFrom(readable, n)` resolves with the first `n`
items and **destroys the source**, so it stops producing. A stream shorter than
`n` yields what it has, without error.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex4
```

## Problem 5 — one stream after another, not all at once

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `concatStreams(sources)` yields everything from the
first source, then the second, and so on. Each source is only **started** once
the one before it has ended, and an error in any source destroys the joined
stream with that error.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a paginated API wearing a stream

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createPagedSource(fetchPage)` is an object-mode
Readable over an injected `fetchPage(cursor)` returning `{ items, next }`: first
call with `null`, then each `next`, **one call at a time**, ending after the
page whose `next` is null. A rejected fetch destroys the stream with that error.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex6
```

## Problem 7 — many sources, one stream

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `mergeStreams(sources)` interleaves every source into
one object-mode Readable as items are produced. It ends when **all** sources
have ended; the first error destroys the other sources and propagates. No
sources at all ends immediately.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a socket pair with no socket

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createDuplexPair()` returns `[a, b]`, two Duplex
streams wired crosswise: what is written to `a` is readable from `b` and vice
versa, the two directions are independent, and `end()`ing one side ends the
**other** side's readable half while its own writable half keeps working.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex8
```

# Reading - node/d15_readable_writable

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **demand-driven production**. A Readable is not a
loop that emits; it is a `read()` callback the machinery invokes when a consumer
wants more, plus one obligation — `push(null)` when there is no more. Every
problem here turns on who moves first: the range stream that must end an empty
range unprompted, the taker that must stop a source mid-flow, the concat that
must not start source two early, the paged source that must not fetch ahead of
demand. The recurring instrument is the async iterator: `for await` subscribes,
converts errors to rejections, and — the part people forget — destroys the
stream when you `break`. Where the iterator is the wrong tool (the merge, the
pair), the answer is hand-built Readables fed by `push`, with a counter or a
flag doing the bookkeeping the iterator would have done.

## ex1 — push(null) is the contract

**What it tested:** the minimal hand-built source: object mode, a cursor in a
closure, and the end signal.

**The classic mistake:** treating `push(null)` as something that happens when
data runs out mid-stream, and never considering the range that was empty from
the start. The first `read()` then pushes nothing, the machinery waits politely
for a push that never comes, and the consumer hangs with no error anywhere. The
lesser mistake is forgetting `objectMode`, which coerces every number into a
Buffer and turns `[2, 4, 6, 8]` into byte soup.

**Model answer:** check "past the end" **before** producing, so the empty range
hits `push(null)` on the very first read — the same line handles both endings.

## ex2 — a partial success is a failure in disguise

**What it tested:** consuming a stream you did not build, with the error path
treated as seriously as the data path.

**The classic mistake:** the `data`/`end` listener pair without `error`, which
resolves with whatever had arrived when the stream broke. A caller receives two
of five records and no signal that three are missing — the worst outcome a
consumer can produce, because it is indistinguishable from success. Adding the
`error` listener but forgetting to remove the others on each terminal path is
the second version of the same bug.

**Model answer:** `for await` — subscription, cleanup, and error-to-rejection
conversion in one keyword; the pending `next()` rejects with the stream's real
error.

## ex3 — fail the write, not the process

**What it tested:** the Writable side of the contract: `callback(error)` is how
a sink refuses, and refusal must be precise about what was and was not taken.

**The classic mistake:** counting the chunk before checking it, so `bytes()`
claims the sink accepted data it refused — an off-by-one-chunk that matters the
moment anyone reconciles the count against what was stored. The other is
throwing from `write()` instead of passing the error to the callback, which
crashes instead of propagating through the stream's error machinery to the
`pipeline()` that fed it.

**Model answer:** test `accepted + chunk.length > limit` before adding —
strictly greater, so landing exactly on the budget is allowed — and put the
number in the message.

## ex4 — break is a shutdown, not just an exit

**What it tested:** early termination as a first-class operation. Taking three
items from a hundred-item source must cost three items, not a hundred.

**The classic mistake:** collecting with a `data` listener and detaching after
`n` items. Detaching does not stop a flowing stream — production continues into
the void, and for a file or socket source the handle stays open until the
source ends on its own. The gate counts productions precisely to catch the
version that "works" while draining everything.

**Model answer:** `for await` with `break`: the loop's exit calls the
iterator's `return()`, which destroys the Readable — laziness and cleanup in
one keyword.

## ex5 — a generator is lazy by construction

**What it tested:** sequencing sources without starting them early. Attaching a
listener, resuming, or iterating a stream *is* starting it, and starting all
sources at once means holding every underlying resource open from the first
read.

**The classic mistake:** subscribing to all sources up front and switching a
"current" pointer between them. The gate plants a flag inside the second
source's `read()`, and any eager subscription trips it while source one is
still open. The subtler miss is the error path: catching a source's failure and
just ending the joined stream presents a broken transfer as a short one.

**Model answer:** an async generator looping `yield* source`, wrapped in
`Readable.from()` — the code that would start source two literally has not run
until source one's loop finishes, and a source error becomes the joined
stream's destruction for free.

## ex6 — demand drives the fetches

**What it tested:** adapting a pull-based API to a stream without turning it
into a download. Two independent disciplines: never two fetches in flight, and
never fetching far ahead of the consumer.

**The classic mistake:** ignoring that `read()` can be called again while your
fetch is still pending — without an in-flight guard the same cursor is fetched
twice and the gate's cursor log shows the duplicate. Second: leaving the
default object-mode `highWaterMark` of 16, which makes the machinery call
`read()` until sixteen items are buffered — for two-item pages, that is the
whole API fetched before the consumer touches item one.

**Model answer:** three closure variables — cursor, finished, inFlight — a
`highWaterMark` of 1, and `destroy(error)` on a rejected fetch rather than a
quiet early end.

## ex7 — the end is a countdown

**What it tested:** the one shape where every source *should* flow at once, and
the bookkeeping that makes the combined stream honest about ending and failing.

**The classic mistake:** ending the merge when the first source ends — the
survivors keep producing into a stream that has already pushed null, and their
items are silently lost. On the error path, forgetting to destroy the other
sources leaves them producing into a dead stream; forgetting the guard boolean
lets a second failure destroy an already-destroyed stream with a different
reason.

**Model answer:** a counter of open sources decremented on each `end`, null
pushed at zero; on the first error, destroy the survivors, destroy the merge
with that error, and ignore everything after.

## ex8 — a Duplex is two independent halves

**What it tested:** that the readable and writable halves of a Duplex are
separate machines, and that "wiring" means crossing them: A's `write()` pushes
into B's readable half.

**The classic mistake:** pushing into your **own** readable half, which builds
two echo chambers instead of a channel — each side hears itself and the gate's
directional assertions catch it immediately. The advanced miss is the
half-close: not implementing `final()`, so ending side A never tells side B the
data has stopped, and any consumer waiting for B's `end` event waits forever.

**Model answer:** two hand-built Duplexes whose `write()` pushes into the other
side and whose `final()` pushes null into the other side — `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`
in stream form, with the reverse direction untouched.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: implementing a Readable](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-readable-stream) — `read()`, `push()`, object mode and `highWaterMark`, for ex1 and ex6.
- [Node.js: implementing a Writable](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-writable-stream) — `write(chunk, encoding, callback)` and failing a write, for ex3.
- [Node.js: streams and async iterators](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streams-compatibility-with-async-generators-and-async-iterators) — why `for await` and `Readable.from()` carry ex2, ex4 and ex5.
- [Node.js: duplex and transform streams](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#duplex-and-transform-streams) — the two-halves model behind ex8.
- [MDN: `for await...of`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — the loop's `return()` semantics that make breaking out of a stream destroy it.

## Hint 1

A hand-built source is `new Readable({ objectMode: true, read() { ... } })`.
The machinery calls `read()` whenever it wants more; you answer with `push`.
Without `objectMode` every number you push is coerced into a Buffer on the way
out.

Keep the cursor in a closure variable and let `read()` push one value and
advance it. The end of the stream is `this.push(null)` — and the empty-range
case falls out for free if the "past the end" check comes **first**, because the
very first `read()` then ends the stream before anything is produced. A stream
that never pushes null is a consumer that hangs forever, which is exactly what
the gate's empty-range test would do.

## Problem 2 — the whole stream, or the real error

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `toArray(readable)` collects any object-mode Readable
into an array, in order. An empty stream is `[]`. A stream that errors part way
through **rejects** with that error — never resolves with a partial array.

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every Readable is an async iterable. The consumer you are asked to write is a
loop, not a listener: `for await (const item of readable)`.

## Hint 2

The reason the loop beats `on("data")` is the error path: an `error` event on
the stream becomes a **rejection** of the pending `next()`, so the promise your
function returns rejects with the real error instead of resolving with whatever
had arrived by then. If you do build it from events, you need all three of
`data`, `end` and `error`, and you must remove the other two listeners in each
terminal case — which is the bookkeeping the iterator exists to do for you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Every Readable is an async iterable. The consumer you are asked to write is a
loop, not a listener: `for await (const item of readable)`.

## Hint 2

The reason the loop beats `on("data")` is the error path: an `error` event on
the stream becomes a **rejection** of the pending `next()`, so the promise your
function returns rejects with the real error instead of resolving with whatever
had arrived by then. If you do build it from events, you need all three of
`data`, `end` and `error`, and you must remove the other two listeners in each
terminal case — which is the bookkeeping the iterator exists to do for you.
