## Problem 3 — a sink with a budget

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createBoundedSink(limit)` returns `{ writable, bytes }`.
The sink accepts chunks until one would take the total **past** `limit` bytes —
landing exactly on it is fine — then fails that write with an error naming the
limit. `bytes()` reports what was actually accepted, and a `pipeline()` feeding
the sink rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A hand-built sink is `new Writable({ write(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.
Calling `callback()` accepts the chunk; calling `callback(error)` fails the
write, destroys the stream, and makes any `pipeline()` feeding it reject.

## Hint 2

The check is `accepted + chunk.length > limit` — strictly greater, tested
**before** you add. Landing exactly on the limit is allowed; going over is not;
and the chunk that would go over must not be counted, or `bytes()` claims to
have accepted data it refused. Put the limit's number in the error message: the
person reading the rejection wants to know the budget, not just that one exists.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A hand-built sink is `new Writable({ write(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.
Calling `callback()` accepts the chunk; calling `callback(error)` fails the
write, destroys the stream, and makes any `pipeline()` feeding it reject.

## Hint 2

The check is `accepted + chunk.length > limit` — strictly greater, tested
**before** you add. Landing exactly on the limit is allowed; going over is not;
and the chunk that would go over must not be counted, or `bytes()` claims to
have accepted data it refused. Put the limit's number in the error message: the
person reading the rejection wants to know the budget, not just that one exists.

## Problem 5 — one stream after another, not all at once

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `concatStreams(sources)` yields everything from the
first source, then the second, and so on. Each source is only **started** once
the one before it has ended, and an error in any source destroys the joined
stream with that error.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An async generator that loops over the sources in order, plus `Readable.from()`
to turn it back into a stream, is the entire implementation. The laziness you
are asked for is a property of the generator: code after the first loop has not
run yet, so the second source has not even been subscribed to.

## Hint 2

`yield* source` inside the generator delegates to the source's async iterator —
items, end, and error all handled. The version to avoid is attaching `data`
listeners to every source up front and switching between them: attaching a
listener **starts** a stream, which is precisely what the gate's `secondRead`
flag catches. Error handling comes free too: a source that errors rejects the
pending `next()`, the generator throws, and `Readable.from` destroys the joined
stream with that error rather than quietly ending early.

## Hint 1

An async generator that loops over the sources in order, plus `Readable.from()`
to turn it back into a stream, is the entire implementation. The laziness you
are asked for is a property of the generator: code after the first loop has not
run yet, so the second source has not even been subscribed to.

## Hint 2

`yield* source` inside the generator delegates to the source's async iterator —
items, end, and error all handled. The version to avoid is attaching `data`
listeners to every source up front and switching between them: attaching a
listener **starts** a stream, which is precisely what the gate's `secondRead`
flag catches. Error handling comes free too: a source that errors rejects the
pending `next()`, the generator throws, and `Readable.from` destroys the joined
stream with that error rather than quietly ending early.

## Hint 1

State in the closure: the cursor to fetch next, whether the last page has been
seen, and whether a fetch is in flight right now. `read()` starts a fetch,
pushes the page's items when it lands, and pushes `null` after the page whose
`next` was null.

## Hint 2

Two traps, both about `read()` being called at awkward moments:

- it can be called again while your fetch is still pending. Without an
  `inFlight` guard you fetch the same cursor twice and the gate's cursor log
  shows the duplicate;
- the default object-mode `highWaterMark` of 16 makes the machinery keep
  calling `read()` to fill its buffer, which for two-item pages means fetching
  most of the API before the consumer has asked for anything. Pass
  `highWaterMark: 1` so demand, not buffering, drives the fetches.

A rejected fetch is `this.destroy(error)` — not a swallowed catch, and not an
`end`, which would present a failed download as a short one.

## Problem 7 — many sources, one stream

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `mergeStreams(sources)` interleaves every source into
one object-mode Readable as items are produced. It ends when **all** sources
have ended; the first error destroys the other sources and propagates. No
sources at all ends immediately.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Unlike ex5, this one *wants* every source flowing at once — that is what makes
it a merge. Attach a `data` listener to each source and forward every item into
one hand-built object-mode Readable.

## Hint 2

The end condition is a countdown, not an event: keep a counter of sources still
open, decrement on each `end`, and `push(null)` only when it reaches zero.
Ending the merge when the *first* source ends is the classic version of this
bug, and it silently drops everything the slower sources still had.

## Hint 3

The error path has three jobs, and each one is checked: propagate the first
error into the merged stream (`merged.destroy(error)`), destroy the **other**
sources so they stop producing into a stream nobody reads, and ignore any
second error — a destroyed stream must not be destroyed again with a different

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Unlike ex5, this one *wants* every source flowing at once — that is what makes
it a merge. Attach a `data` listener to each source and forward every item into
one hand-built object-mode Readable.

## Hint 2

The end condition is a countdown, not an event: keep a counter of sources still
open, decrement on each `end`, and `push(null)` only when it reaches zero.
Ending the merge when the *first* source ends is the classic version of this
bug, and it silently drops everything the slower sources still had.

## Hint 3

The error path has three jobs, and each one is checked: propagate the first
error into the merged stream (`merged.destroy(error)`), destroy the **other**
sources so they stop producing into a stream nobody reads, and ignore any
second error — a destroyed stream must not be destroyed again with a different
reason. A guard boolean covers the last two. What to do about backpressure when
a consumer is slower than the sources is deliberately out of scope here; that is
d17's whole subject.

## Problem 8 — a socket pair with no socket

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createDuplexPair()` returns `[a, b]`, two Duplex
streams wired crosswise: what is written to `a` is readable from `b` and vice
versa, the two directions are independent, and `end()`ing one side ends the
**other** side's readable half while its own writable half keeps working.

```
uv run dojo test node d15_readable_writable ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Duplex` is a Readable and a Writable in one object, and the two halves are
independent. The wiring you want is a cross: side A's `write()` implementation
pushes the chunk into side B's readable half, and vice versa.

## Hint 2

Build both with `new Duplex({ read() {}, write(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.
The empty `read()` is fine — data arrives by the other side pushing, not by
this side pulling. Referring to `b` inside `a`'s options object works because
the closure runs at write time, not at construction time.

## Hint 3

The half-close is the part interviews poke at: implement `final(callback)` —
which runs when this side is `end()`ed — and have it `push(null)` into the
**other** side. That ends B's readable half when A stops writing, while B's
writable half keeps working, exactly like `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` on a real socket.
Whether ending one side should eventually tear down the whole pair (as
`allowHalfOpen: false` would) is a semantics decision the gate leaves to you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `Duplex` is a Readable and a Writable in one object, and the two halves are
independent. The wiring you want is a cross: side A's `write()` implementation
pushes the chunk into side B's readable half, and vice versa.

## Hint 2

Build both with `new Duplex({ read() {}, write(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.
The empty `read()` is fine — data arrives by the other side pushing, not by
this side pulling. Referring to `b` inside `a`'s options object works because
the closure runs at write time, not at construction time.

## Hint 3

The half-close is the part interviews poke at: implement `final(callback)` —
which runs when this side is `end()`ed — and have it `push(null)` into the
**other** side. That ends B's readable half when A stops writing, while B's
writable half keeps working, exactly like `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` on a real socket.
Whether ending one side should eventually tear down the whole pair (as
`allowHalfOpen: false` would) is a semantics decision the gate leaves to you.

# d16 — Transform pipelines

Eight problems on the middle of a stream. Lesson **07_streams_2** taught the
`Transform` and what `pipeline()` does when a link fails; this set drills the
stages you end up writing again in every project — map, filter, batch, expand —
and then the two that are genuinely hard: keeping order while working in
parallel, and fanning one stream out to many destinations without leaving a file
handle behind.

Everything here is in memory, and nothing is graded by timing. Where a stage has
to run work in parallel the gate hands it deferreds it controls and releases
them by name, so "three were in flight" and "nothing came out until the first
one landed" are exact claims.

## Problem 1 — map

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createMapStage(fn)` is an object-mode `Transform` that
pushes `fn(item)` for every item. A throw inside `fn` must fail the **stream** —
it may never escape as an uncaught exception.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex1
```

## Problem 2 — filter, with a receipt

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createFilterStage(predicate)` passes on the items the
predicate likes and drops the rest. The stream it returns also answers `kept()`
and `dropped()`.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex2
```

## Problem 3 — the group is the unit

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createBatchStage(size)` emits arrays of `size` items.
The short final batch is emitted when the input ends; an input whose length
divides exactly emits **no** trailing empty batch, and an empty input emits
nothing at all.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex3
```

## Problem 4 — one in, many out

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createExpandStage(fn)` pushes every element `fn(item)`
produces. `fn` may return an array or an async iterable, and an empty one drops
the item. The output of one input is drained fully before the next is accepted.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a stage that is just a function

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `asyncMapStage(fn)` returns an **async generator stage**
you can drop straight into `pipeline()`. It awaits `fn` per item, one at a time,
yields in input order, and on a rejection stops pulling from the source.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex5
```

## Problem 6 — one source, several destinations

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `tee(source, sinks)` sends every item to every sink and
resolves when all of them have finished. If any sink fails it rejects with that
error and destroys the source and every other sink.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex6
```

## Problem 7 — parallel work, sequential output

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createOrderedParallelStage(worker, limit)` keeps at
most `limit` calls to `worker` in flight and emits their results in **input**
order, whatever order they finish in. A rejection fails the stream.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex7
```

## Problem 8 — one stream in, many files out

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `partitionTo(source, keyOf, openSink)` routes each item
to the sink its key names, calling `openSink(key)` at most **once per key**. It
ends every sink when the source runs out and resolves with the per-key counts;
on any failure it destroys them all and rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex8
```

# Reading - node/d16_transform_pipeline

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **the transform callback**, and what it actually
means. It is not "here is my output" — `push()` is that, and you may call it
zero times or twenty. The callback means "I have finished with this chunk, send
me another", which makes it the only lever a stage has over how much work is in
flight and how much data is buffered ahead of it. Every problem in this set is
that one idea from a different angle: not calling it stalls the stream (ex2),
calling it too early interleaves output (ex4) or lets an unbounded fan-out
happen (ex5, ex7), and calling it with an error is the only way a failure inside
your code becomes a failure the caller can catch (ex1). The other half of the
set is teardown. A pipeline that fails has to leave nothing open, and the two
fan-out problems exist because that is where people forget.

## ex1 — a throw is not a stream error

**What it tested:** that you know who calls `transform()`. Not you — the stream
machinery does, from inside its own tick.

**The classic mistake:** letting `fn` throw. The exception unwinds into Node's
internals and comes out as an uncaught exception on a later tick, where no
`try`/`catch` around `pipeline()` and no `.catch()` on its promise can see it.
The process dies, and the stack trace points at a stream file nobody wrote.

**Model answer:** wrap the call, `callback(error)` on the way out — and note the
two-argument form, `callback(null, value)`, which pushes and continues in one
line.

## ex2 — dropping is not pushing

**What it tested:** that emission and completion are separate signals, which is
the fact that makes a filter possible at all.

**The classic mistake:** forgetting the callback on the dropped path. The stream
stalls at the first dropped item and never recovers — and a stall is the worst
failure mode there is, because it looks exactly like a slow upstream. Nothing
throws, nothing logs, the process just sits there.

**Model answer:** `push` conditionally, `callback()` unconditionally, and keep
the counters in the closure so a caller cannot reach in and reset them.

## ex3 — the remainder is the exercise

**What it tested:** `_flush`, the last word a stage gets before the stream ends,
and the one place a buffered remainder can escape.

**The classic mistake:** no flush at all, so the final partial batch is silently
dropped. It passes every test with a round number of items and loses the last
seventeen rows of every real import. The mirror-image mistake is a flush with no
guard, which emits an empty array whenever the count divides exactly, and every
consumer downstream grows a defensive `if` because of it.

**Model answer:** accumulate, push and reassign a **new** array when full — not
`length = 0`, which mutates the array downstream now owns — and push from flush
only if there is something in it.

## ex4 — drain before you accept the next one

**What it tested:** that `push()` is not once per `transform()`, and that
"finished with this chunk" has to mean finished, including everything the chunk
expanded into.

**The classic mistake:** pushing the array instead of its elements, which is a
map wearing an expand's name. After that: calling the callback before an async
iterable has been drained, so the next input starts producing while yours is
still going and the two outputs interleave — an ordering bug that only appears
when the source is fast enough to have a queue.

**Model answer:** `Array.isArray` to pick the loop, `for await` to drain the
async case completely, and the callback strictly after.

## ex5 — the generator stage

**What it tested:** that `pipeline()` takes an async generator function as a
stage, and that `for await` gives you sequencing, ordering and cancellation
without any bookkeeping of your own.

**The classic mistake:** starting everything and collecting afterwards —
mapping the source into an array of promises and then yielding them. It is
subtly wrong three ways: it is an unbounded fan-out, the rejection arrives long
after the source has been fully drained, and by then the "stop consuming"
guarantee is worthless because there was nothing left to consume.

**Model answer:** `for await (const item of source) yield await fn(item);` —
and the sentence that earns the point is *why* the order is free, not that it is.

## ex6 — a stream is consumed by reading it

**What it tested:** that fan-out is not a thing streams do natively. Two
consumers of one readable share the data; they do not each get all of it.

**The classic mistake:** `source.pipe(a); source.pipe(b)` — which actually does
work for the simple case, because `pipe` broadcasts, and then fails the moment
one sink is slower than the other, since `pipe` pauses the source for the
slowest and no longer tells you which sink that was. Worse is the teardown: a
failing sink leaves the source and the other sink open for ever.

**Model answer:** a `PassThrough` per sink, one `pipeline()` per branch, and a
`Promise.all` whose catch destroys everything — with a placeholder `.catch()` on
each promise first, because teardown makes all of them reject.

## ex7 — the slot is freed by the head, not by the winner

**What it tested:** the only genuinely hard idea in the set. Concurrency and
ordering are both about *which promise you wait on*, and it is the same lever
for both.

**The classic mistake:** freeing the slot when any worker finishes — `Promise.
race` over the in-flight set. That gives you the limit and destroys the order,
and the resulting bug is invisible until a slow item happens to be followed by a
fast one, which is to say: in production, once. Emitting on completion instead
of on retirement is the same mistake spelled differently.

**Model answer:** a FIFO of started promises; when the queue reaches `limit`,
await `queue[0]`, push its value, shift it off, and only then call the callback —
so the callback count is the in-flight count and the queue order is the output
order.

## ex8 — lazily, once, and closed afterwards

**What it tested:** three separate lifecycle rules at once — open per key rather
than per item, end every sink and wait for `finish` before resolving, and
destroy rather than end when anything fails.

**The classic mistake:** resolving when the source runs out. `end()` says "no
more data", not "the data is on the disk", so the caller reads the file, finds
it short, and files a bug about lost records. Second: opening a sink per item,
which is fine in a test with three rows and produces four million files in
production. Third: ending sinks on the failure path, which turns a crashed
export into a set of files that all look complete.

**Model answer:** a `Map` for the routing table, one `finished()` promise per
sink collected as it opens, `allSettled` at the end so the first real error wins
over the teardown noise — and `destroy()`, not `end()`, when anything goes wrong.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: Implementing a Transform stream](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#implementing-a-transform-stream) — `_transform`, `_flush`, and the exact meaning of the callback's two arguments.
- [Node.js: `stream.pipeline()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinesource-transforms-destination-callback) — what counts as a stage, including the async generator form ex5 uses, and what it destroys on failure.
- [Node.js: `stream.finished()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streamfinishedstream-options) — the difference between a stream being ended and a stream being finished, which is the whole of ex8.
- [Node.js: Streams in object mode](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#object-mode) — why every stage in this set sets `objectMode: true` and what changes when you do.
- [MDN: `for await...of`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — the loop ex5 and ex8 are built on, and what it does to the iterator when the body throws.

## Problem 1 — map

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createMapStage(fn)` is an object-mode `Transform` that
pushes `fn(item)` for every item. A throw inside `fn` must fail the **stream** —
it may never escape as an uncaught exception.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new Transform({ objectMode: true, transform(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.
The callback takes an error first and a value second, so
`callback(null, value)` pushes and moves on in one line.

## Hint 2

The whole exercise is the `try`/`catch`. `transform()` is called by the stream
machinery, not by you, so a throw does not travel up to whoever called
`pipeline()` — it becomes an uncaught exception on a later tick, which no
`.catch()` anywhere can see and which ends the process.

Wrap the call to `fn`, and hand the error to the callback instead. Then
`pipeline()` rejects with it, the chain is torn down, and the caller finds out.

## Hint 1

`new Transform({ objectMode: true, transform(chunk, encoding, callback) { ... } })`.

The whole exercise is the `try`/`catch`. `transform()` is called by the stream
machinery, not by you, so a throw does not travel up to whoever called
`pipeline()` — it becomes an uncaught exception on a later tick, which no
`.catch()` anywhere can see and which ends the process.

Wrap the call to `fn`, and hand the error to the callback instead. Then
`pipeline()` rejects with it, the chain is torn down, and the caller finds out.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One array in the closure. `transform` appends to it and pushes it on only when
it is full; `flush` is where the leftovers go.

`flush(callback)` is the second option a `Transform` takes. It runs once, after
the last chunk and before the stream ends, and it is the only place a stage gets
a last word.

## Hint 2

Two details decide whether this is right.

After pushing a full batch, start a **new** array rather than emptying the one
you just pushed — downstream now owns that array, and `batch.length = 0` would
empty it under their feet.

In `flush`, push only if there is something to push. Without that guard an input
whose length divides exactly by `size` ends with a stray `[]`, and every
consumer downstream grows an `if (batch.length)` to work around your bug.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One array in the closure. `transform` appends to it and pushes it on only when
it is full; `flush` is where the leftovers go.

`flush(callback)` is the second option a `Transform` takes. It runs once, after
the last chunk and before the stream ends, and it is the only place a stage gets
a last word.

## Hint 2

Two details decide whether this is right.

After pushing a full batch, start a **new** array rather than emptying the one
you just pushed — downstream now owns that array, and `batch.length = 0` would
empty it under their feet.

In `flush`, push only if there is something to push. Without that guard an input
whose length divides exactly by `size` ends with a stray `[]`, and every
consumer downstream grows an `if (batch.length)` to work around your bug.

## Problem 5 — a stage that is just a function

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `asyncMapStage(fn)` returns an **async generator stage**
you can drop straight into `pipeline()`. It awaits `fn` per item, one at a time,
yields in input order, and on a rejection stops pulling from the source.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`pipeline()` accepts three kinds of middle stage: a `Transform`, a duplex, and
an **async generator function** taking the source as its only argument. So the
whole answer is a function that returns another function — and the inner one is
`async function*`.

## Hint 2

Four lines: `for await (const item of source) { yield await fn(item); }`.

Read what that buys you. The `await` inside the loop means the next item is not
pulled until this one has been handed downstream, so the order is the input
order without any bookkeeping, and only one call to `fn` is ever outstanding.

The failure behaviour is free too: when `fn` rejects, the `for await` loop
unwinds, the generator ends, `pipeline()` rejects, and the source stops being
pulled. Compare that with collecting promises in an array first, where a
rejection arrives long after the source has been drained.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`pipeline()` accepts three kinds of middle stage: a `Transform`, a duplex, and
an **async generator function** taking the source as its only argument. So the
whole answer is a function that returns another function — and the inner one is
`async function*`.

## Hint 2

Four lines: `for await (const item of source) { yield await fn(item); }`.

Read what that buys you. The `await` inside the loop means the next item is not
pulled until this one has been handed downstream, so the order is the input
order without any bookkeeping, and only one call to `fn` is ever outstanding.

The failure behaviour is free too: when `fn` rejects, the `for await` loop
unwinds, the generator ends, `pipeline()` rejects, and the source stops being
pulled. Compare that with collecting promises in an array first, where a
rejection arrives long after the source has been drained.

## Problem 6 — one source, several destinations

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `tee(source, sinks)` sends every item to every sink and
resolves when all of them have finished. If any sink fails it rejects with that
error and destroys the source and every other sink.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot pipe one readable into two sinks and expect both to see everything —
reading a stream consumes it, so the two would race for chunks. Give each sink
its own `PassThrough` branch, wire branch to sink with `pipeline()`, and write
each chunk into every branch yourself.

## Hint 2

Three promises to keep track of: the pump (a `for await` over the source that
writes into every branch and ends them all at the end) and one `pipeline()` per
branch. `Promise.all` over the lot gives you both "all finished" and "the first
failure", which are exactly the two outcomes you owe the caller.

The teardown is the part reviewers look for: on any failure, destroy the source,
the branches and every sink — including the ones that were behaving. A sink left
open holds its file handle, and a half-written file that was never destroyed
looks complete to whatever reads it next.

Attach a no-op `.catch()` to every one of those promises before you await them
together. When the teardown destroys a stream its `pipeline()` rejects too, and
without a handler that becomes an unhandled rejection warning on the way out.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You cannot pipe one readable into two sinks and expect both to see everything —
reading a stream consumes it, so the two would race for chunks. Give each sink
its own `PassThrough` branch, wire branch to sink with `pipeline()`, and write
each chunk into every branch yourself.

## Hint 2

Three promises to keep track of: the pump (a `for await` over the source that
writes into every branch and ends them all at the end) and one `pipeline()` per
branch. `Promise.all` over the lot gives you both "all finished" and "the first
failure", which are exactly the two outcomes you owe the caller.

The teardown is the part reviewers look for: on any failure, destroy the source,
the branches and every sink — including the ones that were behaving. A sink left
open holds its file handle, and a half-written file that was never destroyed
looks complete to whatever reads it next.

Attach a no-op `.catch()` to every one of those promises before you await them
together. When the teardown destroys a stream its `pipeline()` rejects too, and
without a handler that becomes an unhandled rejection warning on the way out.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — one stream in, many files out

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `partitionTo(source, keyOf, openSink)` routes each item
to the sink its key names, calling `openSink(key)` at most **once per key**. It
ends every sink when the source runs out and resolves with the per-key counts;
on any failure it destroys them all and rejects.

```
uv run dojo test node d16_transform_pipeline ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Map` from key to sink is the whole routing table. `for await` over the
source, compute the key, look it up, and open one only when the lookup misses —
`openSink` is creating a file, so calling it per item rather than per key is how
a partitioned export produces four million of them.

## Hint 2

Ending is not finishing. `sink.end()` says "no more data"; the bytes are not
necessarily on the disk until the stream emits `finish`. `finished(sink)` from
`node:stream/promises` gives you a promise for that moment — collect one per
sink as you open it, and await them all before you resolve.

## Hint 3

The failure path is what makes this an ex8. Three things can go wrong: the
source can fail, a sink can fail, and `keyOf` can throw. All three have to end
the same way — every sink **destroyed** rather than ended, the source destroyed,
and the first error thrown.

A sink failing while you are still reading the source is the awkward one,
because you are not awaiting anything at that moment. Attach a handler to each
`finished()` promise when you create it, have it record the failure and destroy
everything, and check that flag as you loop.

`Promise.allSettled` rather than `Promise.all` at the end: on the failure path
several of those promises have rejected, and you want the first real error, not
a race between teardown errors. Which of the three failures deserves to be the
one reported when two arrive together is a decision the gate leaves to you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `Map` from key to sink is the whole routing table. `for await` over the
source, compute the key, look it up, and open one only when the lookup misses —
`openSink` is creating a file, so calling it per item rather than per key is how
a partitioned export produces four million of them.

## Hint 2

Ending is not finishing. `sink.end()` says "no more data"; the bytes are not
necessarily on the disk until the stream emits `finish`. `finished(sink)` from
`node:stream/promises` gives you a promise for that moment — collect one per
sink as you open it, and await them all before you resolve.

## Hint 3

The failure path is what makes this an ex8. Three things can go wrong: the
source can fail, a sink can fail, and `keyOf` can throw. All three have to end
the same way — every sink **destroyed** rather than ended, the source destroyed,
and the first error thrown.

A sink failing while you are still reading the source is the awkward one,
because you are not awaiting anything at that moment. Attach a handler to each
`finished()` promise when you create it, have it record the failure and destroy
everything, and check that flag as you loop.

`Promise.allSettled` rather than `Promise.all` at the end: on the failure path
several of those promises have rejected, and you want the first real error, not
a race between teardown errors. Which of the three failures deserves to be the
one reported when two arrive together is a decision the gate leaves to you.

lessons.briefing:
# d17 — Backpressure

Eight problems on the one question a stream exists to answer: **how do I stop
the fast end from burying the slow end?** Lessons **06_buffers_streams** and
**07_streams_2** taught the mechanism — `write()` returns false, `drain` says
carry on. This set drills the decisions built on top of it: producing only on
demand, dropping on purpose, cancelling a write that is stuck, batching the wait
instead of wasting it, and spreading work across consumers by how far behind
they are.

Nothing here is graded by timing. Every sink in the gate holds its write
callbacks until the gate releases them by hand, and every claim is about
`writableLength`, `readableLength`, or a count of units of work that were
started. If a solution buffers when it should have waited, the number says so.

## Problem 1 — the primitive under every writer

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `writeAndWait(writable, chunk)` writes one chunk and
resolves when it is safe to write another: at once if `write()` returned true,
on `drain` if it returned false. It rejects if the stream fails while you are
waiting, and leaves **no** listeners behind on any path.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a source that waits to be asked

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createDemandSource(items, highWaterMark)` is an
object-mode `Readable` that produces items only as its consumer takes them, and
never runs more than `highWaterMark` ahead. It also answers `produced()`.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex2
```

## Problem 3 — dropping, on purpose

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createLossySink({ capacity })` is a `Writable` that
never asks its writer to slow down. It keeps the newest `capacity` items,
discards the oldest to make room, and answers `items()` and `dropped()`.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex3
```

## Problem 4 — async work in the middle

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createAsyncStage(fn, { highWaterMark })` is an
object-mode `Transform` that awaits `fn` per item. Only one call to `fn` may be
outstanding, and the source must not be drained into the stage while it waits.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex4
```

## Problem 5 — pause high, resume low

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `pumpWithHysteresis(source, sink, { pauseAbove,
resumeBelow })` pauses the source when the sink holds more than `pauseAbove` and
resumes it once it is back below `resumeBelow`. It resolves with `{ written,
maxBuffered, pauses }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex5
```

## Problem 6 — a writer you can call off

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `writeAllOrAbort(writable, chunks, signal)` writes
everything in order, honouring backpressure, until the signal aborts — then
rejects with `signal.reason` **without** waiting for the drain that may never
come. An already-aborted signal writes nothing at all, and the abort listener is
removed on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex6
```

## Problem 7 — spend the waiting time collecting

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createBatchingWriter(sink, { maxBatch })` returns
`{ write, end }`. Items arriving while the sink is busy are collected and sent
as **one** array write when it comes free, never more than `maxBatch` at a time.
`end()` flushes the remainder, ends the sink, and resolves once it has all
landed.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex7
```

## Problem 8 — send the work where there is room

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `balanceAcross(source, sinks)` routes each chunk to
whichever sink currently has the smallest `writableLength`, waits when every
sink is at its own `highWaterMark` rather than buffering, ends them all, and
resolves with the per-sink counts.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex8
```

# Reading - node/d17_backpressure

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **making the fast end wait**. Node gives you exactly
three levers and no more: the boolean `write()` returns, the moment you call a
`_read` or a transform callback, and `pause()`/`resume()`. Everything in this
set is one of those three, and every wrong answer is the same wrong answer —
accepting work you are not ready for, so that the queue moves from somewhere
visible into your own process. That is why none of these problems is graded by
how long anything took. `writableLength` and "how many were started" are the
measurements that matter, because the symptom of getting this wrong is never
slowness; it is a heap that grows until the process dies, on the one day the
consumer is slower than usual. The other thread running through the set is that
waiting has to be cancellable and observable: a wait with no error listener is a
hang, and a hang is worse than a crash.

## ex1 — true does not mean written

**What it tested:** the meaning of the return value, which almost everybody gets
half right. `true` means *there is room for more*, not *this chunk has been
written* — the gate's sink is still holding the chunk when the promise resolves.

**The classic mistake:** ignoring the boolean entirely, which is the bug the
whole lesson exists for. After that, the subtler one: listening for `drain` and
nothing else. A stream that errors or is destroyed never emits `drain`, so the
promise is never settled, and an upload hangs for ever with nothing in the logs
— which is strictly worse than the crash it replaced.

**Model answer:** resolve on the fast path with no listeners at all, and on the
slow path attach `drain`, `error` and `close` with one shared cleanup, because
`once()` only removes the listener that actually fired.

## ex2 — _read means "I have room"

**What it tested:** which direction `_read()` points. It is not "produce your
data"; it is the stream asking, and Node stops asking when its buffer is full.

**The classic mistake:** looping inside `_read` and pushing everything. The
right items come out in the right order and the test passes — and the entire
input is now in the stream's buffer, so you have written a very elaborate array.
The gate measures it directly: produced minus consumed has to stay inside the
highWaterMark.

**Model answer:** push one item per call and return. Doing so means you never
have to look at what `push()` returns, which is the same conversation running in
the other direction.

## ex3 — losing data is a design, not a failure

**What it tested:** that backpressure is a choice with an alternative, and that
the alternative is legitimate. Metrics, traces and access logs should never
stall a request path; the right answer there is to drop.

**The classic mistake:** a "lossy" sink that still buffers — capping the array
but letting the stream's own queue grow, so the memory you were worried about
just moved one layer down. Second: dropping the newest instead of the oldest
without deciding to. Both ends are defensible, and the recent end is usually
worth more, but it has to be a decision somebody made.

**Model answer:** call the write callback synchronously, so `write()` never
returns false, and keep a bounded array with an honest `dropped()` counter — a
drop nobody can count is a drop nobody knows about.

## ex4 — the callback is the throttle

**What it tested:** that the transform callback is a backpressure signal and not
a formality. The number of chunks in flight is exactly the number of callbacks
you have called without finishing the work.

**The classic mistake:** `fn(chunk).then((v) => this.push(v)); callback();`. It
produces correct output in correct order, which is why it survives review. It
also announces that you are ready for the next chunk before you have started
this one, so the whole source pours through: every item in flight at once
against whatever `fn` talks to, and the entire input in memory behind it.

**Model answer:** call the callback inside the `then`, pass a rejection to it as
an error, and let `highWaterMark` decide how many may queue in front of you.

## ex5 — one threshold flaps, two do not

**What it tested:** `pause()` and `resume()`, and the fact that there is no
event for "the buffer got a bit smaller".

**The classic mistake:** resuming on `drain`. `drain` fires only when the buffer
is completely empty, which is not what `resumeBelow` asked for, and on a busy
sink it may not fire for a long time. The other one is pausing and resuming at
the same number, which flaps once per chunk — and a pause is not free.

**Model answer:** the per-chunk write callback, `sink.write(chunk, cb)`, is the
hook that fires exactly when the length has just gone down; check the resume
threshold there and the pause threshold after each write.

## ex6 — cancelling a wait, not just a loop

**What it tested:** that "abortable" has two halves. Stop starting new work, and
stop waiting for work already started — and an implementation can do the first
and still hang for ever.

**The classic mistake:** checking `signal.aborted` only between chunks. The
moment the sink stalls you are parked on a `drain` that is never coming, and the
signal is checked again only after it arrives. Nearly as common: creating the
abort listener inside the loop, so a thousand-chunk write attaches a thousand
listeners and Node starts warning at eleven.

**Model answer:** one abort promise created before the loop, raced against every
drain wait, with a placeholder `.catch()` so an abort on the happy path is not
an unhandled rejection — and `removeEventListener` in a `finally`.

## ex7 — the wait is free capacity

**What it tested:** that a sink being busy is not dead time. Items arriving
during it can be collected and sent as one write, which is how log shippers and
bulk inserts get their throughput.

**The classic mistake:** no cap. A long stall collects everything, and the
"batch" that eventually goes out is the whole backlog in one object — you have
moved the unbounded buffer from the sink into your own array and called it a
feature. Second: resolving `end()` when the last write callback fires rather
than when the sink emits `finish`, so the final batch is still in flight when
the caller thinks it is done.

**Model answer:** one `flush()` reading `busy`, `pending` and `ended`, called
from both `write()` and the write callback, with `splice(0, maxBatch)` doing the
capping and `sink.end(cb)` settling the promise.

## ex8 — measure the consumers, do not schedule them

**What it tested:** that `writableLength` is readable at any moment, and that
this makes adaptive routing about three lines long.

**The classic mistake:** round-robin. It hands the stalled consumer exactly as
much as the healthy one, so one slow sink slows everything to its own pace and
the backlog is invisible until it is a memory graph. The second mistake is
writing to a saturated set anyway rather than awaiting — which is the one the
gate catches by holding both sinks and checking the source was barely read.

**Model answer:** pick the smallest `writableLength`; when every sink is at its
own `writableHighWaterMark`, await the first `drain` from any of them with a
cleanup that removes all the listeners — and let the `for await` loop's
suspension carry the backpressure back up to the source.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `writable.write()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#writablewritechunk-encoding-callback) — the return value, the per-chunk callback ex5 and ex7 are built on, and when `drain` is emitted.
- [Node.js: Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the guide that walks through what happens when you ignore all of this.
- [Node.js: `readable._read()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readable_readsize) — who calls it, when it stops being called, and what `push()` returning false means.
- [Node.js: `stream.Writable` class](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#class-streamwritable) — `writableLength`, `writableHighWaterMark` and `writableEnded`, the three properties this whole set is graded on.
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) — `aborted`, `reason`, and `AbortSignal.abort()` for the already-cancelled case in ex6.

a formality. The number of chunks in flight is exactly the number of callbacks
you have called without finishing the work.

**The classic mistake:** `fn(chunk).then((v) => this.push(v)); callback();`. It
produces correct output in correct order, which is why it survives review. It
also announces that you are ready for the next chunk before you have started
this one, so the whole source pours through: every item in flight at once
against whatever `fn` talks to, and the entire input in memory behind it.

**Model answer:** call the callback inside the `then`, pass a rejection to it as
an error, and let `highWaterMark` decide how many may queue in front of you.

## ex5 — one threshold flaps, two do not

**What it tested:** `pause()` and `resume()`, and the fact that there is no
event for "the buffer got a bit smaller".

**The classic mistake:** resuming on `drain`. `drain` fires only when the buffer
is completely empty, which is not what `resumeBelow` asked for, and on a busy
sink it may not fire for a long time. The other one is pausing and resuming at
the same number, which flaps once per chunk — and a pause is not free.

**Model answer:** the per-chunk write callback, `sink.write(chunk, cb)`, is the
hook that fires exactly when the length has just gone down; check the resume
threshold there and the pause threshold after each write.

## ex6 — cancelling a wait, not just a loop

**What it tested:** that "abortable" has two halves. Stop starting new work, and
stop waiting for work already started — and an implementation can do the first
and still hang for ever.

**The classic mistake:** checking `signal.aborted` only between chunks. The
moment the sink stalls you are parked on a `drain` that is never coming, and the
signal is checked again only after it arrives. Nearly as common: creating the
abort listener inside the loop, so a thousand-chunk write attaches a thousand
listeners and Node starts warning at eleven.

**Model answer:** one abort promise created before the loop, raced against every
drain wait, with a placeholder `.catch()` so an abort on the happy path is not
an unhandled rejection — and `removeEventListener` in a `finally`.

## ex7 — the wait is free capacity

**What it tested:** that a sink being busy is not dead time. Items arriving
during it can be collected and sent as one write, which is how log shippers and
bulk inserts get their throughput.

**The classic mistake:** no cap. A long stall collects everything, and the
"batch" that eventually goes out is the whole backlog in one object — you have
moved the unbounded buffer from the sink into your own array and called it a
feature. Second: resolving `end()` when the last write callback fires rather
than when the sink emits `finish`, so the final batch is still in flight when
the caller thinks it is done.

**Model answer:** one `flush()` reading `busy`, `pending` and `ended`, called
from both `write()` and the write callback, with `splice(0, maxBatch)` doing the
capping and `sink.end(cb)` settling the promise.

## ex8 — measure the consumers, do not schedule them

**What it tested:** that `writableLength` is readable at any moment, and that
this makes adaptive routing about three lines long.

**The classic mistake:** round-robin. It hands the stalled consumer exactly as
much as the healthy one, so one slow sink slows everything to its own pace and
the backlog is invisible until it is a memory graph. The second mistake is
writing to a saturated set anyway rather than awaiting — which is the one the
gate catches by holding both sinks and checking the source was barely read.

**Model answer:** pick the smallest `writableLength`; when every sink is at its
own `writableHighWaterMark`, await the first `drain` from any of them with a
cleanup that removes all the listeners — and let the `for await` loop's
suspension carry the backpressure back up to the source.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `writable.write()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#writablewritechunk-encoding-callback) — the return value, the per-chunk callback ex5 and ex7 are built on, and when `drain` is emitted.
- [Node.js: Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams) — the guide that walks through what happens when you ignore all of this.
- [Node.js: `readable._read()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#readable_readsize) — who calls it, when it stops being called, and what `push()` returning false means.
- [Node.js: `stream.Writable` class](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#class-streamwritable) — `writableLength`, `writableHighWaterMark` and `writableEnded`, the three properties this whole set is graded on.
- [MDN: `AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal) — `aborted`, `reason`, and `AbortSignal.abort()` for the already-cancelled case in ex6.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — the primitive under every writer

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `writeAndWait(writable, chunk)` writes one chunk and
resolves when it is safe to write another: at once if `write()` returned true,
on `drain` if it returned false. It rejects if the stream fails while you are
waiting, and leaves **no** listeners behind on any path.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean, and it is the only thing a stream
ever tells you about how full it is. `true` means there is room — resolve
immediately, and do not attach a single listener. `false` means the buffer is at
or over its `highWaterMark`, and the stream will emit `drain` when it has
emptied.

Note what `true` does **not** mean: it does not mean the chunk was written. The
sink in the gate is still holding that chunk when the promise resolves.

## Hint 2

The `false` branch is a promise around one event, and the whole exercise is the
paths you have to cover besides the happy one. A stream that errors, or is
destroyed, will never emit `drain` — so a promise that only listens for `drain`
is a promise that is never settled, and an upload that hangs for ever with
nothing in the logs.

Listen for `error` (and `close`) alongside it, and remove **all** of them from a
single cleanup function whichever one fires. `once()` removes only the listener
that fired; the other two are still attached, and one leaked listener per chunk
is a `MaxListenersExceededWarning` a few thousand chunks later.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean, and it is the only thing a stream
ever tells you about how full it is. `true` means there is room — resolve
immediately, and do not attach a single listener. `false` means the buffer is at
or over its `highWaterMark`, and the stream will emit `drain` when it has
emptied.

Note what `true` does **not** mean: it does not mean the chunk was written. The
sink in the gate is still holding that chunk when the promise resolves.

## Hint 2

The `false` branch is a promise around one event, and the whole exercise is the
paths you have to cover besides the happy one. A stream that errors, or is
destroyed, will never emit `drain` — so a promise that only listens for `drain`
is a promise that is never settled, and an upload that hangs for ever with
nothing in the logs.

Listen for `error` (and `close`) alongside it, and remove **all** of them from a
single cleanup function whichever one fires. `once()` removes only the listener
that fired; the other two are still attached, and one leaked listener per chunk
is a `MaxListenersExceededWarning` a few thousand chunks later.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`_read()` is not "produce your data". It is the stream saying *I have room for
more* — Node calls it only while the internal buffer is below the
`highWaterMark`, and stops calling it when the buffer is full.

So the shape is: one item per call, then return. `push(null)` when there is
nothing left.

## Hint 2

The tempting version loops inside `_read` and pushes everything it has. It
works, in the sense that the right items come out in the right order — and it
has bought you nothing at all, because the entire input is now sitting in the
stream's buffer. That is the assertion in the gate: the number produced minus
the number consumed must stay inside the highWaterMark.

`push()` returns a boolean of its own, and it is the same conversation in the
other direction: `false` means the buffer is full and you should stop pushing
until `_read` is called again. Pushing one item per call means you never have to
look at it, which is why it is the shape everybody should start from.

## Problem 3 — dropping, on purpose

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createLossySink({ capacity })` is a `Writable` that
never asks its writer to slow down. It keeps the newest `capacity` items,

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Backpressure comes from one place: how long you take to call the write
callback. A sink that calls it synchronously never lets its own queue build up,
so `write()` keeps returning true and the writer is never slowed down.

The bounded array is then just an array: push, and while it is over capacity,
`shift()` and count.

## Hint 2

Notice which end you drop from. Dropping the **oldest** keeps the most recent
data, which is what you want for metrics, traces and logs — the last thing that
happened before the incident is worth more than the first. Dropping the newest
is also a valid policy, and it is the one you want when the early data is a
handshake; the point is that it is a decision somebody made rather than an
accident of where the buffer overflowed.

Hand out a copy from `items()`. If a caller can mutate the array you are using
as your buffer, your sink has no control over its own contents.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Backpressure comes from one place: how long you take to call the write
callback. A sink that calls it synchronously never lets its own queue build up,
so `write()` keeps returning true and the writer is never slowed down.

The bounded array is then just an array: push, and while it is over capacity,
`shift()` and count.

## Hint 2

Notice which end you drop from. Dropping the **oldest** keeps the most recent
data, which is what you want for metrics, traces and logs — the last thing that
happened before the incident is worth more than the first. Dropping the newest
is also a valid policy, and it is the one you want when the early data is a
handshake; the point is that it is a decision somebody made rather than an
accident of where the buffer overflowed.

Hand out a copy from `items()`. If a caller can mutate the array you are using
as your buffer, your sink has no control over its own contents.

## Problem 4 — async work in the middle

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createAsyncStage(fn, { highWaterMark })` is an
object-mode `Transform` that awaits `fn` per item. Only one call to `fn` may be
outstanding, and the source must not be drained into the stage while it waits.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The transform callback means "send me another chunk". So the number of chunks
in flight is exactly the number of times you have called it without finishing
the work — which makes *when* you call it the only backpressure control the
stage has.

## Hint 2

The bug this is built around looks like this:

```ts
transform(chunk, _encoding, callback) {
  fn(chunk).then((value) => this.push(value));
  callback();                                   // <- says "ready for more"
}
```

It works. The right values come out in the right order. And it has told the
stream it is ready for the next chunk before it has done anything with this one,
so the entire source pours through and every item is in flight at once — an
unbounded fan-out onto whatever `fn` talks to, plus the whole input in memory.

Move the callback inside the `then`, and hand a rejection to it as an error. The
gate measures the difference by counting how much the source produced.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The transform callback means "send me another chunk". So the number of chunks
in flight is exactly the number of times you have called it without finishing
the work — which makes *when* you call it the only backpressure control the
stage has.

## Hint 2

The bug this is built around looks like this:

```ts
transform(chunk, _encoding, callback) {
  fn(chunk).then((value) => this.push(value));
  callback();                                   // <- says "ready for more"
}
```

It works. The right values come out in the right order. And it has told the
stream it is ready for the next chunk before it has done anything with this one,
so the entire source pours through and every item is in flight at once — an
unbounded fan-out onto whatever `fn` talks to, plus the whole input in memory.

Move the callback inside the `then`, and hand a rejection to it as an error. The
gate measures the difference by counting how much the source produced.

## Problem 6 — a writer you can call off

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `writeAllOrAbort(writable, chunks, signal)` writes
everything in order, honouring backpressure, until the signal aborts — then
rejects with `signal.reason` **without** waiting for the drain that may never
come. An already-aborted signal writes nothing at all, and the abort listener is
removed on every path.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate obligations, and it is easy to satisfy one and not the other.

*Stop starting new work*: check `signal.aborted` at the top of the loop, and
once before the loop — an already-aborted signal must not write even the first
chunk.

*Stop waiting*: the `await` for a drain has to lose a race against the abort.
Waiting for a sink that has stopped moving is exactly the case cancellation
exists for, so a version that only checks the flag between chunks still hangs
for ever on a stalled upload.

## Hint 2

Build one promise that rejects with `signal.reason` when the `abort` event
fires, and race the drain wait against it. Create it once, outside the loop —
one listener per call, not one per chunk.

Give it a no-op `.catch()` as soon as you make it. On the happy path nobody ever
awaits that promise, and an abort arriving after the writes are done would
otherwise be reported as an unhandled rejection.

Remove the listener in a `finally`, so it goes on the abort path, the error path
and the success path alike. A long-lived signal — a request signal shared by
twenty helpers — collects one listener per call otherwise, and Node starts
printing `MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two separate obligations, and it is easy to satisfy one and not the other.

*Stop starting new work*: check `signal.aborted` at the top of the loop, and
once before the loop — an already-aborted signal must not write even the first
chunk.

*Stop waiting*: the `await` for a drain has to lose a race against the abort.
Waiting for a sink that has stopped moving is exactly the case cancellation
exists for, so a version that only checks the flag between chunks still hangs
for ever on a stalled upload.

## Hint 2

Build one promise that rejects with `signal.reason` when the `abort` event
fires, and race the drain wait against it. Create it once, outside the loop —
one listener per call, not one per chunk.

Give it a no-op `.catch()` as soon as you make it. On the happy path nobody ever
awaits that promise, and an abort arriving after the writes are done would
otherwise be reported as an unhandled rejection.

Remove the listener in a `finally`, so it goes on the abort path, the error path
and the success path alike. A long-lived signal — a request signal shared by
twenty helpers — collects one listener per call otherwise, and Node starts
printing `MaxListenersExceededWarning` at eleven.

## Problem 7 — spend the waiting time collecting

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createBatchingWriter(sink, { maxBatch })` returns
`{ write, end }`. Items arriving while the sink is busy are collected and sent
as **one** array write when it comes free, never more than `maxBatch` at a time.
`end()` flushes the remainder, ends the sink, and resolves once it has all
landed.

```
uv run dojo test node d17_backpressure ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces of state: an array of items not yet sent, a `busy` flag, and an
`ended` flag. One function — call it `flush` — reads all three and decides what
to do, and both `write()` and the sink's write callback simply call it.

## Hint 2

`flush` has exactly three cases, in this order:

- busy → do nothing, the callback will come round again;
- nothing pending → if `end()` has been called, end the sink; otherwise nothing;
- otherwise → `splice(0, maxBatch)` off the front, mark busy, and write that
  array with a callback that clears busy and calls `flush` again.

The `splice` is what enforces the cap. Without it a long stall turns into a
single enormous batch, which is the failure this design was supposed to avoid —
you have moved the unbounded buffer from the sink into your own array.

## Hint 3

`end()` is not "stop". It is "no more items are coming", and it has to return a
promise that stays pending until the remainder has been flushed **and** the sink
has finished. Note that `sink.end(callback)` fires on `finish`, which is later
than the last write callback — resolving any earlier is how the final batch
never reaches the disk.

The decision left to you is what `write()` should do after `end()`. Throwing,
ignoring, and quietly accepting are all defensible; a reviewer will ask which
one you chose.

lessons.briefing:
# d18 — HTTP without a framework

Eight problems on `node:http`, drawn from lesson **08_http_core**. That lesson
taught you to route, read a query string, bound a body and answer a conditional
GET. This set is the layer underneath all of it: the parts of HTTP that a
framework normally hides, and that you end up implementing anyway the first time
a client asks for something the framework did not anticipate.

No express here — `http.createServer`, `IncomingMessage`, `ServerResponse` and
`URL`, nothing else. Every problem exports a factory so the gate gets a fresh
handler with fresh state, and supertest is handed that handler directly, so
nothing binds a port.

## Problem 1 — the same resource, in the type the client can read

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` serves `GET /report` as
`application/json` or `text/plain`, chosen from `Accept` — including `*/*`,
`text/*` and `q=` weights, where `q=0` is a refusal. Every response carries
`Vary: Accept`; nothing acceptable is a 406 naming what was offered.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a GET with the body left off

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` answers `GET /status` with a JSON
document and `HEAD /status` with the same status and the same headers —
including an accurate `content-length` — and no body. An unknown path is a 404
on both, with a content-length too.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex2
```

## Problem 3 — cookies, by hand

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` parses the `Cookie` header on
`GET /session` into `{ cookies: {...} }` (percent-decoded values, split at the
first `=`, malformed pairs dropped), and on `POST /session` sets **two** cookies
on one response: `sid=s-N; Path=/; HttpOnly; Max-Age=3600` and
`theme=dark; Path=/; Max-Age=86400`. Ids count from `s-1`.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex3
```

## Problem 4 — send the bytes that were asked for

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` serves the ten bytes `0123456789` at
`/clip.txt` with `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, and honours `Range`: 206 with an
inclusive `Content-Range` for `bytes=2-5`, `bytes=-4` and `bytes=6-`; an end
past the last byte is clamped; a start past the end is 416 with
`Content-Range: bytes */10`; an unrecognised unit is ignored.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex4
```

## Problem 5 — moving a client without losing what it carried

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` sends 301 for `/old-report`, 308 for
the trailing-slash spelling `/reports/quarterly/`, and 302 for the alias
`/latest` — all to `/reports/quarterly`, all keeping the query string, all with
a `Location` built using `URL`. The canonical path answers 200 and does not
redirect to itself.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex5
```

## Problem 6 — the write that refuses to lose an update

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` returns an ETag from `GET /config`.
`PUT /config` requires `If-Match`: a matching one (or `*`) writes and issues a
new ETag, a stale one is **412** and changes nothing, a missing one is **428**,
and a body that will not parse is 400.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex6
```

## Problem 7 — serving a directory, and only that directory

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createStaticServer(root)` serves files from `root`:
content-type from the extension, `application/octet-stream` for one you do not
know, 404 for a missing file **or a directory**, 405 with `Allow: GET, HEAD` for
any other method, and 403 for a path that resolves outside `root` — including
the percent-encoded `..%2f` form that the client never gets a chance to
normalise away.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex7
```

## Problem 8 — a response that is still being written

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createEventStream(source)` streams an injected
`AsyncIterable<SseEvent>` from `GET /events` as server-sent events:
`content-type: text/event-stream`, `cache-control: no-cache`, no
`content-length`, one `id:`/`event:`/`data:` block per event terminated by a
blank line, multi-line data split across several `data:` lines, and the response
ended when the source ends. A source that throws reports an `error` event and
ends.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d18_http_raw

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **reading the request headers you did not ask for**.
A framework answers `Accept`, `Range`, `If-Match`, `Cookie` and `HEAD` on your
behalf, or quietly does not, and either way you find out at the worst possible
moment. Every problem here follows the same shape: a request header carries a
condition, the handler has to decide what that condition means, and the answer
is a status code that is not 200. The status codes are the content — 406, 412,
416, 428, 405, 206, 301, 308 — because picking the right one is what makes a
client able to recover on its own instead of retrying forever. The other thread
running through the set is that a response is a decision made *before* the first
byte leaves: once the headers are out, the status, the content-type and the
length are all fixed, which is why ex8 has to report a failure inside the body
it is already sending.

## ex1 — content negotiation is a weighted vote

**What it tested:** parsing a structured header into data before deciding
anything, and the two rules of `Accept` that everybody skips: wildcards match,
and `q` is a weight.

**The classic mistake:** `req.headers.accept.includes("json")`. It says yes to
`text/plain` from a client that listed `application/json;q=0` — the one type it
told you it could not read — and it has no answer at all for `*/*`. Nearly as
common: omitting `Vary: Accept`, after which a shared cache stores whichever
representation happened to be requested first and serves it to everyone.

**Model answer:** parse into `{ type, quality }` pairs, score each thing you
offer against the list, keep the best with a **strictly greater** comparison so
your own preference order breaks ties, and start the running best at `0` so a
`q=0` can never win.

## ex2 — a HEAD is a promise about a GET

**What it tested:** that HEAD is the same route, the same status and the same
headers as GET, and that `content-length` is a byte count.

**The classic mistake:** `payload.length`. It is right for ASCII and wrong for
every accented character, emoji or CJK glyph, so it survives the whole test
suite and then understates the size of one real document. The structural mistake
is treating HEAD as a separate endpoint, which drifts from the GET the moment
either one changes.

**Model answer:** build status, headers and body once, then branch on the method
at the single line where they differ — and count the body with
`Buffer.byteLength`, not `String.length`.

## ex3 — one header in, one header each out

**What it tested:** the asymmetry of the cookie protocol. Requests carry all
their cookies in one `Cookie` header; responses need a separate `Set-Cookie` per
cookie.

**The classic mistake:** `res.setHeader("set-cookie", ...)` twice, which
replaces rather than appends, so the second cookie is the only one the browser
ever sees — and the missing one is the session, so the symptom is "login works
locally". On the parsing side, `pair.split("=")` on a base64 value throws away
everything after the first padding character.

**Model answer:** split at the first `=` with `indexOf`, decode the value only,
and set both cookies in one call with an array.

## ex4 — ranges are inclusive, and off by one is silent

**What it tested:** three range syntaxes, the clamp, and the difference between
"I cannot satisfy this" and "I do not understand this".

**The classic mistake:** treating `bytes=-4` as "up to byte 4" instead of "the
last 4 bytes" — a suffix range has no start, and reading it as a start of zero
serves the wrong end of the file. The second is answering 416 for an unknown
unit, when the specification says to ignore it and serve the whole thing; the
third is `slice(start, end)`, which is one byte short every single time because
`Content-Range` is inclusive at both ends.

**Model answer:** parse into a three-way result — none, unsatisfiable, or a
concrete `{ start, end }` — before touching the response, so the 200, 206 and
416 branches cannot leak into each other.

## ex5 — the redirect codes mean different things

**What it tested:** that 301, 302 and 308 are three different promises, and that
a redirect must carry the query string forward.

**The classic mistake:** using 301 for everything. A 301 is cached by browsers
more or less permanently, so a temporary alias pinned with a 301 cannot be moved
back; and a 301 historically permits the client to turn a POST into a GET, which
is why 308 exists and why the trailing-slash canonicaliser has to use it.
Dropping the query string is the quieter one — every link keeps working and
silently loses its filters.

**Model answer:** one helper that builds the `Location` from the canonical path
plus `url.search` using `URL`, and a `switch` that picks the code deliberately —
with the canonical path itself answering 200, because a canonicaliser that
cannot recognise its own output is a redirect loop.

## ex6 — the lost update, caught

**What it tested:** optimistic concurrency. Lesson 08 used `If-None-Match` to
avoid *sending* a body the client already had; this uses `If-Match` to avoid
*accepting* a write based on a version that is no longer current.

**The classic mistake:** treating a missing `If-Match` as permission. If the
header is optional, every buggy client skips it and the protection is worth
nothing — which is what 428 Precondition Required exists to say. The other is
returning the *old* ETag after a successful write, so the next writer believes
it is up to date and the whole scheme silently stops working.

**Model answer:** version counter in the closure, ETag as a quoted string built
from it, and the three PUT outcomes checked in order — no header is 428, a
non-matching header is 412 and changes nothing, `*` or a match writes and bumps
the version.

## ex7 — resolve, then judge

**What it tested:** a static file server, which is four decisions — method,
containment, existence, content-type — and one of them is a security boundary.

**The classic mistake:** checking the raw URL for `..` and then decoding. The
client normalises `/../secret.txt` away before it is ever sent, so the attack
that reaches you is `/..%2fsecret.txt`, and any check performed before
`decodeURIComponent` sees nothing wrong with it. The second mistake is
forgetting to strip the leading slash, because `path.resolve(root, "/index.html")`
discards the root entirely.

**Model answer:** decode, strip the leading separators, resolve once against the
root, and ask one question — is `path.relative(root, target)` non-empty,
relative, and not starting with a `..` **segment**.

# Reading - node/d18_http_raw

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **reading the request headers you did not ask for**.
A framework answers `Accept`, `Range`, `If-Match`, `Cookie` and `HEAD` on your
behalf, or quietly does not, and either way you find out at the worst possible
moment. Every problem here follows the same shape: a request header carries a
condition, the handler has to decide what that condition means, and the answer
is a status code that is not 200. The status codes are the content — 406, 412,
416, 428, 405, 206, 301, 308 — because picking the right one is what makes a
client able to recover on its own instead of retrying forever. The other thread
running through the set is that a response is a decision made *before* the first
byte leaves: once the headers are out, the status, the content-type and the
length are all fixed, which is why ex8 has to report a failure inside the body
it is already sending.

## ex1 — content negotiation is a weighted vote

**What it tested:** parsing a structured header into data before deciding
anything, and the two rules of `Accept` that everybody skips: wildcards match,
and `q` is a weight.

**The classic mistake:** `req.headers.accept.includes("json")`. It says yes to
`text/plain` from a client that listed `application/json;q=0` — the one type it
told you it could not read — and it has no answer at all for `*/*`. Nearly as
common: omitting `Vary: Accept`, after which a shared cache stores whichever
representation happened to be requested first and serves it to everyone.

**Model answer:** parse into `{ type, quality }` pairs, score each thing you
offer against the list, keep the best with a **strictly greater** comparison so
your own preference order breaks ties, and start the running best at `0` so a
`q=0` can never win.

## ex2 — a HEAD is a promise about a GET

**What it tested:** that HEAD is the same route, the same status and the same
headers as GET, and that `content-length` is a byte count.

**The classic mistake:** `payload.length`. It is right for ASCII and wrong for
every accented character, emoji or CJK glyph, so it survives the whole test
suite and then understates the size of one real document. The structural mistake
is treating HEAD as a separate endpoint, which drifts from the GET the moment
either one changes.

**Model answer:** build status, headers and body once, then branch on the method
at the single line where they differ — and count the body with
`Buffer.byteLength`, not `String.length`.

## ex3 — one header in, one header each out

**What it tested:** the asymmetry of the cookie protocol. Requests carry all
their cookies in one `Cookie` header; responses need a separate `Set-Cookie` per
cookie.

**The classic mistake:** `res.setHeader("set-cookie", ...)` twice, which
replaces rather than appends, so the second cookie is the only one the browser
ever sees — and the missing one is the session, so the symptom is "login works
locally". On the parsing side, `pair.split("=")` on a base64 value throws away
everything after the first padding character.

**Model answer:** split at the first `=` with `indexOf`, decode the value only,
and set both cookies in one call with an array.

## ex4 — ranges are inclusive, and off by one is silent

**What it tested:** three range syntaxes, the clamp, and the difference between
"I cannot satisfy this" and "I do not understand this".

**The classic mistake:** treating `bytes=-4` as "up to byte 4" instead of "the
last 4 bytes" — a suffix range has no start, and reading it as a start of zero
serves the wrong end of the file. The second is answering 416 for an unknown
unit, when the specification says to ignore it and serve the whole thing; the
third is `slice(start, end)`, which is one byte short every single time because
`Content-Range` is inclusive at both ends.

**Model answer:** parse into a three-way result — none, unsatisfiable, or a
concrete `{ start, end }` — before touching the response, so the 200, 206 and
416 branches cannot leak into each other.

## ex5 — the redirect codes mean different things

**What it tested:** that 301, 302 and 308 are three different promises, and that
a redirect must carry the query string forward.

**The classic mistake:** using 301 for everything. A 301 is cached by browsers
more or less permanently, so a temporary alias pinned with a 301 cannot be moved
back; and a 301 historically permits the client to turn a POST into a GET, which
is why 308 exists and why the trailing-slash canonicaliser has to use it.
Dropping the query string is the quieter one — every link keeps working and
silently loses its filters.

**Model answer:** one helper that builds the `Location` from the canonical path
plus `url.search` using `URL`, and a `switch` that picks the code deliberately —
with the canonical path itself answering 200, because a canonicaliser that
cannot recognise its own output is a redirect loop.

## ex6 — the lost update, caught

**What it tested:** optimistic concurrency. Lesson 08 used `If-None-Match` to
avoid *sending* a body the client already had; this uses `If-Match` to avoid
*accepting* a write based on a version that is no longer current.

**The classic mistake:** treating a missing `If-Match` as permission. If the
header is optional, every buggy client skips it and the protection is worth
nothing — which is what 428 Precondition Required exists to say. The other is
returning the *old* ETag after a successful write, so the next writer believes
it is up to date and the whole scheme silently stops working.

**Model answer:** version counter in the closure, ETag as a quoted string built
from it, and the three PUT outcomes checked in order — no header is 428, a
non-matching header is 412 and changes nothing, `*` or a match writes and bumps
the version.

## ex7 — resolve, then judge

**What it tested:** a static file server, which is four decisions — method,
containment, existence, content-type — and one of them is a security boundary.

**The classic mistake:** checking the raw URL for `..` and then decoding. The
client normalises `/../secret.txt` away before it is ever sent, so the attack
that reaches you is `/..%2fsecret.txt`, and any check performed before
`decodeURIComponent` sees nothing wrong with it. The second mistake is
forgetting to strip the leading slash, because `path.resolve(root, "/index.html")`
discards the root entirely.

**Model answer:** decode, strip the leading separators, resolve once against the
root, and ask one question — is `path.relative(root, target)` non-empty,
relative, and not starting with a `..` **segment**.

`application/json` or `text/plain`, chosen from `Accept` — including `*/*`,
`text/*` and `q=` weights, where `q=0` is a refusal. Every response carries
