exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`req.headers.accept` is one string holding a comma-separated list, and each
entry may carry parameters after a semicolon. Parse it into
`{ type, quality }` pairs first; deciding what to send is easy once you have
that, and impossible while you are still doing `.includes("json")`.

## Hint 2

Score each thing you offer against the parsed list and keep the best. Three
patterns can match one offer — the exact type, `type/*`, and `*/*` — and the
score is the highest `q` among them.

Two details decide four of the assertions. Use a **strictly greater than**
comparison as you walk your offers, so a tie leaves your own first preference
in place. And start the running best at `0`, not at `-1`: `q=0` is the client
saying "not this one", so a type scoring zero must never be chosen, and if
nothing scores above zero the answer is 406.

`Vary: Accept` goes on the response before you know which branch you are taking,
because it is true of all of them.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`req.headers.accept` is one string holding a comma-separated list, and each
entry may carry parameters after a semicolon. Parse it into
`{ type, quality }` pairs first; deciding what to send is easy once you have
that, and impossible while you are still doing `.includes("json")`.

## Hint 2

Score each thing you offer against the parsed list and keep the best. Three
patterns can match one offer — the exact type, `type/*`, and `*/*` — and the
score is the highest `q` among them.

Two details decide four of the assertions. Use a **strictly greater than**
comparison as you walk your offers, so a tie leaves your own first preference
in place. And start the running best at `0`, not at `-1`: `q=0` is the client
saying "not this one", so a type scoring zero must never be chosen, and if
nothing scores above zero the answer is 406.

`Vary: Accept` goes on the response before you know which branch you are taking,
because it is true of all of them.

## Problem 2 — a GET with the body left off

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` answers `GET /status` with a JSON
document and `HEAD /status` with the same status and the same headers —
including an accurate `content-length` — and no body. An unknown path is a 404
on both, with a content-length too.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build the response — status, headers, body string — before you look at
`req.method`. A HEAD is a GET that stops one line early, so the two paths should
share everything up to `res.end()`.

## Hint 2

`content-length` counts bytes. `"café".length` is 4 and
`Buffer.byteLength("café")` is 5, and the payload here has an accented character
in it precisely so that the difference shows up.

Node will suppress a body you write on a HEAD response whether you ask it to or
not, so the assertion that actually fails when you get this wrong is the header
one: if you never set `content-length`, the HEAD answers with no size at all,
which is the only question the client was asking.

Routing comes before any of it — the 404 needs the same treatment as the 200.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Build the response — status, headers, body string — before you look at
`req.method`. A HEAD is a GET that stops one line early, so the two paths should
share everything up to `res.end()`.

## Hint 2

`content-length` counts bytes. `"café".length` is 4 and
`Buffer.byteLength("café")` is 5, and the payload here has an accented character
in it precisely so that the difference shows up.

Node will suppress a body you write on a HEAD response whether you ask it to or
not, so the assertion that actually fails when you get this wrong is the header
one: if you never set `content-length`, the HEAD answers with no size at all,
which is the only question the client was asking.

Routing comes before any of it — the 404 needs the same treatment as the 200.

## Problem 4 — send the bytes that were asked for

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createHandler()` serves the ten bytes `0123456789` at
`/clip.txt` with `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, and honours `Range`: 206 with an
inclusive `Content-Range` for `bytes=2-5`, `bytes=-4` and `bytes=6-`; an end
past the last byte is clamped; a start past the end is 416 with
`Content-Range: bytes */10`; an unrecognised unit is ignored.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Parse the header into one of three answers before you touch the response: there
is no usable range (serve everything), there is a range (206), or the range
cannot be satisfied (416). A discriminated union makes the three branches
impossible to confuse.

## Hint 2

`bytes=` is the only unit you support, and anything else — including a unit you
have never heard of — means "ignore the header", not "refuse the request". Then
there are three shapes after the `=`:

- `start-end` — clamp `end` to the last byte, and refuse if `start` is past it
- `start-` — runs to the end
- `-suffix` — the **last** `suffix` bytes, so the start is `size - suffix`

Both ends of `Content-Range` are inclusive, which makes the slice `end + 1` and
the length `end - start + 1`. Off by one here is a corrupt download rather than
an error, so it is worth checking twice.

A 416 still has to say `bytes */size`, or the client has no way to ask a better
question next time.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Parse the header into one of three answers before you touch the response: there
is no usable range (serve everything), there is a range (206), or the range
cannot be satisfied (416). A discriminated union makes the three branches
impossible to confuse.

## Hint 2

`bytes=` is the only unit you support, and anything else — including a unit you
have never heard of — means "ignore the header", not "refuse the request". Then
there are three shapes after the `=`:

- `start-end` — clamp `end` to the last byte, and refuse if `start` is past it
- `start-` — runs to the end
- `-suffix` — the **last** `suffix` bytes, so the start is `size - suffix`

Both ends of `Content-Range` are inclusive, which makes the slice `end + 1` and
the length `end - start + 1`. Off by one here is a corrupt download rather than
an error, so it is worth checking twice.

A 416 still has to say `bytes */size`, or the client has no way to ask a better
question next time.

## Problem 7 — serving a directory, and only that directory

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createStaticServer(root)` serves files from `root`:
content-type from the extension, `application/octet-stream` for one you do not
know, 404 for a missing file **or a directory**, 405 with `Allow: GET, HEAD` for
any other method, and 403 for a path that resolves outside `root` — including
the percent-encoded `..%2f` form that the client never gets a chance to
normalise away.

```
uv run dojo test node d18_http_raw ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four gates in order, and the order matters: the method, then the path, then
whether the path is inside the root, then whether it is a file. Only the last
one is allowed to touch the disk.

## Hint 2

`url.pathname` is still percent-encoded, and you have to decode it before you
can use it as a filename. That decode is the dangerous moment: `%2f` becomes a
separator that the client's own URL normalisation never had a chance to remove,
which is why `/..%2fsecret.txt` arrives intact where `/../secret.txt` would have
been collapsed before it was ever sent.

So: decode, strip the leading slash, `path.resolve()` against the root, and then
ask whether the result is still under the root — by taking `path.relative()` and
looking at its first **segment**. `startsWith("..")` also rejects `..config`.

## Hint 3

The leading-slash strip is load-bearing and easy to skip. `path.resolve(root,
"/index.html")` is `/index.html` — resolve discards everything to the left of an
absolute argument — so without it every ordinary request escapes the root and
your own site 403s.

`stat()` answers two questions at once: it throws `ENOENT` for a file that is
not there, and `isFile()` is false for a directory. Both are the same 404 here.

What is left to you is which code the traversal gets. This gate wants 403; a
number of real servers answer 404 instead, so as not to confirm that the file
above the root exists at all. Have a reason for the one you pick.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four gates in order, and the order matters: the method, then the path, then
whether the path is inside the root, then whether it is a file. Only the last
one is allowed to touch the disk.

## Hint 2

`url.pathname` is still percent-encoded, and you have to decode it before you
can use it as a filename. That decode is the dangerous moment: `%2f` becomes a
separator that the client's own URL normalisation never had a chance to remove,
which is why `/..%2fsecret.txt` arrives intact where `/../secret.txt` would have
been collapsed before it was ever sent.

So: decode, strip the leading slash, `path.resolve()` against the root, and then
ask whether the result is still under the root — by taking `path.relative()` and
looking at its first **segment**. `startsWith("..")` also rejects `..config`.

## Hint 3

The leading-slash strip is load-bearing and easy to skip. `path.resolve(root,
"/index.html")` is `/index.html` — resolve discards everything to the left of an
absolute argument — so without it every ordinary request escapes the root and
your own site 403s.

`stat()` answers two questions at once: it throws `ENOENT` for a file that is
not there, and `isFile()` is false for a directory. Both are the same 404 here.

What is left to you is which code the traversal gets. This gate wants 403; a
number of real servers answer 404 instead, so as not to confirm that the file
above the root exists at all. Have a reason for the one you pick.

## Hint 1

Two halves. Formatting one event into the text that goes on the wire is a pure
function and worth writing on its own; the handler is then a `for await` over

## Hint 2

The wire format, in order: `id: ` if there is one, `event: ` if there is one,
then **one `data: ` line per line of the payload**, then a blank line. The blank
line is the dispatch signal — without it the browser sits on a complete message
waiting for the rest of it.

The interesting failure is a source that throws half way. By then the status

event in the stream followed by `res.end()`. Putting the `end()` in a `finally`
is what makes the success path and the failure path agree.

The remaining decision is one this signature quietly makes for you: the source
is a single async iterable, so a second request would find it exhausted. A real
endpoint takes a *factory* and calls it per connection. Worth knowing why before
somebody asks.

lessons.briefing:
# d19 — HTTP routing

Eight problems on dispatch, drawn from lesson **08_http_core** — the half of it
that decides *which* code answers a request. That lesson's challenge built a
router that handled `:params`, 404 and 405; this set takes the pieces apart and
then rebuilds a harder one. Problem 7 is deliberately the interview version of
that challenge: routes tried in specificity order rather than registration
order, async handlers whose rejections become 500s, and `OPTIONS` and `HEAD`
answered by the router itself.

Six of the eight are pure functions with no server at all, which is the point —
a router is string handling wearing a network costume. Problems 6 and 7 are
graded with supertest against a request listener, so nothing binds a port. No
express anywhere: `node:http` and `URL` only.

## Problem 1 — a request line, taken apart

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `splitRoute(url)` returns `{ segments, query }`.
Segments are percent-decoded with empty ones dropped, so leading, trailing and
doubled slashes all mean nothing. `query` maps each key to its value, or to an
**array** when the key repeats.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex1
```

## Problem 2 — does this pattern describe this path

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `matchPattern(pattern, pathname)` returns the bound
parameters or `null`. `:name` takes exactly one segment, `:name?` may be absent
(and then is not in the result at all), and a trailing `*name` takes every
remaining segment joined with `/`, including none. Parameters come out decoded.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex2
```

## Problem 3 — the order a router has to try things in

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `rankPatterns(patterns)` returns them sorted most
specific first: a literal beats a `:param`, a `:param` beats having run out of
segments, and having run out beats a `*wildcard`. Equally specific patterns keep
their original order, and the array you were given is not modified.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex3
```

## Problem 4 — the router, run backwards

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `buildLink(pattern, params, query)` fills the pattern
in: values percent-encoded, an absent optional segment left off entirely, a
wildcard keeping its separators, and the query sorted by key with arrays
becoming repeated keys. A missing required parameter throws an error naming it.

```

```

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `canonicalPath(url)` returns `{ path, changed }`:

not part of the answer and never counts as a change — and nothing is decoded.


Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `mountAt(prefix, handler)` gives `handler` the path with
the prefix removed (`/api/v1/orders` becomes `/orders`, and the mount point
itself becomes `/`), leaves the untouched URL on the request as `originalUrl`,

`/api/v1extra`, which is not under `/api/v1`.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex6
```

over a `/orders/:id` registered before it. Handlers may be async, and a rejection
becomes a 500 plus a call to `onError`. `HEAD` falls back to the `GET` handler;

path with the wrong method is 405 with the same `Allow`.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex7
```

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `resolveRouteTree(tree, method, pathname)` walks nodes
with `children`, a `param` child and an `index` list of methods, returning
`{ chain, params }` or `null`. A static child is tried before the param child —
and when the static branch fails further down, the walk has to back out and try
the param branch instead.

# Reading - node/d19_http_routing

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **turning a URL into a decision**, which is almost
entirely string handling and almost never treated as such. Every problem in this
set is built on the same two-line primitive — split on `/`, drop the empty
pieces — and the differences between them are questions about *when* you decode
and *what order* you try things in. Those two questions account for most routing
bugs in the wild: decoding before splitting turns one segment into two and hands
an attacker a directory separator, and trying routes in registration order makes
a literal route unreachable behind a parameter that was declared first. The last
two problems put the pieces together in the two shapes real routers take — a
ranked flat table (ex7) and a nested tree (ex8) — and both of them turn on the
same idea, that matching is a *search* and a search has to be able to fail and
back out.

## ex1 — split, then decode

**What it tested:** that `URL` already does the parsing, and that the order of
splitting and decoding is a decision rather than a detail.

**The classic mistake:** `decodeURIComponent(url).split("/")`. A `%2f` inside a
segment becomes a separator, one segment turns into two, and a path that was
meant to name a file now names a directory above it. Second most common:
reading the query with `Object.fromEntries(searchParams)`, which silently keeps
only the last value of a repeated key.

**Model answer:** `new URL(url, base)`, split the `pathname`, filter the empties,
map `decodeURIComponent` over what is left — and build the query by iterating
`searchParams` so a repeat can be promoted to an array.

## ex2 — a match has two ways to end

**What it tested:** the three segment kinds, and both ends of the walk.

**The classic mistake:** comparing only as far as the shorter of the two, so
`/orders/:id` happily matches `/orders/42/lines` and every nested route beneath
it becomes unreachable. The mirror image is treating a path that runs out early
as an automatic failure, which breaks optional segments.

**Model answer:** one loop over the pattern; the wildcard returns immediately;
running out of path is a match only if everything remaining is optional; and
after the loop, the path must have run out exactly when the pattern did.

## ex3 — specificity is a per-position score

**What it tested:** that "most specific first" is a total order you can compute,
not a feeling.

**The classic mistake:** sorting by length, or by counting parameters. Neither
one can express that `/orders` should beat `/orders/*rest` while still losing to
`/orders/:id` — that only falls out if "the pattern has ended" is itself a rank,
sitting between a param and a wildcard. And `sort()` mutates, so a router that
ranks its own table in place reorders the array its caller is still holding.

**Model answer:** score each position (literal 3, param 2, absent 1, wildcard 0),
compare position by position over the **longer** of the two, and tie-break on the
original index so equal patterns keep registration order explicitly rather than
by trusting the sort to be stable.

## ex4 — the same table, read the other way

**What it tested:** reverse routing — that a pattern is the single place a route
is written down, and links should be generated from it rather than typed again.

**The classic mistake:** encoding the wildcard with `encodeURIComponent` as one
value, which turns every separator into `%2F` and produces a link that matches
nothing. Close behind: emitting an absent optional as an empty string (giving a
trailing slash) or as the literal text `undefined`.

**Model answer:** build a list of output segments — literals through, params
encoded, wildcards split and each piece encoded — and sort the query keys so the
same inputs always produce the same string, which is what makes a link usable as
a cache key.

## ex5 — normalise without decoding

**What it tested:** dot-segment removal, and the discipline not to decode while
doing it.

**The classic mistake:** decoding first "so the comparison is fair". That is
exactly how `%2f` becomes a separator and the `..` you just removed comes back.
The other one is guarding `..` with a depth counter instead of letting `pop()`
on an empty array do nothing, which is the same rule with more places to be
wrong.

**Model answer:** strip the query, reduce the segments in one pass with `pop()`
for `..`, rebuild — and compare the result against the **path** rather than the
whole URL so a request carrying only a query string is not redirected.

## ex6 — the rewrite is a loan

**What it tested:** what mounting actually is. Express makes this look like a
feature; it is four lines of string manipulation and one `finally`.

**The classic mistake:** `pathname.startsWith(prefix)`, with no segment
boundary. `/api/v1extra` starts with `/api/v1`, so the inner handler is handed
the path `extra` and answers a route that has nothing to do with the request.
The other is never restoring `req.url`, which breaks everything registered after
the mount and produces a symptom somewhere else entirely.

**Model answer:** split the query off, test for the mount point exactly or the
mount point **plus a slash**, rewrite, and restore in a `finally` — recording
`originalUrl` only if it is not already set, so nesting keeps the outermost.

## ex7 — dispatch is three answers, not two

**What it tested:** assembling the pieces, plus the parts of a router that are
protocol obligations rather than features.

**The classic mistake:** trying routes in registration order, which makes
`/orders/new` unreachable behind `/orders/:id` and produces the folklore that
you must "declare specific routes first". The serious one is not awaiting an
async handler: the rejection becomes an unhandled rejection, the response is
never written, and the client hangs until its own timeout — a much worse failure
than a 500, and one that does not appear in the access log at all.

**Model answer:** keep the table sorted on registration; dispatch by walking it;
and when nothing matched, distinguish "no route for this path" (404) from "no
route for this method on this path" (405 or, for `OPTIONS`, 204) by collecting
the matching routes' methods once and reusing the set for both.

## ex8 — matching is a search

**What it tested:** the one thing that separates a real nested router from a
plausible one — backtracking.

**The classic mistake:** committing to the static child. `if (child) return
walk(child, ...)` looks obviously right, and it returns `null` for
`/orders/new/lines` even though the tree can serve it as `/orders/:id/lines`
with `id = "new"`. The bug only appears where a literal route and a param route
overlap, which is to say only in production.

**Model answer:** try the static child, **inspect the result**, and fall through
to the param child on `null`; build the chain and the merged params on the way
back up, so an abandoned branch costs nothing to unwind.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `node:http`](https://nodejs.org/api/http.html) — `req.url`, `req.method`, and the fact that a request listener is just a function you can wrap.
- [MDN: the `URL` API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URL) and [`URLSearchParams`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams) — including `getAll()`, which is the repeated-key problem solved for you.
- [MDN: `encodeURIComponent()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/encodeURIComponent) — what it escapes and, more usefully, what it does not.
- [MDN: 405 Method Not Allowed](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/405) and [the `Allow` header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Allow) — the obligation ex7 is meeting.
- [RFC 3986 §5.2.4, Remove Dot Segments](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-5.2.4) — ex5 as the specification writes it, including why there is nothing above the root.

## Problem 1 — a request line, taken apart

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `splitRoute(url)` returns `{ segments, query }`.
Segments are percent-decoded with empty ones dropped, so leading, trailing and
doubled slashes all mean nothing. `query` maps each key to its value, or to an
**array** when the key repeats.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`new URL(url, "http://localhost")` does most of this. The base is a formality —
`req.url` is always relative, and nothing about the base ends up in your answer.
You then want `parsed.pathname` and `parsed.searchParams`.

## Hint 2

Order matters on the path: **split, then decode**. Decoding first turns a `%2f`
inside a segment into a real separator, and the segment splits into two — which
is the same mistake that lets a filename climb out of a directory.

Dropping the empty strings that `split("/")` produces is what makes a leading
slash, a trailing slash and a doubled slash all mean nothing.

For the query, `searchParams` is already decoded and already knows about
repeats. Iterating it gives you one entry per occurrence, so the array case is a
matter of noticing you have seen the key before — and the three-value case is
what catches a solution that only ever builds a pair.

## Problem 2 — does this pattern describe this path

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `matchPattern(pattern, pathname)` returns the bound
parameters or `null`. `:name` takes exactly one segment, `:name?` may be absent
(and then is not in the result at all), and a trailing `*name` takes every
remaining segment joined with `/`, including none. Parameters come out decoded.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split both sides into segments and walk them together with one index. Three
kinds of pattern segment — a literal, a `:param`, a `*wildcard` — and each one
either fails, or binds something and moves on.

## Hint 2

The two ends are where this goes wrong.

If the **path** runs out first, you are not automatically finished: it is a
match only if every pattern segment left is optional. If the **pattern** runs
out first, the path must have run out too, or `/orders/:id` matches
`/orders/42/lines` and every nested route becomes unreachable.

The wildcard is the exception to both — it consumes the rest, including nothing
at all, and returns immediately.

Decode the path segments once, at the top, rather than at each use. Doing it
per-branch is how the wildcard ends up as the only part that is still encoded.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split both sides into segments and walk them together with one index. Three
kinds of pattern segment — a literal, a `:param`, a `*wildcard` — and each one
either fails, or binds something and moves on.

## Hint 2

The two ends are where this goes wrong.

If the **path** runs out first, you are not automatically finished: it is a
match only if every pattern segment left is optional. If the **pattern** runs
out first, the path must have run out too, or `/orders/:id` matches
`/orders/42/lines` and every nested route becomes unreachable.

The wildcard is the exception to both — it consumes the rest, including nothing
at all, and returns immediately.

Decode the path segments once, at the top, rather than at each use. Doing it
per-branch is how the wildcard ends up as the only part that is still encoded.

## Problem 3 — the order a router has to try things in

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `rankPatterns(patterns)` returns them sorted most
specific first: a literal beats a `:param`, a `:param` beats having run out of
segments, and having run out beats a `*wildcard`. Equally specific patterns keep
their original order, and the array you were given is not modified.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Give every position in a pattern a score, then compare two patterns position by
position and let the first difference decide. The comparison is over the
**longer** of the two, not the shorter — the interesting cases are the ones
where one pattern has run out.

## Hint 2

Four scores, and the surprising one is third:

- a literal segment — highest
- a `:param`
- **no segment at all** (the pattern has ended)
- a `*wildcard` — lowest

Putting "ended" above "wildcard" is what makes `/orders` beat `/orders/*rest`
while still losing to `/orders/:id`, which is exactly the behaviour you want and
very hard to get by comparing lengths separately.

Two more things the gate checks and a first attempt usually misses: `sort()`
mutates the array it is given, so map to a new array first; and it needs a
tie-break that returns `0`-equivalent ordering for equally specific patterns, or
the routing table quietly reorders itself.

position and let the first difference decide. The comparison is over the
**longer** of the two, not the shorter — the interesting cases are the ones

very hard to get by comparing lengths separately.

## Problem 5 — one URL per resource

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `canonicalPath(url)` returns `{ path, changed }`:
duplicate separators collapsed, `.` and `..` resolved without ever climbing
above the root, and a trailing slash dropped except on `/`. The query string is
not part of the answer and never counts as a change — and nothing is decoded.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split off the query first, then reduce the path to a list of segments and
rebuild it. Every rule in the specification falls out of that one loop: an empty
segment is a doubled or trailing slash, `.` is "here", and `..` is "drop the
last one".

## Hint 2

`Array.prototype.pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined` and does nothing,
which is the entire implementation of "never climb above the root" — no counter,
no guard.

`changed` compares your answer to the **path** you were given, not to the whole
URL, so a request that only carries a query string reports `changed: false` and
the caller does not redirect it.

And do not decode anything. It is tempting, and it is how `%2f` turns back into
a separator after you have just finished removing the `..` that goes with it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split off the query first, then reduce the path to a list of segments and
rebuild it. Every rule in the specification falls out of that one loop: an empty
segment is a doubled or trailing slash, `.` is "here", and `..` is "drop the
last one".

## Hint 2

`Array.prototype.pop()` on an empty array returns `undefined` and does nothing,
which is the entire implementation of "never climb above the root" — no counter,
no guard.

`changed` compares your answer to the **path** you were given, not to the whole
URL, so a request that only carries a query string reports `changed: false` and
the caller does not redirect it.

And do not decode anything. It is tempting, and it is how `%2f` turns back into
a separator after you have just finished removing the `..` that goes with it.

## Problem 6 — mounting, without a framework to do it

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `mountAt(prefix, handler)` gives `handler` the path with
the prefix removed (`/api/v1/orders` becomes `/orders`, and the mount point
itself becomes `/`), leaves the untouched URL on the request as `originalUrl`,
restores `req.url` afterwards, and 404s anything outside the prefix — including
`/api/v1extra`, which is not under `/api/v1`.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex6
```

## Hint 1

Three steps: decide whether this request belongs to the mount, rewrite `req.url`
to what the inner handler should see, and put it back when the handler returns.

## Hint 2

Split the query off before you compare anything — the prefix applies to the
path, not to the whole of `req.url`, and the query has to be reattached to

The membership test is two cases, and the second one is the trap:

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 7 — the router, assembled

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createRouter({ onError })` exposes `get/post/put/delete`
and a `handler`. Routes are tried **most specific first**, so `/orders/new` wins
over a `/orders/:id` registered before it. Handlers may be async, and a rejection
becomes a 500 plus a call to `onError`. `HEAD` falls back to the `GET` handler;
`OPTIONS` is answered with 204 and `Allow`; an unknown path is 404 and a known
path with the wrong method is 405 with the same `Allow`.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need a matcher and a ranker again. Write them, or lift your own from ex2 and
ex3 — the point of this problem is the dispatch loop around them, not a third
copy of the parsing.

Keep the route list sorted by specificity as routes are registered, and the
request path becomes a walk down that list taking the first match.

## Hint 2

There are three answers when no handler matched, and telling them apart is what
makes the router usable:

- no route matches this **path**, whatever the method → 404
- some route matches the path, and the method is `OPTIONS` → 204 with `Allow`
- some route matches the path, and the method is anything else → 405 with the
  same `Allow`

So collect the matching routes' methods once and reuse the set for both. `HEAD`
belongs in `Allow` whenever `GET` does, and `OPTIONS` always does — but neither
is a method anyone registers.

## Hint 1

You need a matcher and a ranker again. Write them, or lift your own from ex2 and
ex3 — the point of this problem is the dispatch loop around them, not a third
copy of the parsing.

Keep the route list sorted by specificity as routes are registered, and the
request path becomes a walk down that list taking the first match.

## Hint 2

There are three answers when no handler matched, and telling them apart is what
makes the router usable:

- no route matches this **path**, whatever the method → 404
- some route matches the path, and the method is `OPTIONS` → 204 with `Allow`
- some route matches the path, and the method is anything else → 405 with the
  same `Allow`

So collect the matching routes' methods once and reuse the set for both. `HEAD`
belongs in `Allow` whenever `GET` does, and `OPTIONS` always does — but neither
is a method anyone registers.

## Hint 3

`http.createServer` hands you a synchronous listener, and your handlers are
async. Start an async function inside it and put a `try`/`catch` around the
whole dispatch, or a rejected handler becomes an unhandled rejection: the client
gets nothing at all and waits for its own timeout, which is a much worse failure
than a 500.

non-promise is free, and not awaiting a promise is the bug.

has already written part of the response. `res.headersSent` is how you find out;

unattractive.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — routing as a tree

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `resolveRouteTree(tree, method, pathname)` walks nodes
with `children`, a `param` child and an `index` list of methods, returning
`{ chain, params }` or `null`. A static child is tried before the param child —
and when the static branch fails further down, the walk has to back out and try
the param branch instead.

```
uv run dojo test node d19_http_routing ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A recursive `walk(node, depth)` returning a match or `null`. At each level:
the path has run out (so this node must answer the method), or it has not (so
try the static child for this segment, then the param child).

Build the chain and the params on the way back **up**, by prepending this
level's name to whatever the recursive call returned. That way a failed branch
costs you nothing to undo.

## Hint 2

The static child is tried first because it is the more specific route. But
trying it first is not the same as committing to it.

## Hint 3

That is the whole problem: when the static child matches the segment and then
fails deeper down, you must **back out and try the param child**. The obvious
implementation

```ts
const child = node.children?.[segment];
if (child) return walk(child, depth + 1);   // wrong
```

returns `null` for `/orders/new/lines` even though the tree can serve it as
`/orders/:id/lines` with `id = "new"`. The symptom is a route that looks
unregistered, and it only appears when a literal route and a param route
overlap — which is to say, in production.

Take the recursive call's result, check it, and fall through on `null`.

Left for you: what should happen when two levels bind the same param name. The
gate does not ask, and the two defensible answers disagree.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A recursive `walk(node, depth)` returning a match or `null`. At each level:
the path has run out (so this node must answer the method), or it has not (so
try the static child for this segment, then the param child).

Build the chain and the params on the way back **up**, by prepending this
level's name to whatever the recursive call returned. That way a failed branch
costs you nothing to undo.

## Hint 2

The static child is tried first because it is the more specific route. But
trying it first is not the same as committing to it.

## Hint 3

That is the whole problem: when the static child matches the segment and then
fails deeper down, you must **back out and try the param child**. The obvious
implementation

```ts
const child = node.children?.[segment];
if (child) return walk(child, depth + 1);   // wrong
```

returns `null` for `/orders/new/lines` even though the tree can serve it as
`/orders/:id/lines` with `id = "new"`. The symptom is a route that looks
unregistered, and it only appears when a literal route and a param route
overlap — which is to say, in production.

Take the recursive call's result, check it, and fall through on `null`.

Left for you: what should happen when two levels bind the same param name. The
gate does not ask, and the two defensible answers disagree.

# d20 — Express routes

Eight problems on the express router, drawn from lesson
**09_express_fundamentals** — the mechanics under the routes you have been
writing since then. Nothing in this set is about REST semantics or validation;
it is about what express does with a request between the socket and your
handler, and about the parts of the routing API most people never reach for.

Every problem is graded through supertest against a fresh app from your factory,
so nothing listens on a port and no state survives a test.

## Problem 1 — one path, three verbs

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on
`/notes/:id` through a single `app.route()` chain: 200 with the note, 200 with
the updated note, 204 with nothing. An unknown id is `404 { error: "not_found" }`
on every verb, and a method you did not register falls through to express.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex1
```

## Problem 2 — load it once, before anybody asks

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createApp()` uses `app.param("id", ...)` to look the
note up once per request, answer the 404 centrally, and hand the result to the
handlers — which then contain no lookup at all. `GET /stats` reports the number
of lookups so far; `/health` and `/stats` must never cause one.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a router that knows where it was mounted

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createApp()` mounts a `Router` at
`/projects/:projectId` serving `/notes` and `/notes/:noteId`. Both routes need
`req.params.projectId` alongside their own parameters, and a router-level guard
answers `404 { error: "no_such_project" }` for the whole subtree.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex3
```

## Problem 4 — the handler that decides it is not the one

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp()` registers `/reports/:id` **twice**. The
first route starts with a guard that keeps numeric ids and passes everything
else to the next route with `next("route")`; the second answers those. Each
response carries a `trail` of what actually ran.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a sub-application, and its three urls

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createApp()` mounts a second express app at `/api/v2`
with a `/notes/:id` route reporting `req.baseUrl`, `req.originalUrl` and
`req.url`. Middleware on the parent sets `x-parent` for everything; middleware
on the sub-app sets `x-sub` only inside the mount.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex5
```

## Problem 6 — settings, app.locals, res.locals

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createApp({ strict, caseSensitive, service })` applies
express's `"strict routing"` and `"case sensitive routing"` settings, puts
`service` on `app.locals`, and has middleware write `res.locals.tenant` from the
`x-tenant` header (default `"public"`). `GET /notes` answers `{ service, tenant,
strict }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex6
```

## Problem 7 — the same five routes, for any resource

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `mountResource(app, { name, store })` registers list,
create, show, replace and destroy for that resource: `201` with a `Location` of
`/{name}/{id}`, `204` on delete, `404 { error: "not_found" }` for an unknown id.
Two specs on one app must not share anything.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the status code express will not give you

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET|POST /notes`,
`GET|PATCH|DELETE /notes/:id` and `GET /health`, and answers **405** with a
sorted `Allow` header — including `OPTIONS`, and `HEAD` wherever `GET` exists —
when a known path is asked for with a method it does not have. `OPTIONS` gets
`204` and the same header; an unknown path is still `404`; `HEAD` still reaches
the `GET` handler.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex8
```

# Reading - node/d20_express_routes

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **the express router as a machine**, not as a place
to hang handlers. Everything in this set follows from two facts. First, express
tries its registrations strictly in the order you made them, matching path *and*
method together, and the first layer to respond ends the request — so ordering
is a design decision and not an accident of how you typed the file. Second, a
request carries three separate namespaces as it travels: parameters (which a
router only sees if you let it), the url (which mounting rewrites), and locals
(which live for exactly one response). Half the bugs in real express codebases
are a value put in the wrong one of those three, and the other half are a layer
registered in the wrong place.

## ex1 — one path, declared once

**What it tested:** that `app.route()` exists and why you would use it — three
verbs on one path with the path written a single time.

**The classic mistake:** none in the routing; the trap is state. Seeding the
store directly from the exported `SEED` array rather than from a copy of it
means the first `PUT` mutates a module-level object, and every later app built
by the factory starts from the mutated data. In a test suite that shows up as a
test which passes alone and fails in company.

**Model answer:** one `app.route("/notes/:id")` chain, a store in the closure
seeded with `SEED.map((note) => ({ ...note }))`, and `res.status(204).end()` for
the delete — because a 204 with a body is a contradiction the client is entitled
to trip over.

## ex2 — the parameter callback

**What it tested:** `app.param()`, which most people have never used, and the
distinction it draws that `app.use()` cannot: run for routes that have this
parameter, and only those.

**The classic mistake:** reaching for `app.use("/notes/:id", loader)` instead.
It looks equivalent and is not — it runs for every method and every sub-path,
including ones that were never meant to load anything, and it cannot be reused
by a second route family with the same parameter name. The other mistake is
calling `next()` after responding with the 404, which sends the request onward
to a handler that will try to respond again.

**Model answer:** one `app.param("id", ...)` that counts, loads, responds on
failure and otherwise hangs the note on `req` — so every route below it is three
lines long and none of them contains the word "find".

## ex3 — mergeParams

**What it tested:** that a `Router` has its own `req.params` and does not
inherit the mount path's parameters unless you ask.

**The classic mistake:** forgetting the option and then filtering by
`undefined`. Nothing throws. The endpoint answers `200` with an empty array, the
client renders "no notes yet", and the bug is reported as a data problem weeks
later. It is the quietest failure in this whole set.

**Model answer:** `express.Router({ mergeParams: true })`, routes written
relative to the mount, and one `router.use()` guard at the top that rejects an
unknown project for the entire subtree — which is only possible because the
router can read a parameter it did not declare.

## ex4 — three ways to say "carry on"

**What it tested:** that `next()`, `next("route")` and `next(err)` travel three
different distances, and that the middle one exists at all.

**The classic mistake:** believing `next("route")` passes a string to the next
handler, or using `return next()` where the intent was to abandon the route.
Written the wrong way round, a guard that means "this is not my request" instead
runs the handler it was guarding, and the second route — the one that was
supposed to answer — never gets a look.

**Model answer:** `app.get(path, guard, handler)` twice on the same path, with
the guard calling `next("route")` on the ids it does not want; the trail lives on
`req` so the gate can watch what ran without a shared array accumulating across
requests.

## ex5 — what mounting actually does

**What it tested:** the three url properties, which is the same question as
"what is a mountable application".

**The classic mistake:** building links from `req.url`, or matching on it
against the full public path. Inside a mount, `req.url` has already had the
mount path removed, so a redirect built from it drops the prefix and sends the
client to a 404. The mirror-image mistake is hard-coding `/api/v2` inside the
sub-app, which works perfectly until somebody mounts it somewhere else.

**Model answer:** `req.baseUrl` for where I am, `req.originalUrl` for what was
asked, `req.url` for what is left to route — and middleware registered on the
sub-app rather than the parent when the intent is "only inside this mount".

## ex6 — three lifetimes

**What it tested:** knowing which of `app.set`, `app.locals` and `res.locals`
outlives what, and that two of express's settings are read at router build time.

**The classic mistake:** the one this exercise is really about — putting
per-request state on the app. `app.locals.tenant = ...` in a middleware works
flawlessly for one user at a time and silently serves the wrong tenant's data
the moment two requests overlap, which is exactly the load a test suite never
produces. Second place: calling `app.set("strict routing", true)` after the
routes are registered, where it changes nothing at all.

**Model answer:** settings first, `app.locals` for what the process knows,
`res.locals` for what this response knows, and `app.get(name)` to read a setting
back — the one-argument form of the same function that registers routes.

## ex7 — routes as data

**What it tested:** whether you can see the shape five hand-written routes have
in common and lift it into a function, without the resource name leaking into
seventeen places.

**The classic mistake:** hoisting anything — the router, the store, an id
counter — out of the function and into module scope, so the second resource
shares the first one's state. Close behind: building the `Location` header from
`req.url` or from a hard-coded string, so mounting the same code at a different
name produces links that 404.

**Model answer:** a fresh `express.Router()` per call, routes written as `"/"`
and `"/:id"`, `app.use("/" + spec.name, router)` for the one place the name
appears, and every handler closing over the `store` it was given.

## ex8 — the code express refuses to guess

**What it tested:** that express matches path and method together, so "wrong
method" and "no such path" are indistinguishable to it — and that you can
recover the distinction by declaring it.

**The classic mistake:** writing the 405 check as a global `app.use` that tries
to work out whether the path exists, usually by re-matching patterns by hand.
That is a router reimplemented badly. The other one is an `Allow` header that
lists only the methods you registered: `OPTIONS` and `HEAD` are supported
whether you wrote them or not, and a client that trusts your header will not
send them.

**Model answer:** one `app.all(path, ...)` per path, registered after that
path's real methods, so express's own ordering does the matching; `OPTIONS`
answered with `204` and the header rather than refused; and a final `app.use`
that now means precisely "no path matched".

## Further reading

- [Express: Routing](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/routing.html) — `app.route()`, route parameters, and handler chains.
- [Express 5 API: `app.param()`](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#app.param) — the callback, when it fires, and how often.
- [Express 5 API: `express.Router()`](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#express.router) — `mergeParams`, `strict` and `caseSensitive`.
- [Express 5 API: application settings](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#app.set) — including `"strict routing"` and `"case sensitive routing"`, and `app.locals` next to `res.locals`.
- [MDN: 405 Method Not Allowed](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/405) — and the `Allow` header it is required to carry.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 1 — one path, three verbs

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` on
`/notes/:id` through a single `app.route()` chain: 200 with the note, 200 with
the updated note, 204 with nothing. An unknown id is `404 { error: "not_found" }`
on every verb, and a method you did not register falls through to express.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`app.route(path)` returns a Route object whose `.get()`, `.put()` and
`.delete()` each return the same object, so they chain. The path string is
written once, which is the point: three `app.get("/notes/:id", ...)`-style
registrations are three chances to typo the path.

## Hint 2

The store lives in the closure `createApp()` returns, so each call to the
factory gets its own notes — that is what lets the gate run a fresh app per
test. Seed it with a **copy** (`SEED.map((note) => ({ ...note }))`), or the
first test to mutate a note changes the module-level array for every test after
it.

Two details the gate checks: `PUT` needs `express.json()` mounted before the
route or `req.body` is undefined, and a `204` must have no body at all —
`res.status(204).end()`, never `.json()`.

## Hint 1

`app.route(path)` returns a Route object whose `.get()`, `.put()` and
`.delete()` each return the same object, so they chain. The path string is
written once, which is the point: three `app.get("/notes/:id", ...)`-style
registrations are three chances to typo the path.

## Hint 2

The store lives in the closure `createApp()` returns, so each call to the
factory gets its own notes — that is what lets the gate run a fresh app per
test. Seed it with a **copy** (`SEED.map((note) => ({ ...note }))`), or the
first test to mutate a note changes the module-level array for every test after
it.

Two details the gate checks: `PUT` needs `express.json()` mounted before the
route or `req.body` is undefined, and a `204` must have no body at all —
`res.status(204).end()`, never `.json()`.

## Problem 3 — a router that knows where it was mounted

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `createApp()` mounts a `Router` at
`/projects/:projectId` serving `/notes` and `/notes/:noteId`. Both routes need

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Router` is its own little world, and by default `req.params` inside it holds
only the parameters its own routes declared. The mount path's `:projectId` is
not one of those.

## Hint 2

`express.Router({ mergeParams: true })` is the switch. With it, the parent's
parameters are merged into `req.params` for every route in the router; without
it you get `undefined` and a filter that silently matches nothing — the worst
kind of bug, because the endpoint answers `200` with an empty list.

Mount with `app.use("/projects/:projectId", router)` and write the routes inside
relative to that: `"/notes"`, not `"/projects/:projectId/notes"`.

A `router.use()` guard at the top of the router runs for every route in it, so
"is this a real project" is answered once rather than in each handler.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `Router` is its own little world, and by default `req.params` inside it holds
only the parameters its own routes declared. The mount path's `:projectId` is
not one of those.

## Hint 2

`express.Router({ mergeParams: true })` is the switch. With it, the parent's
parameters are merged into `req.params` for every route in the router; without
it you get `undefined` and a filter that silently matches nothing — the worst
kind of bug, because the endpoint answers `200` with an empty list.

Mount with `app.use("/projects/:projectId", router)` and write the routes inside
relative to that: `"/notes"`, not `"/projects/:projectId/notes"`.

A `router.use()` guard at the top of the router runs for every route in it, so
"is this a real project" is answered once rather than in each handler.

## Problem 4 — the handler that decides it is not the one

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp()` registers `/reports/:id` **twice**. The
first route starts with a guard that keeps numeric ids and passes everything
else to the next route with `next("route")`; the second answers those. Each
response carries a `trail` of what actually ran.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex4
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Express has three different "carry on" signals and they go three different
distances:

- `next()` — the next handler **in this route**;
- `next("route")` — skip the rest of this route, try the next **route** that
  matches the path;
- `next(err)` — skip everything until an error handler.

## Hint 2

Register the two routes on the same path, in order. The first one is
`app.get(path, guard, handler)`; the guard decides. `next("route")` is the
literal string `"route"` — passing anything else is an error, which is exactly
the confusion this exercise exists to clear up.

Keep the trail on `req`, not in a variable in `createApp()`: the gate makes
several requests to the same app and a shared array would accumulate across all
of them.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Express has three different "carry on" signals and they go three different
distances:

- `next()` — the next handler **in this route**;
- `next("route")` — skip the rest of this route, try the next **route** that
  matches the path;
- `next(err)` — skip everything until an error handler.

## Hint 2

Register the two routes on the same path, in order. The first one is
`app.get(path, guard, handler)`; the guard decides. `next("route")` is the
literal string `"route"` — passing anything else is an error, which is exactly
the confusion this exercise exists to clear up.

Keep the trail on `req`, not in a variable in `createApp()`: the gate makes
several requests to the same app and a shared array would accumulate across all
of them.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three storage places, three lifetimes:

- `app.set(name, value)` / `app.get(name)` — express **settings**. Some of them,
  including `"strict routing"` and `"case sensitive routing"`, change how the
  router matches paths.
- `app.locals` — your values, application-wide, alive for the whole process.
- `res.locals` — your values, alive for exactly one response.

## Hint 2

The settings have to be applied **before** the routes are registered. Express
reads them when it lazily builds the router, so an `app.set("strict routing",
true)` underneath your `app.get(...)` calls is a line that does nothing and
looks like it works.

`app.get` is two functions wearing one name: with a path and a handler it
registers a route, with a single string it reads a setting back. That is not a
trick question — it is the API, and knowing it is the exercise.

Anything that differs per request belongs in `res.locals` (or on `req`). The
moment it goes in `app.locals` it is shared by every user on the server at once.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three storage places, three lifetimes:

- `app.set(name, value)` / `app.get(name)` — express **settings**. Some of them,
  including `"strict routing"` and `"case sensitive routing"`, change how the
  router matches paths.
- `app.locals` — your values, application-wide, alive for the whole process.
- `res.locals` — your values, alive for exactly one response.

## Hint 2

The settings have to be applied **before** the routes are registered. Express
reads them when it lazily builds the router, so an `app.set("strict routing",
true)` underneath your `app.get(...)` calls is a line that does nothing and
looks like it works.

`app.get` is two functions wearing one name: with a path and a handler it
registers a route, with a single string it reads a setting back. That is not a
trick question — it is the API, and knowing it is the exercise.

Anything that differs per request belongs in `res.locals` (or on `req`). The
moment it goes in `app.locals` it is shared by every user on the server at once.

## Problem 7 — the same five routes, for any resource

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `mountResource(app, { name, store })` registers list,
create, show, replace and destroy for that resource: `201` with a `Location` of
`/{name}/{id}`, `204` on delete, `404 { error: "not_found" }` for an unknown id.
Two specs on one app must not share anything.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here is new express — it is ex1, ex3 and ex5 used deliberately. The
change of perspective is that the path segment and the storage are *arguments*,
so the same function body serves `notes` and `tags` without knowing either name.

## Hint 2

Build a `express.Router()` per call, register `"/"` and `"/:id"` on it, and
`app.use("/" + spec.name, router)`. Relative paths inside the router mean the
resource name appears exactly once, in the mount.

Each call gets its own router **and** its own closure over `spec.store`. If you
hoist the store into a variable outside `mountResource`, the second mount
silently shares the first one's data — which is the failure the gate checks by
creating a tag and then counting the notes.

## Hint 3

Two places leak the resource name if you are not careful: the `Location` header
on the create, which has to be `/tags/t2` and not `/t2`, and the 404 body, which
must stay the same shape for every resource so one client error handler covers
them all.

What is left for you to decide is whether `mountResource` should also mount
`express.json()`. The gate does it on the app, which is the arrangement that
scales — but a reviewer will ask whether a resource ought to declare its own
body parsing, and there is a real answer either way.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 8 — the status code express will not give you

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET|POST /notes`,
`GET|PATCH|DELETE /notes/:id` and `GET /health`, and answers **405** with a
sorted `Allow` header — including `OPTIONS`, and `HEAD` wherever `GET` exists —
when a known path is asked for with a method it does not have. `OPTIONS` gets
`204` and the same header; an unknown path is still `404`; `HEAD` still reaches
the `GET` handler.

```
uv run dojo test node d20_express_routes ex8
```

— it matches nothing, and falls through to the 404 like any unknown path. There
is no hook that tells you the difference, so you have to build the knowledge in.

## Hint 2

`app.all(path, handler)` matches that path with **any** method. Register one
after the real methods for that path:

an unsupported method.

matched. That is your 404.

lessons.briefing:
# d21 — Middleware

Eight problems on the layer between the socket and your handler, drawn from
lessons **09_express_fundamentals** and **10_middleware_validation**. Lesson 10
gave you one logger, one validator, one error handler and one rate limiter; this
set is the family they belong to — combinators, guards, the error stack, and the
two middlewares that have to wrap the response object to do their job.

Nothing here waits. Anything time-shaped takes an injected `now`, and the
concurrency problem is graded by holding handlers open with deferreds the gate
releases by hand, so "two at once" is a count and not a race.

## Problem 1 — how long did that take

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `timing({ now })` sets `x-response-time` to the
milliseconds elapsed on the injected clock. The header has to be on the response
before it goes out, which rules out the obvious hook.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex1
```

## Problem 2 — the same middleware, but not everywhere

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `only(predicate, middleware)` runs the wrapped
middleware when `predicate(req)` is true and skips it otherwise — without
stopping the request. A `next(error)` from inside must reach the error handler
unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex2
```

## Problem 3 — a stack wearing one middleware's coat

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `compose(...middlewares)` folds them into one: in order,
each waiting for the last to call `next()`; one that responds stops the rest;
a `next(error)` skips the remainder **and** the routes below; and `compose()`
with nothing is a middleware that only calls `next()`.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex3
```

## Problem 4 — two error handlers, and one that knows when to give up

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp({ log })` has a first error handler that
answers what it recognises with 422 and passes everything else on with
`next(error)`, an ordinary middleware between the two, and the exported
`finalErrorHandler` at the bottom: 500, nothing revealing, one log line — and
`next(error)` instead when `res.headersSent` is already true.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex4
```

## Problem 5 — bodies at the edge

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createApp()` configures `express.json({ limit, type })`
and translates every refusal into one JSON error shape: 413
`payload_too_large`, 400 `invalid_json`, 415 `unsupported_media_type`, 400
`empty_body`. Two of those four the parser raises for you; two it does not.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex5
```

## Problem 6 — who you are, and whether that is enough

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `bearerAuth({ verify })` reads `Authorization: Bearer`,
calls `verify`, and attaches the principal — 401 with `WWW-Authenticate` for no
token, the wrong scheme, or a token `verify` rejects. `requireRole(role)` then
answers 403, with no challenge, for a principal who is who they say and still
may not.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex6
```

## Problem 7 — how many requests are allowed inside

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `concurrencyLimit({ max, queue })` admits `max` at a
time, parks up to `queue` more, and refuses the rest with `503 { error:
"too_busy" }` and `Retry-After`. A request that failed gives its slot back like
any other.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex7
```

## Problem 8 — answering without running the handler

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `responseCache({ ttl, now })` stores successful `GET`
responses per method and url and replays them with `x-cache: HIT` (fresh is
`MISS`). Never a non-2xx, never when the request says `cache-control: no-store`,
expiring on the injected clock, and dropping everything stored for a path when a
write arrives at it.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d21_middleware

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **middleware as a value**. A middleware is a function
of `(req, res, next)`, which means it can be wrapped, combined, generated and
handed around like any other function — and four of these eight problems are
combinators rather than features. The other four are about the two moments a
middleware does not naturally have access to: *after* the handler has decided
what to send, and *when the request is over*. Express gives you neither directly,
so both are reached the same way — by replacing something on the response object
and calling the original afterwards, or by listening for the events the response
emits when it ends. Once you have seen `res.end` wrapped for a timer and
`res.json` wrapped for a cache, most of the middleware ecosystem stops being
mysterious.

## ex1 — a last word before the headers go out

**What it tested:** knowing that a response has a point of no return, and where
it is.

**The classic mistake:** `res.on("finish", () => res.setHeader(...))`. It reads
correctly — finish is when the response is done — and it is one moment too late:
the headers were serialised and sent before `finish` fired, so the call either
throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` or is silently discarded. The header simply never
appears, and nothing in the logs says why.

**Model answer:** record the start time in the closure for *this* request, wrap
`res.end` so the header is set on the way past, and guard on `res.headersSent`
so a second call cannot throw.

## ex2 — a combinator, and the missing next()

**What it tested:** that middleware composes, and that "do nothing" is an
action you have to take.

**The classic mistake:** writing the skip branch as a bare `return`. The request
stops dead — no response, no error, no timeout on the server side — and the
client hangs until *its* timeout fires. It is the one express bug that produces
no output at all, which is why it takes people so long to find.

**Model answer:** `next()` to skip, and `middleware(req, res, next)` to run —
handing the outer `next` straight through, so `next(error)` and `next("route")`
keep meaning exactly what the wrapped middleware meant by them.

## ex3 — the chain, rebuilt by hand

**What it tested:** whether you can express "in order, each waiting for the
last" when the waiting is asynchronous and controlled by somebody else's code.

**The classic mistake:** a `for` loop calling each middleware in turn. That runs
all of them immediately, ignores the fact that one might respond, and turns the
second argument of `next(error)` into nothing at all. The subtler version gets
the recursion right and then advances the chain even when it was handed an
error, so a failure quietly becomes a continue.

**Model answer:** a recursive `step(index)` whose `next` inspects its argument —
anything not `undefined` goes to the outer `next` and stops the chain — and
which calls the outer `next()` when it runs off the end, so the composition is a
drop-in for the stack it replaced.

## ex4 — arity is the API

**What it tested:** that express identifies error handlers by counting declared
parameters, and that "handled" and "answered" are different things.

**The classic mistake:** dropping the unused `next` from
`(err, req, res, next)`. The function now takes three arguments, express files
it as ordinary middleware, and it never runs in the error path — while looking
exactly like an error handler in the source. Second place: one handler that
tries to recognise everything, so a new error type gets whatever the last
`else` said.

**Model answer:** a first handler that answers what it knows and calls
`next(error)` for the rest; a last handler that logs the truth and tells the
client nothing; and the `res.headersSent` branch, where the only correct move is
`next(error)` — the response has already begun, so express destroying the
connection is more honest than a second answer appended to the first.

## ex5 — what the parser will and will not tell you

**What it tested:** the boundary of `express.json()`. It refuses two things
loudly and ignores a third completely, and knowing which is which is the whole
question.

**The classic mistake:** assuming a wrong `content-type` produces an error. It
does not — `express.json({ type })` skips a body it was not configured for and
leaves `req.body` as `undefined`, so the first sign of trouble is a handler
reading a property off undefined and a 500 in the logs. The mirror mistake is
treating that `undefined` and the `{}` from an empty body as the same case, when
one is a 415 and the other is a 400.

**Model answer:** switch on `error.type` (`entity.too.large`,
`entity.parse.failed`) in a four-argument handler for what the parser raises,
and write your own guard for the two it does not — checking `req.body ===
undefined` before checking whether it is empty.

## ex6 — 401 and 403 are not synonyms

**What it tested:** the distinction every API gets wrong at least once, and the
header that makes 401 useful.

**The classic mistake:** answering 401 for a permission failure. The client's
correct response to a 401 is "get credentials and retry", so a user who is
already logged in is sent round a login loop that cannot possibly help — and in
a browser client, often literally an infinite one. The other mistake is a 401
with no `WWW-Authenticate`, which is the status code without the part that says
what to do about it.

**Model answer:** `bearerAuth` checks the scheme before the token, awaits
`verify` (async is fine — express 5 forwards a rejected promise on its own), and
attaches the principal; `requireRole` is a separate middleware so a route can
ask for identity without asking for a role, and its 403 carries no challenge
because there is nothing to retry.

## ex7 — a semaphore with a response attached

**What it tested:** the lesson-03 limiter, moved into a place where you do not
control when the work finishes.

**The classic mistake:** releasing the slot after `next()` returns. `next()`
returns as soon as the handler *starts*, not when it finishes, so the limit is
enforced against nothing at all. The runner-up is releasing only on `finish`, so
a client that disconnects mid-request keeps its slot forever and the service
degrades one connection at a time until it accepts nothing.

**Model answer:** listen for `finish` **and** `close` with a `released` boolean
so the pair cannot double-count, and hand a returning slot straight to the
longest waiter rather than decrementing and re-checking — because that gap is
where a brand-new request jumps the queue.

## ex8 — the middleware that has to see the future

**What it tested:** capturing a response from a position that runs before it
exists, and the four policy decisions that separate a cache from a bug.

**The classic mistake:** caching everything that comes back. A stored 404 or 500
outlives its cause: the resource is created, the outage ends, and every client
keeps getting the failure until the ttl expires. Almost as common is never
invalidating, so a client that has just written cannot see its own work — the
single most reported "the site is broken" bug in any cached API.

**Model answer:** wrap `res.json` to record the body while it is still a value;
store only 2xx; key on `req.originalUrl` so the query string is part of the
identity; honour `no-store` by neither reading nor writing; and clear a path's
entries on the way *in* to a write, before the handler runs, so no concurrent
read can repopulate them from data that is about to be wrong.

# Reading - node/d21_middleware

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **middleware as a value**. A middleware is a function
of `(req, res, next)`, which means it can be wrapped, combined, generated and
handed around like any other function — and four of these eight problems are
combinators rather than features. The other four are about the two moments a
middleware does not naturally have access to: *after* the handler has decided
what to send, and *when the request is over*. Express gives you neither directly,
so both are reached the same way — by replacing something on the response object
and calling the original afterwards, or by listening for the events the response
emits when it ends. Once you have seen `res.end` wrapped for a timer and
`res.json` wrapped for a cache, most of the middleware ecosystem stops being
mysterious.

## ex1 — a last word before the headers go out

**What it tested:** knowing that a response has a point of no return, and where
it is.

**The classic mistake:** `res.on("finish", () => res.setHeader(...))`. It reads
correctly — finish is when the response is done — and it is one moment too late:
the headers were serialised and sent before `finish` fired, so the call either
throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` or is silently discarded. The header simply never
appears, and nothing in the logs says why.

**Model answer:** record the start time in the closure for *this* request, wrap
`res.end` so the header is set on the way past, and guard on `res.headersSent`
so a second call cannot throw.

## ex2 — a combinator, and the missing next()

**What it tested:** that middleware composes, and that "do nothing" is an
action you have to take.

**The classic mistake:** writing the skip branch as a bare `return`. The request
stops dead — no response, no error, no timeout on the server side — and the
client hangs until *its* timeout fires. It is the one express bug that produces
no output at all, which is why it takes people so long to find.

**Model answer:** `next()` to skip, and `middleware(req, res, next)` to run —
handing the outer `next` straight through, so `next(error)` and `next("route")`
keep meaning exactly what the wrapped middleware meant by them.

## ex3 — the chain, rebuilt by hand

**What it tested:** whether you can express "in order, each waiting for the
last" when the waiting is asynchronous and controlled by somebody else's code.

**The classic mistake:** a `for` loop calling each middleware in turn. That runs
all of them immediately, ignores the fact that one might respond, and turns the
second argument of `next(error)` into nothing at all. The subtler version gets
the recursion right and then advances the chain even when it was handed an
error, so a failure quietly becomes a continue.

**Model answer:** a recursive `step(index)` whose `next` inspects its argument —
anything not `undefined` goes to the outer `next` and stops the chain — and
which calls the outer `next()` when it runs off the end, so the composition is a
drop-in for the stack it replaced.

## ex4 — arity is the API

**What it tested:** that express identifies error handlers by counting declared
parameters, and that "handled" and "answered" are different things.

**The classic mistake:** dropping the unused `next` from
`(err, req, res, next)`. The function now takes three arguments, express files
it as ordinary middleware, and it never runs in the error path — while looking
exactly like an error handler in the source. Second place: one handler that
tries to recognise everything, so a new error type gets whatever the last
`else` said.

**Model answer:** a first handler that answers what it knows and calls
`next(error)` for the rest; a last handler that logs the truth and tells the
client nothing; and the `res.headersSent` branch, where the only correct move is
`next(error)` — the response has already begun, so express destroying the
connection is more honest than a second answer appended to the first.

## ex5 — what the parser will and will not tell you

**What it tested:** the boundary of `express.json()`. It refuses two things
loudly and ignores a third completely, and knowing which is which is the whole
question.

**The classic mistake:** assuming a wrong `content-type` produces an error. It
does not — `express.json({ type })` skips a body it was not configured for and
leaves `req.body` as `undefined`, so the first sign of trouble is a handler
reading a property off undefined and a 500 in the logs. The mirror mistake is
treating that `undefined` and the `{}` from an empty body as the same case, when
one is a 415 and the other is a 400.

**Model answer:** switch on `error.type` (`entity.too.large`,
`entity.parse.failed`) in a four-argument handler for what the parser raises,
and write your own guard for the two it does not — checking `req.body ===
undefined` before checking whether it is empty.

## ex6 — 401 and 403 are not synonyms

**What it tested:** the distinction every API gets wrong at least once, and the
header that makes 401 useful.

**The classic mistake:** answering 401 for a permission failure. The client's
correct response to a 401 is "get credentials and retry", so a user who is
already logged in is sent round a login loop that cannot possibly help — and in
a browser client, often literally an infinite one. The other mistake is a 401
with no `WWW-Authenticate`, which is the status code without the part that says
what to do about it.

**Model answer:** `bearerAuth` checks the scheme before the token, awaits
`verify` (async is fine — express 5 forwards a rejected promise on its own), and
attaches the principal; `requireRole` is a separate middleware so a route can
ask for identity without asking for a role, and its 403 carries no challenge
because there is nothing to retry.

## ex7 — a semaphore with a response attached

**What it tested:** the lesson-03 limiter, moved into a place where you do not
control when the work finishes.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the clock once on the way in and keep the value in the closure for **this**
request — a variable in `timing()` itself would be shared by every request the
server ever handles.

## Hint 2

The obvious place to finish the measurement is `res.on("finish", ...)`, and it
is exactly one moment too late: `finish` fires after the headers have gone out,
so `res.setHeader()` there throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT` (or is silently lost).

Every response — `res.json()`, `res.send()`, even express's own 404 — ends up in
`res.end()`. Replace it with your own function that sets the header and then
calls the original. Bind the original first, guard on `res.headersSent`, and
remember to return what the original returned.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — the same middleware, but not everywhere

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `only(predicate, middleware)` runs the wrapped
middleware when `predicate(req)` is true and skips it otherwise — without
stopping the request. A `next(error)` from inside must reach the error handler
unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A middleware is just a function of `(req, res, next)`, so a combinator that
returns one has exactly two branches: call the wrapped middleware, or do not.

## Hint 2

The branch that does not is where people lose the request. "Skip it" means
`next()` — calling nothing at all leaves the connection open until the client
gives up, and there is no error anywhere to tell you why.

The branch that does should hand your own `next` straight through. Do not wrap
it, do not swallow an argument: if the inner middleware calls `next(error)` the
error has to arrive at the error handler unchanged, and if it calls
`next("route")` that has to keep meaning what it means.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A middleware is just a function of `(req, res, next)`, so a combinator that
returns one has exactly two branches: call the wrapped middleware, or do not.

## Hint 2

The branch that does not is where people lose the request. "Skip it" means
`next()` — calling nothing at all leaves the connection open until the client
gives up, and there is no error anywhere to tell you why.

The branch that does should hand your own `next` straight through. Do not wrap
it, do not swallow an argument: if the inner middleware calls `next(error)` the
error has to arrive at the error handler unchanged, and if it calls
`next("route")` that has to keep meaning what it means.

## Problem 4 — two error handlers, and one that knows when to give up

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp({ log })` has a first error handler that
answers what it recognises with 422 and passes everything else on with
