exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Express tells error handlers apart from ordinary middleware by **arity**: four
declared parameters means "error handler". Once a request is in the error path
express walks the stack looking only for four-argument functions, and once it is
not, it skips them.

That is the whole reason `(err, req, res, next)` must keep all four names even
when you do not use `next` — dropping it turns your error handler into a
middleware that never runs.

## Hint 2

Two handlers, in order. The first knows a specific failure and answers it; for
anything else it calls `next(error)` and the request keeps travelling — past the
ordinary middleware in between, which is not part of the error path at all — to
the last handler, which logs the real error and tells the client nothing.

The gate calls `finalErrorHandler` directly with a fake `res`, so it has to be
exported on its own rather than written inline in `createApp()`.

## Hint 3

The `res.headersSent` branch is the one people have never thought about. If some
bytes have already gone out, the status line is decided and gone; calling
`res.status(500).json(...)` now either throws or appends garbage to a body the
client is already parsing.

The correct move is `next(error)`. Express's own final handler takes it from
there and destroys the connection, which is honest: the client sees a truncated
response and knows something went wrong, instead of a valid-looking one that
lies.

What you still have to decide is whether the last handler should log *every*
error it sees or only the ones it is inventing a 500 for — the gate settles one
of those, and a reviewer will ask about the other.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Express tells error handlers apart from ordinary middleware by **arity**: four
declared parameters means "error handler". Once a request is in the error path
express walks the stack looking only for four-argument functions, and once it is
not, it skips them.

That is the whole reason `(err, req, res, next)` must keep all four names even
when you do not use `next` — dropping it turns your error handler into a
middleware that never runs.

## Hint 2

Two handlers, in order. The first knows a specific failure and answers it; for
anything else it calls `next(error)` and the request keeps travelling — past the
ordinary middleware in between, which is not part of the error path at all — to
the last handler, which logs the real error and tells the client nothing.

The gate calls `finalErrorHandler` directly with a fake `res`, so it has to be
exported on its own rather than written inline in `createApp()`.

## Hint 3

The `res.headersSent` branch is the one people have never thought about. If some
bytes have already gone out, the status line is decided and gone; calling
`res.status(500).json(...)` now either throws or appends garbage to a body the
client is already parsing.

The correct move is `next(error)`. Express's own final handler takes it from
there and destroys the connection, which is honest: the client sees a truncated
response and knows something went wrong, instead of a valid-looking one that
lies.

What you still have to decide is whether the last handler should log *every*
error it sees or only the ones it is inventing a 500 for — the gate settles one
of those, and a reviewer will ask about the other.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`express.json()` takes options, and two of them matter here: `limit` (bytes, or
a string like `"200b"`) and `type` (which content-types it will parse at all).

When it refuses a body it does so by calling `next(error)`, and those errors are
tagged: `error.type` is `"entity.too.large"` or `"entity.parse.failed"`. Switch
on that, not on the message.

## Hint 2

The two cases the parser does **not** raise are the interesting half of this
problem.

A content-type it was not configured for is not an error to it — it simply does
not parse, and leaves `req.body` as `undefined`. Nothing warns you; the first
symptom is a handler reading a property off undefined. That check, and the 415,
are yours.

An empty body with the right content-type *is* parsed, into an empty object. So
`req.body === undefined` and `Object.keys(req.body).length === 0` are two
different questions with two different answers, and you need both.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — who you are, and whether that is enough

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `bearerAuth({ verify })` reads `Authorization: Bearer`,
calls `verify`, and attaches the principal — 401 with `WWW-Authenticate` for no
token, the wrong scheme, or a token `verify` rejects. `requireRole(role)` then
answers 403, with no challenge, for a principal who is who they say and still
may not.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two middlewares, two questions, and the whole exercise is refusing to let them
blur:

- **401 Unauthorized** — I do not know who you are. Retrying with credentials
  might work, so the response carries `WWW-Authenticate` to say how.
- **403 Forbidden** — I know exactly who you are, and no. Retrying will not
  help, so there is no challenge.

## Hint 2

The header is `Authorization: Bearer <token>` — a scheme, a space, a token.
Split on the space and check the scheme case-insensitively before you look at
the token; a `Basic` header is not a bearer token, and passing its payload to
`verify` is how a password ends up in a token lookup.

`verify` may return a promise, so the middleware is `async` — which is fine in
express 5: a rejected promise reaches the error handler on its own, and you do
not need a try/catch or a wrapper.

`requireRole` reads what `bearerAuth` attached. It is a separate middleware
precisely so that one route can require identity and another can require a role.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two middlewares, two questions, and the whole exercise is refusing to let them
blur:

- **401 Unauthorized** — I do not know who you are. Retrying with credentials
  might work, so the response carries `WWW-Authenticate` to say how.
- **403 Forbidden** — I know exactly who you are, and no. Retrying will not
  help, so there is no challenge.

## Hint 2

The header is `Authorization: Bearer <token>` — a scheme, a space, a token.
Split on the space and check the scheme case-insensitively before you look at
the token; a `Basic` header is not a bearer token, and passing its payload to
`verify` is how a password ends up in a token lookup.

`verify` may return a promise, so the middleware is `async` — which is fine in
express 5: a rejected promise reaches the error handler on its own, and you do
not need a try/catch or a wrapper.

`requireRole` reads what `bearerAuth` attached. It is a separate middleware
precisely so that one route can require identity and another can require a role.

## Problem 7 — how many requests are allowed inside

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `concurrencyLimit({ max, queue })` admits `max` at a
time, parks up to `queue` more, and refuses the rest with `503 { error:
"too_busy" }` and `Retry-After`. A request that failed gives its slot back like
any other.

```
uv run dojo test node d21_middleware ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is the semaphore from lesson 03 with a request attached: a count of what is
in flight, a FIFO queue of parked continuations, and three branches — take a
slot, join the queue, or be refused.

The parked continuation is the request's own `next`. Calling it later is what
"resuming" a request means; there is nothing else to store.

## Hint 2

The hard half is giving the slot back. There is no "handler finished" hook — the
handler may be async, may throw, may be replaced by an error handler — so hang
the release on the **response** instead: `res.on("finish")` for one that was
sent, `res.on("close")` for one whose client went away.

Both can fire for the same response, so guard with a boolean: releasing twice
raises your effective limit by one, permanently, and the symptom is a limiter
that quietly stops limiting.

## Hint 3

Release straight into the queue rather than through the counter. If you write
`active -= 1` and then look for a waiter, there is a window where `active` is
below `max` and a brand-new request can take the slot the waiter was owed — a
queue that is FIFO on paper and last-in-first-served under load.

The gate holds every handler open with a deferred it controls, so "two at once"
is counted, never timed.

What is left for you is the `Retry-After` value. The gate only insists that it
is there; choosing a number honestly — and whether it should grow with the
length of the queue — is the part a reviewer will want to talk about.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the semaphore from lesson 03 with a request attached: a count of what is
in flight, a FIFO queue of parked continuations, and three branches — take a
slot, join the queue, or be refused.

The parked continuation is the request's own `next`. Calling it later is what
"resuming" a request means; there is nothing else to store.

## Hint 2

The hard half is giving the slot back. There is no "handler finished" hook — the
handler may be async, may throw, may be replaced by an error handler — so hang
the release on the **response** instead: `res.on("finish")` for one that was
sent, `res.on("close")` for one whose client went away.

Both can fire for the same response, so guard with a boolean: releasing twice
raises your effective limit by one, permanently, and the symptom is a limiter
that quietly stops limiting.

## Hint 3

Release straight into the queue rather than through the counter. If you write
`active -= 1` and then look for a waiter, there is a window where `active` is
below `max` and a brand-new request can take the slot the waiter was owed — a
queue that is FIFO on paper and last-in-first-served under load.

The gate holds every handler open with a deferred it controls, so "two at once"
is counted, never timed.

What is left for you is the `Retry-After` value. The gate only insists that it
is there; choosing a number honestly — and whether it should grow with the
length of the queue — is the part a reviewer will want to talk about.

## Problem 8 — answering without running the handler

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `responseCache({ ttl, now })` stores successful `GET`
responses per method and url and replays them with `x-cache: HIT` (fresh is
`MISS`). Never a non-2xx, never when the request says `cache-control: no-store`,
expiring on the injected clock, and dropping everything stored for a path when a
write arrives at it.

```

## Hint 1

A middleware sits *before* the handler, so by the time it runs there is no

lessons.briefing:
# d22 — Validation with zod

Eight problems on the boundary where somebody else's JSON becomes your typed
data. Lesson **10_middleware_validation** taught `validateBody` and the 400 that
lists every failing field; lesson **11_rest_capstone** used schemas to keep a
client from patching an `id`. This set drills the rest of zod: coercion,
discriminated unions, cross-field rules, transforms, unknown keys, whole-request
validation, error rendering, and a schema that contains itself.

Two things run through all eight. A schema is a *parser*, not a checker — what
comes out is allowed to be a different shape from what went in, and most of
these answers depend on that. And an issue is only useful if the client can act
on it, which means every failure carries a **path** pointing at the field that
has to change.

## Problem 1 — the query string is all strings

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET /articles`, parsing `limit`
(a number, 1–50, default 10), `page` (a number, at least 1, default 1) and
`order` (`asc` or `desc`, default `asc`). Valid queries answer 200 with the
typed values; anything else is a 400 `{ error: "invalid_query", issues }` where
each issue is `{ path, code, message }` — **every** failing parameter, not the
first.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex1
```

## Problem 2 — one field decides the shape of the rest

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /events` over a
`z.discriminatedUnion("type", ...)` of `click` (`x`, `y`: numbers), `keypress`
(`key`: a non-empty string) and `scroll` (`delta`: a number). Success is 202
with `{ summary }` — `click at 3,4`, `key Enter`, `scroll by -120`. An unknown
tag is 400 `{ error: "unknown_event_type", discriminator: "type", issues }`; a
known tag with the wrong fields is 400 `{ error: "invalid_event", issues }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex2
```

## Problem 3 — the rules that need two fields

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Export `bookingSchema`: `startsAt`, `endsAt` (non-empty
strings), `seats` (an integer, 1–8), and optional `email` and `phone`. Two
rules that no single field can check: `endsAt` must be after `startsAt`
(reported on `endsAt`), and at least one of `email` and `phone` must be present
(reported on `email`). All problems come back at once.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex3
```

## Problem 4 — parsing is allowed to change what comes out

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Export `signupSchema`: `email` is trimmed, lowercased
and *then* checked as an address; `joinedAt` is an ISO string that comes out as
a real `Date` (and an unparseable one is rejected); `tags` is a comma-separated
string that comes out as a trimmed, de-duplicated array, defaulting to `[]`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a key the schema never mentioned

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves the same body — `{ title, pages }`
— on three routes, one per decision. `POST /strip` uses the default and answers
201 with the extras gone. `POST /strict` answers 400
`{ error: "unknown_fields", keys }`, naming them. `POST /passthrough` answers
201 with everything kept. An ordinary schema failure on `/strict` is
`{ error: "validation_failed" }`, not an unknown-key report.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex5
```

## Problem 6 — three places one request can be wrong

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `validate({ params, query, body })` returns one
middleware that parses each part it was given, puts the results on `req.valid`,
and on failure answers 400 `{ error: "validation_failed", issues }` with paths
namespaced by part — `body.title`, `query.dryRun`, `params.id`. Every part is
checked before it answers. `createApp()` mounts it on
`PATCH /projects/:id/tasks` (`id` matches `proj-<digits>`, `dryRun` is
`true`/`false` defaulting to `false`, the body is `{ title }`) and answers with
`req.valid`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a ZodError is not a response

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `toProblem(error)` returns
`{ error: "validation_failed", issues: [{ path, code, message }] }`. Paths

# Reading - node/d22_validation_zod

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **treating a schema as the boundary of your program**
— the one place where unknown input becomes a value the rest of the code can
trust. Two ideas unite all eight answers. First, zod *parses*: `safeParse`
returns a new value, not a verdict, so coercion, defaults and transforms are
part of the schema rather than clean-up code scattered through the handler. Get
that wrong and every route acquires a `Number(req.query.limit) || 10` that
drifts out of step with the next one. Second, an issue is a message to a human
who has to fix something, which makes `issue.path` the load-bearing field: a
failure with no path, or with a path the client cannot map back to a form
control, is a 400 that tells nobody anything. Four of these problems are about
producing the right path, and two are about producing *all* of them in one
response instead of one per round trip.

## ex1 — coercion, and what a default is for

**What it tested:** that you know `req.query` holds strings, and that the
conversion belongs in the schema rather than in front of it.

**The classic mistake:** `z.number()` on a query parameter, which rejects every
request ever sent — followed by the "fix" of parsing by hand before the schema
and losing the range checks. The other one is mapping `issues[0]` into the
response, so a client with two bad parameters learns about them one deploy at a
time.

**Model answer:** `z.coerce.number().int().positive().max(50).default(10)` —
convert, then constrain what was converted, and let `.default()` short-circuit
an absent parameter so the handler needs no fallbacks at all.

## ex2 — the tag is read before the body

**What it tested:** the difference between a union and a *discriminated* union,
and the two distinguishable ways a tagged payload can be wrong.

**The classic mistake:** reaching for `z.union([...])`. It works, and then an
invalid click reports nine issues — three per branch, contradicting each other —
because every branch was tried. Almost as common: collapsing both failures into
one 400, so a client cannot tell "there is no such event type" from "your
keypress is missing its key".

**Model answer:** `z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])`, and then a single test
on the issue code — `invalid_union_discriminator` means the tag matched nothing,
anything else means the branch it chose was not satisfied.

## ex3 — rules that belong to the object

**What it tested:** where a rule lives when it needs more than one field, and
whether you attach it to something the client can display.

**The classic mistake:** `ctx.addIssue({ code, message })` with no `path`. The
issue is perfectly true and completely unusable — it arrives with an empty path,
the form has nowhere to put it, and it ends up in a toast that says
"Validation failed". The second mistake is assuming a refinement is skipped once
a field has failed, and splitting the rules across two round trips to be safe.

**Model answer:** one `.superRefine` on the object with an explicit `path` per
issue — and a deliberate choice about *which* field "email or phone" is reported
on, since neither is wrong by itself.

## ex4 — the output type is not the input type

**What it tested:** `.transform()` and `.pipe()`, and the fact that a transform
ends the chain unless you reopen it.

**The classic mistake:** `.transform((s) => new Date(s))` with nothing after it.
`new Date("the fourth of May")` does not throw — it returns an Invalid Date,
which passes straight through and lands in the database as `null`, `NaN` or
`1970-01-01` depending on which driver gets to it first. The mirror image is
validating the email *before* trimming it, so `" ADA@Example.COM "` is rejected
for a problem the schema was about to fix.

**Model answer:** `.trim().toLowerCase().pipe(z.string().email())` and
`.transform(...).pipe(z.date())` — tidy first, judge second — with `.default()`
placed before the transform because it answers for a missing *input*.

## ex5 — three defensible answers, chosen on purpose

**What it tested:** that stripping unknown keys is a *decision* zod made for
you, and that you know the two alternatives and when each is right.

**The classic mistake:** never learning that the default strips, and writing a
hand-rolled "reject unknown keys" check that duplicates `.strict()` badly. The
sharper one is reaching for `issue.keys` without narrowing on
`code === "unrecognized_keys"` first — it exists on exactly one member of the
`ZodIssue` union, and a strict schema fails for ordinary reasons too.

**Model answer:** one shape, three schemas derived from it, and a 400 that looks
for the `unrecognized_keys` issue before falling back to the generic report.

## ex6 — a request is three inputs, not one

**What it tested:** validating params, query and body together, and reporting
them in a way that says which was which.

**The classic mistake:** returning as soon as one part fails. It is one `if` and
it costs the client two extra round trips. Close behind, and specific to express
5: assigning the parsed value back to `req.query`. That property is a getter
now, the assignment throws a `TypeError`, and the route answers 500 with a stack
trace that mentions none of this.

**Model answer:** loop the three part names, accumulate issues with the part
name prefixed onto `issue.path`, and put the parsed results on a new property
the framework does not own.

## ex7 — rendering a path a client can use

**What it tested:** turning zod's structured path — an array mixing keys and
array indices — into one string that unambiguously names a field.

**The classic mistake:** `issue.path.join(".")`, giving `items.0.qty`. A client
splitting that back apart cannot tell an index from a key called `0`, and no
form library accepts it as a field name. The other temptation is flattening an
`invalid_union`'s `unionErrors` into the list, which shows the user "expected
string" and "expected number" for the same input and helps nobody.

**Model answer:** a fold over the path where a number appends `[n]` and a string
appends `.key` — with the first segment taking no dot — plus a name for the
empty path, and no sorting, because zod's order is already the schema's order.

## ex8 — recursion, and a rule the nodes cannot see

**What it tested:** `z.lazy()` for a self-referential schema, and the
recognition that a depth limit is a property of the tree rather than of any node
in it.

**The classic mistake:** trying to express the limit on the node schema.
A node genuinely does not know how deep it sits, so this cannot be written, and
the usual next step is a depth *parameter* threaded through a schema factory —
which builds a different schema per level and produces paths that no longer
match the payload. The other one is forgetting the `z.ZodType<Category>`
annotation and watching TypeScript give up on the whole file.

**Model answer:** `z.lazy()` for the node, one `superRefine` on the outside
walking from the root, and a `path` accumulated during the walk so the issue
lands on the node that went too far rather than on the tree that contains it.

## Further reading

- [zod: basic usage and `safeParse`](https://zod.dev/?id=basic-usage) — the parse-do-not-validate model these eight problems are built on.
- [zod: coercion](https://zod.dev/?id=coercion-for-primitives) — `z.coerce`, and why it exists for exactly the ex1 situation.
- [zod: refinements](https://zod.dev/?id=refine) — `.refine`, `.superRefine`, `ctx.addIssue` and the `path` option.
- [zod: `.transform()` and `.pipe()`](https://zod.dev/?id=transform) — including why nothing can follow a transform without a pipe.
- [zod: recursive types](https://zod.dev/?id=recursive-types) — `z.lazy()` and the annotation TypeScript needs.
- [Express 5 migration notes](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html) — `req.query` is a getter now, which is the ex6 trap.
- [RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html) — the standard shape the ex7 document is a step towards.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — one field decides the shape of the rest

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /events` over a
`z.discriminatedUnion("type", ...)` of `click` (`x`, `y`: numbers), `keypress`
(`key`: a non-empty string) and `scroll` (`delta`: a number). Success is 202
with `{ summary }` — `click at 3,4`, `key Enter`, `scroll by -120`. An unknown
tag is 400 `{ error: "unknown_event_type", discriminator: "type", issues }`; a
known tag with the wrong fields is 400 `{ error: "invalid_event", issues }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])` takes the name of the tag and a list of
object schemas, each of which pins that tag with `z.literal(...)`. Zod reads the
tag first, picks the one branch it names, and judges the body against that
branch alone.

## Hint 2

The two failures you have to tell apart both arrive as issues, and the `code`
is what separates them:

- `invalid_union_discriminator` — the tag matched no branch. Nothing was even
  attempted, and the useful answer names the field that decides.
- anything else — the tag was fine and the branch it chose was not satisfied.
  The paths point at the branch's own fields.

A plain `z.union()` would have tried all three and handed you every branch's
complaints at once, which is why the response could not tell the client
anything useful. That is the whole reason the discriminated form exists.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])` takes the name of the tag and a list of
object schemas, each of which pins that tag with `z.literal(...)`. Zod reads the
tag first, picks the one branch it names, and judges the body against that
branch alone.

## Hint 2

The two failures you have to tell apart both arrive as issues, and the `code`
is what separates them:

- `invalid_union_discriminator` — the tag matched no branch. Nothing was even
  attempted, and the useful answer names the field that decides.
- anything else — the tag was fine and the branch it chose was not satisfied.
  The paths point at the branch's own fields.

A plain `z.union()` would have tried all three and handed you every branch's
complaints at once, which is why the response could not tell the client
anything useful. That is the whole reason the discriminated form exists.

strings), `seats` (an integer, 1–8), and optional `email` and `phone`. Two

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A rule that reads two fields cannot live on either of them, so it goes on the
object: `.superRefine((value, ctx) => { ... })` runs after the fields have been
parsed and gets the whole value.

`.refine()` is the shorter form and it can only add one issue. Two independent
rules want `.superRefine`, which can call `ctx.addIssue` as many times as it
likes.

## Hint 2

`ctx.addIssue({ code: z.ZodIssueCode.custom, path: [...], message })` — the
`path` is the part everybody forgets. Leave it out and the issue attaches to the
object itself, arriving at the client with an empty path and nowhere to be
displayed.

For "end after start" the path is obvious. For "email or phone" it is a choice:
neither field is wrong on its own, so pick one deliberately and say why in a
comment. Note also that `superRefine` still runs when a field underneath it has
already failed — which is what lets a bad `seats` and both cross-field problems
come back in one response instead of three.

## Hint 1

A rule that reads two fields cannot live on either of them, so it goes on the
object: `.superRefine((value, ctx) => { ... })` runs after the fields have been
parsed and gets the whole value.

`.refine()` is the shorter form and it can only add one issue. Two independent
rules want `.superRefine`, which can call `ctx.addIssue` as many times as it
likes.

## Hint 2

`ctx.addIssue({ code: z.ZodIssueCode.custom, path: [...], message })` — the
`path` is the part everybody forgets. Leave it out and the issue attaches to the
object itself, arriving at the client with an empty path and nowhere to be
displayed.

For "end after start" the path is obvious. For "email or phone" it is a choice:
neither field is wrong on its own, so pick one deliberately and say why in a
comment. Note also that `superRefine` still runs when a field underneath it has
already failed — which is what lets a bad `seats` and both cross-field problems
come back in one response instead of three.

## Hint 1

The same object shape, three times, differing only by one call: nothing (the
default), `.strict()`, and `.passthrough()`. Build the shape once and derive the

The interesting half is the 400. A strict schema reports one issue with

reasons too. The gate posts a body that is simply missing a field to check you
kept the two apart.

## Hint 1

The same object shape, three times, differing only by one call: nothing (the
default), `.strict()`, and `.passthrough()`. Build the shape once and derive the
three schemas from it, or the exercise becomes a copy-paste question.

## Hint 2

The interesting half is the 400. A strict schema reports one issue with
`code: "unrecognized_keys"`, and that issue carries a `keys` array naming what
it refused — which is what turns "your request was wrong" into "you spelled
`colour` and I expected nothing of the sort".

Narrow on the code before you reach for `keys`: on a `ZodIssue` union, `keys`
only exists on that one member, and a schema can fail for perfectly ordinary
reasons too. The gate posts a body that is simply missing a field to check you
kept the two apart.

## Problem 6 — three places one request can be wrong

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `validate({ params, query, body })` returns one
middleware that parses each part it was given, puts the results on `req.valid`,
and on failure answers 400 `{ error: "validation_failed", issues }` with paths
namespaced by part — `body.title`, `query.dryRun`, `params.id`. Every part is
checked before it answers. `createApp()` mounts it on
`PATCH /projects/:id/tasks` (`id` matches `proj-<digits>`, `dryRun` is
`true`/`false` defaulting to `false`, the body is `{ title }`) and answers with
`req.valid`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a ZodError is not a response

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `toProblem(error)` returns
`{ error: "validation_failed", issues: [{ path, code, message }] }`. Paths
render as `items[0].qty` — array indices in brackets, keys after dots, no
leading dot — and an empty path renders as `(root)`. Zod's own issue order is
kept.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`error.issues` is already a flat list — one entry per failure, however deep in
the object it happened. There is no tree to walk. The whole exercise is
rendering `issue.path`, which is an array of strings *and numbers*.

## Hint 2

A `fold` over the path, with one rule per kind of segment:

- a **number** is an array index: append `[n]` with nothing in between;
- a **string** is a key: append `.name`, except at the very start where there is
  nothing to put a dot after.

## Problem 8 — a schema that contains itself

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `categorySchema` describes a category — a non-empty
`name` and `children`, an array of categories defaulting to `[]` — to any depth,
with a rule that the tree may be at most `MAX_DEPTH` (3) levels deep counting
the root as 1. The offending node is reported at its own path, ending in
`name`. `createApp()` serves `POST /categories`: 201 `{ depth }`, or 400
`{ error: "invalid_category", issues: [{ path, message }] }` with paths rendered
like `children[1].children[0].children[0].name`.

```
uv run dojo test node d22_validation_zod ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A schema cannot mention itself while it is being defined — the constant does not
exist yet. `z.lazy(() => ...)` wraps the definition in a function that is not
called until something is parsed, by which time it does.

TypeScript needs help too: give the constant an explicit
`z.ZodType<Category>` annotation, because it cannot infer the type of a value
defined in terms of itself.

## Hint 2

The depth rule does not belong on the node. A node has no idea how far down the
tree it sits, so no amount of `.refine()` on the node schema can express
"at most three levels" — the rule belongs to the *tree*, which means one
`superRefine` on the outside, walking from the root with a depth counter.

## Hint 3

The point of the walk is the `path` you build as you descend. Every time you
step into a child, push `"children"` and the index; when you find a node that is
too deep, the accumulated path is exactly where it lives, and adding `"name"`
points at something the client can highlight.

`ctx.addIssue` takes that array as-is; the bracket rendering happens later, in
the handler. And note that `superRefine` runs even when the fields underneath it
already failed, so guard the walk against a shape you were not given — or accept
that a tree with a bad name *and* a bad depth reports both.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A schema cannot mention itself while it is being defined — the constant does not
exist yet. `z.lazy(() => ...)` wraps the definition in a function that is not
called until something is parsed, by which time it does.

TypeScript needs help too: give the constant an explicit
`z.ZodType<Category>` annotation, because it cannot infer the type of a value
defined in terms of itself.

## Hint 2

The depth rule does not belong on the node. A node has no idea how far down the
tree it sits, so no amount of `.refine()` on the node schema can express
"at most three levels" — the rule belongs to the *tree*, which means one
`superRefine` on the outside, walking from the root with a depth counter.

## Hint 3

The point of the walk is the `path` you build as you descend. Every time you
step into a child, push `"children"` and the index; when you find a node that is
too deep, the accumulated path is exactly where it lives, and adding `"name"`
points at something the client can highlight.

`ctx.addIssue` takes that array as-is; the bracket rendering happens later, in
the handler. And note that `superRefine` runs even when the fields underneath it
already failed, so guard the walk against a shape you were not given — or accept
that a tree with a bad name *and* a bad depth reports both.

# d23 — REST patterns

Eight problems on the part of an API that is not code you write but promises you
keep. Lesson **11_rest_capstone** built the task service — a store, a
collection, the four verbs, one error shape. This set drills what the capstone
had no room for: what each verb owes the client, how a collection is paged when
it is changing, what an error body looks like when it follows a standard, and
the two hard ones — retries and batches.

Validation is deliberately trivial here. The schemas are one `typeof` check
apiece so that nothing distracts from the status codes, and every app is a fresh
`createApp()` driven by supertest on a port the OS picks.

## Problem 1 — the verb decides the code

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `/tasks` (seeded with `seed-1`,
"write the spec", not done). `POST` creates with 201 and a `Location`. `PUT
/tasks/:id` **creates** an id nobody is using (201 + `Location`) and
**replaces** one that exists (200) — replace meaning a field the body omits
returns to its default. `PATCH` merges, and 404s rather than creating. `DELETE`
is 204, and 404 the second time. `GET /tasks` lists.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex1
```

## Problem 2 — send what was asked for

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET /tasks` (as
`{ items, total }`) and `GET /tasks/:id` over resources with
`id`, `title`, `done`, `owner` and `createdAt`. `?fields=title,owner` returns
only those — plus `id`, always, and never twice. An absent or empty `fields` is
the whole resource. An unknown name is 400
`{ error: "unknown_field", field }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex2
```

## Problem 3 — one error shape, and nothing leaking through it

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `problem(input)` builds an RFC 9457 document —
`{ type, title, status, detail, instance }`, `type` defaulting to
`about:blank`. `createApp(logError)` answers every failure with one, sent as
`application/problem+json`: a 404 for an unknown task, a 400 for
`?status=elephant` (detail `status must be one of open, done`), a 409 for
re-archiving `seed-1` (type
`https://example.com/probs/already-archived`), and — for the throw at
`GET /boom` — a 500 whose detail is `an unexpected error occurred` while the
real error goes to `logError`.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex3
```

## Problem 4 — pages that do not slip

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET /tasks?limit=&cursor=` over
five tasks `t-1`…`t-5` in id order, answering `{ items, nextCursor }`. The
cursor is the last id served, base64url-encoded and opaque; the last page
carries `nextCursor: null`. `limit` defaults to 2 and is **capped** at 3. A
cursor that names no task in the collection is 400
`{ error: "invalid_cursor" }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a resource inside another one

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `/projects/:projectId/tasks` over
projects `p-1` and `p-2`. Listing answers `{ items, total }` for that parent
only; a parent that does not exist is 404
`{ error: "project_not_found" }`, not an empty list. `POST` creates with 201 and
a **nested** `Location`. `GET /projects/:projectId/tasks/:id` matches on both
halves, so a real task read through the wrong parent is a 404.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex5
```

## Problem 6 — the retry that must not charge twice

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /payments` (`{ amount }`) and
`GET /payments`. A request carrying `Idempotency-Key` is executed once: a replay
with the same key **and the same body** returns the original status and body
with `Idempotency-Replayed: true` and creates nothing. The same key with a
different body is 409 `{ error: "idempotency_key_reuse" }`. Different keys are
different payments, and no key at all means no de-duplication.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex6
```

## Problem 7 — all of it or none of it

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /tasks/bulk` with
`{ operations: [...] }` — `{ op: "create", title }`, `{ op: "update", id, title }`,
`{ op: "delete", id }` — over tasks `t-1` and `t-2`. Every operation is checked
**before any is applied**, walking the batch as if it were running. Success is
200 `{ results }` in request order. A failure is 422
`{ error: "bulk_failed", index, reason }` with the store untouched.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the whole small service

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createApp(deps)` — `deps.seed` overriding the built-in
tasks — assembles it: `GET /tasks` with cursor pagination *and* `?fields=`,
`POST /tasks` (201 + `Location`), `GET /tasks/:id`, `PATCH /tasks/:id`,
`PATCH /tasks/:id/subtasks/:subtaskId`, `DELETE /tasks/:id`. Every failure is
`application/problem+json`, and one business rule: moving a task to `done` while
a subtask is still open is a 409 with type
`https://example.com/probs/open-subtasks`.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex8
```

# Reading - node/d23_rest_patterns

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **answering with the truth**, in the vocabulary HTTP
already has. Almost every problem in this set has a version that "works" — the
data ends up right, the client eventually copes — and is still wrong, because
the response said something that was not so: a 200 for a resource that was
created, an empty list for a parent that does not exist, a 400 for a request
that was perfectly well formed, a page that silently skipped a row. Two habits
run through all eight answers. The status code is chosen from what *this
request* did rather than from whether the handler threw, which is why 201 and
200 differ on the same PUT and why 409 is not 400. And the failure body has one
shape across the whole service, because a client that has to parse two error
formats will only ever handle one of them. Validation is kept deliberately thin
here — that was d22 — so that nothing distracts from the codes.

## ex1 — four verbs, four contracts

**What it tested:** that you know PUT is not "update" and PATCH is not "upsert".

**The classic mistake:** treating PUT as a partial update, so a body that omits
`done` leaves the old value in place. That makes the verb unusable for its one
real purpose — sending a whole representation and knowing what is there
afterwards — and it makes two identical PUTs able to produce different states.
Close behind: PATCH creating the resource when it is missing, which turns a
typo in an id into a new record nobody meant.

**Model answer:** build the replacement object from the request alone for PUT,
merge field by field for PATCH, and pick 201 versus 200 by whether the id was
already in use — with `Location` on every creation, whichever verb caused it.

## ex2 — the client knows what it needs

**What it tested:** projection driven by a whitelist, and the difference between
refusing a request and silently under-delivering.

**The classic mistake:** validating the requested fields against
`Object.keys(task)`. It looks equivalent and it means the day a
`passwordHash` joins the record, `?fields=passwordHash` starts working. The
second is ignoring an unknown field name and returning 200 — the client waits
for a key that is never coming, and the bug surfaces as "the UI shows blank"
three services away.

**Model answer:** a `FIELDS` constant that is the contract, one function that
turns the parameter into "everything" or a validated list, and one that projects
— with `id` seeded first so it is present exactly once however it was asked for.

## ex3 — a standard error body

**What it tested:** RFC 9457, and the discipline that an unexpected error tells
the client nothing.

**The classic mistake:** `res.status(500).json({ error: error.message })`. The
thrown message here is a connection failure containing a database password, and
that response publishes it — to a browser console, a log aggregator, a bug
report screenshot. The other one is skipping `type`, leaving clients to
recognise a problem by matching its `title` with a regular expression that
breaks the first time somebody improves the wording.

**Model answer:** an error class carrying a problem document, one four-argument
`app.use` at the bottom that renders it as `application/problem+json`, and a
default branch that logs everything and says nothing.

## ex4 — a cursor is a position, not a count

**What it tested:** keyset pagination, and why the cursor is opaque.

**The classic mistake:** `?page=2` translated to an offset. The list is changing
while the client reads it, so a row inserted before the cursor shifts everything
down and page 2 repeats an item page 1 already showed — or a deletion shifts
everything up and page 2 skips one entirely. Nobody notices, because the pages
look plausible. The other mistake is a readable cursor: the moment a client can
decode it, a client will construct one, and the encoding is now your public API
forever.

**Model answer:** remember the last id served, base64url it so it survives a
query string, and treat a cursor naming nothing as a 400 — an empty page would
say the collection had ended, and starting over would loop the client forever.

## ex5 — a child is not addressable on its own

**What it tested:** the two checks a nested route owes, and the fact that they
are different checks.

**The classic mistake:** `tasks.find((t) => t.id === req.params.id)` inside a
route mounted under `/projects/:projectId`. It works in every test where you
happen to use the right parent, and it is the bug that shows one customer
another customer's data through a url they guessed. The other is answering a
missing parent with `[]`, which asserts that the project exists and is empty —
two false statements for the price of one.

**Model answer:** one `requireProject` middleware in front of every nested
route so the parent check cannot be forgotten on one of them, and a lookup that
matches the id **and** the parent.

## ex6 — the network eats responses

**What it tested:** idempotency keys, and the fact that the interesting state is
the *response*, not a flag.

**The classic mistake:** recording only that a key was used, then answering a
replay with 200 and an empty body — the client cannot tell what happened and has
no id for the resource it created. The sharper one is skipping the fingerprint:
the same key with a different body then replays the *old* payment, telling the
client that its 250 succeeded when nothing was ever charged.

**Model answer:** store `{ fingerprint, status, body }` per key; replay it
verbatim with a header saying so; 409 on a mismatch; and no key means no
promise, because two identical requests really can be two intentional payments.

## ex7 — check everything, then apply everything

**What it tested:** atomicity without a transaction, and choosing an identifier
that always exists.

**The classic mistake:** one loop that validates and applies each operation as
it goes. The batch fails at index 3 with three changes already made, the client
gets a 422, and neither side knows what is true. Subtler, and the one the gate
is built around: validating every operation against the store *as it is now*, so
a batch with two deletes of the same id passes the check and then fails half way
through — the check has to walk the batch as if it were running.

**Model answer:** a first pass over a `Set` of live ids that mutates as it goes,
returning the first `{ index, reason }`; then a second pass that cannot fail,
because everything in it was already proved applicable.

## ex8 — the rule that makes it a service

**What it tested:** assembling the set, and one status code that only exists
because the *data* said no.

**The classic mistake:** answering the open-subtask refusal with a 400. Nothing
about the request was bad — the JSON was well formed, the field was valid, the
task existed. What refused it was the state of the resource, and that is
precisely what 409 means; a 400 tells the client to fix its request, which it
cannot. The other habit worth breaking: letting the unmatched-route 404 fall
through to express's HTML page, so the one path a confused client is most likely
to hit is the one that does not answer in your error format.

**Model answer:** one `sendProblem` helper used by every failure including the
final catch-all, a seed that is copied rather than borrowed, and the conflict
given a `type` URI of its own so a client can recognise it without reading
English.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html) — the five members of ex3, and what `type` and `instance` are actually for.
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html) — the definitions behind ex1: PUT versus PATCH, idempotency, and when 409 is the right refusal.
- [MDN: HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status) — a fast reference for 201, 204, 409 and 422.
- [Express 5: `res.location()` and `res.status()`](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#res.location) — the response helpers these eight apps are built from.
- [MDN: `Idempotency-Key`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers) — the header in ex6, and the retry story it exists to make safe.

## Problem 1 — the verb decides the code

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `/tasks` (seeded with `seed-1`,
"write the spec", not done). `POST` creates with 201 and a `Location`. `PUT
/tasks/:id` **creates** an id nobody is using (201 + `Location`) and
**replaces** one that exists (200) — replace meaning a field the body omits
returns to its default. `PATCH` merges, and 404s rather than creating. `DELETE`
is 204, and 404 the second time. `GET /tasks` lists.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four verbs, four questions to answer for each: does it need the resource to
exist already, does it create one, what status says so, and does it owe a
`Location` header.

Write that table out before you write the routes. The code falls out of it.

## Hint 2

The two that trip people up:

**PUT is not "update".** It means "let this url hold this representation", so a
PUT to an id nobody has used creates it — and a creation is a 201 with a
`Location`, however it happened. A second PUT to the same id replaces, which is
a 200. `express` gives you `res.status(201).location(url).json(task)` in one
chain.

**Replace means replace.** If the incoming representation does not mention
`done`, the stored resource does not have it either — it goes back to its
default. A PUT that merges the fields it was given onto the ones it was not is a
PATCH with the wrong name on it, and the gate has an assertion for exactly that.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four verbs, four questions to answer for each: does it need the resource to
exist already, does it create one, what status says so, and does it owe a
`Location` header.

Write that table out before you write the routes. The code falls out of it.

## Hint 2

The two that trip people up:

**PUT is not "update".** It means "let this url hold this representation", so a
PUT to an id nobody has used creates it — and a creation is a 201 with a
`Location`, however it happened. A second PUT to the same id replaces, which is
a 200. `express` gives you `res.status(201).location(url).json(task)` in one
chain.

**Replace means replace.** If the incoming representation does not mention
`done`, the stored resource does not have it either — it goes back to its
default. A PUT that merges the fields it was given onto the ones it was not is a
PATCH with the wrong name on it, and the gate has an assertion for exactly that.

## Problem 3 — one error shape, and nothing leaking through it

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `problem(input)` builds an RFC 9457 document —
`{ type, title, status, detail, instance }`, `type` defaulting to
`about:blank`. `createApp(logError)` answers every failure with one, sent as
`application/problem+json`: a 404 for an unknown task, a 400 for
`?status=elephant` (detail `status must be one of open, done`), a 409 for
re-archiving `seed-1` (type
`https://example.com/probs/already-archived`), and — for the throw at
`GET /boom` — a 500 whose detail is `an unexpected error occurred` while the
real error goes to `logError`.

uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

RFC 9457 gives an error body five members. Four of them are easy; the two worth
thinking about are `type` — a URI that *identifies the kind of problem*, and the
thing a client should branch on — and `instance`, the path this particular
failure happened at. `about:blank` is the honest `type` when the status code
already says everything there is to say.

`req.originalUrl` is the `instance` you want.

## Hint 2

Routes should not build responses. Give yourself an error class that carries a
problem document, throw it from anywhere, and write **one** four-argument
`app.use((error, req, res, next) => ...)` at the bottom that turns it into a
response. Express 5 forwards a throw from a sync handler and a rejection from an
async one to exactly that place.

Two details the gate checks. The media type is `application/problem+json`, not
`application/json` — `res.type(...)` before `.json(...)` sets it. And an error
you did *not* mean to produce gets a generic detail: the thrown message here
contains a database password, and repeating a thrown message back to the client
is how it gets published. Log the real thing, answer with nothing.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

RFC 9457 gives an error body five members. Four of them are easy; the two worth
thinking about are `type` — a URI that *identifies the kind of problem*, and the
thing a client should branch on — and `instance`, the path this particular
failure happened at. `about:blank` is the honest `type` when the status code
already says everything there is to say.

`req.originalUrl` is the `instance` you want.

## Hint 2

Routes should not build responses. Give yourself an error class that carries a
problem document, throw it from anywhere, and write **one** four-argument
`app.use((error, req, res, next) => ...)` at the bottom that turns it into a
response. Express 5 forwards a throw from a sync handler and a rejection from an
async one to exactly that place.

Two details the gate checks. The media type is `application/problem+json`, not
`application/json` — `res.type(...)` before `.json(...)` sets it. And an error
you did *not* mean to produce gets a generic detail: the thrown message here
contains a database password, and repeating a thrown message back to the client
is how it gets published. Log the real thing, answer with nothing.

## Problem 4 — pages that do not slip

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `GET /tasks?limit=&cursor=` over
five tasks `t-1`…`t-5` in id order, answering `{ items, nextCursor }`. The
cursor is the last id served, base64url-encoded and opaque; the last page
carries `nextCursor: null`. `limit` defaults to 2 and is **capped** at 3. A
cursor that names no task in the collection is 400
`{ error: "invalid_cursor" }`.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A cursor answers "where was I", and the only durable answer is **the last row I
served** — not an offset. Offsets count from the front of a list that other
people are inserting into, which is why page 2 shows you an item page 1 already
did.

So: decode the cursor to an id, find that id, start one past it.

## Hint 2

`Buffer.from(id).toString("base64url")` and
`Buffer.from(cursor, "base64url").toString("utf8")` are the two halves.
`base64url` rather than `base64` because the value is going into a query string
and `+`, `/` and `=` all have to be escaped there.

Opaque matters: the moment a client can read a cursor, it will build one, and
then you can never change what a cursor contains.

Note what "invalid" means. Decoding never fails — any string is bytes. A cursor
is invalid when the id it names is not in the collection, and that is a 400,
not an empty page and not a silent jump back to the start. And `nextCursor` on
the last page is `null` rather than absent: a missing key and a null one look
the same to a person and different to every JSON parser.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A cursor answers "where was I", and the only durable answer is **the last row I
served** — not an offset. Offsets count from the front of a list that other
people are inserting into, which is why page 2 shows you an item page 1 already
did.

So: decode the cursor to an id, find that id, start one past it.

## Hint 2

`Buffer.from(id).toString("base64url")` and
`Buffer.from(cursor, "base64url").toString("utf8")` are the two halves.
`base64url` rather than `base64` because the value is going into a query string
and `+`, `/` and `=` all have to be escaped there.

Opaque matters: the moment a client can read a cursor, it will build one, and
then you can never change what a cursor contains.

Note what "invalid" means. Decoding never fails — any string is bytes. A cursor
is invalid when the id it names is not in the collection, and that is a 400,
not an empty page and not a silent jump back to the start. And `nextCursor` on
the last page is `null` rather than absent: a missing key and a null one look
the same to a person and different to every JSON parser.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 6 — the retry that must not charge twice

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /payments` (`{ amount }`) and
`GET /payments`. A request carrying `Idempotency-Key` is executed once: a replay
with the same key **and the same body** returns the original status and body
with `Idempotency-Replayed: true` and creates nothing. The same key with a
different body is 409 `{ error: "idempotency_key_reuse" }`. Different keys are
different payments, and no key at all means no de-duplication.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Keep a map from key to **what you answered**, not merely to "this key has been
used". A replay has to reproduce the original status and the original body, and
you cannot reproduce them from a boolean.

Three fields per entry are enough: a fingerprint of the request, the status, and
the body.

## Hint 2

The fingerprint is what separates a retry from a mistake. The same key with the
same body is the network having eaten your response — replay it. The same key
with a *different* body is a client bug, and answering it with the old payment
would report success for a payment that was never attempted: that is the 409.

Two more things the gate checks. The replayed response carries
`Idempotency-Replayed: true` and the first one does not, which is how a client
knows which happened. And with no key at all there is nothing to de-duplicate
on, so two identical requests are two payments — the guarantee is something the
client has to ask for, and inventing one from the body alone would break every
legitimate repeat purchase.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Keep a map from key to **what you answered**, not merely to "this key has been
used". A replay has to reproduce the original status and the original body, and
you cannot reproduce them from a boolean.

Three fields per entry are enough: a fingerprint of the request, the status, and
the body.

## Hint 2

The fingerprint is what separates a retry from a mistake. The same key with the
same body is the network having eaten your response — replay it. The same key
with a *different* body is a client bug, and answering it with the old payment
would report success for a payment that was never attempted: that is the 409.

Two more things the gate checks. The replayed response carries
`Idempotency-Replayed: true` and the first one does not, which is how a client
knows which happened. And with no key at all there is nothing to de-duplicate
on, so two identical requests are two payments — the guarantee is something the
client has to ask for, and inventing one from the body alone would break every
legitimate repeat purchase.

## Problem 7 — all of it or none of it

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createApp()` serves `POST /tasks/bulk` with
`{ operations: [...] }` — `{ op: "create", title }`, `{ op: "update", id, title }`,
`{ op: "delete", id }` — over tasks `t-1` and `t-2`. Every operation is checked
**before any is applied**, walking the batch as if it were running. Success is
200 `{ results }` in request order. A failure is 422
`{ error: "bulk_failed", index, reason }` with the store untouched.

```
uv run dojo test node d23_rest_patterns ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two passes, and they must not be interleaved. Pass one decides whether the whole
batch can be applied; pass two applies it. As soon as you check-and-apply in one
loop, a failure at index 3 leaves the first three changes in place and the
client has no way to find out which.

## Hint 2

The identifier in a bulk failure is the **index**. Ids are absent on a create,
duplicated across operations, and meaningless for an unknown `op` — the position
in the array the client sent is the only thing that always identifies one
operation.

Pass two can be total: every operation has already been proved applicable, so
there is nothing left to check and nothing left to fail.

## Hint 3

The subtle half is what pass one checks *against*. Validating each operation
against the store as it is now lets a batch containing two deletes of the same
id through — both ids are present, both look fine — and then the second delete
finds nothing during pass two, half way through.

Walk the batch as if it were running: keep a `Set` of the ids that are live,
remove one when you pass a delete, add one when you pass a create. The gate
sends exactly that batch.

What to do about an update *after* a delete of the same id in one batch is left
to you: the same technique answers it, but whether it should be an error or a
resurrection is a product decision.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two passes, and they must not be interleaved. Pass one decides whether the whole
batch can be applied; pass two applies it. As soon as you check-and-apply in one
loop, a failure at index 3 leaves the first three changes in place and the
client has no way to find out which.

## Hint 2

The identifier in a bulk failure is the **index**. Ids are absent on a create,
duplicated across operations, and meaningless for an unknown `op` — the position
in the array the client sent is the only thing that always identifies one
operation.

Pass two can be total: every operation has already been proved applicable, so
there is nothing left to check and nothing left to fail.

## Hint 3

The subtle half is what pass one checks *against*. Validating each operation
against the store as it is now lets a batch containing two deletes of the same
id through — both ids are present, both look fine — and then the second delete
finds nothing during pass two, half way through.

Walk the batch as if it were running: keep a `Set` of the ids that are live,
remove one when you pass a delete, add one when you pass a create. The gate
sends exactly that batch.

What to do about an update *after* a delete of the same id in one batch is left
to you: the same technique answers it, but whether it should be an error or a
resurrection is a product decision.

lessons.briefing:
# d24 — The mixed gauntlet

The last set. Nothing here belongs to one lesson: every problem needs two or
three parts of the track at once, the way real code does — a limiter and a retry
policy and a clock, a stream and a schema, an HTTP route and a file handle. If a
problem stalls, the fix is almost never a new idea; it is remembering which of
the eight drills that came before it already answered half the question.

The rules are the ones you have been working under all along. Anything counted
is held open by the gate and released by hand. Anything timed takes an injected
clock. Streams stay in memory, HTTP is driven through supertest with no port,
and anything that touches the disk gets a temp directory and gives it back.

## Problem 1 — configuration, layered and frozen

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `loadConfig(dir, { env })` reads `config.json`,
deep-merges `config.<env>.json` over it when that file exists, and returns the
result deeply frozen. Objects merge key by key; arrays and scalars are replaced.
A missing base file, or one that will not parse, rejects with a message naming
the file. *(filesystem + paths + immutability)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## Problem 2 — a limiter that retries without growing

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `retryingLimitedMap(items, worker, { limit, retries,
delayFor, sleep })` keeps at most `limit` items in flight, retries a failing item
**inside the slot it already holds**, waits `delayFor(attempt)` on the injected
`sleep` between attempts, returns results in input order, and fails the whole
call — starting nothing further — when an item runs out of attempts.
*(concurrency + retry policy + injected time)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```

## Problem 3 — the end of a very large file

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `tailLines(file, n)` returns the last `n` lines in file
order, without their line endings, by reading the file **backwards** a block at a
time. A trailing newline does not produce an empty last line; a file that ends
without one still has a last line; `\r\n` is a line ending.
*(filesystem handles + buffers)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```

## Problem 4 — a pipeline that says what it is doing

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `runNamedPipeline(source, stages, sink, emitter)` runs
the chain, emits `progress` with `{ done }` for every item that reaches the sink,
and resolves with the total. A failing stage rejects with a `StageFailure` whose
`stage` is that stage's name and whose `cause` is the original error, and emits
`failed` with the same object. *(streams + events + custom errors)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

## Problem 5 — a schema in the middle of a stream

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `createValidatingStage(schema, { onInvalid, failFast })`
is an object-mode Transform: records the schema accepts are pushed as the
**parsed** value, records it rejects go to `onInvalid` with their index in the
input and their issues — or, with `failFast`, fail the stream with a message
naming the record. *(streams + zod validation)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

## Problem 6 — an upload endpoint

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `createApp({ dir, limit, nextId })` serves `POST
/uploads`, streaming the raw request body to a file — no body parser — and
answering 201 with `{ id, bytes }` and a Location header. Over `limit` bytes it
answers 413 and leaves nothing on disk. `GET /uploads/:id` answers `{ id, bytes }`
or 404. *(HTTP + streams + filesystem)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```

## Problem 7 — a client that knows when to stop calling

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. `createResilientClient({ call, failureThreshold,
cooldownMs, now })` returns `{ get, state }`. Callers sharing a key while one
call is in flight share its outcome; `failureThreshold` consecutive failures open
the circuit, which then rejects with `CircuitOpenError` without calling anything;
after `cooldownMs` on the injected clock exactly one probe is allowed through,
and its outcome closes or re-opens the circuit.
*(de-duplication + circuit breaking + injected time + custom errors)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```

## Problem 8 — the gateway

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. `createApp({ apiKey, upstream, logError })` guards every
request on `x-api-key` (401 in the shared JSON shape), mounts a router at
`/api/v1` with `GET /orders` returning `{ items, total }`, `GET /orders/export`
streaming NDJSON, and `GET /orders/:id`; answers 404 in the same shape for
anything unmatched; and turns an upstream rejection into a 502 that leaks
nothing, logged once in full. *(express + routing + middleware + error handling +
streams)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - node/d24_mixed_gauntlet

What each problem was really testing, the mistake that costs people the
question, and one line of the model answer's reasoning.

## Notes

The skill being drilled is **composition** — and the thing that makes it a skill
rather than an exam is that the individual pieces are all familiar. Every
problem here is two or three drills you have already done, wired together, and
the difficulty is never in the pieces; it is in the seam. A retry loop and a
concurrency limit are each five lines, and where you put one relative to the
other decides whether a burst of failures is absorbed or amplified. A schema and
a Transform are each obvious, and the choice of pushing the parsed value rather
than the raw chunk is the whole reason for the schema. A stream and an HTTP
response are each routine, and the order in which you set the content type
against the first write decides whether the endpoint works at all. Read every
problem for its seam.

## ex1 — filesystem, paths, and a value nobody can quietly edit

**What it tested:** three habits at once — ENOENT as the one error that means
"nothing has happened", a recursive merge that knows what is mergeable, and a
freeze that goes all the way down.

**The classic mistake:** `{ ...base, ...overlay }`. It reads as a merge and is a
replacement: the overlay's `server` object overwrites the base's wholesale, so
the port that only the base mentioned disappears and the service starts on 0.
Second: a shallow `Object.freeze`, which protects exactly the keys nobody was
going to overwrite anyway.

**Model answer:** a recursive merge guarded by a plain-object test that excludes
arrays and `null`, a recursive freeze applied bottom-up, and two distinct
failures — missing base and unparseable file — that each name their file.

## ex2 — where the retry goes

**What it tested:** the interaction between two limits, not either one of them.
Retrying and limiting are both easy; only their arrangement is interesting.

**The classic mistake:** implementing the retry by pushing the item back onto
the queue. Every runner is then free to pick up a fresh item while the failed
one waits, so under a burst of failures the number of calls in flight is `limit`
plus everything retrying — a retry storm aimed at a service that is already
struggling. The other one: sleeping after the final failure, which delays the
rejection by a backoff nobody is waiting for.

**Model answer:** the retry loop lives inside the runner, before it takes its
next index, so a retrying item costs exactly the one slot it already had; a
shared `failed` flag stops the other runners from taking new work; and `sleep`
is a parameter, so the test suite never waits.

## ex3 — reading a file from the wrong end

**What it tested:** `FileHandle.read` with an explicit position — the API you
reach for when a stream is the wrong shape — plus the buffer discipline from
lesson 06.

**The classic mistake:** decoding each block as it is read. Blocks are cut at
byte offsets and characters are not one byte, so a boundary lands inside a
multi-byte sequence and both halves decode to replacement characters. It is
invisible in ASCII test data and appears the first time somebody logs a name.
Nearly as common: stopping after `n` newlines rather than `n + 1`, which returns
a truncated first line.

**Model answer:** walk backwards prepending Buffers, count `0x0a` bytes as you
go, stop when there is one more newline than lines wanted, and decode the
concatenation exactly once.

## ex4 — a stream error with an address on it

**What it tested:** that `pipeline` gives you teardown and nothing else. Progress
and attribution are yours to add, and both are small once you see them as
streams and listeners rather than as bookkeeping.

**The classic mistake:** counting at the source. "Read 10,000 rows" is a
comforting number and a useless one — on a run that fails at the sink it is an
overstatement of exactly the amount that was lost. The second: catching the
pipeline's rejection and rethrowing `new Error(error.message)`, which discards
the stack and the `code` and leaves the on-call engineer with a sentence.

**Model answer:** a counting Transform immediately before the sink, an `error`
listener per stage recording the first name to fire, and a wrapper error built
with `{ cause }` so nothing is lost.

## ex5 — validation as a stage, not a gate

**What it tested:** that a schema in a stream has two legitimate policies —
report and continue, or stop — and that the choice belongs to the caller.

**The classic mistake:** pushing the original chunk instead of `result.data`,
which throws away the stripping, defaults and coercion that were the entire
point of validating. And counting only the records that got through, so the
index in the error report does not match any line in the file the operator is
looking at.

**Model answer:** `safeParse` per chunk; push `result.data`; keep an index that
counts every arrival; `callback(error)` — never `throw` — for fail-fast, and
`callback()` with nothing pushed to drop a record.

## ex6 — the request is a stream, and it is not yours to buffer

**What it tested:** an HTTP route that must not use a body parser, a byte limit
enforced on what actually arrived, and a filesystem write that leaves nothing
behind when it goes wrong.

**The classic mistake:** trusting `content-length`. A chunked upload does not
send one and a hostile client will happily send a small one, so the limit has to
be the running total of the chunks you have counted. Second: destroying the
request the moment you go over, which the client sees as a connection reset
rather than as your 413. Third: answering before the write stream's callback,
which lets a reader following your Location header find a short file.

**Model answer:** count in `data`, stop writing but keep draining once over the
limit, answer from inside `end(callback)`, and remove the partial file before
sending 413.

## ex7 — two mechanisms, one function

**What it tested:** single-flight de-duplication and circuit breaking sharing a
call path, with every decision derived from an injected clock so the whole thing
is testable without waiting.

**The classic mistake:** storing the state as a string and keeping it in step
with a timer. Two sources of truth, one of which fires whether or not anybody is
calling — and a `setTimeout` in a client is a handle somebody has to clean up.
The other is releasing the whole backlog the instant the cooldown expires, which
is the thundering herd that knocks the recovering service straight back down.

**Model answer:** `state()` computed from `openedAt` and `now()`, the in-flight
map cleared on both outcomes, and a `probing` flag so exactly one call decides
for everybody.

## ex8 — everything, in the order express runs it

**What it tested:** the assembly. A guard above the router so it also covers the
404, routes ordered so a literal beats a parameter, a streamed response, and one
error handler that is the only place a failure chooses a status.

**The classic mistake:** registering `/orders/:id` before `/orders/export`, so
`export` becomes an id and the endpoint 404s for the rest of its life — a bug
that survives review because the code looks tidy. Close behind: letting the
upstream error's message reach the client, which in the gate's case ships an
internal address and a database user to whoever asked.

**Model answer:** guard, router, catch-all, error handler, in that order; the
upstream call wrapped in an error type the handler can recognise so 502 and 500
are distinguishable; and the export written as an async generator piped into the
response, so the content type is set before the first byte and the client can
start parsing before the server has finished.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: `stream.pipeline()`](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html#streampipelinesource-transforms-destination-callback) — the teardown guarantee ex4 and ex8 lean on, including the array form.
- [Node.js: `FileHandle.read()`](https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#filehandlereadbuffer-offset-length-position) — positional reads, which is how ex3 gets to the end of a file without passing through the front of it.
- [MDN: `Error.cause`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Error/cause) — wrapping without losing, used by ex4 and ex8.
- [Express: error handling](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/error-handling.html) — the four-argument handler, and express 5 forwarding rejected promises without a wrapper.
- [Martin Fowler: Circuit Breaker](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html) — the pattern ex7 implements, including why half-open lets exactly one request through.

exercises.prompt:
## Problem 2 — a limiter that retries without growing

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `retryingLimitedMap(items, worker, { limit, retries,
delayFor, sleep })` keeps at most `limit` items in flight, retries a failing item
**inside the slot it already holds**, waits `delayFor(attempt)` on the injected
`sleep` between attempts, returns results in input order, and fails the whole
call — starting nothing further — when an item runs out of attempts.
*(concurrency + retry policy + injected time)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from the limiter you already know: a shared cursor and `limit` runners
that each take the next index, do the work, and come back for another. The retry
is not a new mechanism — it is a loop **inside** the runner, before it goes back
for the next index.

## Hint 2

That placement is the whole exercise. Put the retry inside the slot and a
retrying item costs you one worker, exactly as it did on its first attempt. Push
the item back onto the queue instead and a burst of failures can have `limit +
retries` calls in flight against a service that is already unwell.

Attempt numbering: the first call is attempt 1 and is not a retry, so `retries:
2` means three calls and two sleeps — never a sleep after the last failure.

## Hint 3

Fail-fast needs a flag the runners can see: set it when an item exhausts its
attempts, check it at the top of the loop, and the other runners finish what
they are holding and stop taking new work. `Promise.all` over the runners then
rejects with the error that set the flag.

The decision the gate leaves you: whether an item that fails *after* the flag is
set should still be retried. The reference does not bother — there is nobody
left to want the answer.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the limiter you already know: a shared cursor and `limit` runners
that each take the next index, do the work, and come back for another. The retry
is not a new mechanism — it is a loop **inside** the runner, before it goes back
for the next index.

## Hint 2

That placement is the whole exercise. Put the retry inside the slot and a
retrying item costs you one worker, exactly as it did on its first attempt. Push
the item back onto the queue instead and a burst of failures can have `limit +
retries` calls in flight against a service that is already unwell.

Attempt numbering: the first call is attempt 1 and is not a retry, so `retries:
2` means three calls and two sleeps — never a sleep after the last failure.

## Hint 3

Fail-fast needs a flag the runners can see: set it when an item exhausts its
attempts, check it at the top of the loop, and the other runners finish what
they are holding and stop taking new work. `Promise.all` over the runners then
rejects with the error that set the flag.

The decision the gate leaves you: whether an item that fails *after* the flag is
set should still be retried. The reference does not bother — there is nobody
left to want the answer.

## Problem 3 — the end of a very large file

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. `tailLines(file, n)` returns the last `n` lines in file
order, without their line endings, by reading the file **backwards** a block at a
time. A trailing newline does not produce an empty last line; a file that ends
without one still has a last line; `\r\n` is a line ending.
*(filesystem handles + buffers)*

```
uv run dojo test node d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`readFile` is not available to you here — the point of a `tail` is that the file
may be gigabytes. `open()` gives you a `FileHandle` with `stat()` for the size
and `read(buffer, offset, length, position)` for reading a block from anywhere
in the file, and a `finally` to close it.

## Hint 2

Walk backwards: start at the end, read a block, prepend it to a list, count the
`0x0a` bytes you have seen, and stop when you have seen more newlines than the
number of lines asked for — the extra one is what proves the first line in your
region is whole. Also stop at the start of the file.

Do not decode a block when you read it. Keep the Buffers, `Buffer.concat` them
once, and decode the result. A block boundary lands inside a multi-byte
character eventually, and decoding either side of the cut gives you replacement
characters in a log line that was perfectly fine on disk.

## Hint 3

The line-ending rules are worth writing down before you code them: a file that
ends with a newline has no empty last line, a file that does not still has a
last line, and a `\r` before the `\n` belongs to the ending rather than to the
text. Three of the gate's cases are exactly those.

What is left for you: whether `n` larger than the file should be an error. The
gate says no — but say so on purpose rather than by accident.
